News.title: Military base asylum plans granted planning approval
News.content:
Planning permission to house asylum seekers at a former military site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington has been granted by the government.

The Home Office's application to house up to 1,256 men at the MoD Bicester site was fast-tracked using an Urgent Crown Development application.

The nearby village of Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK in opposition to the planned site, which has also been legally challenged by campaigners.

A Home Office spokesperson said the planning permission "allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester" but no final decision on the proposal had been taken.

A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against, and one in support.

It also said Housing Secretary Angela Rayner ruled permission should be granted because "national demand for asylum accommodation remains high".

The permission allows for demolition of existing buildings, the erection of new modular accommodation, and provisions for health and welfare facilities.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "Angela Rayner and the Labour government have betrayed the people of Piddington by abusing their emergency powers in this way."

He continued: "Instead of accommodating illegal immigrants, the government should leave the ECHR so they can be rapidly deported."

News.title: Junior doctor burnout putting maternity patients at risk, says regulator
News.content:
Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is warning.

The General Medical Council (GMC) says the fully qualified doctors, who are still training in obstetrics and gynaecology, are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation than similar trainees in any other field of medicine or surgery, and are also more wary of escalating concerns.

Author Adam Kay, who left medicine in 2010 after dealing with a traumatic birth incident, says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture.

The Department for Health and Social Care said ensuring every maternity unit "meets the highest standards" was a priority.

The GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors, which includes registrars, representing almost 52,000 people.

It found:

Almost one in three trainee doctors working in obstetrics and gynaecology felt hesitant or apprehensive approaching a senior colleague about a patient, compared with one in five across all specialties

They were also more likely to be at moderate to high risk of burnout - 70% versus 61% across all specialties

One in three said they regularly suffered from sleep deprivation compared to one in five across the wider pool of trainees

Charlie Massey, head of the GMC, said having doctors who feel they cannot speak up, could have a critical impact on patients.

"Creating environments where staff are supported, listened to and feel able to raise concerns is essential."

He told the BBC: "Sadly, when we see when things go wrong, it is it is very often because of failures in terms of culture and leadership."

News.title: The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds
News.content:
Two years ago, I stood in a school hall in Sunderland on GCSE results day and watched the pride and surprise in the faces of teenagers as the envelopes were opened.

Even after years of covering results days, I was emotional to see a set of outstanding results in a school facing so many challenges. Almost half of the school's pupils receive free school meals, meaning their parents are on low incomes. In fact, the results in the ex-mining town of Hetton-le-Hole were as strong as the most affluent parts of southern England.

This summer, Hetton Academy hit another milestone, with 80% of its pupils getting a pass of at least a grade 4 in maths and English. A grade 4 is roughly equivalent to a 'C' under the old system, and is seen as a passport to jobs and further education.

Another striking detail about Hetton is that almost all of its pupils are from a white, working-class background, a group that's been in the spotlight for some time. This week saw the launch of the second phase of an independent inquiry, led by former Cabinet minister Baroness Morris, into why children from those communities lag behind their peers at school. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "Right now, too many white, working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education."

But Hetton Academy seems to have defied the odds. The school's principal, Vicky Pinkney, refuses to accept low incomes should mean low results. "I don't think we should be accepting less just because of the community you work in," she says.

News.title: Timothée Chalamet among Hollywood stars and charity heroes stepping up for BBC Children In Need
News.content:
This year's BBC Children In Need show is taking place on Friday, with highlights including Timothee Chalamet pranking Rylan Clark, and a "challenge squad" of young people completing feats in the name of charity.

Oscar-nominated actor Chalamet and co-stars Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy will be seen making Rylan sweat during an interview for their new film Dune: Part Three, with the help of three children, hidden behind the scenes.

The show will also feature Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans, on a 400-mile cycle challenge through Scotland, Northern Ireland, England and Wales.

Last year's appeal raised more than Â£45m to help children and young people across the UK, and this year's TV event will be broadcast from 19:00 GMT.

News.title: Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
News.content:
Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016.

The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November.

Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire".

The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.

Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

News.title: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
News.content:
BBC's Asma Khalid explains how the Nvidia affair could threaten US national security and risk sensitive US technology getting into China. This comes after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of tech giant Nvidia after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs.

Read more about the rise and fall of Jensen Huang here.

News.title: Cricket sandpaper scandal claims '100% wrong', Australia captain says
News.content:
Australia captain Pat Cummins has hit back at former team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims over the sandpaper scandal, calling them "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".

In 2018, Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished for a plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town.

Khawaja has published his autobiography this week and the former batter has said the entire Australia team, which included Cummins, knew about the sandpaper scheme and should have taken responsibility.

But in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney, Cummins countered and said: "When he says we all knew, if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100% wrong.

"I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Cummins and Khawaja played 56 Tests together until Khawaja retired from international cricket in January.

Khawaja was in the Australia XI when Cummins made his Test debut in 2011 and the pair were also once team-mates in domestic cricket with New South Wales.

"Usman is a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," said Cummins.

"In his book he's been casual with my life and the lives of many others - and, I think, Australian cricket.

"I support him to tell his story, 100%, I'm glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

In a media conference he arranged himself, Cummins began by promising to answer all questions because, he said: "I don't want to talk about this again after today."

At times emotional, Cummins addressed a wide range of topics, including:

Advice that some of Khawaja's claims are defamatory, but he will not take legal action

He had been in contact with Khawaja and Smith since the book was published, but not Warner

His belief that the one-year bans handed to Smith and Warner, and a nine-month suspension to Bancroft were "heavy handed"

He had no recollection of Australia tampering with the ball in the 2017-18 Ashes series against England

He had met with Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg, who has reviewed the files from the original investigation

Explaining why sandpaper would have been present in the dressing room and that it was sometimes used by bowlers in training in order to practise with a reverse-swinging ball

Khawaja's allegations have reopened the debate about the sandpaper plot, the investigation into the cheating, the culture of Australian cricket and the reputations of those involved.

The story has dominated the media in Australia and caused headlines around the cricketing world.

Khawaja has been supported by Warner and Chadd Sayers, a seam bowler who was part of the Australia squad on the 2018 tour of South Africa.

However, his allegations have been rejected by Darren Lehmann, who was then the Australia head coach and former England batter Graeme Hick, one of Lehmann's assistants. Mitchell Starc, another bowler on the tour, has also denied Khawaja's claims.

Khawaja has put a spotlight on Cummins and his fellow bowlers Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon. The four were Australia's attack in Cape Town and remain their first-choice bowlers eight years later.

The quartet have always denied any knowledge of the plot, including in the release of a joint-statement in 2021.

In his book - Sabr - Khawaja alleged Australia were urged to find ways of getting the ball to swing by a coach, while Bancroft was later encouraged to cheat.

Khawaja also said he asked for the entire team to take responsibility for the controversy in Cape Town, but his request was rejected by two unnamed players.

Cummins said he does not recall any suggestion that the team should have shared the responsibility, or that it was rejected.

On the idea that the whole team were aligned in a plot to tamper with the ball, he said: "There was no masterplan around using illegal methods. People assume you've gone from very legal methods to suddenly taking sandpaper, and there must have been some huge masterplan.

"That is not the case. There's no grand plan. There's no team meeting. There's no bowlers saying this is what must happen."

"There's big leaps where Usman is being vague."

News.title: Brand will face 'hell on earth' in Wandsworth prison, says former inmate
News.content:
Russell Brand will face "hell on earth" inside HMP Wandsworth, a former inmate at the London prison has said.

Brand, 51, was convicted a week ago of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and was sentenced on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison.

He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons.

Chris Atkins, who served eight months at HMP Wandsworth for tax fraud, described the prison as "hell on earth".

He continued: "The first month is hands-down the worst. The mental shock is absolutely colossal. It was colossal for me and it's going to be 10 times worse for him because of the nature of his offences and the height from which he's fallen.

"He has to come to terms with it and the pure physical shock of suddenly being trapped in a dungeon for weeks on end with nobody to talk to most of the time is ghastly."

News.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
News.content:
ï»¿The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures, external show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.

News.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
News.content:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

As reported in the Times,, external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment.

Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes.

People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.

In his interim report,, external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

News.title: Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?
News.content:
Andy Burnham has committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but he knows just how the high the political stakes are.

He saw how last year's welfare rebellion marked the beginning of the end for his predecessor in Downing Street.

Sir Keir Starmer's authority was shredded when 120 - more than a quarter - of his own MPs threatened to derail his reforms.

To defuse this, Sir Keir was compelled to guarantee that existing claimants of personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales, wouldn't lose out.

Even then, 49 of the 120 potential Labour rebels still voted against their own government.

Next week, a review from former New Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn has the capacity to create another internal row in Labour's ranks.

Milburn has spent a year grappling with how to reduce the nearly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets).

In an interview with the Times, he has now confirmed he is set to recommend cutting benefits for some 16-24 year olds who currently receive Pip, or the enhanced health-related payment of Universal Credit.

Taking benefit cuts to the Parliamentary Labour Party would usually have a similar effect to adding phosphorous to water.

But from my soundings, the deep waters of the Labour ranks are calmer than might be expected.

News.title: Some childhood offenders may no longer have to reveal convictions to employers
News.content:
Some job applicants in England and Wales would no longer need to declare criminal convictions they received as children under government proposals designed to improve the employment prospects of rehabilitated young people.

The changes would mean criminal records for people detained when they were under 18 years old would no longer show up for life during checks carried out by employers.

The Ministry of Justice has also launched a consultation on relaxing disclosure requirements for some specific drug-related and violent crimes committed by children.

Young people who have not re-offended as adults struggle to find work because of their past behaviour, the government says.

Many employers require applicants to undergo a background check, which in their most basic form require people to self-declare if they have a criminal record.

For more sensitive roles, such as working with children or joining the police, an employer can carry out a standard or enhanced check, which allows them to request information from the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS).

How long a criminal record must be volunteered for or will show up in those checks differs depending on the severity of the offence, the punishment received and how long ago the crime was committed - sometimes referred to as whether a conviction is 'spent'.

For example, a young person who was convicted and fined for an offence when they were under-18 will have that information show up in checks for five-and-a-half years. If they were given a custodial sentence, that will be disclosed for the rest of their lives.

The government wants to reduce the number of young people those disclosure rules apply to if an applicant has not continued to offend as an adult.

Five offences would be removed from a list of crimes which will show up in background for checks for life if committed by an adult. They are: affray, violent disorder, supplying a controlled drug to a child, robbery and assaults occasioning actual bodily harm.

Between March 2022 and March 2026, around 8,500 under-18s were convicted of those offences, according to Ministry of Justice data.

The government says that type of crime is often a result of peer pressure, exploitation and "adolescent impulsivity" by individuals who are still developing, as opposed to a broader propensity for crime and violence.

Under the new rules, they would cease to show up in checks after five-and-a-half years.

Lifelong disclosure would also be removed for offences which led to a detention period of less than two years, the maximum which can be handed out by a youth court, and replaced by a new 11-year disclosure period.

In cases where a child was given a sentence longer than two years - which can only happen if the severity of the crime meant they were dealt with by an adult crown court - the rules would stay the same.

The most serious offences - including severe violence, terrorism-related crimes and sexual offences - would be exempted from the reforms.

Other proposed changes include:

Cutting or removing altogether the disclosure period for offences which led to a fine, the majority of which are for driving-related crimes

Ending disclosure of offences which were dealt with via an out of court resolution, which have primarily been used to tackle knife possession and assault

Reforming how long earlier offences appear in checks for young people who committed more than one crime as a child

Announcing a consultation on proposals, justice minister Jake Richards said: "Many young people who offend do not go on to lead lives of crime.

"They take responsibility, turn their lives around and want to make something of themselves.

"When they do, we should recognise that progress and support them â not put unnecessary barriers in their way."

The proposals come as the government prepares to publish a long-awaited report authored by former Labour minister Alan Milburn on tackling the number of young people not in work or education.

In May, he warned the UK was at risk of a raising a "lost generation" as almost one in eight young people are not working or studying.

Richards pointed to that intervention as he announced the disclosure reforms, saying barriers to employment can be "particularly difficult to overcome" for people who committed crimes as children.

News.title: Teenage girl admits murder in row over boy
News.content:
A teenager has admitted murdering a 16-year-old girl who she stabbed to death in a pre-planned fight over a boy.

Leeds Crown Court heard that Chloe Watson Dransfield was attacked by 18-year-old Kayla Smith after going to Smith's home with her boyfriend Blake Dowling in the early hours of 28 March.

Smith had pleaded guilty to manslaughter but denied murder. She then changed her plea to guilty on the second day of her trial.

Dowling, 18, who took Chloe to the house in Kennerleigh Avenue in Leeds, and Archie Rycroft, 20, who followed Smith to the fight, are also charged with murder and manslaughter and their trial will continue. They both deny the charges against them.

The judge, Mr Justice Cavanagh KC, said he would sentence Smith once the trial was over.

He told her the only sentence he could give was life imprisonment, but that he would need to set the minimum term she must spend in custody.

The trial previously heard that Dowling had been in a relationship with both Chloe and Smith and "knew of the bad feeling between the two females".

Dowling's mother told the court that Smith was "jealous and obsessed" over her son's relationship with Chloe.

News.title: Poundland gets more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
News.content:
Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended to find a rescue deal.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the retail chain was set to expire at midnight, but a court has given Poundland an extra 10 days to find a buyer.

The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by owners Gordon Brothers from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 shops and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just Â£1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock shops, and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims.

However, pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About Â£50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further Â£11m today from Poundland's accounts, on top of Â£10m announced earlier, as the firm seeks to find a new buyer.

Gordon Brothers said it was in talks with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and it had received "several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business".

News.title: Man jailed for 'appalling' catalogue of coercive control and abuse against partner
News.content:
Warning: This article contains details and references to suicide and abusive behaviour

A man subjected his partner to an "appalling" catalogue of abuse, including beating and abusive messages, which the judge said was "one of the worst" cases of coercive control the court had seen.

John Gizzi, 55, from St Asaph, Denbighshire, was jailed for four years and 11 months after pleading guilty to coercive and controlling behaviour towards Natasha Farah, 32, and for intentional strangulation of her sister.

There were shouts of "scumbag" and "rot in hell" from the public gallery towards Gizzi who appeared at the hearing via video link from prison.

Farah's mother said she would campaign in her daughter's name for sentences around coercive and controlling behaviour to be longer.

At Mold Crown Court, some people called out that the sentence was too short, until they were asked to be quiet by a court usher.

The court heard that a catalogue of physical and verbal abuse of Farah by Gizzi was unearthed after she made a suspected suicide attempt that left her with severe brain damage.

In his sentencing remarks, Judge Mills said Farah and her family and friends had faced an "appalling tragedy" and said the case of coercive control was one of the worst the court had seen, telling Gizzi he had subjected her to "appalling" behaviour.

Judge Mills said Gizzi had used "dreadful misogynistic language" towards Farah which was "part of the process of humiliation" and "destroying" her self worth.

Farah's mother, wearing a T-shirt saying Justice for Natasha, read a lengthy victim impact statement, saying she wanted to detail the "sheer devastating" impact Gizzi's behaviour had had and the "pain, grief, anger, torture" he had inflicted.

She described her daughter as "the most beautiful, funniest, kindest soul in the world" and told Gizzi, who was appearing by video link, that he was a "smiling devil monster".

Judge Mills said Natasha was often seen to have bruises, and was once assaulted by Gizzi with a dumbbell.

"You would accuse her of sleeping with other menâ¦ assaulted her frequentlyâ¦ sometimes in front of other peopleâ¦ you assaulted her in front of her child," he said.

The judge also said Gizzi had assaulted her on Valentine's Day and Mother's Day.

"She would plead with you to desist," he added.

News.title: Rolls-Royce gas leak prompts emergency response
News.content:
Emergency services have responded to a gas leak at a Rolls-Royce factory in Derby.

Derbyshire Fire and Rescue Service said it was called to the site in Raynesway at about 15:40 GMT on Thursday.

It said police, fire crews and ambulances responded to a "small chemical and gas leak", adding this was "not a nuclear incident", and that all employees were accounted for.

A 300m (985ft) cordon was put in place and locals were asked to remain indoors with windows and doors shut, however the guidance was lifted shortly before 22:00.

A BBC reporter at the scene was advised by police to stay in her car for her safety, and an alarm was heard coming from the building.

A number of roads were closed around the factory, including Royal Scot Way, Pride Park Way, from Derby Audi to the London Road roundabout, Harrow Street, and London Road, from the junction of Harrow Steet to Meadow Lane. They have all reopened, the fire service said.

In a statement, a fire service spokesperson added: "Emergency services and Rolls-Royce would like to thank local residents and businesses for their co-operation while the incident was resolved safely and as quickly as possible.

"The incident has now been handed over to Rolls-Royce."

News.title: What’s next for Ukraine-Russia peace talks as war approaches fifth year?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

U.S. envoys met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin before heading to Ireland for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as Washington sought new momentum for its peace efforts.

Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law, brokered talks this week between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv.

The session in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, brought the first direct discussions between Ukrainian and Russian representatives in nine months as the push for a settlement stalled.

The talks produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.

Plans for another round of talks were announced as well, with Witkoff and Zelensky saying Europe will join, though they gave no details about which countries or how many.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham (left) sits next to the President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky during the Ukraine security meeting (Stefan Rousseau/PA) ( PA Wire )

Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin for about two hours before going to Dublin, where they met with Zelensky for more than an hour as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.

Europe seeks a place at the negotiating table

Kushner said one goal of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader’s blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent’s broader security arrangements.

In Abu Dhabi, several European security advisers were involved on the sidelines but not in the main three-way talk.

Speaking to reporters before boarding a plane to leave Moscow, Witkoff said the next round of talks has been agreed upon.

Russian state TV showed Witkoff saying that “the Europeans will join at the next meeting,” but he did not elaborate.

Zelensky in Dublin indicated the Europeans would not be on the sidelines.

“Next meeting, Europe will be during negotiations, will be a negotiation team – not some way, not separately. They will have a voice,” he said.

The U.S. and Zelensky want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

open image in gallery ( PA )

Russia, meanwhile, doesn’t want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent.

But Washington and European capitals have sometimes seemed at odds in their diplomatic efforts.

Trump has repeatedly sided with Putin, last month waiving sanctions and striking a deal to import Russian diesel, in moves that dismayed Ukraine and European leaders.

The Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov argued that for Europe to join peace talks, it first must name a representative.

“The Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar. If someone takes the initiative to establish contact with the Russian side, such people are facing ostracism.”

Many in Europe also see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO’s eastward expansion as a main security threat and has demanded the alliance’s troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders.

Putin's aide calls the talks ‘constructive’

Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine – a possibility that alarms European leaders.

Thursday’s talks were “substantive, constructive, frank and useful,” Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov said.

He added that the Kremlin leader reminded Witkoff and Kushner about Moscow’s proposals from 2021 – before it sent troops into Ukraine – demanding that NATO roll back the alliance’s military deployments in Central and Eastern Europe.

open image in gallery ( AP )

Russia will update those with “fresh considerations,” Ushakov said.

Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire — an idea long floated by Europe to prevent a new attack by Moscow — would be “absolutely unacceptable” and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate target.

“In other words, the war would resume immediately,” the Russian president said.He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.

Fighting continues as another bitter winter approaches

Zelensky is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are “very much aligned” on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January.

“But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire,” Rutte said.

Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.

Russia’s bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow’s drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a “weaponization of winter.”

Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.

open image in gallery ( AP )

US Starlink problems return, Zelensky says

Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelensky said Thursday on social media.

Military units have recorded “significant disruptions,” including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelensky said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.

Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.

Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn’t be used for offensive strikes against Russia.

Zelensky said the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on.

Russian colonel reportedly killed by a car bomb

A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to the Investigative Committee, the country’s main criminal investigation agency.

It didn’t identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing. The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.

Several senior Russian military officers have died in bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

News.title: Who is Yuanjun Tang? Chinese dissident who admitted to spying for Beijing avoids prison time
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A member of New York’s Chinese dissident community who admitted spying for five years on his fellow activists on behalf of the Chinese government avoided prison time at his sentencing Thursday in Manhattan federal court.

Yuanjun Tang, 69, an outspoken critic of the Chinese Communist Party for over three decades, was sentenced to three years’ probation by Judge John G. Koeltl. The judge said claims by some individuals who believe they and their families were targeted for harm because of Tang’s actions could not be proven.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Jane Chong had asked the judge to impose a five-year prison sentence, the maximum Tang could face after pleading guilty in September 2025 to a charge that he failed to register as an agent of the People’s Republic of China with the U.S. attorney general’s office.

Defense attorney Michael Bradley said Tang was a democracy advocate, writer and activist who desperately wanted to return to China to visit his ailing parents and brother and made a connection with an individual who thought he could make it happen.

The lawyer said Tang didn’t know the man was a spy until he actually got to China, where, as it turned out, his mother and brother had already died.

Speaking through a Chinese interpreter, Tang told the judge that he betrayed his ideology to visit China and “see my parents again.”

“I deeply regret my actions,” he said. “My actions have caused a certain harm to other people.”

Tang’s October 2024 arrest followed several high-profile investigations into China’s attempts to harass and silence dissidents abroad, part of what federal officials have called a campaign of “transnational repression.”

Ms Chong said that the betrayal by Tang, a prominent Tiananmen Square protester, of those who joined him in the protest movement in the U.S. furthered the “story of transnational repression that is still playing out in America today.”

The betrayal came after Tang won the trust of others in the pro-democracy China movement by joining monthly protests outside China’s Manhattan consulate and founding a nonprofit in Flushing, Queens, where he has lived since 2002.

Ms Chong said Tang provided information to Chinese authorities on dozens of individuals from at least 2018 to 2023, including enabling a Chinese handler to join a group online chat titled “Friends of the Chinese Democracy Party” he had begun with 140 Chinese-American individuals.

Four individuals who believe they were victimized spoke at the sentencing. Several of them said they believe the deaths of family members in China were suspicious after their activities in the U.S. were exposed. One man said he did not believe it was a random attack when he was stabbed in the throat with a knife one day.

“They can never stop looking over their shoulders,” the prosecutor said of those who were victimized by Tang’s spying.

She said his actions “had a chilling effect on an entire community of people.”

Tang participated in the 1989 student-led Tiananmen Square demonstrations calling for democracy and political reform that ended with a deadly military crackdown. He was held in a Chinese prison for 12 years for his involvement in the student-led protests, according to reports at the time.

In 2002, he defected to Taiwan and then to the U.S., where he was granted political asylum. He became a naturalized U.S. citizen in July 2018.

By then, Ms Chong said, he was already providing information to the Ministry of State Security, China’s principal civilian intelligence agency.

At the direction of a Chinese intelligence officer, Tang agreed to photograph and record local protests against China, including a 2023 event in Manhattan dedicated to victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre, according to court documents.

In court papers, prosecutors said the FBI met with Tang in June 2023 to tell him that his phone likely contained malware planted by the People’s Republic of China. They said he then confessed that he had been carrying out tasks for China’s Ministry of State Security for years in return for about $4,200 annually.

News.title: Godzilla returns in special-effects glory in the latest movie with an anti-war message
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Japan’s most famous monster is back in “Godzilla Minus Zero” in all its fire-breathing, stomping glory, delivering its trademark allegorical message of the destruction of nuclear war and the pathos of human folly.

“Godzilla is not just any old monster but a metaphor for war and nuclear weapons, reflecting all the uncertainties of this world that still exist everywhere, in people’s hearts,” said Takashi Yamazaki, the director, writer and head of special effects.

“Being able to see that, taking shape, is important, even if it’s destroying a city.”

The new movie is proving to be a huge hit, topping $31.6 million over the opening weekend, scoring a record debut for a foreign-language live-action film at the North American box office.

Yamazaki also directed “Godzilla Minus One,” released three years ago, which won the Oscar for best visual effects. Except this time, the Godzilla story moves forward in time, from 1947 to 1949.

In his latest Godzilla, the same human characters are back: the pilot with a heart of gold, played by Ryunosuke Kamiki, and his sweetheart, portrayed by Minami Hamabe, who suffers from a mutative sickness inflicted by Godzilla’s earlier attack on Tokyo.

Hidetaka Yoshioka is cast in the role of the well-meaning-but-hapless official trying to save Japan, along with new characters, including a Hiroshima bombing survivor who became a mad scientist of sorts, portrayed with angst by seasoned dancer and actor Min Tanaka.

But the star of the show is undeniably Godzilla, first concocted in the 1954 classic directed by Ishiro Honda.

Since then, Godzilla, or Gojira in Japanese, based on the words for gorilla and “kujira,” or whale, has been featured in more than 30 films, mostly from Toho Co., the Japanese studio behind the original.

Yamazaki stressed he made sure to tackle the big question of “what makes for a Godzilla.” And he swears it turns out to be pretty basic, while also being surprisingly freeing and flexible, as there have been so many Godzillas over the years.

“As long as it has those spikes on its back,” he told The Associated Press in a recent interview. “Our Godzilla stays true to the original.”

The human melodrama might drag on at first. But when Godzilla finally appears, shuddering as it belts out its roar, dorsal spikes glowing fluorescent blue, it’s the moment filmgoers have all been waiting for.

The storyline is scripted to get the audience cheering for Godzilla, as it fights the golden winged dragon Ghidorah, according to Yamazaki. Ghidorah is to Godzilla, he added with a laugh, what the Joker is to Batman.

The latest Godzilla is the first in that franchise to be filmed using IMAX technology, meaning it feels tingingly immersive, delivering the illusion that everything is up close and coming right at you.

“It’s such an experience it’s something you get soaked in, not just a movie you watch. It’s overpowering,” said Ryosuke Matsui, who designed the shoes for the filmmaker’s red carpets.

IMAX is a challenge for filmmaking because the viewer is seeing a much bigger image with clearer resolution, which means more work for the special-effects team. But IMAX is perfect for framing Godzillian scenes, which typically have the giant monster chasing tiny fleeing people.

IMAX also delivers tremendous sound quality that’s effective for evoking terror, Yamazaki said.

He also made sure the new score by Naoki Sato kept the original Godzilla theme by Akira Ifukube in key scenes. Ifukube also created Godzilla's scream, as the legend goes, by running a leather glove across the strings of a contrabass.

“It’s so iconic it’s unavoidable. That has to be the centerpiece. It’s how you create on top of that,” said Yamazaki.

The late Haruo Nakajima, the stunt actor who portrayed Godzilla in the early works, used to say he was careful to show through his movements how Godzilla simply could not stop itself.

It had no choice but to keep going, stomping, one heavy step at a time, a tragic creature that went on to become an enduring artistic statement from the only nation in the world to suffer atomic bombings.

Yamazaki expressed openness to keeping the Godzilla franchise going, although he is now busy with a Hollywood film starring English-speaking actors. Details are still under wraps for the work, likely set for release in 2028.

___

Yuri Kageyama is on Threads: https://www.threads.com/@yurikageyama

News.title: UN climate summit pushes electrification goal as groups call for mining safeguards
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Clean public transport. Energy-efficient buildings. Affordable energy.

Those are a few of the things the president of the U.N. climate talks — known as COP31 — asked global leaders, delegates and climate activists to pledge as part of the global electrification plan laid out during the world's largest annual climate summit.

But environmental and human rights organizations caution that without strong safeguards, the mining boom for the minerals and metals needed to make the power lines, batteries, wind turbines and other energy infrastructure that can make the pledge a reality could have serious environmental and human rights impacts across the globe.

Mining has come at a cost to communities and habitats around the globe: Forests have been felled, water supplies poisoned and Indigenous peoples have lost access to land. Rights groups have urged COP31 officials to focus on how to fairly source the materials needed for the transition.

COP31 sets ambitious electrification goal

Turkey announced that electrification would be one of the main priorities during its copresidency of COP31 with Australia. The “35-by-35” global electrification pledge aims to increase the use of electricity from 21% to 35% by 2035 to reduce planet-warming greenhouse emissions, preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind.

The pledge builds on commitments made at previous U.N. climate summits: At COP28, countries agreed to work toward tripling renewable energy capacity and transitioning away from fossil fuels. COP29 focused on energy storage, grid modernization and climate finance.

The COP31 presidency said electrification is the next logical step, translating earlier pledges into changes in how energy is consumed.

“This transition brings together renewable energy, strong grids, storage capacity, energy efficiency, clean transport and green industry. Each supports the others,” said COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey’s environment minister. “We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs.”

Environmental activists note that the pledge does not require that electricity must come from renewable sources, meaning coal and other fossil fuels could be used. But as countries try to move away from fossil fuels, renewable energy is expected to play a major role.

Experts warn of a mining boom

From Indonesia to Brazil, the boom in demand for the metals and minerals needed to create wind turbines, solar panels, electric vehicle batteries, high-speed railways and other technologies crucial for the renewable energy transition has been underway for some time, according to the International Energy Agency.

Countries are also exploring new ways, like deep-sea mining, to secure their own mineral supplies, especially as the Iran war drives clean energy development.

The 35-by-35 pledge is expected to push demand even higher.

Data released by the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre shows those threats are on the rise. The international nonprofit recorded over 300 human rights allegations linked to transition mineral mining in 2025, up 73% from the previous year.

And experts warn that a boom in mining would likely lead to an increase in abuses.

“If mining is going to ramp up without proper protections in place, I think we can probably expect to see some of these problems ramp up as well,” said Emily Iona Stewart, the head of policy and advocacy at environmental and human rights group Global Witness.

Environmentalists call for guardrails against abuse

Environmental and human rights groups are urging governments to strengthen safeguards across critical material supply chains.

In an open letter to the COP31 presidencies, over 120 international civil society groups laid out conditions they want met for the 35-by-35 target, including protecting ecosystems, having binding human rights and environmental due diligence, and protecting Indigenous peoples.

“The transition must not repeat the harms of the fossil fuel era or replace one dependency with another,” the letter stated.

Experts said better recycling of already-mined materials is also key to reducing the reliance on mining. The IEA estimates that a successful scaleup of recycling could also lower the need for new mining by 25‑40% by 2050.

Yet, most countries don't have waste management programs or supportive regulations that would enable recycling, according to the IEA.

Rights experts also point out that the official negotiations and main talking points of COP31 do not contain explicit language on critical minerals and mining, leaving the door open for mining abuses to spread.

“If we want to do good by communities, bringing electricity to communities who don’t have it right now is a basic human need and right,” said Aimee Boulanger, executive director of the Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance. “But we can’t do good by some communities by doing inherent harm against others where the raw materials are extracted.”

The COP31 presidencies — Turkey is the official host while Australia is leading the negotiations — did not respond to requests for comment.

___

Milko reported from Islamabad.

News.title: Trump already eyeing another war before he leaves office
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump said he would consider ordering a military campaign against Cuba before the end of his term, even as his administration pulls back from diplomatic talks over the war with Iran following recent midterm election losses.

In an interview on “The Hugh Hewitt Show,” Trump said he wanted to “get Cuba done” before leaving office and suggested Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents immigrated from the island, would be eager to take on the effort.

“Well, I want to get Cuba done before I leave, yeah,” Trump told Hewitt when asked if he would order military force to free Cuba. “And we have a very good, talented guy for Cuba named Marco. Because Marco’s parents are from, Marco Rubio, his parents are from Cuba as you probably know. And he would love to do that.”

Trump described Cuba as a “failed” nation and said he was watching the situation closely, pointing to his past electoral support among Cuban Americans in Florida.

“I would like to be able to do it,” Trump said. “I won the Cuban vote by 94% in Florida, and I think I’m more popular now than I was then. And frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America.”

open image in gallery In an interview on ‘The Hugh Hewitt Show,’ President Donald Trump said he would ‘certainly consider’ a brief military campaign against Cuba before leaving office ( AFP/Getty )

When Hewitt pressed him on whether he would approve a brief military operation — specifically asking if he would be comfortable with “a little bit of military force, a week campaign” — Trump replied: “I would be, I would certainly consider that, yes.”

The president's remarks on Cuba come as the White House shifts its approach to the ongoing war with Iran, which began on February 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched military strikes.

Earlier Thursday morning, Trump announced in a series of Truth Social posts that he had instructed Vice President JD Vance to abandon diplomatic negotiations with Tehran and focus instead on investigating alleged fraud in Democratic-led states and cities.

“We don't need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

open image in gallery Calling Cuba a ‘failed’ nation, the president told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt he wanted to ‘get Cuba done’ before leaving office for the Cuban Americans who backed him in Florida ( AFP via Getty Images )

Oil prices rose, and stocks fell following the announcement as markets reacted to the renewed uncertainty, as reported by Axios.

The directive marks an abrupt shift for Vance, who has spent months leading U.S. negotiating delegations to secure a ceasefire and resume nuclear talks. Just days ago, the vice president had been weighing direct discussions with senior Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei, as reported by The Wall Street Journal.

On Tuesday, Rubio told G7 counterparts in Paris that Trump had decided against resuming major military strikes or pursuing a diplomatic settlement with Iran, opting instead to isolate the regime. The U.S. has repeatedly rejected an existing Iranian ceasefire proposal, which Rubio dismissed as “outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”

Though Trump told reporters on Monday that the war with Iran was “effectively over” and that the U.S. would hold off on threatened strikes at the request of Gulf neighbors including Qatar and Saudi Arabia, he intends to maintain a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.

open image in gallery After the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance took to X to blame his party’s losses on the war with Iran ( Reuters )

Low-level attacks have also continued, with Iranian state media reporting U.S. strikes on Iran's Qeshm island earlier this week following Iranian attacks on tankers in the Gulf.

The war’s economic toll, including higher gas prices, was widely seen as a factor in the Republican Party's recent midterm losses, which cost the GOP control of Congress. Days before Trump's Thursday announcement, Vance publicly broke with the president over the war's political impact.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote on X last week. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost."

Trump has defended the war in Iran, saying he would not have handled it differently.

News.title: Olive oil shots are popular with influencers - but might not be a magic health elixir
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Viral olive oil shots are promoted by celebs like model Hailey Bieber, reality star Kourtney Kardashian and actress Jennifer Lopez to benefit the skin and support overall health.

“I sound so old! I’m like, ‘Ah, I gotta take my olive oil shot in the morning,’” Bieber told TIME in April, saying she mixes it with lemon. “It really kind of just tastes like a big gulp of salad dressing.”

There are serious benefits to the oil, which is naturally anti-inflammatory - but experts say people should be cautious about how much they consume. You might be adding more calories to your morning than you think.

Just a teaspoon of olive oil has 40 calories, according to Rochester Medicine. A shot glass has about nine teaspoons, or 360 calories - around the same as a bacon, egg and gouda sandwich at Starbucks.

"Taking an olive oil shot or two every day can add several hundred calories to your daily calorie consumption," Megan Meyer, a science communication consultant based in North Carolina, told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

open image in gallery ‘It really kind of just tastes like a big gulp of salad dressing,’ says model Hailey Bieber ( Reuters )

"Consuming more calories than your body burns each day leads to weight gain, so taking an olive oil shot or two daily will most likely lead to weight gain over time,” she said.

A fat problem

The problem is that olive oil is primarily made of fat. Fortunately, the fat in olive oil is considered good for you when not consumed in excess.

One of those fats is oleic acid, which has been found to support heart health and lower levels of bad cholesterol that increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Oleic acid is part of why the U.S. Food and Drug Administration says consuming about 1.5 tablespoons of olive oil instead of other fats and oils may reduce the risk for heart disease.

The recommended daily amount is typically just under 2 tablespoons, per 2025 federal guidelines.

open image in gallery There are many benefits to including olive oil in your diet, including vitamin E and polyphenols ( AFP via Getty Images )

Proven benefits

If you’re not consuming olive oil in excess, there are other proven benefits.

Olive oil has vitamin E, which supports a strong immune system, and has been tied to a reduced risk of dementia-related death. It also has beneficial plant compounds known as polyphenols, according to U.C. Davis Health.

Polyphenols can help the body manage inflammation that leads to disease. Though, the polyphenol content in olive oil varies. There are more polyphenols in extra virgin olive oil, which costs at least $20 a bottle.

“Any habit that gets polyphenols into your body is a step in the right direction,” Dr. Frank Lipman, a longevity expert and bestselling author, told HOLA! magazine. “If you're doing the olive oil shot, quality matters. Make it high-quality extra virgin.”

News.title: Right-wing influencer claims Democrats will tank the economy so they can blame Trump
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Conservative commentator Ben Shapiro said Thursday on Sean Hannity’s “Hang Out” podcast that Democrats would seek to deliberately weaken the U.S. economy over the next two years in an effort to hurt President Donald Trump politically.

Shapiro, a founder of conservative media company The Daily Wire, told Hannity that congressional Democrats planned to push populist measures designed to look as though they were addressing the cost of living while actually slowing economic growth.

“The Democrats right now have a strong incentive to basically crater the American economy over the course of the next two years and blame President Trump for it,” Shapiro said.

According to Shapiro, this strategy involves targeting the artificial intelligence sector under the guise of protecting workers and addressing the cost of living, which he argued would appeal to the “legacy media” and uninformed voters.

As an example, Shapiro pointed to opposition against AI infrastructure, referencing a recent campaign in which an activist gathered thousands of signatures to stop a planned $5 billion AI data center in Maryland.

open image in gallery On Thursday’s episode of Sean Hannity’s ‘Hang Out’ podcast, conservative commentator Ben Shapiro predicted that congressional Democrats would intentionally damage the U.S. economy over the next two years ( AFP/Getty )

“I think they will offer, quote, unquote, affordability bills to help with the legacy media that aren’t actually about affordability,” Shapiro said. “They’ll say that the way we’re going to save your job is by destroying the AI industry, which is responsible for the vast majority of economic growth in the country right now, and they’ll do it in the name of populism.”

He added that the resulting economic “fallout” would ultimately be pinned on Trump.

Hannity appeared taken aback by the claim, letting out a long breath during their discussion of the midterm results before pressing Shapiro on whether he really meant it.

open image in gallery Hannity predicted during his ‘Hang Out’ podcast that voters would experience ‘buyer’s remorse’ over the new congressional majorities within five months ( AFP/Getty )

“That is a powerful statement,” Hannity said. “They will purposefully crater the economy?”

Hannity went on to suggest that voters would experience “buyer’s remorse” regarding the new congressional majorities within five months. He also questioned how Democrats might respond if the president attempted to find common ground on economic legislation.

Naturally, Shapiro was unfazed and stuck to his talking points — the Dems will wreck it all just to spite Trump.

News.title: Pat Cummins says Usman Khawaja’s sandpaper scandal claims are ‘utter nonsense’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Australia captain Pat Cummins has come out fighting against former team-mate Usman Khawaja, branding his allegations over the sandpaper scandal as “complete and utter nonsense” and “100 per cent wrong”.

Khawaja’s newly released autobiography contained a series of explosive claims about the ball-tampering drama of 2018, suggesting that the entire squad were party to a plot which ended with Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft assuming all blame.

In an interview with the Sydney Morning Herald, the former opener concluded: “It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.”

Cummins previously distanced himself from the conspiracy in 2021, co-signing a statement alongside fellow bowlers Mitch Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon denying knowledge.

In the aftermath of Khawaja’s bombshell claims, which have been backed up by Warner, Cummins invited the media to question him at Cricket Central in Sydney and launched a passionate defence.

“When he says we all knew, if that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he’s 100 per cent wrong,” Cummins said.

“I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening. But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that.

“He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense. There was no master-plan around using illegal methods. There’s no grand plan. There’s no team meeting. There’s no bowlers saying this is what must happen.”

open image in gallery Usman Khawaja’s new book has reopened old wounds for Australian cricket. (Rory Dollard/PA) ( PA Wire )

Cummins also shared his frustration at Khawaja’s conduct, suggesting he has acted carelessly by casting inflammatory aspersions on his former team-mates.

“Usman is a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,” Cummins said.

“In his book, he’s been casual with my life and the lives of many others and, I think, Australian cricket. I support him to tell his story, 100 per cent. I’m glad he feels like he can but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do.

“It affects real people. This really affects Australian cricket and I think the way that he’s presented his story, I think he’s done that in a very casual manner. That’s what I’m grappling with at the moment because I don’t think it’s okay.”

Cummins went as far as suggesting he and others could have a legal case against Khawaja, only to rule out pursuing such action.

“I did get advised this week that some of the things that have been said are probably defamatory,” he said.

open image in gallery Cummins (left) and Khawaja (right) in happier times together. (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Archive )

“I won’t be doing that (suing). You got to move on. It’s been eight years. You’ve got to draw the line at some point.”

Cummins took questions for over an hour, rejecting a media adviser’s offer to wrap the session, ostensibly in a bid to exhaust the matter once and for all.

Yet, given the level of intrigue and the contrasting opinions on both sides, that seems optimistic.

“I’m here to answer it today and I won’t speak about it again,” he said.

“We dealt with this at the time, we told everyone in the investigation everything we knew. We had to defend ourselves in 2021, we’ve had to defend ourselves now.

“If we have to do this every time another book or idea comes out, it’s pretty ridiculous.”

Cummins’ wide-ranging account of events came less than 24 hours after a bizarre press conference by Mitch Marsh, the stand-in ODI captain and another survivor from the 2018 team, during which he repeatedly refused to speak on the subject.

News.title: Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of England vs Croatia in the Nations League, with the hosts’ captain Harry Kane set to become the country’s most-capped player.

The 33-year-old has enjoyed a memorable few weeks, becoming the first English Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years and following it up with a new Bayern Munich contract, and an appearance at Wembley tonight will take him clear of Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Kane scored twice in his record-equalling appearance against Czech Republic at Wembley last month, extending his international tally to 91 goals – a total that is unrivalled for England.

“It’s not about me – it’s about the team,” Kane said before tonight’s landmark moment. “I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

The 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic left England on nine points after four Nations League group games, with a 2-0 win in the away contest and a 7-0 thumping of Croatia coming after a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

Thomas Tuchel will be hoping that his side can inflict another heavy defeat on Croatia this evening, but a draw will be enough to book their place in the quarter-finals, with the group’s top two teams progressing.

While Kane will collect plaudits for his 126th cap, attention will also be on a potential first, with Jude Bellingham’s younger brother, Jobe, included in a senior England squad for the first time.

The two Bellinghams appearing together in a senior match would be a new experience for them, while it would be the first time that brothers have taken to the field together for England in 19 years.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the Football Association’s England app. “It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great.”

News.title: Experts hail a “milestone” as TB deaths fall by more than a third in 10 years
News.content:
The number of people dying from tuberculosis has dropped by more than a third over the last 10 years but progress against the disease is still too slow, according to the World Health Organization.

Figures from WHO’s annual TB report showed that the lung disease took the lives of an estimated 1.13 million people in 2025, down from 1.7m in 2015, a drop of 35 per cent.

While WHO hailed this as a major milestone in achieving global targets - albeit five years too late - it said that progress in wiping out TB was still too slow.

Africa and Europe have made the greatest progress in reducing deaths, with numbers halving on both continents over the 10-year period. India and China - countries that have high burdens of the disease - also cut deaths by 35 per cent.

The report also showed that an estimated 10.6million people contracted the disease in 2025, a reduction of just 75,000 since 2024.

TB - still the world’s leading infectious disease killer - is preventable and curable, and is caused by the bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is spread when infected people cough or sneeze.

The disease has been around for centuries, and has been described as the quintessential disease of poverty as it spreads in areas of low quality housing, among people with poor nutrition and immunity. It is a particular risk to people who are HIV positive.

Treatment requires a six-month long regimen of medication, and while treatments have become less toxic in recent years, they still take a heavy toll on patients and have a range of side effects, including at the most extreme deafness. Adherence to medication is also a problem.

News.title: Low-cost parenting app halves rates of sexual violence amongst teenagers in Tanzania
News.content:
A low cost parenting intervention has more than halved rates of sexual violence among teenage girls in Tanzania, a study has shown.

The ParentApp digital parenting programme for families is aimed at reducing rates of violence experienced by teenagers of both sexes.

Researchers found the programme helped bolster family relationships and enabled mothers and fathers to better communicate with their children at what is often a tricky stage of their development.

The programme, led by Oxford University and the University of Cape Town in partnership with the Tanzanian government, the World Health Organization and Unicef, combines in-person and mobile parenting support.

Parents have an introductory session with a facilitator and then undertake 12 weekly sessions online. They also join a WhatsApp group with other parents where they can discuss problems and support one another.

The randomized controlled trial, published in The Lancet, included 2,396 children aged 10–17 and 2,396 parents and carers across 80 urban and rural areas.

Families were randomly assigned to receive either ParentApp or a comparison app focused on safe water and hygiene. Researchers analysing the results did not know which app each family received.

At the 14-month follow-up, girls in families participating in the ParentApp initiative reported a 67% reduction in sexual violence; a 54% reduction in sexual exploitation and an improvement in parent-child relationships. The successes were less marked in boys, however.

Violence against children is widespread globally: Unicef data shows that around one in five girls and women and one in seven boys and men globally have experienced sexual violence as children.

Lucie Cluver, professor of child and family social work at Oxford University and one of the authors of the study, said the intervention was aimed at helping parents and children talk to one another and discuss situations before they arise.

In Tanzania, for example, teenage girls might get a motorbike taxi late at night, potentially putting them in a dangerous situation.

“What you’re doing is making plans and problem solving ahead of these risky situations that teenagers end up in. And you’re building trust and the relationship so you can have these difficult conversations,” said Prof Cluver.

She said she was surprised at how big an impact the intervention had on sexual violence: teenage girls reported that because the app helped improve communication with their parents and carers they did not feel the need to go out as much.

The programme cost around $6 per family but researchers calculated that it goes up to around $10 per family if 20% are given smartphones. A traditional in-person parenting intervention generally costs around $120 per family.

Engagement in the sessions was high - around 70 per cent of participants completed the course - and some parents kept in touch with one another after the programme.

However, the authors of the study stressed that while the app focused on families there remains a need to prevent violence against children in other settings, such as schools and religious institutions. There also needs to be a broader societal push to address the scourge.

“The app isn’t the answer to everything - it’s just one part of the puzzle,” said Prof Cluver.

Prof Cluver said she hoped future versions of the programme would include greater focus on digital harms and test whether parents could take the lead themselves.

The programme is being rolled out in other countries, including Mexico, Panama and South Africa, and is easily adaptable for different contexts.

“Tanzania only has 20% smartphone use and we thought if it works in one of the hardest places to do a digital intervention it could work anywhere,” she said.

She said the study showed how parenting was a universal experience, with the majority focused on what is best for their children.

“Parents feel powerless. We live in a world where our kids are facing risks and parents just want to help,” added Prof Cluver.
