News.title: AI fuels fastest economic growth in two years
News.content:
The Prime Minister and the Chancellor should not claim credit for the AI-fuelled expansion of Britain’s economy in the third quarter, a think tank said.

Julian Jessop, economics fellow at the Institute of Economic Affairs, said the 0.7pc expansion in the economy was “a tribute to the resilience of the private sector in the face of the energy shock and policy headwinds”.

He said: “This resilience is despite rather than because of anything the Government has done. In particular, the persistent weakens of the construction sector underlines the failure of flagship policies to boost housebuilding and infrastructure spending.

“The Government’s clumsy interventions are also continuing to add to labour and housing costs, including rents. Instead, the key driver of growth and business optimism has been the rollout of AI. This is an area that the Government has not got round to messing up, though that may yet be coming.

“In the meantime, the Government is still borrowing more than expected and the labour market remains weak.

“The full impact of higher inflation and higher interest rates has also yet to be felt. Early surveys for the fourth quarter already show that consumer confidence, retail spending, private sector hiring and housing market activity are all starting to slide again.

“2026 will still be a year when the economy performed much better than expected – at least in terms of GDP. But the new year will start with further increases in energy bills and high levels of job insecurity, which will matter far more to most people.”

News.title: Bird flu viruses changing through natural mixing, warn scientists
News.content:
The bird flu virus’ resurgence began with an 11-year-old. In February 2023, the schoolgirl was admitted to a hospital in Phnom Penh with severe pneumonia – within a day, she was dead.

Tests soon revealed that she had contracted avian influenza: Cambodia hadn’t reported a human case of bird flu since 2014, but the hiatus was over. Since then, 39 more people have been infected and 15 have died in the Southeast Asian country – a case fatality rate of roughly 40 per cent.

Researchers have been scratching their heads as to why, after nine years, this particular stain of H5N1 suddenly started jumping from birds to people again. The strain or clade called 2.3.2.1 had been circulating for almost a decade without spilling into humans. What changed?

Now, a paper in Emerging Infectious Diseases offers clues.

Scientists say the apparent rise in human cases has coincided with the virus gaining new genetic material and, potentially, new powers of infection, from a second flu virus via a process known as “reassortment”.

News.title: The country where diabetes is more feared than HIV
News.content:
Furthermore, even when antiretrovirals suppress the virus, the immune system can stay chronically activated, causing a low-grade inflammation that damages organs and blood vessels. The Lancet HIV Commission reported that, by one measure of biological ageing, people with HIV appeared about five years older on average than peers without the virus.

HIV also makes other infections more dangerous. For example, those living with the virus are more likely to contract human papillomavirus (HPV), the leading cause of cervical cancer, and they are less able to clear HPV from their bodies.

“With HIV, you don’t channel your mind into dying,” Ms Shongwe said. “But when I got to know that I have cervical cancer, I thought it was the end of the world.”

In 2018, Ms Ginindza moved from the Ministry of Health’s HIV programme to its NCD programme, but almost immediately, she asked to go back to her old job. “There is nothing here,” she recalled, “no tools, no data collection system, no guidelines”.

Even today, the ministry doesn’t have any dedicated NCD posts. While there are hundreds of people working on HIV, there are just 10 NCD staff, all borrowed from other programmes, Ms Ginindza said.

Although latest figures show that NCDs account for almost half of Eswatini’s deaths the government’s programme for NCDs, injuries and mental health received about one million emalangeni - roughly £45,000 - or 0.03 per cent of the health budget.

Foreign aid hasn’t filled the gap: international partners cover about five per cent of NCD spending, Ms Ginindza said, compared with 60 per cent of the HIV response. Donors “cannot give you money when they also need that money to address their own NCDs”, she added.

So, when it comes to these chronic diseases, patients struggle to get diagnosed, obtain their medicines or see a specialist for complications. In a 2024 government survey, fewer than 30 per cent of people with high blood pressure were on medication, and only 14 per cent had their hypertension under control.

The government’s own NCD report puts the stock-out rate for key medicines at 79 per cent, and the public system has no nephrologists, endocrinologists or cardiologists, Ms Ginindza said, relying instead on private specialists and Taiwanese medical missions to provide these services.

Faced with one of the worst HIV epidemics, Eswatini poured almost everything into fighting it. “The focus was HIV,” Ms Ginindza said, “so we forgot about the other conditions.”

Fighting on two fronts



Now, Eswatini is trying to turn its HIV machinery towards chronic diseases.

Since 2020, a government-led scheme has delivered NCD medication refills, blood pressure checks and glucose tests in hundreds of community settings, integrating this with existing HIV services. As it once did with antiretrovirals, the ministry is also shifting NCD care from hospitals to local clinics, Ms Ginindza said, aiming to train at least two nurses at each.

For Mr Mamba, that means he sees the same clinician for his HIV, diabetes and blood pressure. It saves time, he said, since he can get everything under one roof.

The challenge is not just extending HIV services to NCD patients but finding the money to sustain both. The Eswatini government aims to increase NCD funding to 20 million emalangeni, or £900,000, by 2028.

But last year, the Trump administration gutted the US President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar), the backbone of Eswatini’s HIV response.

In December, Eswatini signed a five-year deal with the US to restore some HIV funding - on the condition that the government shoulders more of the cost itself. So, as the country scrambles to protect its HIV gains, NCDs risk remaining a secondary priority.

With his diabetes and blood pressure medicines so often out of stock, Mr Mamba has come to dread his check-ups, convinced each one will show his numbers have climbed again - and that his luck is running out.

Many of his neighbours have the same conditions and probably share these fears, he said, but much as people once kept quiet about HIV, they rarely discuss such things.

Over 30 years ago, Ms Gwebu contemplated suicide after being diagnosed with HIV. But today, she hopes Eswatini can sustain its hard-won progress against the virus without leaving those with other diseases behind. “What is going to kill our people,” she said, “is not going to be HIV.”

News.title: Ebola could be raging in DRC for another year, expert warns
News.content:
The Ebola epidemic currently raging in the Democratic Republic of Congo could last at least another year, a leading UK epidemiologist has warned.

Experts have struggled to contain the current outbreak since the first cases of the rare Bundibugyo strain of the disease were reported in May.

There have so far been almost 11,000 cases including 5,000 deaths, making it the second largest outbreak in history, after the devastating West Africa epidemic of 2014-16. Cases have also been reported in Nigeria and Kenya, although transmission has not been widespread.

The outbreak is taking place across a vast area of DRC - North Kivu and Ituri - where conflict and widespread mistrust of authorities, including health workers, have hampered the response.

Neil Ferguson, professor of epidemiology at Imperial College, London, told a press briefing that at the current rate of disease spread that the epidemic could still be ongoing at the end of next year.

“Controlling Ebola outbreaks takes a long time so it is highly likely we’ll still be seeing transmission in a year’s time,” he said.

“We’re ticking over at about 70 confirmed cases a day at the moment and that’s almost certainly quite a significant underestimate of the true number of infections,” said Prof Ferguson, who rose to prominence at the beginning of the Covid pandemic when he advised government on the likely trajectory of the outbreak.

News.title: Many more cattle ranch workers infected with H5N1 than reported, says US farming union
News.content:
Far more US farm workers are infected with bird flu than officially reported, with some suffering “very severe” symptoms, according to the country’s largest farming union.

H5N1 is currently spreading rapidly across US cattle farms in dozens of US states.

Officially, just three people have been diagnosed with the virus in the past month, all following close contact with infected cows.

In total, 73 people in the US have been officially been recorded as infected with H5N1 since 2024, mostly dairy farm workers. Three have died.

But United Farm Workers (UFW), which represents thousands of workers across the US, said it was aware of many more farmers experiencing symptoms consistent with H5N1 who had not been tested.

“We have now connected with a number of workers and have confirmed that more workers are sick with avian flu symptoms who have not been tested,” the UFW wrote on X.

Symptoms range from “very mild to very severe”, the post added, including mild upper respiratory infections and conjunctivitis to severe flu-like symptoms, bone pain, persistent coughing and high fever.

The ongoing outbreak is worrying disease experts.

“H5N1 is not a virus to be casual about- or to let spread unchecked, given every mutation is like the virus buying a lottery ticket to acquire human-to-human transmission,” said Dr Devi Sridhar, a public health researcher at the University of Edinburgh.

Referring to the statement by the UFW, Professor Francois Balloux, director of the UCL Genetics Institute, added: “The most puzzling aspect to me is not even the incompetence and paralysis of the authorities but the resignation and fatalism. It feels like reading some chronicle by a mediaeval peasant.”

Of the roughly 1,000 people infected with H5N1 since the virus was first identified in the late 1990s, almost half have died. However, most historical cases have resulted from contact with wild birds, while the strain circulating in cattle, known as genotype B.12, is thought to cause much milder illness.

Concerns have nevertheless grown after an unidentified farm worker in Washington state died in late October from the cattle-derived H5N1 strain, raising questions about whether the virus may have mutated.

The Trump administration has been heavily criticised for allowing bird flu to run rampant through America’s wild and domestic animals, putting people at risk.

Deep cuts to the federal agencies responsible for managing human and animal health, the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and the Department of Agriculture (USDA), have resulted in the scaling down of surveillance and testing programmes amongst both livestock and farm workers.

Every infection, animal or human, raises the chance the virus could mutate and eventually gain the ability to spread between people – something which experts have long warned could trigger the next pandemic.

As flu season begins, experts are concerned a dairy worker infected with ordinary seasonal flu could catch H5N1 at the same time, and the two viruses could mix to create a new, more dangerous strain that could spread between people – a phenomenon known as “reassortment.”

“It is clear that workers are not being informed of the risks of handling sick cattle and infected milk. They are being given no information on flu shots or avian flu testing,” the UFW said.

Estimates suggest that over half of the 150,000-strong dairy workforce in the US are immigrant or undocumented workers, driven in part by high demand for intensive year-round labour and a lack of domestic applicants.

Many are reportedly worried about coming forward for testing over fears they will come into contact with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the federal agency emboldened under Trump, which has been tasked with deporting one million immigrants every year.

Yakima Valley, the region of Washington State where the three recent H5N1 cases have been reported and where the virus is spreading through dozens of dairy herds, is in the midst of an ICE crackdown.

Sports.title: Cummins dismisses Khawaja's sandpaper claims as 'utter nonsense'
Sports.content:
Australia Test captain Pat Cummins dismissed his former team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims as "utter nonsense" after the recently retired batter said in his autobiography that the whole side were aware of ball-tampering that took place on their 2018 tour of South Africa.

Khawaja made the revelations in his new book 'Sabr', which was released earlier this week, bringing the scandal back onto the agenda eight years after Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera using sandpaper on the ball while Australia were fielding.

Only Bancroft, then-captain Steve Smith and his vice-captain David Warner were punished, with each receiving lengthy bans as the rest of the Australian team and coaching staff denied knowledge of the scheme.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Nasser Hussain and Michael Atherton react to Usman Khawaja suggesting the whole Australian side knew about the Sandpaper scandal on their 2018 tour of South Africa

Cummins, who was a relatively junior member of the side playing in just his 13th Test match, in 2021 issued a joint-statement with fellow bowlers from the fixture Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, in which they denied knowing that a foreign substance had been taken onto the field to alter the ball in order to try to make it swing.

"When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, ​he's 100 per cent wrong. I've said that consistently for the last eight years," ‌Cummins told reporters on Friday morning in Sydney having called the press conference himself on social media.

"I did not know that was happening, but Usman actually says things that ​are actually far more serious than that.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player David Warner took to his Instagram to back Khawaja's claims the entire team knew about 2018 ball-tampering plan against South Africa (Credit: @davidwarner31)

Following the publication of the book, Warner, who received a year-long ban from all cricket and a lifetime ban from leadership roles, said on Monday that Khawaja's version of events was "100 per cent accurate".

Cummins, who was appointed Australia captain in November 2021, criticised Khawaja for being "casual" with the lives of his former team-mates and Australian cricket as a whole.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and ​reputations," Cummins said.

"In his book, Ussie has been casual with my life and the ​lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket."

Cummins, who appeared to become emotional at times in a press conference that lasted more than an hour, revealed that a video taken of him and his wife Becky in a heated discussion a day earlier had been prompted by her anger with Khawaja's actions.

Despite that and his clear disagreement with Khawaja's statements, Cummins said that he does not intend to pursue legal action.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Martin Samuel explains what impact Khawaja's claims that the entire Australia team were aware of the ball-tampering scheme in South Africa in 2018 could have on next summer's Ashes series in England

"I did get advised this week that some of the things ​that've been said are probably defamatory, but I won't be doing that," Cummins said.

"You've got to move on. It's been eight years. We're moving on. So ‌you got to draw a line ​at some point."

Cummins has been rested for England's white-ball tour of Australia, which resulted in him holding his press conference on Friday morning in Sydney just hours before the first ODI was scheduled to begin in Perth.

How have other Australian players reacted?

Cummins' extraordinary press conference came a day after Australia ODI captain Mitchell Marsh, who was also part of the team that toured South Africa in 2018, declined to comment on a series of questions about Khawaja's book.

Khawaja also claimed in the book that Australia experimented with lifting the seam on the ball during the 2017-18 Ashes at home to England, which they won 4-0 under the captaincy of Smith.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Australia's stand-in captain Mitchell Marsh declined to comment on 'Sandpapergate' ahead of their series-opening ODI against England

Starc, who had spoken to reporters on Tuesday, took a similar line to Cummins as he insisted that his recollections hadn't changed.

Starc, who is also not part of Australia's limited-overs side to face England, said of Khawaja's claims: "I haven't really paid much attention to it to be fair.

"There are differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process, at the time and since.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but from where I stand my opinion hasn't changed, my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mitchell Starc responds to Khawaja's claims that Australia's entire dressing room knew about the ball-tampering scheme in Cape Town in 2018

"As far as our statement said, we weren't aware of things being taken on the field. That's where I'll leave it.

"I will be sticking to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time eight years ago, so clearly there are differing versions from different people.

"We weren't aware of anything taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town.

"As far as the book is concerned, I haven't read it. I probably won't read it, so that's for Usman to elaborate on."

Sports.title: Korda two shots off lead on return at The Annika as Woad also starts well
Sports.content:
World No 1 Nelly Korda made an impressive return to LPGA Tour action after a two-month absence to finish the opening round of The Annika within two shots of the lead.

Korda, whose last competitive golf came at the Solheim Cup in September after her most recent LPGA Tour outing in August, shot a bogey-free seven-under par round of 63 at Pelican Golf Club in Florida.

Korda trails Japan's Minami Katsu and Korean Hye-Jin Choi by two shots, with fellow American Lindy Duncan also ahead of her on eight under after making a hole-in-one during her 62.

"It was nice to kind of feel those juices flowing again, especially playing with Hye-Jin who just had a great round today," Korda said.

So much attention was on Korda, who captured two majors early in the season. Her last tournament was the FM Championship outside Boston and then the Solheim Cup, where Korda went 2-1-1 in an American loss in the Netherlands.

"I needed to take that break, and right after Solheim I was burned out," Korda said. "I just needed to mentally step away for a few days."

Sports.title: Pochettino agrees two-and-a-half-year deal to become Man Utd boss
Sports.content:
Manchester United and Mauricio Pochettino have agreed a deal for him to become the club's next head coach.

Pochettino is expected to sign a two-and-half-year contract at Old Trafford, replacing Michael Carrick, who was sacked earlier on Thursday.

Pochettino - who had a £7m release clause in his USA contract - will take charge of United after overseeing the USA's games against Haiti on Saturday and Wednesday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The six stats that got Michael Carrick sacked as Man Utd head coach

The formal announcement of Pochettino's appointed is expected on Friday, with the Argentine set to be United's eighth permanent appointment since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Pochettino's first game in charge will be the trip to Anfield to face Liverpool on November 22, live on Sky Sports.

Carrick departed less than six months after signing a two-year contract having overseen the club's worst start to a Premier League season, with United in the relegation zone after picking up one win in 10 matches.

In a statement on Thursday morning, shortly after Carrick left the training ground, United said they reached "the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions".

Carrick took training in Manchester on Wednesday as United reached a verbal agreement with Pochettino.

Meanwhile, club chiefs were at a Monaco summit with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. That is where the decision to sack Carrick was ratified by Ratcliffe following the recommendation of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

United's hierarchy, including Wilcox and Berrada, are understood to feel that the current squad is much better than results and performances have shown.

Carrick's exit follows United's 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on Sunday, when they fell 2-0 down inside four minutes and then 4-2 down early in the second half before mounting a last-gasp comeback to draw.

The rescue job followed a similar turnaround to beat Roma in the Champions League last Tuesday but was not enough to convince the United hierarchy to continue with the former midfielder in charge.

Jonny Evans and Jonathan Woodgate, who were part of the coaching set up under Carrick, have also left the club, along with Steve Holland, Travis Binnion and goalkeeping coach Craig Mawson.

The only coach who remains is assistant first-team goalkeeping coach Connor King, who joined the club two months ago.

Carrick was initially appointed as United boss in January 2026 on a contract until the end of the season following Ruben Amorim's sacking earlier in that campaign. He delivered a brilliant run of results, winning 12 of 17 matches to earn a third-place finish in the Premier League and a return to the Champions League.

Carrick was nominated for Premier League Manager of the Season and, on May 22, signed a new contract running to 2028. However, just three wins in 15 matches this term have cost him his job.

Former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain boss Pochettino has been considered for the United job on three previous occasions, but will now finally take the Old Trafford hot seat.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Carragher believes Mauricio Pochettino is the right man for Manchester United and sets out the minimum expectations he must meet by the end of the season

Neville: United need bigger solution than sacking Carrick

Sky Sports' Gary Neville to NBC:

"You can keep changing the manager and thinking that's going to be the answer. But this has been proven now over 12 years, that's not the answer.

"It's rinse and repeat. Ruben Amorim, Erik ten Hag, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Carrick, Jose Mourinho, Louis van Gaal, David Moyes, Ralf Rangnick - some of them are world-class managers who have had success. There are a lot of promising young managers there, ex-players who know the club as well.

"None of it has worked because if you've got a poor performance department, poor recruitment department, you've not got leadership that is strong right through the spine of the football club, you will fail."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News reporter Rob Dorsett reveals the inside details of Manchester United's pursuit of USA head coach Mauricio Pochettino

Carrick's Man Utd reign in numbers

United won 12 out of 17 games last season under Carrick - a 70.1 per cent win rate, which saw him comfortably sit with the best record of permanent Old Trafford managers.

But he leaves with a record of 15 wins in 32 matches - a rate of just 46.9 per cent, which leaves him only ahead of Ruben Amorim, the man he replaced in the dugout last season, in the years since Ferguson's retirement.

Carrick has overseen three wins in 15 matches this campaign (20 per cent). They won eight out of 21 games before Amorim's sacking last year (38.1 per cent).

His drop-off brings echoes of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. The former United striker's win percentage fell from 73.7 per cent as interim manager (14 wins in 19 games) to 51.7 per cent having been appointed on a permanent basis (77 out of 149).

Carrick had three games as caretaker boss after Solskjaer's departure, wins over Villarreal and Arsenal and a draw with Chelsea. These matches are not counted towards his record as permanent manager.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News reporter Adam Binnie looks at Mauricio Pochettino's spell at Chelsea, examining the challenges he faced and what Manchester United could look like under the Argentine

Ferguson's shadow

Since the retirement in 2013 of Ferguson, who won 26 major trophies in 27 years at Old Trafford and had a 59.7 per cent win ratio, United have struggled to find a long-term figurehead.

Ferguson took charge of 1,500 games with United. In 731 games since he retired in 2013, Carrick was the club's seventh permanent manager in addition to interim boss Ralf Rangnick and caretakers Ryan Giggs, Carrick himself, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher.

Jose Mourinho has the best win percentage of those permanent managers, with 58.3 per cent, 84 out of 144 games.

Mourinho also won the most trophies of any manager since Ferguson, with a League Cup and Europa League double in 2016-17 having opened that season with the Community Shield.

Erik ten Hag won both domestic cups, Louis van Gaal lifted an FA Cup and David Moyes another Community Shield.

Timeline: INEOS' time in charge at Man Utd so far

December 2023: Sir Jim Ratcliffe's deal to purchase a stake in United is announced.

January 2024: United appoint Omar Berrada from rivals Manchester City as their new chief executive. The move was made by Ratcliffe in consultation with Joel and Avram Glazer but INEOS were the driving force behind the move.

February 2024: Ratcliffe completes deal to acquire 27.7 per cent stake in Manchester United, which gives his company, INEOS, control of football operations.

April 2024: INEOS and Ratcliffe shake-up continued as United appoint Jason Wilcox as technical director after less than a year as director of football at Southampton, which was his first executive role in senior football.

Image: Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Omar Berrada (centre) and Jason Wilcox

July 2024: Man Utd agree deal with Newcastle United to appoint Dan Ashworth as sporting director after a lengthy period of gardening leave.

July 2024: Erik ten Hag is handed a one-year contract extension after winning the FA Cup by beating Manchester City 2-1 in the final. He is backed with the signings of Matthijs De Ligt, Noussair Mazraoui, Joshua Zirkzee, Manuel Ugarte and Leny Yoro.

July 2024: Christopher Vivell is hired as director of global talent on a temporary basis.

October 2024: United sack manager Ten Hag after winning just four of their 14 games to start the 2024/25 season. United in 14th and Ruud van Nistelrooy appointed as interim boss.

November 2024: Ruben Amorim is confirmed as the club's new head coach, signing a contract until June 2027. United paid £9.2m to release him from Sporting.

December 2024: Ashworth leaves his role as sporting director after just five months. He oversaw a £200m spend in the transfer market.

December 2024: Wilcox steps into Ashworth's role as sporting director.

February 2025: Vivell is appointed as permanent director of recruitment.

June 2025: Wilcox is promoted to director of football after Sir Dave Brailsford ends association with the club. He is tasked with overseeing football operations, including recruitment.

January 5 2026: Amorim is sacked after 14 months in charge after winning only 24 of his 63 games in charge. Darren Fletcher is appointed as interim boss.

January 13 2026: Michael Carrick is appointed as head coach until the end of the 2025/26 season.

May 2026: After securing Champions League football and winning 12 of his 17 games in charge, Carrick is rewarded with a two-year deal at Old Trafford.

November 12 2026: Carrick leaves United following a draw with Aston Villa, which left the club in the Premier League relegation zone after 10 games.

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United head coach, so how did his Old Trafford reign go so wrong, so quickly?

The former midfielder guided United to a Champions League finish last season but after their worst start to a season in 40 years, they are in the Premier League relegation zone at the start of November.

United salvaged a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa in Carrick's final game in charge, but they have only won once in 10 Premier League fixtures so far despite finishing last term on a high, with former Spurs and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino set to take over.

Sports.title: Kane the hero on historic night as England book Nations League QF spot
Sports.content:
Record-breaker Harry Kane scored from the spot to seal England's place in the Nations League quarter-finals with a 2-1 victory over Croatia, capping a memorable Wembley night as the captain became his country's most-capped player.

There was an inevitability about Kane hitting the net on his 126th appearance. There had been pre-match tributes and accolades as the Ballon d'Or holder passed the mark of legendary goalkeeper Peter Shilton and once again Kane was England's match winner with his second-half spot-kick. That's 92 goals now in England colours for the record scorer.

The win means England will now have the chance to win Nations League Group A3 and be seeded for the quarter-finals - but they will have to be far better than this if they are to beat table-toppers and world champions Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

When are the Nations League quarter-finals? The Nations League quarter-finals will take place in March, with the top two from each League A group going into the draw.



Teams which finish top of their group will be seeded and drawn against teams which have finished second for the two-leg ties which will determine who make it into the Nations League finals in June.

England thumped Croatia 7-0 last month but this was a performance far shy of that previous display, lacking intensity and final-third spark for long periods, and littered with jittery moments at the back.

Thankfully for Thomas Tuchel, he has Kane. The captain orchestrated the opener in his trademark style, dropping deep before clipping a fine pass for Jude Bellingham to cross for Morgan Rogers to bundle in when Josko Gvardiol failed to clear.

Image: England's Morgan Rogers scores a goal against Croatia

But moments after Kane's Bayern Munich team-mate Josip Stansic made a key block on the England skipper, Jarell Quansah's blunder gave Croatia a gift. His header back to Jordan Pickford was too casual and pounced on by Petar Sucic.

Quansah almost immediately made amends, being hauled down from an England corner by Ivan Smolcic for Kane to have his big moment.

But still England couldn't go up through the gears. James Garner's celebrations were cut short by an offside flag but the final stages were nervy for the hosts, with Nikola Vlasic wastefully clipping wide and Ante Budimir heading over.

On Kane's historic night, England were again indebted to their captain fantastic.

Image: Harry Kane scores a penalty against Croatia

Pre-match tributes for record-breaker Kane

Image: Harry Kane proudly shows off his Ballon d'Or to the Wembley crowd

Image: England fans showed off a Harry Kane tifo before kick-off

Image: Harry Kane poses with the Prince of Wales

Image: Harry Kane is presented with an award by Peter Shilton, whose record for England appearances he surpassed

Tuchel defends performance despite 'sloppy' moments

England head coach Thomas Tuchel:

"It was an okay performance overall. It took us a while to figure the press out because they played in a back five. It needed a lot of communication because we wanted to stay in our structure.

"Once we figured that out after 15 minutes we were the better team. You felt the confidence coming. We got a bit sloppy in the last five minutes of the first half. Good reaction at the start of the second half. Created more and more.

"We got again sloppy for five minutes and were punished from a set-piece which is uncharacteristic from us. Then we needed to show a reaction because we were desperate for a result.

"Croatia had nothing to lose and you have to overcome these moments."

Kane on 'incredible' night

England captain Harry Kane:

"It was incredible. Everything was amazing. Thank you to everyone who organised [the build-up], with the tifo and presentations. Thank you to Luka [Modric] and Croatia for their gift.

"I knew there would be something before the game. It's been a crazy few weeks with a lot happening, but it's an important moment in our history as a national team.

"But once the game started it was full focus. These occasions feel much better when you win and now I can take a breath and enjoy this."

As it happened at Wembley...

15: CLOSE! Elliot Anderson goes close to his first England goal with a decent snapshot from 20 yards.

18: BLOCK! A Bellingham cross is cleared as far as Trent Alexander-Arnold, who strikes it well but into the body of Josip Misic.

24: GOAL! Kane's fine pass into the box finds Bellingham to volley a cross for Rogers to bundle in.

48: WIDE! Anthony Gordon takes aim but doesn't get the bend on his shot he'd like and it flies well wide.

51: BIG BLOCK! Kane is denied a goal when his Bayern Munich team-mate Stanisic gets in the way as the England captain tries to turn in Declan Rice's cutback.

55: PENALTY APPEALS! But there's deemed to be no foul when Gordon is bundled over by Misic before Bellingham hits the target with a follow-up shot.

59: GOAL! Quansah tries to head the ball back to Jordan Pickford from a Croatia corner but Sucic is there to pounce and poke in. A bad mistake from the England centre-back!

63: PENALTY TO ENGLAND! After a VAR check referee Morten Krogh awards England a penalty for Quansah being pulled down from an England corner by Smolcic.

64: GOAL! Record-breaker Kane scores from the spot for England goal number 92.

82: BIG CHANCE! But Vlasic clips his shot wide when he looked set to equalise.

86: NO GOAL! Garner is denied his first England goal by the offside flag.

88: BLOCK! Quansah slides in to block Budimir's shot.

90+2: CHANCE! But Budimir heads over from a late corner.

Analysis: An historic night for Kane - but forgettable performance from England

Sky Sports News' Rob Dorsett at Wembley Stadium:

"As a game, it was instantly forgettable. As an occasion, it will live long in the memory. But that is all about what happened pre-match, rather than during the 90 minutes.

"Captain Kane being recognised as not only the best player in the world, but also as England's most capped player of all time, was a proper "I was there" moment. Inevitably, he scored to mark the occasion, with a coolly-slotted second-half penalty.

"But beyond that, England were disappointing. Flat. Lifeless, in the main. Lacking energy, spark and invention. The two full-backs, Alexander-Arnold and Hall, came out of it with some credit. And Elliot Anderson was as industrious and effective as ever. But that was about it.

"It was enough to ensure a victory - just about - and to set up a winner-takes-all Nations League group finale against the world champions Spain in Madrid on Sunday. Maybe England's players had that game in the back of their minds, and held back a bit. Let's hope that's what it was, anyway."

Sports.title: Harry Kane spot on to seal England win over Croatia on his record-breaking night
Sports.content:
It was an historic occasion for Harry Kane, the one when he made his 126th England appearance and overtook Peter Shilton as the nation’s most capped men’s player. And for much of the night, it felt as though the desire to celebrate him, certainly beforehand, was the main thing. The actual football in this Nations League group game felt like a sideshow.

England had demolished Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka last month; it was Croatia’s heaviest defeat. It was a different story here. England lacked cut and thrust. There was a flatness to the Wembley atmosphere. Croatia were never likely to be humbled again and they sensed redemption when Petar Sucic capitalised upon a defensive aberration from Jarell Quansah to equalise for 1-1 just before the hour.

It was at that point that Kane got a hold of the script. It was supposed to be his night during the 90 minutes, wasn’t it? There was a tussle on an England corner inside the Croatia area, Quansah feeling Ivan Smolcic tug at his shirt and when he went down, it felt as though the video assistant would be interested. He was, deciding that it added up to a penalty – and not that Quansah went to ground too easily.

It was over to Kane from the spot. There was the familiar stutter and the conversion was clipped up the middle, narrowly avoiding the trailing leg of the goalkeeper, Dominik Livakovic. It was Kane’s 92nd England goal; his 27th successful penalty.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane celebrates after restoring England’s lead. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Croatia fought until the end and they had a clutch of late chances, none better than when Nikola Vlasic took a touch and shot just wide in the 82nd minute. England were good value for the result. They are guaranteed a place in the quarter-finals of this competition in March and will go to Madrid to play Spain on Sunday with a shot at winning the group. They would have to beat the world champions to do that. And, really, play better than this.

Kane had walked out for kick-off with his four children and there was a lot for him – and them – to take in before a ball was kicked. First of all, there was the giant tifo behind one of the goals, which acclaimed Kane as “England’s finest”. Then, after he had hoisted aloft his Ballon d’Or trophy, there were presentations from Shilton, Luka Modric and Prince William. The gifts they bore, respectively, were a small trinket, a replica of the first football brought to Croatia in 1880 and a commemorative, framed Kane shirt.

View image in fullscreen A tifo in tribute to Harry Kane towers above a stand as the players take to the pitch. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane poses with Prince William and his commemorative shirt. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

It was quickfire. Rarely has so much been handed out so swiftly. Somewhat inevitably, there was a hangover when the game got under way. Was the show not already over? The Wembley crowded slumbered. Thomas Tuchel always wants intensity at the outset. It was not there.

Kane was involved in the breakthrough goal midway through the first-half, floating a lovely diagonal out to Jude Bellingham on the right-hand side of the Croatia area. Bellingham volleyed over first-time and what followed was a personal disaster for Josko Gvardiol. He got his feet into a tangle and allowed the ball to get to Morgan Rogers, who reached back and slashed it down and in from close-range.

Tuchel’s most eye-catching selection was to start Trent Alexander-Arnold over Ben White at right-back and the Real Madrid player got into advanced positions. He played some good balls. He wanted to quicken the collective pulse. As did Bellingham with those surges. It was all rather room temperature in the first half; England in control but not an awful lot happening.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Croatia goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic is unable to prevent Morgan Rogers from giving England the lead. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Kane dropped deep. He wanted to spark England’s moves. He even took throw-ins. Rogers, who Tuchel played on the right wing, had the license to get into central attacking areas. Alexander-Arnold pushed high; sometimes as far as the centre-forward position.

Kane went close at the start of the second-half, seeing a close-range shot blocked and Bellingham did not get hold of a drive after Anthony Gordon had tried to buy a penalty with an obvious dive.

England were sleepwalking. It felt as though complacency set in. Elliot Anderson played a couple of loose passes. Lewis Hall needed to win a one-versus-one against Igor Matanovic, conceding a corner. From it, England got their wake-up call. Gvardiol challenged for the high ball and when it broke, Quansah tried to head back for Jordan Pickford; a high-risk move. He did not see Sucic, who stretched out a leg to touch home.

Enter Kane. The closing stages were notable for the booing of White when he came on to replace Alexander-Arnold and Croatia threatening a second equaliser. Quansah redeemed himself with a saving tackle on the substitute, Ante Budimir. At the other end, James Garner, on as a substitute, had the ball in the net only for Bellingham to be flagged offside. For England, it is on to the showdown with Spain.

Sports.title: Fitness, Fernandes and a back four: how next head coach can reignite Manchester United | Will Unwin
Sports.content:
Improve internal discipline

One of the final images of Michael Carrick’s time in charge will be of him standing in the rain on the Old Trafford touchline watching his side succumb to Bournemouth, while his sullen captain sat unused on the bench. Bruno Fernandes was dropped after calling out his head coach’s tactics, although Carrick said it was for football reasons. It was the second combustible television interview in as many Champions League games after Lisandro Martínez pointed the finger at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, for failing to provide a squad suitable for fighting on all fronts.

Fernandes was soon back in the fold, and Martínez apologised for his outburst, but it is clear internal discipline is an issue and will be central to getting the team back on track. United will always draw more attention than almost any other club in the world and creating a circus around a failing team merely complicates matters when there are already enough problems to sort out on the pitch. The players need to harness their anger to ensure they create headlines for performances, not interviews.

View image in fullscreen Bruno Fernandes (centre) was left on the bench against Bournemouth, reportedly for tactical reasons. Photograph: Gary Oakley/EPA

Work out the best back four

One player Jason Wilcox could claim as a recruitment success was Senne Lammens but the goalkeeper’s form has joined that of his teammates in the gutter. The Belgian endured a horror show for Bournemouth’s third goal when he rushed out of his area, and he made two errors in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa. Leny Yoro was another to make a terrible mistake against Bournemouth, while Diogo Dalot’s efforts as a makeshift left-back can be categorised as somewhere between woeful and inept. No team in Europe’s top five leagues have conceded more than United’s 30 in all competitions, which is clearly a worry.

Morale is at rock bottom but the chopping and changing in defence is creating more uncertainty. The new head coach should pick a back four and stick with it where possible. If Harry Maguire’s experience is deemed mandatory, he needs pace around him to make up for what he lacks. Luke Shaw’s absence has created a left-back tombola as Dalot, Ayden Heaven and Noussair Mazraoui have been placed there.

View image in fullscreen Leny Yoro is among the United defenders to have made costly errors. Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP

Settle on a central focal point

Benjamin Sesko’s injury has cost United a No 9 for most of the season and Joshua Zirkzee has rarely been trusted in the role. Matheus Cunha gave it a go as a false 9 and Bryan Mbeumo was tried as a more traditional centre-forward but without much success either. Cunha has become more productive in a deeper role behind the striker, cutting in from the left as he did at Wolves, but United require someone to be a classic No 9, someone who can occupy defenders and be serviced by deliveries from wide. Zirkzee, for his faults, has been a presence when used in recent weeks and scored against Aston Villa. If a new coach can rebuild his confidence, the Dutchman could provide a short-term solution. Alternatively, greater demands should be made of Marcus Rashford to play through the middle.

View image in fullscreen An option up top? Marcus Rashford could fill in for the injured Benjamin Sesko. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA

Put pressure on the hierarchy

A mix-and-match of expletives were aimed at those above Carrick at recent home games. Wilcox has taken most of the individual criticism, but the ownership were told in no uncertain terms to sell up. The Glazers have been instrumental in driving the club downwards in recent years and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s investment and involvement in football operations have yielded little success.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen From left to right: Sir Jim Ratcliffe; Manchester United chief executive, Omar Berrada; and director of football, Jason Wilcox. Photograph: Jacob King/PA

Carrick was the face of the operation, as the new head coach will be, and he needs to put pressure on someone at the top to speak to the media to explain why the club is in such a mess because it is unfair to expect the coach to do so. United fans know the person in the dugout cannot take all the blame and someone else has to be publicly accountable.

Make demands on signings

Three central midfielders and a backup goalkeeper did not make for an inspiring summer when everyone knew United’s squad required improvement in numerous positions. Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba and Youri Tielemans started together against Bournemouth and offered no evidence for why so much was spent on them.

Whoever comes in needs to be clear about what is required, whether in the winter or summer windows, because the deficiencies in the squad mean United cannot compete on all fronts and are struggling to cope with the rigours of the Premier League. A new left-back and striker are a given, but there is plenty more work to be done.

View image in fullscreen Andrey Santos has struggled to prove his worth since joining from Chelsea for £50m in July. Photograph: Conor Molloy/ProSports/Shutterstock

Create fast starts

Outrunning the opposition does not guarantee success but United have looked pedestrian on far too many occasions this season. This could explain the number of slow starts to games in recent times: in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid and Como they conceded in the first and second minute respectively, and were two down at home to Roma after 17 minutes last week. Worse still, Aston Villa, aided by errors, were two goals ahead within four minutes at Old Trafford, giving United a monumental task to turn things around. The players deserve credit for finding some fight to do so but need to make life easier for themselves because it does not take a genius to work out starting with a deficit is ill-advised. They will face a fiery atmosphere at Anfield, and that will be a fine place to show a shift in dynamic.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers says ‘it’s a lie’ that Cole Palmer does not want to play for England
Sports.content:
Morgan Rogers has said accusations that his Chelsea teammate Cole Palmer is not committed to playing for England are “a lie”.

Palmer, who was left out of the squad for this week’s Nations League ties against Croatia and Spain, has faced questions over his desire to play international football since withdrawing from last month’s camp with a groin injury. Thomas Tuchel, who did not take the 24-year-old to last summer’s World Cup, expressed irritation at the time, saying the Chelsea attacker “misses too many opportunities” to play for his country.

Tuchel last week insisted Palmer’s latest exclusion was “not personal” but he has placed plenty of store in players showing up to camp. The German has previously said it was “hard to argue” when it was put to him that Palmer does not want to play for the national team after his fourth withdrawal from a squad. But Rogers, who scored in England’s 2-1 win over Croatia on Thursday, delivered a strong rebuttal to claims his friend and teammate is not dedicated to the national team.

“It’s a lie,” Rogers said. “He wants to be here. He wanted to get called up and he wanted to come and represent his country as he always has done. People just see it as news and say the easy thing.

“We all know he had a difficult year last year with injuries and I know personally he’s been managing them injuries ever since. He was in quite a low place with his injuries last year and didn’t feel 100% himself on the pitch, so he wants to be here and he wants to be the best version of himself. Of course he does, who wouldn’t? But he also has to look at his body. He wants to play for 10 to 15 years, he also has to manage himself.

“If he has to manage himself in the short term for the greater good then he has to do that and you have to fully support it. It has nothing to do with England or not wanting to play with England. It’s a nonsense really that people are questioning someone that wants to play for England. You see the joy and smile on his face, how much he loves the game, so I honestly don’t get it and he doesn’t get it. But it’s something he has to deal with but I can assure you he wants to be here and he wants to play for his country.”

Tuchel had no issue with Rogers’s defence of Palmer. “It’s totally fine, it’s his teammate and friend,” England’s manager said. “I was very happy with the emotional commitment and physical commitment of Morgan. He was our standout player today.”

Tuchel is not short of options at No 10 and has selected Eberechi Eze, Rogers and Josh King as cover for Jude Bellingham. Rogers played on the right against Croatia and opened the scoring as England secured the win that secured England’s place in the Nations League quarter-finals next March.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

England were pegged back by Petar Sucic’s equaliser but they restored their lead thanks to Harry Kane converting a penalty on the night when the captain became his country’s most capped player. Tuchel’s side will win Group A3 if they beat Spain in Madrid on Sunday. But the occasion was slightly overshadowed by Ben White being booed when he came on in the second half. Some fans are yet to forgive White for his self-imposed exile after his early departure from the camp at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

“I didn’t hear the boos,” Tuchel said. “I thought we were past it. I hope it doesn’t happen again. He is a player for us. Since I came in he is desperate to be in the group. He hasn’t put a foot wrong since I am in charge. He is part of our group and I will protect our group. He deserved to be with us and I hope to open a new chapter for him.”

Sports.title: Nations League: Italy roar back to beat France despite Donnarumma’s early howler
Sports.content:
Pio Esposito struck twice to inflict a first defeat on Zinedine Zidane as France head coach as Italy stormed back to win 3-1 at San Siro and go top of their Nations League group.

Michael Olise profited on a Gianluigi Donnarumma error to put the visitors in front after 10 minutes, but Italy hit back through Esposito and Davide Frattesi either side of half-time.

Inter striker Esposito’s second came from the penalty spot after his brother Sebastiano had earlier fired a spot-kick wide, while France were twice denied by the woodwork in an entertaining encounter.

The result sent Italy top of Group A1 on 10 points, level with France but above them on head-to-head record, while Belgium are third on nine points after inflicting a fifth straight defeat on rock-bottom Turkey.

France were without Kylian Mbappé and Ousmane Dembélé through injury, but it did not show as they made an electric start under pouring rain in Milan. Désiré Doué hit the side netting and first-time captain Adrien Rabiot tested Donnarumma before Lucas Da Cunha’s rasping half-volley flew narrowly wide.

However, the opener was gifted to France when Donnarumma passed the ball straight to Olise, who skipped past a defender before firing home his fifth goal in five Nations League games – a record only bettered by England captain Harry Kane’s seven.

The hosts struck back in the 26th minute with their first chance of the game when Nicolò Cambiaghi drove to the byline and cut back a cross, which Esposito converted with a deft touch. The goal brought San Siro to life as the older Esposito sibling, Sebastiano, threatened a quickfire comeback two minutes later when he forced a sharp save from Mike Maignan.

Bradley Barcola came closest to a third goal before the break with a curling shot from the edge of the box that struck the foot of the far post.

The end-to-end nature of the game continued in the second half as Rayan Cherki’s rasping strike was tipped on to a post by Donnarumma before Italy charged up the other end and forced Maignan into a point-blank save from Cambiaghi. Italy had a glorious chance to go in front when Cambiaghi was tripped by Malo Gusto to earn a penalty, but Sebastiano Esposito failed to join his brother on the scoresheet as he hammered his spot-kick wide on the hour mark.

The Azzurri did not dwell on the disappointment for long, taking the lead just three minutes later when Frattesi drilled in a shot from a Federico Dimarco cross moments after the Inter wing-back was brought off the bench. Fellow substitute Antonio Vergara earned the home side another penalty when he was tripped by Dayot Upamecano, and this time Pio Esposito stepped up to drill a shot into the bottom corner.

The result continued a strong start to Roberto Mancini’s second spell as Italy coach as his side stretched their unbeaten run to four matches and notched their first home win over France since 1962.

Belgium are third after Kevin De Bruyne scored in their 2-1 triumph in Turkey.

During a goal-frenzied first half at Gursel Aksel Stadium, Arda Güler put Turkey ahead with a stunning free-kick from 25 yards out before De Bruyne levelled seven minutes after a cutback from Jérémy Doku. Charles De Ketelaere fired in after Diego Moreira’s shot was saved to earn Belgium all three points.

Belgium host Italy and Turkey travel to France in the final round of group games on Sunday.

View image in fullscreen Charles De Ketelaere jumps for joy after scoring Belgium’s winning goal. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters

Álex Baena scored from the spot and Marc Pubill added another seconds from time as Spain beat 10-man Czechia 2-0 in Group A3. The win in Prague leaves Spain unbeaten for 44 competitive games, including five wins in as many Nations League games this season.

Spain, who already secured a quarter-final berth before travelling to Prague, will face England in Madrid on Sunday in their final Group A3 game.

Baena scored on 39 minutes after a VAR check revealed Czechia midfielder Lukas Ambros had handled the ball inside the box. The Atlético Madrid winger blasted his spot-kick past Matej Kovar who touched the ball but failed to clear it.

Home captain Ladislav Krejci was sent off in the 69th minute after bringing down second-half substitute Roberto Fernández on a counterattack. Pubill, another substitute, beat Kovar with a low shot deep into stoppage time after the Czechia back four left him alone facing the Eindhoven goalkeeper.

Luis de la Fuente missed Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo, Rodri and Eric García with injuries while Mikel Oyarzabal was sidelined with flu.

Fabián Ruiz hit a post with a curling right-footer three minutes from half-time, while Dean Huijsen’s header found Kovar’s arms.

View image in fullscreen Marc Pubill makes Spain’s victory safe in the dying moments against Czechia. Photograph: Michal Čížek/AFP/Getty Images

Yéremy Pino, replacing Yamal on the right flank, saw his goal overturned by VAR for offside just two minutes into the second half.

Czechia showed higher spirits after the break, but David Zima put an effort over on 50 minutes and Adam Hlozek’s glancing header landed on the top of the crossbar.

The hosts lost momentum after the red card, but Baena had two efforts cleared by Kovar who also denied Fernández from close range.

The hosts, led by De la Fuente’s long-time collaborator Santi Denia, have lost all their Nations League games this season. They are next travelling to Croatia for a game they need to win to stay in the top tier of the competititon for the next edition.

Sports.title: Arsenal dig deep to earn WCL draw in face of Barcelona dominance
Sports.content:
Arsenal continue to be a sharp thorn in the side of the European champions, Barcelona, and they dug deep to hold on to a draw at the Camp Nou on Thursday night. Frida Maanum put the Gunners ahead despite a hugely dominant performance from Barcelona, but Caroline Graham Hansen’s equaliser ensured the spoils would be shared.

Barcelona have been formidable when playing at the club’s main stadium, winning nine and drawing twice, against Chelsea in the semi-finals in 2023 and now Arsenal.

“Grit, resilience, discipline, clarity, communication, leadership, bravery – that’s a lot of words,” said Renée Slegers. “There’s a lot of really good things in this performance that we definitely want to build on.”

The last time these two teams met, Arsenal lifted the Champions League trophy at Barcelona’s expense after the most perfect defensive performance and a Stina Blackstenius goal in Lisbon in 2025. It was a far less perfect defensive performance this time but Arsenal showed the guts they have been missing at times this season, against the team that retook their crown last season, and showed they can play ugly when needed.

There was one change to the team that earned a 2-1 win against Liverpool on Sunday, but it was a significant one. Olivia Smith was replaced by Maanum and the Norwegian slotted into the No 10 role with Alessia Russo, who has scored 12 goals in nine games for club and country, moving into the centre-forward position.

It was the England forward’s play on the left that set up the shock first-half goal that temporarily silenced the crowd. She beat two and worked the ball to Maanum. Barcelona got the ball away but Russo was there again and delivered a perfect cross across the face of goal for Caitlin Foord. The Australian forced a close-range save from Cata Coll only for Maanum to power in the loose ball.

The pocket of travelling fans behind plexiglass in the upper tier were jubilant. About 1,000 had travelled despite the late switch of the match to Thursday due to a 24-hour general strike in Spain on Wednesday.

Quick Guide Benfica bounce back to see off Austria Vienna Show Benfica rebounded from their humbling defeat by Arsenal last time out to claim a second Women’s Champions League victory of the season by seeing off struggling Austria Vienna 3-1. Beaten 3-0 at Meadow Park a fortnight ago following Alessia Russo’s hat-trick, Benfica had the ideal opportunity to get back to winning ways against a Vienna side who had picked up one point in three games. They went ahead at Lisbon’s Estadio da Luz through Andreia Norton in the fifth minute before Carina Wenninger levelled after half-time when Valentina Potzl was upended in the area by Lena Pauels. But Vienna goalkeeper Jasmin Pal’s 73rd-minute red card proved a turning point as Caroline Møller headed home before she teed up Nycole Raysla to score in time added on. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

The goal came decidedly against the run of play but Barcelona struggled to capitalise on their first-half dominance. Ewa Pajor and Graham Hansen were particularly threatening as Barcelona targeted Arsenal’s left, made up of the less experienced Taylor Hinds and Lisa Baum.

The scoreline at the break was a little unfathomable based on the run of play and the domestic fortunes of both sides. While Arsenal languish in sixth in the WSL, 12 points behind the league leaders, Manchester City, Barcelona have won nine of their 10 games in Liga F, having scored 41 goals and built a five-point lead over their nearest rivals, Real Madrid.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal’s Alessia Russo shows her dismay after a missed chance. Photograph: Álex Caparrós/Uefa/Getty Images

Arsenal’s gameplan felt familiar. It was as if they had studied the blueprint religiously followed by teams that have sat back in a low block and frustrated them week-in, week-out in the WSL this season.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Aitana Bonmatí, the three-time Ballon d’Or winner, was surprisingly relegated to the bench but her arrival shortly before the hour elevated Barcelona’s threat, causing Arsenal’s defending to look even more calamitous at times, and lifted the mood in a frustrated stadium.

Three minutes after her arrival they were level. Esmee Brugts found an unmarked Graham Hansen on the right and she cut inside and swept in past Misa Rodríguez.

It was no surprise that Baum and Hinds, who had been run ragged, were removed soon after, with former Barcelona player Ona Batlle and Smith, Arsenal’s record signing, replacing them.

Arsenal were better after the goal and the changes, occasionally breaking free of their prison of a final third. At the end they were clinging on, but cling on they did.

“If we were to do it again, we’d try to stay on the ball for longer and play our game even more,” said Slegers. “Definitely there were moments in the first half and in the second half where we were really, really dangerous and created big chances, open chances. I’m just really pleased with the way we played the game tonight because it’s a very different game to what we usually play and that we can do it this way is a big boost for us as a team and that’s what we’re going to take with us going forward.”

Sports.title: Pierre Sage’s failure to fix defensive flaws leaves Crystal Palace seeking new solution
Sports.content:
The moment that summed up Crystal Palace’s season under Pierre Sage came five minutes before half-time at Selhurst Park on Sunday. After Palace had gone close to taking the lead on numerous occasions against Liverpool, the Frenchman must have feared the worst when Alexis Mac Allister headed in from a soft free-kick conceded by Jefferson Lerma. The TV cameras immediately panned to Steve Parish in the stands. After the Palace chair removed his hands from in front of his eyes, his expression said everything you needed to know. The only surprise was that Sage had to wait until Thursday before his inevitable fate was confirmed.

Not since the start of the 2017-18 season, after Frank de Boer was appointed as Palace’s first permanent foreign manager and sacked after five matches, have the club found themselves bottom. In their record 14th consecutive season in the top flight, and with preliminary work having started on building a new £200m main stand despite major doubts over funding, Palace cannot afford to be relegated.

Sage has been walking a tightrope since the 5-0 thrashing at Brighton last month when it was made clear to the 47-year-old that he must tighten a defence that had conceded the most goals in the Premier League. Some players are thought to have questioned his training methods, although Dean Henderson, the captain, was among those believed to have pledged their support for Sage after defeats by Newcastle and Tottenham.

There was some evidence Palace’s players were adapting to his desire to play more on the front foot rather than relying on the counterattacking approach that brought his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, so much success. But they have been far too open at the back and Liverpool’s second goal from Florian Wirtz was almost a copy of Hoffenheim’s in Thursday’s 1-1 Europa League draw, when Palace were extremely fortunate to snatch a point in a game Parish did not attend because he was in New York.

Palace have conceded eight goals from set plays in the Premier League, including four in their current run of four straight defeats. Fixing a problem that dates back to Glasner’s spell has to be the priority for Thomas Frank, who looks poised to take over. The Dane met with Palace in the summer but decided he wasn’t ready to return after a difficult spell at Spurs. He is now believed to be very keen for a new challenge and offers proven Premier League experience - a prerequisite for Parish after Sage. Sean Dyche also had his supporters among the Palace hierarchy. The former sporting director Iain Moody, an influential consultant for Palace who was heavily involved in Sage’s appointment after Sage’s success at Lens last season, worked with the former Nottingham Forest manager at Watford and was thought to favour him.

Frank has played with a back three – a consideration that was a major factor in Palace opting for Sage in an attempt to provide continuity from Glasner – more often than Dyche. Palace could benefit, though, from a change of formation, in the short term at least, given the lack of experienced options owing to the long-term absences of Chadi Riad and Takehiro Tomiyasu.

Palace were rescued from the relegation zone by Sam Allardyce in the 2016-17 season and Parish went back to basics again with Roy Hodgson after De Boer’s disastrous spell, and the team finished 11th despite losing their first seven games. That was without the added complication of European football, however.

View image in fullscreen Pierre Sage’s suggestion that Crystal Palace had to invest in the winter transfer window is not believed to have gone down well with Steve Parish (front). Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/Shutterstock

Palace signed 11 players in the summer and Sage’s suggestion after the Liverpool game that adjustments may be needed in “some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions” is not believed to have gone down well with Parish. Last month, the 61-year-old hired the Raine Group to field interest in investment or a possible sale of the club he helped to rescue from administration in 2010. His American billionaire co-owners Woody Johnson, David Blitzer and Josh Harris are understood to have reservations about funding the new stand.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Parish is said to view the squad as too good to be in this position, although Palace failed to adequately replace the key defenders Maxence Lacroix and Marc Guéhi this year, bringing in Tomiyasu on a free and Axel Disasi and the 18-year-old Honest Ahanor on loan. It is telling that Coventry and Hull – Palace’s next two opponents after the international break – have a higher net spend over the past five years despite being in the Championship until this season. Palace broke their transfer record twice last January and providing mid-season funds will be essential.

Much of the blame for the summer’s haphazard recruitment has been pinned on Matt Hobbs, the sporting director brought in from Wolves to replace the influential Dougie Freedman, who moved to Saudi Arabia in spring 2025. Freedman is said still to be a sounding board over transfers and there have been questions over the influence of the agents Unique Sports Group given the large number of players it has, or has had, on Palace’s books, but it is Parish who calls the shots despite owning less than 10% of the shares. His next move will be crucial to their hopes of avoiding relegation.

Sports.title: Robertson pays tribute to Dalglish as he matches Scotland cap record
Sports.content:
Andy Robertson insists his matching of Kenny Dalglish’s Scotland cap record by no means brings reputational parity. Four decades after Dalglish, widely regarded as the country’s finest player, ended his international run at 102 games Robertson will hit the same figure with the visit of North Macedonia to Hampden Park on Friday.

The Tottenham full-back is understandably delighted by his own tally – and should surpass Dalglish in Switzerland on Monday – but paid glowing tribute to the man he got to know well during nine years at Liverpool.

“For how long the record stood, for starters, for what he achieved in his career, for the person he is,” Robertson said.

“Tomorrow is another reason for our country to honour one of the greatest players that has played a game. He’s definitely the greatest from Scotland. I think it’s another reason for everyone to speak about him and realise his achievements in his footballing career. And also the person that he has been throughout his whole life.

“Obviously, in terms of number, I will stand side by side with him but I don’t want people to forget how important this man has been to our country.”

The Liverpool connection between Robertson and Dalglish adds an endearing, personal element. “He reminds me all the time that getting into the 100 caps back then was a lot harder than it is now,” said Robertson with a smile. “I never set myself personal goals. For me it’s always about the team and how I best deal with the team and things like that.

“When I overtook Darren Fletcher, when I was in the 80s, it felt like it took ages for me to get to Jim Leighton [at 91]. Then I thought: ‘I’ve only got one more to go.’

That’s when I started thinking about it a little bit more, starting to believe that it might happen a little bit more, starting to wind-up Kenny a bit more that it was going to happen. Sat here today, if it happens, it’s something I couldn’t be more proud of.’’

Sébastien Pocognoli, the Scotland manager, has said the country is stepping up efforts to convince eligible players born in England to commit their international futures to Scotland. Archie Gray and Hayden Hackney are among those who qualify to play for Scotland but have, thus far, resisted overtures. In conjunction with others at the Scottish Football Association, Pocognoli would like that to change. Gray’s position as a club-mate of Robertson’s may be significant in this context.

“We are on it,” Pocognoli said. “We are always proactive in all of these situations. What is very exciting about those two names [Gray and Hackney] is that they are young players.

“That’s interesting. We have to look and manage the situation. But it won’t be a definitive choice from them because we weren’t proactive. That has to be clear. We are proactive.”

Sports.title: ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts
Sports.content:
Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

“I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”

For many years, says the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa launched its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

View image in fullscreen Claire Emslie on her return to football: ‘It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.’ Photograph: Elsa/NWSL/Getty Images

“I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” says Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

“Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”

Up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she says. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

“There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”

Some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she says. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”

View image in fullscreen Newcastle’s Emma Kelly became pregnant earlier this year. Photograph: Michelle Mercer/Newcastle United/Getty Images

Though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie says candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”

The other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she says bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

Even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an important fact.
