World.title: The rise and fall of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
World.content: Jensen Huang, who once led the most valuable company in the world, resigned from his post as Nvidia CEO today after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang had co-founded Nvidia in 1993, and it became a juggernaut making the chips underpinning much of the AI boom.Nov. 12, 2026

World.title: Howard Lutnick agrees to testify as bipartisan pressure grows over Nvidia scandal
World.content:
Earlier Thursday, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told reporters that Lutnick should appear voluntarily, though if he doesn’t, “He may need to be subpoenaed.”

Blumenthal said one thing he wants to know is, “Were export controls relaxed?”

Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., said in an interview with Fox News that he’d like Lutnick to testify before Congress “ASAP,” noting concerns about chips being exported that should not have.

“We have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns about what’s happened over the last year that would allow some of these issues to continue, to chips being exported, it appears, to defy President Trump’s orders for those exports to be stopped,” Banks said.

Huang’s extramarital activity has added to concerns that Nvidia chips may have been smuggled or illegally accessed by AI companies in China. Nvidia has said that it complies with U.S. laws on exports.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., told reporters on Capitol Hill Thursday that Lutnick “certainly should” testify before Congress.

“I think he should be given the opportunity and the strong encouragement to do it without a subpoena,” Cramer said. “If a subpoena becomes necessary, that would be too bad. But yes, he absolutely should.”

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement that Lutnick needs to “explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military.”

The White House has defended Lutnick, writing in a statement that the president “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.”

Huang has previously praised Lutnick’s role in uplifting the U.S. efforts to lead in AI.

“Howard is the person I talk to most in the administration — he’s on top of the technology and learning the industry quickly,” Huang said while appearing at a Nvidia panel alongside Lutnick in September 2025.

Reps. Gregory Meeks of New York, Gabe Amo of Rhode Island and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California — top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee — signed a letter Monday demanding answers from Lutnick over the Trump administration’s “approval of advanced AI chip exports,” noting “concerning links to China” and “alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties” to Huang.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., said Thursday that Huang had agreed to brief lawmakers, though the date and venue were still being negotiated. In a new letter to Huang on Thursday, Mast asked that he appear before the committee on Dec. 1 for a “closed-door, transcribed interview,” adding that a subpoena would be issued if Huang did not confirm the interview by Friday evening.

Some members of Congress said they want answers from Lutnick much sooner than next month, when the Senate Banking Committee has scheduled its hearings.

“Come here before Thanksgiving. Give us the facts,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said Thursday.

Tillis, who is leaving Congress in January, said it would be wise for Lutnick to testify to Congress now, before Democrats take control of both chambers next year, adding the secretary “should recognize right now he’s got a lot of Republicans that are pulling for him.”

“I’m not one of them, but he does,” Tillis said. “So it would seem to me that he would do himself a favor by getting in a room with Republicans, whether it’s a committee hearing or not, and lay out the facts so that he’s got a group of people that are generally going to take at face value what he says.”

World.title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for majority leader
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced Thursday he will run for Senate majority leader, becoming the first to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the position.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement.

Van Hollen’s move follows attempts by grassroots progressives — and some newly elected Democratic senators — to draft him for the position as some seek an alternative to Schumer.

“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader,” he added.

Schumer, who has led the Senate Democratic caucus since 2017, remains favored to retain the position of Democratic leader. Still, it’s likely to be the most serious challenge he has gotten for the job.

Democratic senators will hold a vote in December to choose their leadership for the next Congress. That vote is held behind closed doors and requires a simple majority of the caucus.

Van Hollen said in an interview with MS NOW Thursday night that more than 10 senators have pledged to support him.

“We have a lot of people, but here’s the thing about an election like this: As you say, I’m the underdog,” Van Hollen said. “I told people I was thinking about it, and so now we are opening up the process, right?”

He added, “Now people will have to make a decision, one way or the other, and they have to decide whether they want to vote for change or whether they want to vote for the status quo.”

Van Hollen plans to run on having the new Democratic majority use every available tool to end the Iran war, starting with the upcoming government funding measure to avoid a December shutdown, according to his team. He’s also proposing to reverse President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” get money out of politics and tackle corruption.

Van Hollen, 67, is newer to Congress than Schumer, 75, but both men have served in Congress for decades. Van Hollen was first elected to the Senate in 2016. Before that, he served in the House for over a decade, beginning in 2003. Schumer was first elected to the House in 1980 and moved up to the Senate in 1999.

Schumer responded on X to Van Hollen’s announcement, saying he has the votes to win.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” he said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Wednesday that he would support Van Hollen if he decided to launch an official bid for the leadership role. The day prior, Sanders had said he would not back Schumer, saying at a press conference that “in my view, the time is now for change.”

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan endorsed Van Hollen for the role shortly after his announcement Thursday night, writing in a post on X, “I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience.”

“We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” El-Sayed wrote, adding that to “earn our mandate,” Democrats “will require bold leadership.”

Still, Schumer has maintained support from longtime colleagues who point to his work as minority leader ahead of Democrats’ landslide midterm victories.

“Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, wrote in a statement on Thursday night. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

King wrote that Schumer “outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen.”

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., also urged Democrats not to turn their backs on Schumer earlier this week, saying that “no one has put in the time and effort that anyone has put into this cycle than he did.”

Gillibrand, who oversaw Senate Democrats’ campaign arm for the midterms, said Schumer ensured that resources were provided to help 100,000 new voters register in Mississippi, where Sen.-elect Scott Colom just captured a stunning victory.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done, and that’s why you will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position,” Gillibrand said.

World.title: Democrats can’t wait until after Trump to produce results, James Talarico says
World.content:
DENVER — Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico told a gathering of Democrats Thursday that voters are expecting them to immediately deliver, and that means making President Donald Trump’s last two years in office the “most productive of any presidency in American history.”

Talarico, who just made history by becoming the first Democrat elected senator in Texas since 1988, urged his party to put aside vitriol and distractions and immediately provide economic relief to Americans. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, but Trump will remain in the White House — and wield the veto pen — until 2029.

“The American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump,” Talarico said. “If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”

It was a reference to President Lyndon B. Johnson, who was from Texas.

Talarico spoke at the two-day What’s Next conference, an event organized by the group Majority Democrats, tapping into campaign themes he stressed on the trail. Then, Talarico said his goal wasn’t to turn all of Texas blue because he believes voters want a divided, but balanced, government. He also spoke against politicians who pit communities against one another, saying those in power wanted Americans to focus on the “wrong 1%,” instead of billionaires who were growing their wealth.

In his speech, Talarico noted his historic win and what he described as a Democratic mandate “the size of Texas,” but stressed the need to reach across the aisle, and down Pennsylvania Avenue, to deliver results, even if it means Trump takes some of the credit.

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history, because this moment is so much bigger and so much more important than the red team or blue team,” Talarico said. “It’s so much bigger than a party. We are tired of being pitted against each other. We’re tired of being told to hate each other. It’s been 10 years of this kind of politics.”

Whether Democrats deliver on an agenda and to what extent they focus on investigations of Republicans remains a central debate within the party. The White House has signaled it plans to fight attempts by Congress to investigate the administration.

Talarico has previously called not only for accountability for the Trump administration, but also for Democrats to work with Trump.

“It is not an either-or choice,” Talarico told NBC News earlier this month. “We need accountability and we need to deliver.”

Talarico swept into office after campaigning against corruption and framing himself as David versus Elon Musk, the Goliath, who single-handedly spent more than $168 million to support Talarico’s Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.

“We went up against the richest man in the world, and we won,” Talarico said at Thursday’s event.

World.title: Democrat Cindy Holscher defeats Republican Ty Masterson in Kansas governor’s race
World.content:
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher has narrowly won Kansas’ race for governor, NBC News projected Thursday, extending the party’s hold on the office in the red state.

Holscher defeated Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, who was backed by President Donald Trump, to succeed two-term Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.

While Trump carried Kansas — a state where registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats nearly 2 to 1 — by double digits in the latest three presidential elections, polling had shown a close race down the stretch due mostly to voter frustrations with Trump and his handling of the economy. Democrats also benefited from increased attention on the traditionally conservative state as its Senate race tightened.

Kansas Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher. Evert Nelson / The Capital-Journal / USA Today via Imagn

Holscher’s victory came despite a nearly 3-to-1 Republican ad spending advantage in the general election, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

In the general election, Holscher aggressively tied Masterson to Trump, while also maintaining that she’d find areas to work with the administration.

“I think that’s a concern that [Masterson] has the ear of the administration, because the administration also has a hold on him. You won’t see Ty Masterson pushing back against bad policy, like tariffs that are hurting our farmers or the importing of beef that are hurting our ranchers,” she told local news station KMBC in October. She added that will also “work with folks” in the administration “to make sure we bring good things to Kansas.”

Masterson, who was endorsed by Trump, attempted to distance himself from the president on his website and in campaign materials. But his connection to Trump, who faced increasingly lower approval ratings in the traditionally red state, was unmistakable: the president came to Kansas over the last weekend before Election Day to campaign alongside Masterson and the Republican candidate in the state’s Senate race, Sen. Roger Marshall, who lost his re-election bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty

Meanwhile, Holscher also prominently highlighted her opposition to new data center construction throughout her campaign.

“This field of Kansas sunflowers is under threat because big tech wants to build a day out of center. As governor, I’ll hit pause on data centers until we can set up firm guardrails to protect our communities and our budgets,” she said in one spot featuring her standing in a field.

Masterson has opposed a moratorium on data centers and has defended a 2025 law he voted for giving a sales tax exemption for data center investments. Holscher has called for a statewide moratorium on the new data center construction. Building the Future, a pro-data center super PAC, jumped into the race last month to boost Masterson.

Holscher’s win followed a primary that featured Democratic infighting. Kelly, who has maintained strong job approval ratings in the state, had endorsed Holscher’s Democratic primary opponent, state Sen. Ethan Corson, and issued stark warnings to voters about being “very concerned about the direction Kansas will go in” if Holscher were to win.

Holscher had run a more progressive-styled campaign, while Corson ran as a moderate. Kelly endorsed Holscher following the primary.

World.title: GOP lawmakers press Huang and Lutnick to testify over Nvidia
World.content:
Republicans on Capitol Hill are pressing now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear before Congress early next month about the scandal that has rocked one of the most important companies in the world — as a Senate panel asks Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.

"We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk," the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, Foreign Affairs Committee and Intelligence Committee said in a statement requesting Huang's presence.

The three committee chairs wrote a letter Thursday asking Huang to appear for a closed-door interview on Dec. 1. They said if he does not accept their request by Friday evening, the House Foreign Affairs Committee will issue a subpoena.

The upper chamber has also pushed Huang to appear. Republican Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, asked Huang to testify voluntarily before the panel in the first week of December, but warned the committee is prepared to use its subpoena power if needed.

"The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote on X.

Nvidia, whose chips have fueled the AI boom, announced on Thursday that Huang had stepped down following a scandal over his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang's resignation from the company he co-founded has not dampened calls from members of Congress for answers about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to highly prized chips that are banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.

Moments before Nvidia announced Huang's resignation, Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said on CNBC on Thursday morning that he would happily support subpoenaing Huang. A Cramer spokesperson said he would still support subpoenaing the tech founder.

The controversy has also raised questions about whether the federal government has done enough to prevent Nvidia's chips from being diverted to China — and about the Trump administration's close relationship with Huang.

Scott asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear for a public hearing next month. The House Foreign Affairs Committee also requested testimony from Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler, who leads the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency that oversees export controls.

Some critics have argued Lutnick's Commerce Department should have taken action to prevent Megaspeed from buying chips. The New York Times reported that a Bureau of Industry and Security probe into the firm was halted last year.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told CNN on Thursday he wanted to hear from both Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, saying: "This is serious as an aneurysm."

Earlier Thursday, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China, GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, said lawmakers were "in discussions" with Huang "on a date to come and meet with us." But he added, "If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power."

Moolenaar and two other chairs — Rep. Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rep. Rick Crawford of the Intelligence Committee — first asked Huang to appear in a letter last week. They said the purpose of the closed-door briefing would be to discuss Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset." The lawmakers gave Huang a deadline of Wednesday to respond.

Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Thursday that they received a response. Mast said Huang indicated he's willing to appear. Moolenaar said that Huang's resignation "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony.

"I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune also told CBS News that he expects "there'll be an interest in doing oversight" in the Senate. Asked whether he wants Huang to testify, Thune said, "I think that it would make sense because of the, again, the nature of the association and the governments and the national security interests, what we're talking about here."

Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said Democrats have questions for the Trump administration, too.

"Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer said on X. "The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset."

President Trump, a friend of Huang's, has downplayed the scandal and said he doesn't believe Huang knew the Megaspeed executive was a spy. The president said Thursday that Huang had done a "fantastic job."

"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place — TIM COOK of Apple," the president posted to Truth Social.

World.title: Van Hollen will challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader
World.content:
Washington — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.

"In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person – it's about answering that call," Van Hollen said in a post on X. "That's why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

The decision by Van Hollen, who said earlier this week he was in "listening mode" about running for majority leader, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership since it decisively won last week's midterms. Some Democrats have not committed to voting for Schumer in leadership elections, which are expected next month.

Van Hollen, 67, has been in the Senate since 2017 after representing the state in the House for more than a decade. The Maryland Democrat has gained attention from progressives in recent years. In 2024, he vocally supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticized the Biden administration's posture toward the war in Gaza. Van Hollen also gained attention when he traveled to El Salvador last year to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who lived in Maryland and had been sent to the country's notorious CECOT prison.

Supporters see Van Hollen as someone who's willing to speak to the issues progressives hold most dear. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told NPR in an interview this week that Van Hollen is "willing to take risks when it matters," citing his trip to El Salvador.

Schumer, 75, responded to Van Hollen's announcement in a post on X, saying he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead."

"I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," the New York Democrat said. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."

Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who chairs the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, defended Schumer's continued leadership at a news conference earlier this week, crediting his "strategic leadership."

"You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position," Gillibrand said. "We are about to win nine Senate seats — that has never happened in my political history."

The challenge comes as Schumer is still widely expected to hold on to the top leadership post, especially after the strong showing for Democrats in the midterm elections. Despite a Senate map that appeared unfavorable for the party heading into the cycle, Democrats flipped at least eight Senate seats — with one race remaining up in the air in Alaska — securing a sizable majority in the new Congress.

With the election results, Schumer has appeared to improve his position with the caucus, following a tumultuous tenure in recent years. The pushback took hold after the New York Democrat maneuvered to avoid a government shutdown in early 2025, prompting frustration from his party's left flank.

Later that year, he changed course and kept Democrats largely united through a record-breaking government shutdown as they sought to prevent the expiration of health insurance tax credits.

In an interview with MS NOW announcing his run for majority leader, Van Hollen acknowledged he is an "underdog," but said he has spoken with caucus members and believes the race is "very much in flux."

Asked what he would do differently from Schumer, Van Hollen suggested the current leader hasn't taken a firm enough stance on using the power of the purse to force the Trump administration to end the Iran war. He told host Jen Psaki that Democrats should use the Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government as leverage, saying it "should not be a finger-in-the-wind issue."

Van Hollen also criticized Schumer for, in his view, moving behind the scenes to back certain candidates in Democratic primaries — a longstanding point of contention for progressives.

"On the political side of the equation, we shouldn't have a Democratic leader who is getting involved in picking sides in open Democratic primaries. … We have two senators right now in the United States Senate who wouldn't be there if the current majority leader had his way," Van Hollen said, referring to El-Sayed and Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan.

Some members of the Democratic caucus — including both progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and moderates like Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas — have called for new leadership.

"I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader," Sanders said in a news conference this week, adding that the caucus needs to have "a vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party."

Sanders was flanked by the more moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who said she was "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."

"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

World.title: Crews begin excavating site of building collapse in Brooklyn
World.content:
The death toll rose to eight Thursday after a Brooklyn building collapsed and an adjacent building was significantly damaged.

A three-story, multi-use building on Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a nearby construction site just after 4 p.m. Wednesday, tearing off the side of another building.

At least eight people were killed and 17 others were injured as of Thursday afternoon, according to the FDNY. Six people were found dead at the scene, and two died at the hospital.

"We know that this morning they pulled out, I believe a couple of construction workers that were on site last night, which added to the death toll this morning," said Councilwoman Farrah Louis.

The structure was fully occupied by residents, and workers were in the construction pit performing excavation work at the time of the collapse.

Emergency crews worked through the night under floodlights with the help of drones and K-9 units to get through the massive piles of rubble.

Video showed dozens of firefighters at the scene Thursday morning searching for additional victims. First responders also used machinery to excavate debris.

The FDNY completed its rescue operations just after 3:30 p.m. Thursday after searching the entire site and determining there were no remaining victims.

Members of the New York City Fire Department and first responders search for victims in the rubble a day after a building collapsed in Brooklyn. Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

The building collapse site has now been turned over to the Department of Buildings and the NYPD. Officials are trying to determine what caused the ground to give way.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the incident devastating, praising first responders for executing a grueling, high-risk technical operation.

"Rescue workers have spent the night searching the site of yesterday's building collapse, working under extremely dangerous conditions to find and save anyone who may still be trapped. I am heartbroken that eight New Yorkers have now lost their lives and at least 17 have been injured, including three firefighters. There are no words for a loss of this magnitude," he said in a post Thursday.

Investigators are conducting comprehensive reviews of the conditions at the collapsed building and neighboring construction site. Investigators said developers have active permits for excavation and foundation work associated with a new building project.

Records revealed the site had been cited for violations months before the disaster. Those were corrected, and work was allowed to resume in May.

Investigators have not determined whether that work contributed to the collapse.

A full stop-work order has been issued as recovery operations continue.

The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office is also investigating whether any criminal conduct contributed to the collapse.

World.title: Is Outlook down? Widespread outage hits Microsoft email and other apps
World.content:
Is Outlook down? Widespread outage hits Microsoft email and other apps

toggle caption i Lindsey Wasson/AP

A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.

Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook just after 1 p.m. ET. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they couldn't send and receive emails or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether.

Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft's workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft said it was investigating disruptions, notably related to its email and Teams applications.

In updates posted on social media, Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft said it was aware of users "experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas."

Microsoft explained that a portion of its infrastructure was "experiencing elevated load" — which it said was "likely contributing to the connectivity errors." The company determined a number of servers were "unexpectedly unavailable" due to a problem that caused them to fail during "automated health checks."

Sponsor Message

It was not immediately clear what exactly caused that failure. But Microsoft later said it was testing a fix and rolling out an alternative method for these checks to bring impacted servers back online.

"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X.

Earlier in the day, the company said it had "successfully restored" problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

Cindy Holscher wins in Kansas, holding governor's office for Democrats

Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher will hold onto the Kansas governor's office for her party after defeating Republican Ty Masterson, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Masterson, the president of the state Senate, was endorsed by President Trump. Of the 36 elections for governor across the country, Kansas was seen as the most likely to flip from Democratic to Republican control.

Current Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly is term-limited after serving for eight years in a state with a heavily Republican legislature and that usually votes for Republicans for other offices and in presidential elections.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

Holscher, 57, ran a campaign with notes of populism, promising to fight "sweetheart deals" for billionaires. She tied Masterson to his work in the state Senate when it passed a tax cut under former Republican Gov. Sam Brownback that led to a series of budget crises and was later repealed.

Holscher opposed school vouchers, calling for more support for public schools, in contrast with Masterson, who backed school vouchers. She also called for a moratorium on new data centers and for legalizing cannabis as a way to generate state revenue.

Masterson, 57, called for lower property taxes and said faith influenced all his decisions, including in politics. He promised to be the "most pro-ag, pro-business, pro-oil and gas governor," the state has seen. He called Holscher, "the most radical, liberal, socialist Democrat ever" on a ticket in Kansas.

"He likes to throw around a whole lot of labels," Holscher responded. "You know why? Because that's all he's got."

World.title: What's a Honey Trap? The spy tactic that helped topple Jensen Huang
World.content:
What's a Honey Trap? The spy tactic that helped topple Jensen Huang

toggle caption i CTI via Reuters

One of the world's oldest spy tactics appears to have helped topple one of the world's richest men. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday amid revelations that he had an affair with a female client that U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese spy, according to the New York Times.

NPR has not independently confirmed the reporting by the Times, which said Huang also had an unrelated affair with a company executive who reported to him. The Chinese government has called the accusation of spying, "nothing but smears against China."

Using a romantic relationship to gather intelligence from foreigners – known as a honey trap – has a long history in China and beyond. The Chinese Ministry of State Security, the country's main civilian intelligence agency, routinely tries to recruit women and occasionally men for honey traps, according to former CIA officers and other U.S. officials familiar with Chinese spy craft.

Sponsor Message

Some target businessmen for industrial espionage or to gain insights into the economic and political strategy of foreign governments. Peter Mattis , a former CIA counter-intelligence analyst, said honey traps also serve as influence operations with spies trying to gain enough trust to shape the target's thinking about China.

'A whole of society approach'

"The biggest thing here that we should pay attention to is that the Ministry of State Security celebrates a tradition of getting inside the enemy's decision-making," said Mattis, president of the Jamestown Foundation , a national security think tank in Washington, D.C., that focuses on America's geopolitical rivals.

Nicholas Eftimiades , who spent more than 34 years with the CIA and Defense Intelligence Agency and now teaches at Penn State, said the honey trap is just one tactic among many that use ordinary Chinese citizens to gather information at home and abroad.

"Unlike the CIA, or MI6 or any of the other Western services, China has a 'whole of society approach,'" said Eftimiades, the author of Chinese Intelligence Operations: An Analysis of the People's Republic of China's Intelligence Services. "Chinese law supports this. The National Intelligence Law of 2017 requires citizens to cooperate with intelligence collection efforts."

A long list of honey traps

The Chinese government has employed honey traps in the United States and elsewhere in the West. In the 2010s, Christine Fang worked as a political fundraiser in California where she developed a physical relationship with Democrat Rep. Eric Swalwell before and after he became a congressman.

Sponsor Message

The FBI warned Swalwell they thought Fang was a spy. He denied doing anything wrong and she fled back to China.

In the 1980s and 1990s, the FBI paid Katrina Leung – a Los Angeles businesswoman – $1.7 million over 18 years to spy on China. However, Leung had affairs with two FBI agents and the bureau later determined she was a double-agent.

The most remarkable honey trap case dates to the 1960s, when a young French diplomat began a nearly two-decade affair with a male Peking opera performer, whom he thought was a woman. The story inspired the play and movie, M Butterfly.

The woman implicated in the Nvidia case, Alice Huang, is a Chinese businesswoman whose company, Megaspeed, was a major buyer of advanced chips from Nvidia. The Times reported the U.S. had her under surveillance and learned of her connections to Chinese state security through her communications.

toggle caption i Taryn Ng/AFP via Getty Images

Desmond Shum, a Hong Kong businessman and former China insider, says Alice Huang doesn't fit the usual profile in these cases. She appears to be what the Chinese call a "white glove" – or front-person for multi-billion-dollar commercial deals, which Shum says could have insulated her from the Ministry of State Security.

Shum doesn't think Alice Huang is a professional spy, pointing out that she hasn't been discreet on social media, posting photos from her visits to luxurious country clubs and fancy foreign destinations.

"A spy wouldn't do that," Shum told NPR from his home in the United Kingdom.

Isaac Stone Fish , a former reporter in China who runs Strategy Risks, a China-focused business intelligence firm, says the Ministry of State Security – or MSS – could have approached Alice Huang after it learned of her affair with the Nvidia head.

"One imagines that every time a Chinese person enters into a romantic relationship with a very, very powerful American, MSS notices that," Stone Fish said.

The stuff of spy novels and movies

Honey traps are a staple of spy novel and movie plots, including the Netflix series, Black Doves, The Americans on FX, Apple TV's Slow Horses as well as James Bond films, such as From Russia with Love.

Sponsor Message

In reality, when Chinese state security approaches women for these operations, it's embarrassing and humiliating. The tactic perpetuates racist, sexist stereotypes while casting suspicion on the vast majority of Chinese people, who have nothing to do with intelligence gathering.

In addition to China, many intelligence services have engaged in honey traps. The Russians historically used sex workers for blackmail and leverage. During the Cold-War, East Germany sent well-educated and well-mannered male spies – known as Romeos – to West Germany.

Mossad, the Israeli intelligence service, used honey traps from the 1950s into the 1970s in countries such as Egypt, Iraq and Iran. But investigative reporter Yossi Melman, who's written many books on Israeli intelligence, says the practice has dwindled as cyber spying and digital traps have proven more efficient.

The U.S. used sexual entrapment against the Soviets, but several former officials said the Americans now prefer to appeal to people on ideological grounds and provide financial carrots, such as money for college tuition or health care for a sick family member.

Even though countries repeatedly warn businessmen and government officials about the tell-tale signs of a honey trap, ego and vanity remain human weaknesses and men continue to succumb, said Eftimiades.

"Welcome to the male of the species," he said. "Is everyone aware of this? Yes. Does everyone think it'll happen to them? No. And, you know, and it happens all the time."

World.title: 'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years
World.content:
'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.

Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.

"It was a punch in the gut," said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com . "We expected to see a soft month but not the softest month since 2010."

Expensive mortgages are a big factor

The drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.

In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023. Rates have gone down a bit since then, but are still well above where they were a year ago.

Sponsor Message

Higher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September to increase the cost of borrowing, including home mortgages. Fewer home sales and other purchases mean less economic activity, which the Fed wants in order to reach its goal of lowering inflation.

Policymakers at the Fed have signaled another rate hike could come in December, which could further slow down the housing market.

"It might seem like kicking the housing market while it's down right now for the Fed to continue a rate raising cycle but in the long run getting inflation under control is really the goal," Berner said.
