World.title: Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?
World.content:
Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

President Trump's efforts to remake Washington, D.C., have dominated his second term, even after his party's resounding midterm defeat.

He started his election week at the scandal-plagued Reflecting Pool and ended it with an order declaring his gilded Oval Office a national monument to "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space."

That proclamation, like any executive order, could be undone by a future president. But many of Trump's construction projects are changing D.C. in more permanent ways.

Sponsor Message

His administration has already downed hundreds of trees at East Potomac Park and demolished the East Wing of the White House to make space for a ballroom — which he called "the safest place in Washington" as he showed it to reporters the day after the midterms.

Trump has taken a uniquely unilateral approach to construction, packing regulatory commissions with his allies and bypassing Congress entirely. Most of his projects — from the triumphal arch to the Kennedy Center — are now playing out in court.

Critics accuse the Trump administration of skirting federal laws and misleading judges in its effort to progress as quickly as possible before the end of his term.

Democrats have vowed to use their soon-to-be congressional majority to push back on what they describe as Trump's "vanity projects."

When asked about that, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in an email that "no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump." He cited park cleanups, the Reflecting Pool and the White House helipad and ballroom as examples, and said Democrats "should work with President Trump to make our nation's capital beautiful again."

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Imags

Rep. Jared Huffman, D.-Calif., told NPR in an interview that the Trump administration has "played this game of Catch Me If You Can, where they roll ahead with the bulldozers and the tree cutters … and they wait for courts to shut them down." He says a Democrat-led Congress will fight back.

Sponsor Message

"There's no way that we could look away while these sacred, iconic places are being permanently changed in ways that violate the law and could have really terrible lasting impacts," said Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, which has a legislative purview over public lands and national parks.

Huffman says blocking Trump's construction projects — and holding people accountable for potential wrongdoing — will be a top priority when he leads the committee. Earlier this week, he sent letters ordering dozens of administration officials and private companies to preserve their records for a future investigation.

"Whether it is the arch or … or the East Potomac golf course or any number of other examples around the United States capital, that is federal land, and we have a direct statutory responsibility to either authorize those changes or to stop them if they're proceeding without the proper authorization," Huffman said.

What would that actually look like? Democrats have many tools at their disposal, from legislation to lawsuits. But experts say only two are likely to succeed: funding and oversight.

Democrats could block funding for specific projects, potentially as soon as next month

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

Congress could — at least in theory — pass laws to block specific projects from moving ahead. Some Democratic lawmakers have already introduced bills to protect the Kennedy Center from demolition and prohibit the construction of an arch at Memorial Circle.

But Trump has promised to "veto everything," and Democrats won't have a big enough majority to override him on their own.

"Legislation in principle is the cleanest way of doing it, but it's also not achievable," said David Super, who teaches administrative and constitutional law at Georgetown. "So what they're likely to do is cut off funds."

The Constitution says that the federal government may spend money only if is appropriated by Congress. But Trump has neither sought nor received congressional authorization for projects like the arch and the White House ballroom — he maintains he doesn't need it.

Sponsor Message

Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine is one of many who disagree. She's the top Democrat on the House committee that oversees funding for the Interior Department.

"Certainly Congress should have been involved, because we have the power of the purse," Pingree told NPR. "That is our ultimate tool. And Republicans have refused to use that. But we can use that in very many ways to block him or to use it for leverage."

Pingree says a Democratic majority will be able to write appropriations bills with clear language from the outset about where money can and can't be spent — and potentially take the president to court if he doesn't follow it.

Super expects Congress would prevail in such a challenge, because it has clear-cut authority over federal funds.

For example, he noted that some of Trump's D.C.-area beautification projects have been funded at least in part by diverted national park entrance fees. Congress could "cap how much money can be used in the greater Washington area, and force the money to be used in the Everglades and Yosemite and Great Smoky Mountains," he said.

Congress will have to make some appropriations decisions in the coming weeks, since it needs to pass a short-term funding bill by Dec. 11 to avoid a government shutdown. Democrats could use that opportunity to try to limit funding for at least one of Trump's construction projects.

Huffman has proposed language that would prevent Trump from using federal funds for the East Potomac golf course renovations, limiting them instead to repairs of the park's crumbling seawall. Pingree said she will join him in fighting to negotiate that into next month's bill.

toggle caption i Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images

"Whether or not the president will sign that with that in there, I don't know yet," she said. "But certainly those are the most … immediate crisis points … People want the president to stop cutting down the trees on the golf course and stop trying to take that over, and they want to make sure that no shovel goes into the ground on building the arch."

Sponsor Message

Earlier this year Pingree introduced an amendment that would have outright blocked construction of the arch; it failed along party lines. She wonders whether any Republicans might vote differently after the midterms, given the message Americans sent at the polls.

"They want the president to be focused on the issues they're dealing with: the cost of health care, the cost of food, the cost of gasoline," she said. "And if every time the president gives a speech, he's either standing in front of the Reflecting Pool, which he spent millions of dollars on, or showing you the new marble choices he's putting into the ballroom, it just makes a lot of people mad."

Pingree said she's been surprised to hear how strongly people feel about these projects – even people well outside D.C. And she agrees with them that potential corruption and misuse of taxpayer dollars are worth fighting: "After the first of the year, we will use every tool in our toolbox."

Democrats want to hold people and companies accountable

Lawmakers and experts acknowledge that not every project is reversible, or potentially even worth the fight. Huffman suggested he will focus on bigger projects, and ones that are moving too fast for courts to adequately rein in.

"Are we going to throw all of our efforts at stopping the gilding of every statue in Washington, D.C.? Probably not," said Huffman. "But these are iconic places that we're talking about, with permanent damage that we need to engage on to try to prevent."

Even so, Democrats could decide that certain construction projects are "the price they pay for other priorities," said Claire Leavitt, a professor of government at Smith College. Voters made clear they want lawmakers to focus on ending the Iran war and making life more affordable, big asks that may take a lot of political capital.

"And that's not corruption or Democrats not doing their job," Leavitt said. "It's just the natural trade-offs of dealing with who you're dealing with, and understanding that what matters to Trump more than anything seems to be building the arch, building the ballroom … remaking the Kennedy Center."

Sponsor Message

Whether or not these projects move forward, Congress can provide a fuller public accounting of how they came to be — in the hopes of preventing more in the future.

"They can gavel in hearings. They have agenda-setting power," Leavitt said. "They determine what the public hearing roster is. They decide which witnesses to invite. And that means they have a unique opportunity to draw negative public attention to the Trump administration."

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

That may be easier said than done, especially with an administration that has pointedly refused to comply with congressional oversight and is now warning Democrats that their future investigations could constitute criminality. Huffman was coy when asked how he is preparing to handle such challenges.

"We are going to have to have a strategy and a plan to do these things that prior Congresses have never imagined they would have to do," he said.

One investigative priority, lawmakers say, will be following the money — especially when it comes to donations for the ballroom and other projects. Leavitt says that focus has an added benefit: Private companies and individuals are likely more willing to testify than a member of the administration.

Another example: Congress could subpoena for information about the decision-making processes of the Kennedy Center board and the physical state of the building, which trustees say must be closed for two years of repairs. And it can put that information in the Congressional — and therefore historical — Record.

"Both the current public can make its judgments, and history can make its judgments," Leavitt said.

Leavitt said oversight can often lead to policy change in the longer term. For example: The committee investigating the Jan. 6 insurrection didn't stop Trump from eventually pardoning Capitol rioters, but it did lead Congress to pass an electoral reform act.

"The frustrating part about congressional oversight is Congress can draw attention to a problem, and they can demand accountability for something that's already been done," Leavitt said. "But it's very hard for Congress to stop something from happening that the president is determined to do."

Sponsor Message

Super agrees that Democrats are playing a long game. He expects to see more bipartisan support after Trump leaves office for preventing future presidents from following his playbook.

"The process in the past has been built on trust, and President Trump certainly broke that trust in numerous ways," he said. "Laws can be written so that we don't depend on trust, we depend on law. And I'm guessing we're going to do that."

World.title: The SS United States takes its final voyage to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico
World.content:
The SS United States takes its final voyage to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico

toggle caption i JEWEL SAMAD/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

A giant ship sunk off the coast of Florida yesterday—and the coast guard didn't do a thing to stop it.

The SS United States is a retired ocean liner that was deliberately sunk on Wednesday to create the world's largest artificial reef. After hours of slow descent, it finally disappeared beneath the waves at 10 p.m. ET last night. It now rests 180 feet beneath the surface at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico in an upright position.

Measuring almost 1,000 feet from bow to stern, the giant ship is longer than the Titanic. After it's settled on the ocean floor, the ship's hundreds of rooms, corridors and elevator shafts will become a deep-sea playground for divers, fish and other aquatic life.

Sponsor Message

This transformation gives the SS United States the opportunity for a second life and a new species of passenger.

Susan Gibbs has mixed feelings about the ship's final voyage to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. She chairs the board of the SS United States Conservancy, and her grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the ship more than 70 years ago.

"It's a combination of grief, that I will be saying goodbye to her in her current form, but, gratitude and hope in terms of what she will continue to give to the world," she told Morning Edition

The ocean liner took its maiden voyage in 1952, and it shattered the trans-Atlantic speed record, winning the coveted Blue Riband on her opening sail. It still holds the record more than 60 years later.

In the event of war, the SS United States could have been converted from a luxury liner to a military transport vessel able to carry 14,000 troops for 10,000 miles without refueling, though it was never used for this purpose, according to the SS United States Conservancy.

toggle caption i M. Fresco/Getty Images/Hulton Archive

By the end of her time on the water in 1969, the SS United States carried several notable passengers, including Harry Truman, Walt Disney, Marilyn Monroe, Walter Cronkite and a young Bill Clinton.

Sponsor Message

"She embodied the spirit of a nation so confident in its ability to accomplish the extraordinary," said Gibbs.

The conservancy wanted to transform the ship into a hotel or museum, but due to legal and financial issues, they eventually sold it to Okaloosa County, Florida in 2024. It was the county's decision to sink it.

Realistically, it's not easy to sink something that's designed to stay above water. So, Okaloosa County called in the professionals.

Coleen Marine, a marine engineering contracting company who specializes in creating artificial reefs, led the project. Their President and co-founder Coleen O'Malley said they did their best to preserve the ship's original design.

"We've maintained the actual hull. So she's very recognizable," O'Malley said. "We've made it so that the structure under the water is going to look like she did above the water."

To sink the ship, the Coleen Marine team had to repair holes and irregularities in the hull to ensure it would sink properly. O'Malley detailed that "the biggest thing with sinking a ship is not how much water you put in. It's making sure the air comes out."

The team also cleaned much of the rusted exterior to make a more welcoming environment for aquatic life. Most importantly, the team wanted to ensure that the ship sank straight down, without flipping or turning. Overall, O'Malley said construction took more than 18 months.

Both O'Malley and Gibbs made the journey to the coast of Destin and Fort Walton Beach to watch the SS United States disappear below the waves Wednesday.

In the wake of its last moments above the surface, the SS United States Conservancy is planning to construct a museum in the ship's honor in Florida.

World.title: Nvidia CEO's resignation after affair with suspected Chinese spy rattles markets, tech world
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nvidia's stock dove again on Thursday as the massive affair and alleged spying scandal led longtime CEO Jensen Huang to step down, forcing investors to question what the company's future would look like without him.

Shares in the AI chipmaker plunged by 14 per cent after the stock market opened following Huang's resignation as CEO and a board member, before climbing back up and closing the day down 4.3 per cent.

The broader market mostly escaped the Nvidia fallout, with major indexes dipping to only moderate losses to finish the day.

Michael Dehal, a senior portfolio manager at Dehal Investment Partners, says the appointment of chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO likely helped pull Nvidia stock back up.

"That quick resolution on a temporary basis was reassuring to investors," Dehal said.

But this has still been a major slide for a company which first reached a $5 trillion US valuation a year ago and has lost more than $1 trillion US of that in the wake of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang has admitted to having an affair but did not say whether it was with Alice Huang, the woman U.S. intelligence services allege is working for Beijing. He is alleged to have had another affair with a vice president within the company who reports directly to him, according to a report published by the New York Times on Wednesday.

WATCH | Huang resigns, stocks plunge: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns, stocks plunge | Duration 1:17 Nvidia, the U.S.-based tech giant, was rocked by allegations that president and CEO Jensen Huang had two extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Following his resignation, CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO of the world's dominant chipmaker and AI powerhouse. CORRECTION (Nov. 12, 2026): This video erroneously shows an image of the Dow Jones Industrial index instead of Nasdaq.

It's unwelcome news to industry-watchers who are now re-evaluating Nvidia's worth without its seemingly irreplaceable leader and co-founder .

And such big swings can impact investments and retirement funds held by many Canadians too, say financial planners and money managers.

As one of the most valuable companies in the world, Nvidia makes up a big part of major stock indexes, where companies with bigger market values are given more weight.

Because of its size, the Santa Clara, Calif.-based company makes up about six per cent of the S&P 500, and about nine per cent of the tech-heavy Nasdaq.

Dehal says a lot of Canadians hold index funds through exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which track those major indexes, meaning they may be exposed to big swings in Nvidia's value. Mutual funds may also be tech-heavy, but might be more diversified since they are actively managed by professionals.

A screen on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange displays news about Nvidia's stock price in New York, on Monday. (Yuki Iwamura/Associated Press)

Those indexes have become dominated by tech companies in recent years as the AI boom has made other companies like Apple, Microsoft and Google's parent company Alphabet more valuable. With tech outfits now making up an estimated 40 per cent of the S&P 500, certified financial planner Zainab Williams says investors who have parked their money in basic ETFs might be exposed to big changes in tech stocks — AI in particular.

"People often hold so many different ETFs and they feel that they are well diversified," Williams said. But if those ETFs are made up of a lot of the same companies, "you are exposing yourself to the same type of volatility."

Portfolio manager Michael Dehal says Huang's quick exit from Nvidia was 'reasuring to investors.' (Submitted by Michael Dehal)

Some industry analysts worry the Nvidia scandal could ripple throughout the broader tech market because of the company's role in the AI buildout.

With an estimated 80 per cent market share for its chips that power everything from AI data centres to ChatGPT or drones, the company is an integral player in the industry. It's also poured money into funding other AI companies, bankrolling the likes of Anthropic, Toronto-based Cohere and the cloud computing outfit CoreWeave.

Because Huang was a driving force behind those financing deals, Dehan says whether Nvidia keeps funding other tech companies is an open question, and could be a short term drag on other AI firms.

But he and other investors expect the tech sector won't take a major hit. In fact, tech companies like Broadcom and AMD that make their own chips made gains on Thursday, picking up some of the slack left behind by Nvidia, according to the president of Murray Wealth Group, Jamie Murray.

"The money's still there, it's still going to be spent. And we don't really see this slowing down everything, just maybe a shifting of the deck chairs," Murray said.

Outside of tech stocks, Dehan says those with a diversified portfolio shouldn't worry — but it does drive home the importance of not putting all your eggs in one basket.

Williams says the situation could serve as a reminder for investors to "look under the hood" of their investments to get a better sense of whether they might be exposed to certain industries or companies.

"If what happened [in the] last week really gave you heart palpitations, take a look at what you can start doing to reduce some of that exposure and to look at investing in different countries, different sectors," Williams said.

World.title: Feds say Stellantis owes 'hundreds of millions' in subsidies, company offers $24M
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Automaker Stellantis says it will pay back $24 million in federal subsidies after it announced plans to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant — but Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says the company owes far more than what it is offering.

The company announced Monday that it plans to sell the Brampton facility to armoured vehicle manufacturer Roshel Inc., which the federal government says is in violation of a 2022 agreement that put up millions in subsidies to help retool the plant.

In a statement on Thursday, Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said the company will return the subsidies to the government to the tune of $24 million.

"We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility. While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use," the statement reads.

The amount conflicts with the government's characterization of what Stellantis owes.

"Stellantis is on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars," Joly told reporters following a Thursday meeting with representatives from the automaker, the Ontario government and the union representing the plant's workers.

When pressed, Joly didn't specify a number, simply replying that "Stellantis knows how much it owes." The government's own records previously showed that roughly $220 million worth of subsidies were given to the company to help upgrade its plants across the province.

WATCH | Joly gives update on Stellantis: 'I'm fed up': Joly says Stellantis's planned sale of Brampton plant breached contract | Duration closed caption 1:06 Days after Stellantis announced a plan to sell its Brampton, Ont., plant to an armoured vehicle manufacturer, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Stellantis 'is on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars.'

Asked for a response to Stellantis's suggestion that it owes $24 million, Joly's office said the minister's earlier statements stand.

Joly wrote to Longley on Thursday saying the government is terminating a resolution process and notifying the automaker that it is in default of a 2022 government funding agreement.

"Patience has its limits. To be frank, I'm fed up. I'm fed up and Canadians are fed up and workers are fed up," Joly said after Thursday's meeting. She also said the government plans to meet with Stellantis's global CEO.

The minister's letter to Stellantis suggests that the company has 30 days to take corrective action or the government could seek to terminate the 2022 agreement and recoup its subsidies.

WATCH | Deal or no deal? Did Stellantis violate its deals with the feds? Funding contract provided exceptions around Brampton | Duration closed caption 2:19 On Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney called Stellantis' now-confirmed plans to sell an automotive assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., "a betrayal." But a previously obtained copy of the multi-million-dollar funding deal between Stellantis and the federal government suggests the carmaker had a way out when it came to closing the Brampton plant. The CBC's Emma Loop explains.

Stellantis had been engaged with the government to find a possible alternative for the Brampton facility after the company announced last year that it wouldn't be going ahead with plans to build the Jeep Compass at that plant.

The government had signed an agreement to provide subsidies to the automaker to retool the plant to produce the Jeep model. Joly's letter says the planned sale to Roshel indicates Stellantis is not interested in finding a satisfactory solution.

"I must conclude that Stellantis is no longer diligently working in good faith to prepare a satisfactory plan under the Resolution Process. Accordingly, the Resolution Process is terminated," the letter reads.

Union says government should've acted sooner

Joly had promised nearly a year ago that the government would serve a default notice to Stellantis.

Lana Payne — the national president of Unifor, the union representing the workers at the plant — said the federal government should've acted sooner.

"We have the sale of a plant and everybody in the country says they didn't want to have the sale of a plant. Yet here we are, the plant has been sold," Payne told reporters following Thursday's meeting.

"Why could not something have been done last week? Or the week before? Or the week before that?"

WATCH | Unifor on the plant sale: Stellantis auto plant sale is 'last possible outcome that we would have wanted': union | Duration closed caption 2:27 Unifor national president Lana Payne said the time to stop Stellantis's announced sale of its Brampton, Ont., plant has passed. 'We would need to reverse the sale, which is doubly difficult,' Payne said.

Stellantis and Roshel signed a memorandum of understanding regarding the potential sale in September. The automaker announced on Monday that it intends to go ahead with the sale.

When pressed during Thursday's news conference, Joly indicated that the government will be unable to block the sale.

More than 2,000 workers at Stellantis's Brampton plant have been out of work since the company halted operations in 2023 to retool the facility for the Jeep Compass.

In the deal announced by the Trudeau government in 2022, Ottawa said it would inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them retool to increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.

Stellantis paused the retooling plan at the Brampton plant in early 2025, announcing in October of that year that the Jeep Compass would be built at the Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois instead.

Part of the deal with Roshel that was announced on Monday could see Stellantis lease some of the property back.

Stellantis says there are still about 1,800 workers from the Brampton plant on layoff. Since 2023, those workers have continued to receive 70 per cent of their pay, as well as benefits.

WATCH | Carney clarifies stance: 'What was the betrayal?' Carney clarifies stance on Stellantis plant deal | Duration 0:22 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking from Dublin on Nov. 12, was asked what he meant when he called the planned sale of the idled Brampton, Ont., Stellantis plant to an armoured vehicle maker a 'betrayal' of workers. 'A partial solution is a step, it is not a global solution,' he said, adding that is a 'betrayal.'

Last week, Unifor demanded a meeting of all stakeholders, including the Ontario government, Stellantis and the federal government.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that his government had been informed of "some aspects" of Stellantis's plan to sell the auto plant to Roshel before the deal was announced earlier this week.

The prime minister made the comments a day after reports that his office and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's office had been aware for months of the details of what was going to be made public.

Joly's office has insisted that the minister "had no part in negotiating the deal with Stellantis or Roshel" and didn't meet with the armoured vehicle manufacturer.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has called on Carney to remove Joly as minister over the plant sale. He reiterated that call on Thursday and said all the details of the 2022 agreement should be made public.

"Why not release the deal, Mr. Carney? Your government handed over our money. Canadians deserve to know how much they paid and what they got in return," he said during a news conference in Calgary.

World.title: Maryland's Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for U.S. Senate leadership post
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate majority leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.

Van Hollen said in a statement that "the American people called for change" and that is why he is running.

"It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said. "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.

U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win. (Mariam Zuhaib/The Associated Press)

The race will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades.

The question of whether to re-elect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators will not say publicly how they will vote. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election, and Schumer recruited many of the party's winning candidates and raised money for them.

'I'm going to win it': Schumer

Schumer has been talking to Democratic senators since the election about forming an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer laid out a broad plan for their first 100 days in power.

"I'm going to win it," Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week.

In a statement after Van Hollen's announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus.

"I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."

While Schumer is the favourite to win, Van Hollen's run exposes a rift in the party that has put Schumer on the defensive since he sided with Republicans on a spending vote in March 2025.

Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change.

Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president.

El-Sayed backs Van Hollen

While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least one backer in next year's caucus: Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need "bold leadership."

U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is backing Van Hollen to be the Democrats' leader in the U.S. Senate. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

"I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience," El-Sayed wrote. "We need both right now. Which is why I'm proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority."

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin also called for new leadership at a news conference Tuesday, though neither endorsed a specific candidate.

Several senators have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week.

Maine Sen. Angus King, an Independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the election, issued a statement after Van Hollen's announcement: "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?

"Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible," King wrote.

World.title: Microsoft says services being slowly restored after widespread outages across its platforms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Microsoft said it was returning some of its affected servers to full service late Thursday afternoon, after widespread outages hit many of its platforms including Outlook, with users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.

"We’ve... shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions," the company said in a statement on its website. But a short time later, it warned that while its servers seemed to be handling the recovery, "we've observed that they can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic."

It said it was also "temporarily limiting which types of traffic can reach the affected infrastructure in specific locations."

Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook just after 1 p.m. ET. New reports fell following that peak, but many said they couldn't send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether.

Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft's workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services.

In updates posted on social media, Microsoft said it was aware of users "experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas."

We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543. —MSFT365Status

Microsoft later explained that a portion of its infrastructure was "experiencing elevated load," which it said was "likely contributing to the connectivity errors." The company determined a number of servers were "unexpectedly unavailable" due to a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.

It later said it was "implementing protective traffic management measures in a specific location to reduce load on the affected infrastructure," and would expand those measures if the results were positive.

"As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect to the service," it said.

CBC News reached out to Microsoft for more details about how users in Canada were affected.

Via Rail said on social media that, due to the outage, some of its customers may not be receiving email communications about their trip and encouraged them to consult its tracker or 

Earlier in the day, the company said it had "successfully restored" problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

World.title: A PAL Airlines flight lost a wheel less than 2 weeks ago. It's happened again — to the same plane
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A plane that appeared to be missing a wheel landed at St. John's International Airport on Thursday afternoon.

Less than two weeks after a PAL flight lost a wheel, the airline has confirmed the same plane lost another one Thursday.

Flight 411 was bound for Deer Lake, Newfoundland and Labrador, but instead landed safely in St. John's around 4:10 p.m. NT because of mechanical problems, according to PAL.

Emergency vehicles rushed to the plane moments after landing.

On Oct. 30, CBC News reported on a PAL flight where a wheel fell off upon landing in Wabush, N.L.

In a written statement, PAL senior vice-president of public affairs Joseph Galimberti said "extensive maintenance procedures" were completed after that incident. He also confirmed that plane is the same as one that experienced mechanical problems on Thursday.

Emergency vehicles followed PAL flight 411 moments after it landed. (Ted Dillon/CBC)

The airline is now removing the plane from service and will complete another inspection.

"In addition, out of an abundance of caution and in the interest of safety, PAL Airlines has initiated a process to complete wheel assembly inspections on the remainder of its Dash 8-400 aircraft to ensure the integrity of our fleet," wrote Galimberti.

Galimberti said the company has been in contact with Transport Canada and manufacturer De Havilland Aircraft of Canada to review the cause of the problem.

WATCH | PAL says plane will be removed from service for ‘comprehensive inspection’: PAL Airlines removes plane from service after a wheel falls off for the second time in less than 2 weeks | Duration closed caption 1:44 PAL Airlines says it is removing a plane from service after a second incident of a wheel falling off the same plane. On Thursday afternoon, the aircraft made an emergency landing in St. John’s, missing one of its wheels. The CBC’s Madison Taylor reports.

The aircraft in question was on a flight from Happy Valley-Goose Bay chartered by Vale Base Metals. In a written statement, corporate affairs specialist Angela Sullivan said all passengers and crew are accounted for.

"Vale Base Metals is liaising with PAL Airlines to further understand the incident. The safety of people remains our priority," Sullivan wrote.

PAL Airlines said passengers have been rescheduled to complete their trips as soon as possible.

World.title: Will U.S. travel pick up after midterm 'blue wave'? Not so fast, say these Canadians
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

John May had low expectations ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

But he was glad to see the Democratic Party take control of both chambers of Congress in a Nov. 3 vote that many observers have described as a resounding rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump.

"It's encouraging, isn't it? To see that there's finally some common sense coming around down there," said the 73-year-old from Manotick, Ont., an Ottawa suburb.

May, who stopped travelling to the United States last year amid Trump's repeated threats against Canada, said he and his wife Patti aren't ready to go south of the border again just yet though.

The couple had spent winters in Florida for more than a decade before May said the atmosphere turned "toxic" as Trump mocked Canadian leaders and pushed to turn Canada into the "51st state."

"We'd like to, but we're not feeling like we want to go back yet," May told CBC News.

"I think we've got to wait until they've got a different president down there and a whole different attitude," he said. "Things haven't changed enough. We'll need a couple more years, I think."

John and Patti May pose for a photo in Key West, Fla., in February 2024. (Submitted by John May)

Drop in travel

Many Canadians, including those with relatives or business interests south of the border, have continued to travel to the U.S. amid Trump's threats and the trade war with Canada.

But data shows travel to the U.S. has dropped alongside the strained relationship.

According to Statistics Canada, return border crossings from the U.S. fell by about 25 per cent in 2025 compared with the previous year.

There has been a slight increase in 2026: A total of 1.9 million return trips by car and air from the U.S. were reported in October, marking the seventh consecutive month of year-over-year growth and a three per cent increase from October 2025, Statistics Canada reported.

But when compared with October 2024, return trips by car were down 29 per cent while those by air were down 19.6 per cent.

WATCH | People in Windsor, Ont., have mixed reactions post-midterms: Elbows up or down? Windsorites are mixed on returning to the U.S. post-midterms | Duration closed caption 2:19 Some say they're feeling optimistic. Some say they're waiting for concrete change.

Possible 'softening' of travel plans

It's too soon to say whether the midterms will lead to a major increase in Canadian travel south.

McKenzie McMillan, a travel consultant and co-owner of The Travel Group in Vancouver, said that, anecdotally, there may be some "softening" around U.S. travel.

Are you changing your holiday plans due to the cost of domestic airfare in Canada? Getting creative to find cheaper alternatives? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.

"But it hasn't really translated at this point into new bookings, or a real change in the overall sentiment to avoid the United States," McMillan said. "We are still hearing overall that travellers are looking to alternative destinations for their winter travel and beyond."

Spokespersons for Air Canada and Porter Airlines also told CBC this week that it was too early to say whether the midterms have had an effect on travel. Air Transat said it did not have sufficient data to identify a trend.

WATCH | What the midterms could mean for border cities: What the U.S. midterm results could mean for border cities | Duration 2:12 CBC Windsor's Acton Clarkin checks in with the Detroit Regional Chamber of Commerce to find out what the Democratic blue wave in the U.S. midterms could mean for trade and jobs on both sides of the border.

But the midterms may help ease the negative feelings that some Canadians have had.

Marja Vermeer, a 67-year-old from Strathroy, Ont., said the vote results, coupled with messages over the past two years from Americans rejecting the Trump administration's attacks against Canada, make her more open to visiting the U.S.

"Especially to the states where they voted Democrat, I think they're ... a bit more comfortable and a bit more welcoming," she said.

Midterms provide 'great relief'

Jill Ellis-Worthington, 65, of London, Ont., also said the midterms made a recent trip to the U.S. more palatable.

Ellis-Worthington — who is originally from the U.S. but has been living in Canada since age 25 — said she went to her home country this month to deal with issues at a Texas property she owns. It was her first visit since 2024, and one she had put off for as long as possible.

"There's just so much chaos and so much denial of everything that is America going on now with the government, so I just didn't want to support that in any way," she told CBC.

"I think there are a lot of people who feel great relief [after the midterms] and feel that there might be some light on the horizon."

Ellis-Worthington said Americans had been "nothing but friendly, gracious [and] hospitable" during her trip. But she acknowledged that some Canadians likely won't be going back soon, despite last week's vote. "And some won't ever go back, I don’t think."

The Peace Bridge U.S.-Canada border crossing is seen on March 20 in Buffalo, N.Y. (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)

Distrust persists

Indeed, the new Congress doesn't take office until January, and many observers say the Trump administration's policies — including an immigration crackdown that has led to the detention of several Canadian citizens in recent months — continue to fuel distrust.

Mary Thurber, who lives in Lake Country in B.C.'s Okanagan Valley, said she has avoided going to the U.S. for several reasons.

"It's a combination of anger at their policies and disgust with some of the treatment of their own citizens, and frankly, a little bit of fear," said Thurber, 70. "And do I want to support the economy of ... an administration that is actively attacking my country?"

But she said visiting the U.S. is now "an active discussion" in her home after the midterms.

"My husband sometimes says, 'I know! Let's only go to the blue states,'" she said with a laugh. "And I'm like, 'Yeah but that doesn't quite deal with the fact that their president is still actively attacking us.'"

Thurber said she doesn't know when she might feel comfortable going back, adding she expects the Trump administration's policies to have a lasting impact. "That's a hard one," she said.

World.title: Original Star Wars returning to theatres for 50th anniversary
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Missed the initial release of Star Wars in 1977? Maybe you thought it looked weird, didn't want to line up for tickets, or — if you're under 50 — you just weren't born yet.

You'll get another chance on Feb. 19, when Disney re-releases both the original film and a 70-millimetre Imax version to mark its anniversary.

"It is incredibly special to mark the 50th anniversary by returning the original version of Star Wars to theatres so audiences can experience this part of film history on the big screen," said Lynwen Brennan, co-president of Lucasfilm, in a press release.

This won't be the first time Star Wars — now also known as Star Wars: A New Hope — has returned to theatres. For its 20th anniversary, in 1997, creator George Lucas rereleased it with a number of changes, including some CGI touchups, additional scenes and — infamously — the villainous Greedo shooting at Han Solo first in the Mos Eisley Cantina scene.

Disney — which bought the franchise and Lucasfilm in 2012 — says the upcoming release will be a "restored version" of the 1977 film.

The franchise has been under the leadership of Brennan and Dave Filoni since Kathleen Kennedy stepped down in January.

The re-release is part of a slate of projects for 2027, which will also include a new season of the live-action series Ahsoka, a documentary on the making of A New Hope, and the theatrical release of Star Wars: Starfighter.

Ryan Gosling, left, and Shawn Levy speak on stage at Comic-Con in San Diego, Calif., on July 25, 2026. Levy will direct Gosling in next year's new Star Wars film. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

The new movie will hit theatres on May 28 and feature a pair of Canadians.

Ryan Gosling (The Fall Guy, Blade Runner 2049) will star as a cynical rogue (sound familiar?) who has a mysterious past and is thrust into a galactic adventure, working under Montreal-born director Shawn Levy, best known for Big Fat Liar, Night at the Museum and, most recently, Deadpool & Wolverine.

The film will take place five years after the events of 2019's The Rise of Skywalker, according to Lucasfilm.

It will be the first Star Wars film in theatres since last year's The Mandalorian and Grogu, which broke the drought since Rise of Skywalker but grossed just $345.8 US million worldwide, making it the franchise's lowest grossing live-action film ever.

WATCH | Ahsoka season 2 trailer:

The franchise has recently had better luck on the small screen and will release the second season of Ahsoka on Disney+ on Jan. 20, bringing back both Rosario Dawson as the titular former jedi and Hayden Christensen as Anakin Skywalker.

It will pick up where the first season left off, as Ahsoka chases down Grand Admiral Thrawn, a former leader of the Empire who has once again declared war on the Rebel Alliance.

The show will also feature Rory McCann as the recast antagonist Baylan Skol, following the death of Ray Stevenson in 2023.

The documentary The Hero Awakens will be released on Disney+ on May 4 — also known as Star Wars Day.

From filmmaker R.J. Cutler, best known for documentaries such as 1993's The War Room and The September Issue it will, according to a press release, feature never-seen-before archival footage and audio from the making of the 1977 film.

World.title: Indigenous women leaders say budget doesn't address their realities
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Indigenous leaders from across Canada gathered in Ottawa on Thursday to say Prime Minister Mark Carney's new budget leaves Indigenous women out of the decisions made in the more than 500-page document.

"Budget 2026 represents a missed opportunity to make Indigenous women's safety and healing a sustained national priority," said Josie Nepinak, president of the Native Women's Association of Canada.

She was joined by Lisa Pigeau, director of intergovernmental relations for Les Femmes Michif Otipemisiwak, former executive director of Pauktuutit Inuit Women of Canada Rose Mary Cooper, Quebec Native Women President Marjolaine Étienne and Ontario Native Women's Association CEO Cora McGuire-Cyrette.

Cooper said the budget does not account for the dangers Indigenous women face in northern and remote Indigenous communities, adding that Inuit women were not mentioned once in the document.

"For many Indigenous women, safety is a plane ride away," Cooper said, adding that most communities in Inuit Nunangat can only be reached by air, and 60 per cent have no shelters or other safe spaces.

One in six Indigenous women have experienced at least one form of intimate partner violence, according to Statistics Canada. According to federal data, while Indigenous women make up only five per cent of all women in Canada, they made up approximately 26 per cent of women killed by an intimate partner in 2022.

"When an Indigenous woman needs to flee violence, she often must leave her family, her language, her land and her whole surrounding," Cooper said. "A model designed for seven cities does not work in small flying communities where food and housing costs weigh much more. One size does not fit all."

Cooper added that responses "must be tailored to where Indigenous women live and be designed and led by the women who live there."

While Carney's budget pledges $50 billion over the next 10 years to Indigenous programs and services — including $32 billion over 10 years for First Nations housing and infrastructure — many Inuit and Métis groups have expressed concerns over their asks not being met in this year's proposed spending.

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK) told CBC News in a statement earlier this week that while it welcomes the budget's promise of $575 million over five years to fund the Inuit Child First Initiative and transition to the new Inuit-led initiative Pirutsiagutiit, it was "disappointed" by the lack of specific references to Inuit in other areas of the document.

Métis leaders were also concerned earlier this week with the budget's lack of Métis-specific funding, with the word "Métis" only appearing once in the document. Manitoba Métis Federation (MMF) President David Chartrand said he was "appalled" by the absence of distinct funding for Métis.

During Thursday's news conference, the leaders also raised concerns about the government's plan to end homelessness in 10 years. McGuire-Cyrette said this will not be achieved "unless the government works with the agencies on the ground."

Citing a 2024 Ontario Native Women's Association study that 83 per cent of Indigenous women live off reserve in rural and urban centres, she said "the budget is silent for the majority of urban Indigenous agencies" with the majority of investments are going to on-reserve services.

"If we're not at the table, how can you work with us?" she said.

Funding welcome, gaps remain

One significant provision from this year's budget for Indigenous women was providing $3.6 million to renew the Red Dress Alert pilot, which was developed with Indigenous partners to address the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls in Canada (MMIWG).

Nepinak said that while she welcomes the funding and believes it will save lives, it "doesn't fix or address all of the gaps that continue to exist" in safety and protections for Indigenous women.

McGuire-Cyrette added that the investments in the pilot were nice to see, but are for the "aftermath of violence" against Indigenous women, girls and two-spirit people as opposed to prevention.

"We're not seeing those upstream investments," McGuire-Cyrette said.

Cooper added that for Inuit women living in Inuit Nunangat, "the needs are greater and reflecting what those needs are will be important" on how the pilot rolls out.

Pigeau said that while the leaders have not requested a meeting with Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations Rebecca Alty since the budget's tabling last week, they spoke with her before the budget release and look forward to meeting with "all ministers that would be involved" because it's "beyond just one issue."

"It's a multi-systemic approach that is needed to address the gender and orientation-based violence that faces Indigenous women," Pigeau said.

Nepinak added that the leaders brought up the need for supports and investments for Indigenous women's lives in Ottawa in a February conference that Alty attended, but "it feels like it fell on deaf ears."

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Cuban Regime Crackdown on Cell Phone Signal Boosters
World.content:
The use and importing of cellphone signal boosters is prohibited in Cuba.

By Yenys Laura Prieto (El Toque)

HAVANA TIMES – The Cuban government is calling for “citizen surveillance” of unauthorized equipment but offers no solutions to the island’s telecommunications network deficiencies.

In a post on its official Facebook page, Cuba’s Ministry of Communications urged residents to report the installation of cell phone signal boosters without legal authorization. The warning comes as thousands of users struggle with the state telecommunication monopoly Etecsa’s poor network coverage. Those who attempt to improve their reception on their own risk fines and confiscation of their equipment.

Government control also extends to satellite connections. According to the newspaper 14ymedio, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent a notice to diplomatic missions warning that they are prohibited from importing or using Starlink devices. The communication was reportedly addressed to foreign embassies and international organizations accredited in Havana.

Meanwhile, stepped-up repression continues. The arrest of a community activist sparked a neighborhood protest in Guamuta, part of the town of El Cobre in Santiago de Cuba. Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano had been distributing food to people in need. Following his detention, a group of women accompanied by their children took to the streets to demand his release. According to opposition activist Jose Daniel Ferrer, as of November 10, Yoel remained detained at the provincial headquarters of State Security in Santiago de Cuba.

Published in Spanish by El Toque and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Mamma Soul – Song of the Day
World.content:
By Indi Rivero

HAVANA TIMES – Today we feature the Chilean band Mamma Soul with the song “Fe” (Faith) first recorded in 2001.
