Peru’s central bank has raised its benchmark rate to 4.50% to pull inflation, now 5.3%, back toward its 1% to 3% target.

What Happened

The BCRP’s board took the decision at its monthly monetary policy meeting, known as the Programa Monetario, and announced it on Thursday 12 November 2026. The reference rate is the interest rate the bank uses to steer short-term borrowing costs across the economy.

The bank said this is its first increase since 2023. It said the aim is to return inflation to the target range, citing strong supply shocks, expectations above that range and lively domestic demand.

The bank also said the decision does not necessarily start a run of increases. It will weigh core inflation, expectations, economic activity and how long the supply shocks last before changing the rate again.

Apartment towers on the cliffs of Miraflores, a district of Lima, Peru’s capital.

Why It Matters

Annual inflation in Lima, the measure the bank follows, rose from 4.5% in September to 5.3% in October, the bank said. INEI, Peru’s national statistics institute, put the October figure at 5.25% and the monthly rise at 0.57%.

INEI said food and non-alcoholic drinks rose 1.62% in the month, led by fish, vegetables and potatoes. Transport costs also climbed on higher air, road and fuel prices.

Expectations are the bank’s second worry, because they can lock in higher prices. Twelve-month inflation expectations held at 3.1%, slightly above the 3% ceiling of the target range.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, edged up from 4.5% to 4.6%, the bank said. Without transport as well, it stood at 2%, the middle of the target range.

The bank points to El Niño, a warming of Pacific waters that disrupts weather and food supply, and to tensions in the Middle East. It said some of their effects have already reached prices and could prove more lasting than expected.

The bank expects headline and core inflation to return to about 2% over its forecast horizon as the supply shocks fade. It added that most early indicators of activity for October still showed good performance.

What to Watch Next

The next releases on growth and unemployment will show whether domestic demand is cooling. The bank has said a series of hikes is not necessarily coming.

A slowing economy would test the bank’s view that domestic demand is still strong. The bank’s own forecast is that inflation returns to about 2% over its projection horizon as supply shocks fade.

What Is Not Known

The bank has not said whether more increases will follow. It says that depends on core inflation, expectations, activity and the length of the supply shocks.

It is also unclear how long El Niño and the Middle East tensions will push prices up. The bank itself says some of their effects may be more persistent than expected.

What It Means for You

A higher policy rate generally makes borrowing in soles dearer and saving in them more rewarding. The sol traded at about 3.41 per US$ early on Friday 13 November 2026 (market-data rate), and more background is in our Peru coverage.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the BCRP’s reference rate?

It is the interest rate the Central Reserve Bank of Peru sets to guide short-term borrowing costs. It now stands at 4.50%, up from 4.25%.

Why did Peru raise its interest rate?

Annual inflation reached 5.3% in October, above the 1% to 3% target, and expectations also sit above that range. The bank also cited food and energy prices, El Niño and Middle East tensions.

Will more increases follow?

The bank says this does not necessarily begin a series of increases. It will decide on further moves from core inflation, expectations, activity and the length of the supply shocks.

Sources: Central Reserve Bank of Peru, Programa Monetario; INEI, October 2026 consumer prices for Lima.

World.title: Brazil Bank Backs Three Climate Funds
World.content:
Brazil’s state development bank walked into the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, with a headline number and a catch. On Thursday 12 November 2026 it said it could help mobilise R$39 billion (about US$6.9 billion) for clean-energy and decarbonisation projects.

The catch is that most of that money does not exist yet. It is a potential figure that depends on three new private funds raising their equity and attracting loans.

BNDES, Brazil’s state development bank, and the Green Climate Fund, a UN-backed climate fund. —What. The Green Climate Fund backs two private funds with US$300 million; BNDES invests in three. —When. Announced Thursday 12 November 2026 at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. —Next step. The funds must now raise their money and attract private investors.

The bank, known as BNDES, picked three climate funds in a public call and is now putting its own money into them, with a US$300 million boost from the world’s largest multilateral climate fund.

What Happened

BNDES, the Brazilian National Development Bank, said the Green Climate Fund (GCF) approved money for two of the three funds it chose in a public call launched in 2025. The GCF is the largest multilateral climate fund, set up under the United Nations climate process to channel money to developing countries.

The GCF’s project page shows its board approved US$250 million on Wednesday 28 October 2026 for the Catalytic Transition Fund Brazil, run by the Canadian asset manager Brookfield. BNDES said the GCF also approved US$50 million for the Flying Rivers Fund II, run by the Brazilian manager eB Capital.

BNDES said it will invest in the Brookfield fund and in the Flying Rivers fund. It will also back Just Climate Brasil, managed by the London investment firm Generation Investment Management.

Solar panels in Chile’s northern desert, the kind of clean-energy asset such funds target across Latin America. Photo: Ministerio Bienes Nacionales, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

BNDES expects the three funds to attract further private investment. It says that brings the total mobilised to R$39 billion.

The R$39 billion is converted at about 5.64 reais per US dollar, a market rate on 13 November 2026. BNDES describes it as the total it expects the three funds and their investors to mobilise.

Why It Matters

The GCF’s US$250 million anchors a vehicle of up to US$1.3 billion. It is the first GCF project in Brazil channelled through a Brazilian accredited entity.

Brookfield, a Canadian asset manager, is the partner for the vehicle. How quickly the money will be put to work has not been announced.

BNDES says it wants to combine public money, international concessional capital and private investment. The GCF decision gives that plan an international backer.

What to Watch Next

The first test is fundraising: each fund must reach its target before it can invest. Brookfield’s vehicle is the largest, so its progress will signal how much appetite foreign investors have for Brazilian climate assets.

The second test is the debt. Whether lenders supply the rest of the money will show if the R$39 billion headline turns into projects, and no date for that has been published.

What Is Not Known

BNDES has not said when each fund will close its fundraising or make its first investment. The US$50 million for the Flying Rivers fund rests on BNDES’s own account.

The split between equity and loans is BNDES’s own expectation, not a commitment from named lenders. Nor is it known how much will come from foreign rather than Brazilian investors.

What It Means for You

For US investors, the funds are a way to see how a state bank and a UN climate fund try to share risk with private capital in Brazil. Anyone considering exposure should treat the R$39 billion as a ceiling, not a forecast.

More coverage is in our Brazil section, our report on Turkey’s green ambitions at COP31 and our look at BNDES’s first-half profit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the R$39 billion already available?

No. It is a potential total that depends on the three funds raising money and attracting private investment.

Who is putting in public money?

BNDES says it is investing in three climate funds. The Green Climate Fund approved US$250 million for the Brookfield fund and, per BNDES, US$50 million for the Flying Rivers fund.

What do the funds invest in?

BNDES describes the whole package as aimed at industrial decarbonisation and energy transition. It says the funds will draw in private money alongside public capital.

World.title: Haiti Police Retake Stadium From Gangs
World.content:
HAITI · SECURITY

Published Thursday, Nov. 12, 9:40 p.m. ET (same time in Port-au-Prince) · Source: Haitian National Police, Salvadoran presidency

Key Facts Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Haiti story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? What Haiti’s police say they retook Sylvio Cator Stadium in Port-au-Prince from gangs after about two years.

Who Police and a special unit called the Task Force; Salvadoran soldiers now guard the site.

Next El Salvador’s president says his troops will build a base there to push deeper into gang territory.

Unknown Police gave no exact hour, no troop numbers and no casualty figures.

This story is part of our coverage of the haiti crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Haiti Gang Chief Wants UN Drone Probe

In plain English Gangs have held much of Haiti for years, and in 2024 they seized the national football stadium in the capital. Haiti’s police and troops from El Salvador, whose president Nayib Bukele is known for a harsh crackdown on gangs at home, say they have taken it back.

For two years, Haiti’s national football stadium belonged to gangs. On Thursday, 12 November 2026, police said it is theirs again.

Haiti’s National Police said they retook Sylvio Cator Stadium in downtown Port-au-Prince in the early hours of that day. It is the latest turn in the Haiti crisis, in which armed groups control much of the country.

Police said in a statement that they regained control of the stadium and its surroundings together with a special unit they call the Task Force. They then handed security of the site to Salvadoran soldiers, troops sent by El Salvador to help fight Haiti’s gangs.

Why This Stadium Matters

Sylvio Cator opened in 1953 and holds about 10,000 spectators. It was the home ground of Haiti’s national football team until the violence forced the players abroad.

The stadium stands in central Port-au-Prince, near the Bicentenaire district, the Portail-Léogâne area and the roads leading to Martissant. That position gives its holders a view of key access routes into the city.

Haiti played its home World Cup qualifiers in Curaçao instead. The team, coached by France’s Sébastien Migné, still reached its second World Cup finals, then lost all three group games, to Scotland, Brazil and Morocco.

File photo, 23 November 2022. Soldiers of the Salvadoran armed forces at a ceremony. (Photo: Casa Presidencial El Salvador, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Haiti Email address Follow

Bukele Promises an Offensive

Bukele wrote on X (formerly Twitter) in Haitian Creole on Thursday that his forces would now set up an operational base in the stadium. He said they would use it to advance into the heart of gang-held territory.

He told gang members to leave and warned that those who stay to fight will bear the consequences. His video shows soldiers and armoured vehicles inside the stadium.

About 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers arrived in late October. Bukele’s methods at home have drawn accusations of human rights abuses.

The Gang Suppression Force, the United Nations-backed multinational mission in Haiti, is a separate body. On Tuesday, 10 November, Bukele said his troops had destroyed the headquarters of 400 Mawozo, one of Haiti’s main gangs, based around Croix-des-Bouquets near the capital.

What It Means for US Readers

The 400 Mawozo gang kidnapped 17 missionaries from Christian Aid Ministries, an Ohio-based charity, in October 2021. Sixteen were Americans and one was Canadian, and all had been freed or had escaped by mid-December 2021.

A Salvadoran-led push against that gang is therefore a story with an American memory attached. Travellers should keep treating Haiti as unsafe; our Haiti travel safety guide has the details.

What Is Not Known

The police statement gave no exact hour, no count of the officers or soldiers involved and no casualty figures. How the work was split between police, the Task Force and Salvadoran troops, is unclear.

The base is so far Bukele’s announcement alone. We had found no reaction from the United Nations, the Gang Suppression Force (the UN-backed multinational mission) or Haiti’s government at the time of writing.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Haitian police announce?

They said they retook Sylvio Cator Stadium in Port-au-Prince from gangs in the early hours of Thursday, 12 November 2026. Salvadoran soldiers then took over security of the site.

What happens next at the stadium?

El Salvador’s president Nayib Bukele says his troops will set up an operational base there. He says it will support an offensive into gang-held areas.

Sources: Statement of the Haitian National Police Communications Directorate, 12 November 2026; post by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele on X, 12 November 2026 and his announcement of 10 November 2026; UN Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH); Rio Times reporting on the Haiti crisis.

World.title: Pope Leo Moved to Tears at Lima Youth Vigil
World.content:
Key Facts —What. Pope Leo XIV led a youth vigil at Lima’s national stadium on Thursday 12 November, starting at 18:00. —Crowd. Media counts range from about 50,000 to about 60,000 people, and no official figure has been published. He called the young people “the sign of hope” and told them not to rush their answers. —Next. He travels to Chiclayo on Friday 13 November, and the Lima Mass follows on Monday 16 November. —As of 12 November 2026, 9:00 pm Lima time (02:00 GMT 13 November)

A stadium full of young people chanted “¡Se siente, se siente, León está presente!” (“You can feel it, Leo is here”) on Thursday evening, and the man they were cheering was moved to tears, local outlets report. Pope Leo XIV, the first US-born pope, led a youth vigil at Lima’s Estadio Nacional, the national stadium, on day two of his visit to Peru, which began with the arrival we covered in Pope Leo Lands in Lima, Greeted by Fujimori.

Peru was his home for years as a missionary and bishop, which is why Catholics in the United States are following this trip closely. Local media counted tens of thousands in the stands, from about 50,000 to about 60,000, and no official figure exists.

What We Know

The vigil began at 18:00 Lima time on Thursday 12 November. Cardinal Carlos Castillo, the Archbishop of Lima, welcomed the Pope and asked, “¿has visto que estos jóvenes del medio bailan precioso?” (“have you seen how beautifully these young people in the middle are dancing?”).

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 53.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The crowd then chanted the line that means “You can feel it, Leo is here.” Local outlets report that the chant greeted his arrival.

Young people then sang the hymn “Alma misionera” (“Missionary Soul”) for him. Leo was visibly moved, and local outlets describe him close to tears at several moments.

Lima’s Plaza Mayor, the historic main square, at night.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Lima (Peru) Email address Follow

What the Pope Told the Young People

Three young people shared testimonies before his talk: Joao, Emily and Sister Luzbinda, a Catholic nun. He thanked them with the words “nos han abierto sus corazones” (“they have opened their hearts to us”).

He said someone had told him that Peru needs a sign of hope. “Hoy son ustedes ese signo de esperanza,” he said (“today you are that sign of hope”).

His theme was passion, vocation and friendship. He built it on a question from the Gospel of John, “¿Qué buscas?” (“What are you looking for?”), and added “No tengan prisa por responder” (“Do not rush to answer”).

He spoke about pain directly: “Cuando sufran, acudan a Jesús” (“when you suffer, go to Jesus”). He asked them not to fear speaking to Jesus honestly, even when they struggle to find words to pray.

He also told them “No se conformen con vivir siguiendo lo que otros esperan de ustedes” (“do not settle for living as others expect of you”). God, he said, made each of them able to do a good that no one else can do in exactly the same way.

He urged silent time before the Blessed Sacrament, the consecrated bread at the heart of Catholic worship, to discern a path. That path could be priesthood, consecrated life, marriage or service to others, and he said past mistakes do not stop a fresh start.

He quoted an earlier pope, Benedict XVI: “El mal envenena siempre” (“evil always poisons”). The quotation is dated to a homily of 8 December 2005.

Remembering Two Young Protesters

Castillo also remembered two young protesters, Inti Sotelo (24) and Bryan Pintado (22), whom he called “mártires de los jóvenes” (“martyrs of the young”). RPP, a Lima news outlet, reports that they died in November 2020 from police pellets during marches against the government of Manuel Merino, then interim president.

What Is Not Known

No official attendance figure has been published, so the range of 50,000 to 60,000 rests on media counts. We have also found no official security or health figures, and the contents of any private meetings are unknown.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The Pope travels north on Friday 13 November to Chiclayo, the city where he served as bishop, for a Mass at the Pampas de Pimentel, an open field near the city. Local reports describe long queues and uncertainty about free entry.

The Lima Mass is on Monday 16 November, and our guide explains how the free tickets work. Our trip schedule lists the other stops.

For US readers, the vigil shows how warmly the first US-born pope is received in the country where he lived for years. Our report on how the Pope received the keys to Lima shows the same welcome from the city.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where was the Pope’s youth vigil in Lima?

It began at 18:00 Lima time on Thursday 12 November at Estadio Nacional, Lima’s national stadium, on day two of Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Peru.

How many people attended the vigil?

Media counts range from about 50,000 to about 60,000 people. No official attendance figure has been found.

What did Pope Leo tell the young people?

He called them “the sign of hope,” urged them to turn to Jesus when they suffer, and asked them not to settle for living as others expect.

Where does the Pope go next?

On Friday 13 November he travels to Chiclayo in northern Peru, where he served as bishop, for a Mass at the Pampas de Pimentel, an open field near the city. The Lima Mass is on 16 November.

03 Why it moved

First, supply, with fairly high confidence. Wheat has been sliding for a month on expectations of ample global stocks, and the fund is down 11.16% over 20 sessions.

Second, the dollar and borrowing costs, with medium confidence. The dollar index rose 0.25% on the day and the US 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.10%, a combination that makes dollar-priced grain dearer for foreign buyers.

Third, the cross-asset picture is mixed. The S&P 500 slipped 0.35% and the gold fund fell 2.82%, which points to broad selling of assets rather than a grain-specific panic, while the oil fund rose 3.25% and did not lift grains.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. Wheat has lost 11.16% over 20 sessions and 14.9% over 60, while corn is down 6.87% over 20 sessions and 8.9% over 60.

Soybeans are the exception. They are 8.6% below their 10 September high of 28.14, yet only 1.7% lower over 60 sessions.

Our own archive adds perspective. Wheat has fallen 11.2% in 20 sessions before; in 23 earlier cases that large it was higher 20 sessions later only 10 times (43%), with a median change of 0.0% and a worst case of 23.9% lower.

Corn fell 6.9% in 20 sessions in 52 earlier cases, and was higher 20 sessions later in 25 of them (48%), with a median of 0.7% lower. Soybeans fared best: in 61 earlier cases of a 4.5% drop, 38 (62%) were higher 20 sessions later. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil is the world’s biggest soybean exporter and Argentina a giant in wheat, corn and soy products, so lower prices cut the dollars flowing to farmers, port towns and national budgets. Because a stronger dollar usually weakens the Brazilian real and the Argentine peso, growers’ local-currency income is cushioned, though input costs rise too.

Mexico, a heavy corn importer, and Chile and Peru, which buy wheat, gain from cheaper cargoes.

06 The names to watch

For investors the proxies are SOYB, CORN and WEAT, which are US-listed funds that track grain futures. In São Paulo, farm-exposed listed companies and fertiliser or machinery makers tend to follow the same direction.

Corn is the one to watch: it sits only 3.8% above its 29 June low of 16.47, so any further slide tests that floor. Wheat has no nearby floor in the 12-month data, and its high of 28.00 is far above.

07 What would end it

The levels are plain. Corn must hold 16.47, soybeans have support at their January low of 21.71 and resistance at 28.14, and wheat needs to reclaim the round figure of 25 to ease the selling.

The catalysts are the dollar, US interest rates and the next crop reports. A weaker dollar or smaller crops would stop the slide.

The honest answer is that wheat has little reason to stop soon. Corn and soybeans are closer to turning points.

08 What to watch

It stands at 103.17; a retreat would lift all three grains. US Treasury yields: The 10-year at 5.10% raises the cost of holding commodity positions.

Ample global wheat supply, a firmer dollar and rising US yields pushed prices down. Wheat fell most.

Does the dollar affect grain prices?

Yes. Grains are priced in dollars, so a stronger dollar makes them dearer for foreign buyers and tends to depress prices.

Who gains from cheaper grain?

Importers such as Mexico, Chile and Peru, and consumers of bread and meat. Exporters such as Brazil and Argentina lose revenue.

01 The session in one read

Oil rose because a peace bet was partly unwound. President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran. US crude for December delivery (WTI) rose about 3% to roughly US$89 a barrel, and Brent, the international benchmark, about 3.5% to roughly US$96.

Traders who had sold oil on hopes of de-escalation bought it back. That is why a fund tracking US crude jumped 3.25% in one day.

For a reader outside the market, the lesson is simple: oil is being priced on diplomacy, not on shortages.

Assessment — A bounce inside a bigger retreat MEDIUM The best-supported reading is that Thursday was a rebound inside a correction, not a new uptrend: the fund is down 7.15% over 20 sessions even after the gain, and the 5-session change is still negative at 1.44%. We hold this view with medium confidence because the geopolitical news can reverse within hours; the variable to watch is whether talks with Iran resume or finally collapse.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest: Iran diplomacy. Mr Trump’s statement removed some of the peace premium that had pulled oil down since late October, and the market reacted at once.

Second: stocks of oil in the United States. The US Energy Information Administration (eia.gov) reported commercial crude stocks up 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million in the week to 6 November, against a forecast draw of 1.1 million in the RT economic calendar. Gasoline stocks rose 1.8 million barrels and distillates (diesel and heating oil) 4.1 million, which tempers the rally.

Third, the conflicting signals. The dollar index is not the cause here; it edged up 0.25% to 103.17 and the US 10-year yield rose to 5.10%, both normally negative for oil, while the S&P 500 fell 0.35% and the VIX fear gauge rose 6.92% to 18.70.

So geopolitics outweighed the macro backdrop on the day. We are fairly sure of that ranking, around 70% confident, because the timing of the Trump remarks matches the move and the usual drivers pointed the other way.

04 The trend behind it

The fund hit its 12-month high of 169.53 on 23 October and has retreated 13.8% since. Over 60 sessions it is still up 11.6%, so the longer run is higher, while the recent month is lower.

This looks like a continuation of an October-to-November pullback, with Thursday as a pause.

Our own history since 2007 gives some perspective. After 91 earlier falls of this size, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 52 cases (57%), with a median gain of 1.2% but a worst case of a 50.1% drop; history is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil is the clearest loser from the slide in the equity. Petrobras is down 28.46% in 20 sessions and 30.8% below its October high, even though crude has fallen only 7.15% over the same stretch; on Thursday its New York shares rose 1.57% to US$18.10.

Colombia’s Ecopetrol is 16.1% below its 15 September high of 18.26 and has lost 13.45% in 20 sessions, a reminder that Bogotá’s budget leans on oil. Argentina’s YPF slipped only 0.43% on Thursday.

Guyana’s boom, led by ExxonMobil’s Stabroek block, an offshore oil field, matters more for volume than for Thursday’s price.

06 The names to watch

Petrobras is the stress test. Its shares have fallen far more than crude, so investors are pricing company-specific worries on top of the commodity.

Ecopetrol and YPF are the other two Latin American names to follow, because both are tied to the oil price but trade on different local stories.

07 What would end it

The decisive event is Iran: renewed talks would push oil down again, while a clear breakdown would send it back towards the 12-month high of 169.53. The 20-session low area, and below that the 66.17 low, sit far beneath and would need a genuine collapse in demand to be tested.

Next in the calendar are the weekly US inventory reports, and any further statement from Washington or Tehran. Does the pullback stop? Not until the peace-or-war question is settled, and on Thursday’s evidence it is not.

08 What to watch

Iran diplomacy: Any restart or breakdown of talks is the single biggest swing factor for oil.

Any restart or breakdown of talks is the single biggest swing factor for oil. US inventories: Weekly crude and fuel builds can cap rallies; draws would support them.

Weekly crude and fuel builds can cap rallies; draws would support them. Treasury yields: The 10-year at 5.10% is a headwind for commodities if it keeps rising.

The 10-year at 5.10% is a headwind for commodities if it keeps rising. Petrobras 18.10 area and its 20-session slide: Whether the company stabilises after losing 28.46% in 20 sessions.

No. USO is a fund that tracks US crude futures, so it follows oil closely but is not the spot price itself.

03 Why it moved

First cause, with the most weight: American borrowing costs. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.10% from 4.98% on Tuesday (the US bond market was shut on Wednesday), while the dollar index rose 0.25% to 103.17. A hot US inflation report earlier in the week keeps traders pricing a Federal Reserve rate rise rather than a cut.

Higher yields hurt steel twice: they make factories and building projects costlier to finance, and they pull money out of emerging-market shares. Confidence in this link: medium to high.

Some signals disagreed. Oil rose and the gold fund fell sharply, so this was not a simple flight to safety. We found no company news for Gerdau, CSN or Usiminas on the day, so the CSN overshoot is our reading of a thinly priced share, with low confidence.

04 The trend behind it

The fund SLX is 7.3% lower over 60 sessions and 2.81% lower over 20, though it is 2.78% higher over five. It sits 12.9% below its 2 June high of 113.57 and 30.4% above its November 2025 low of 75.82, so this is a correction inside a year of recovery.

Gerdau is 12.28% lower over 20 sessions and 15.5% below its 20 October high of 5.24. CSN’s ADR is 32.84% lower over 20 sessions and 63.6% below its 28 January high of 2.12, only 8.2% above its 3 November low of 0.71.

On balance this is a continuation of a weak autumn rather than a new phase.

05 What it means for Latin America

Mexico is the relative winner on the day. Ternium, the Luxembourg-based steelmaker with large Mexican operations, fell 2.11%, well below the 7% drop at CSN, which suggests Mexican demand is seen as steadier than Brazil’s.

Brazil is the harder case. Gerdau lost 3.49% and CSN 7% in New York. For Brazilian savers and for investors holding steel in São Paulo, the point is that rates, not just trade policy, are driving the sector.

06 The names to watch

Gerdau is the one with history on its side. In our own price record since 2007 there were 75 earlier cases when it fell 12.3% or more in 20 sessions; 20 sessions later it was higher in 39 of them (52%), the median change was +1.4% and the worst was -58.0%. History is not a forecast.

CSN’s record is gloomier. In 17 earlier cases of a fall as deep as 32.8% in 20 sessions, it was higher 20 sessions later in only 7 (41%), with a median of -1.4% and a worst case of -45.5%.

Ternium is the steadier holding on the day. Its New York shares closed at US$50.45, and Usiminas had no verified move to report.

The selling stops when US yields stop rising. A calmer 10-year yield below Thursday’s 5.10% would take pressure off all three names, while another leg up would keep it on.

The slower catalysts are company results and any change in trade policy, neither with a confirmed date. Does it stop? Not until rates stop rising.

The trigger was a surge in US bond yields, the interest rate the American government pays to borrow for ten years. Zinc coats steel to stop it rusting and goes into buildings and cars, so its price follows global growth. Thursday, 12 November 2026 was a day when money ran from anything tied to metals. Buenaventura, Peru’s big gold and silver miner, and Nexa both fell, and for Buenaventura it was the third losing day in a row.

Zinc is the quiet workhorse of the metals world: roughly half of it galvanises steel, and the rest goes into die-castings, brass and batteries. We read it today through two listed proxies, because shares of miners tell us how investors feel about the metal’s outlook.

Assessment — Rates shock, not a mine problem MEDIUM The best-supported reading is that a rising US yields and a firmer dollar hit gold hard and pulled miners down with it. 03 Why it moved

Cause one, and the heaviest, is the bond market. The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to 5.10% from 4.98% on Tuesday (the US bond market was shut on Wednesday), and the dollar index edged up 0.25% to 103.17. A hot US inflation report earlier in the week strengthened the case for the Federal Reserve to raise rates again.

Cause two is the gold sell-off. The gold fund GLD fell 2.82%, its lowest close in 12 months. Buenaventura, which digs gold and silver as well as zinc, feels this directly.

Cause three is Nexa’s own slide. We found no company news for Nexa or Buenaventura on the day, so we treat their moves as market-driven; Nexa has lost 19.3% over 60 sessions.

The signals do not fully agree. The S&P 500 slipped only 0.35% and oil rose 3.25%, so this was not a general panic, although the VIX fear gauge rose 6.92% to 18.70. We are fairly confident (medium) that rates and gold explain most of the fall; the exact split between them and Nexa’s own news is our judgement.

04 The trend behind it

Nexa has lost 19.3% over 60 sessions and 8.41% over 20, and sits 31.6% below its 12-month high of US$16.72, reached on 6 May 2026. It remains 91.5% above its November 2025 low of US$5.97, so the longer picture is of a huge rebound that is now unwinding.

Buenaventura is in a harsher phase: it has fallen 18.78% over 20 sessions and 25.5% over 60, and sits 42.1% below its 12-month high of US$43.67 from 27 February 2026. Its 12-month low of US$22.78 was set on 20 November 2025, only 11.1% below Thursday’s close, which makes this a continuation of a long downtrend, with the floor now close.

History offers context, not a forecast. After earlier falls of this size, Nexa was higher 20 sessions later in 27 of 53 cases, or 51%, with a median gain of 1.5% and a worst case of a 54.5% loss. Buenaventura was higher in 22 of 37 cases, or 59%, with a median gain of 3.4% and a worst case of a 28.1% loss.

05 What it means for Latin America

Peru is the most exposed. Zinc and gold are among its biggest exports, and Buenaventura and Nexa’s Peruvian operations are major employers and taxpayers, so weak shares signal a weaker tax take if prices stay low.

Brazil, Mexico and Bolivia, also large producers, tend to move with the same global price, so their mining budgets face the same pressure. For savers holding Latin American mining funds, the lesson is that US interest rates can matter as much as local mine news.

06 The names to watch

Nexa is the cleaner zinc play. Its New York shares fell 4.59% to US$11.43, 31.6% below their 12-month high of US$16.72, though still 91.5% above their November 2025 low.

Buenaventura is the gold-and-silver barometer. It is the stock that tells you whether the gold sell-off is spreading, and its fall to the lowest close in at least six months shows how far confidence has gone.

07 What would end it

The first level is Buenaventura’s 12-month low of US$22.78, because a fall below it would open a new leg lower. For Nexa the nearest marker is the recent trading range under US$12, with the 12-month high of US$16.72 the distant ceiling.

The decisive event is the next US inflation reading and the Fed’s December meeting: a cooler number that pulls the 10-year yield back below 5% would likely lift both stocks. Does it stop? Only when yields stop climbing, and nothing on Thursday’s board suggests that has happened yet.

US Treasury yields rose to 5.10% and gold fell, which made metals and miners less attractive. Nexa Resources lost 4.59% and Buenaventura 3.07%.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Fire 36 Finance Ministry Workers Over Mouse-Jiggler App
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Finance Ministry is still working to fire 36 employees accused of installing a mouse-jiggler program to make it look as if they were working during remote-work shifts. The ministry will not yet say whether the software exposed any of its systems. The ministry announced the dismissal proceedings on Sept. 10.

Vice Minister of Revenue Víctor Carvajal said at the time that the program simulated mouse movement on institutional computers, so the employees appeared active and their screens did not lock during the workday. Carvajal said the 36 work in the ministry’s revenue, expenditure and administrative areas. He said the evidence pointed to possible job abandonment and that the employees would lose their telework arrangements while the dismissal process runs its course.

The program identified in the case is called Move Mouse. The ministry says it uses web-browsing controls and monitors the security of its equipment, yet the employees were able to install the program on government computers without authorization. Jeffrey Taylor, the ministry’s director of technology and digital innovation, said the ban on unauthorized software rests on the institution’s information-security and software-management policies, along with other general regulations. He did not specify which provisions apply or what sanctions they carry.

Asked whether the program led to data theft, infections or exposed credentials, Taylor said the state of the investigation did not allow the ministry to provide further information. He said the ministry took immediate steps to stop the installation and use of the software once the cases were identified. A technical team is now drafting a plan to tighten controls, he said.

The ministry oversees the country’s tax collection and holds tax records for individuals and businesses. In April 2022, a ransomware attack by the Conti group knocked its tax and customs systems offline for weeks. Costa Rica’s professional association for computing, the Colegio de Profesionales en Informática y Computación, said mouse-jiggler tools are not malicious in themselves and have legitimate uses. It warned, however, that keeping a session open with no one at the keyboard can expose information and systems to unauthorized access.

The association also cautioned that the mere presence of such a program on a computer does not prove misconduct. It said investigators should establish who installed it, who ran it and why, noting that the user account linked to an installation does not always identify the person responsible.

The dismissals must still clear administrative proceedings before they become final. The ministry, now headed by former President Rodrigo Chaves, has not named the employees.

World.title: Two Arrested in Killing of American Surfer Kurt Van Dyke in Costa Rica
World.content:
Costa Rican investigators have arrested two people in the February killing of Kurt Van Dyke. He was the 66-year-old American surfer and Puerto Viejo hotel owner found dead in his home near Cahuita on Valentine’s Day. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) detained a 31-year-old woman and a 34-year-old man today. The arrests came during three raids in the Guápiles area of Limón.

Both are suspects in an aggravated homicide investigation. Both were handed over to prosecutors, who will decide whether to seek charges or precautionary measures. Neither has been charged. Investigators now say the attack was not the random robbery it first appeared to be. According to the OIJ’s preliminary findings, the suspects allegedly planned the assault to obtain the PINs of bank cards linked to Van Dyke’s hotel.

The woman was in the home on the morning of Feb. 14 and was initially reported as a survivor of the attack. OIJ deputy director Vladimir Muñoz said she had a direct personal relationship with Van Dyke. Investigators allege she helped the attackers get into the house. Muñoz said Gutiérrez entered the home with two other men who have not yet been identified. According to his account, the group used violence to try to force Van Dyke to give up his card PINs. When that failed, Muñoz said, they beat and tortured him.

Van Dyke was found under a bed with apparent stab wounds and signs of asphyxia. The OIJ received the report at about 10:50 a.m. that Saturday. Investigators also allege that the group staged the theft of the woman’s car to hide her role. The vehicle was later found undamaged in the Atlantic region, which the OIJ considers evidence supporting her alleged participation.

Agents seized cell phones and a vehicle believed to have carried Gutiérrez and the two other men to the scene. Muñoz said two more people remain to be arrested in the case. Van Dyke grew up in Santa Cruz, California. He came to Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean in the 1980s, drawn by Salsa Brava, the powerful reef break off Puerto Viejo.

Known in surfing circles as “King,” he was a nephew of Hawaii big-wave pioneer Fred Van Dyke. For decades he ran Hotel Puerto Viejo, a regular stop for traveling surfers. His death drew international coverage. It also led the Costa Rican Hotel Chamber and local tourism leaders to voice concern about the region’s image. Tourism Minister William Rodríguez offered condolences at the time and said Costa Rica remains a safe destination.

The Public Ministry is expected to request precautionary measures in the coming days, which could include pretrial detention. The OIJ has not identified the two remaining suspects. Anyone with information can contact the agency’s confidential line at 800-8000-645.

World.title: 5 Costa Rica Parks With Closed Trails or New Rules This High Season
World.content:
High season is starting, and several of Costa Rica’s best-known national parks have a trail, an entrance or a whole sector closed. Others are open but are letting in fewer people under stricter rules. Here’s what’s shut, what’s open with conditions, and what to check before you buy a ticket.

Entry to most national parks is sold only online, and many parks close one day a week. Volcano parks can change their rules with little notice, so check the park’s official page the day before you go.

1. Marino Ballena National Park

The Piñuela sector closed on Monday, Nov. 9, and is expected to stay closed for six months because its facilities have deteriorated. You can’t walk in, and boats can’t drop off or pick up passengers there. The bathrooms and showers at Piñuela are also closed. The Uvita, Colonia and Ballena sectors stay open.

If your tour lands at Piñuela, ask your operator how the plan has changed.

2. Manuel Antonio National Park

The Punta Catedral trail is temporarily closed. It’s the loop over the headland between the park’s two main beaches, with lookouts over the Pacific. No reopening date has been given. The rest of the park is open Wednesday through Monday. It closes every Tuesday.

3. Poás Volcano National Park

Poás is open, but since Aug. 28 it has admitted about half as many people and you must wear a helmet. The rules followed a moderate eruption that threw rock from the crater. The park now admits 1,064 visitors a day, down from 2,052. Only two trails are open: the main trail to the crater lookout and the Sombrilla de Pobre trail. Up to 56 people at a time can stand at the lookout, for 20 minutes per group.

The limits stay in place until volcanic activity drops enough to lower the risk. Book early, because half the daily tickets means they sell out faster.

4. Rincón de la Vieja National Park

The trail to the active crater is still closed. It stays shut until activity drops enough for the climb to be considered safe. The volcano has been one of the country’s most active this year. Five districts of Upala and Liberia near the volcano have been under a yellow alert since Oct. 1.

The Las Pailas sector, with its mud pots and steam vents, is open Tuesday through Sunday, well below the summit.

5. Corcovado National Park

The Sirena, Los Patos and El Tigre sectors were closed to tourists through October for maintenance and the heaviest rains. Only San Pedrillo and La Leona stayed open.

Daily limits also apply. Sirena takes 366 visitors a day, San Pedrillo 120, and La Leona, Los Patos and El Tigre 80 each. Before you travel, confirm with your guide or lodge that your sector has reopened.

Playa Langosta, near Tamarindo

This isn’t a trail closure. Environmental authorities are investigating a die-off of fish, sharks, rays and birds in the San Francisco estuary at Playa Langosta. They have asked people not to alter the estuary’s mouth to the sea without permission.

The national park system has more than two dozen protected areas open to visitors, and most trails are running normally this season. Tickets, schedules and closures are posted on each park’s official page, and those pages are the most reliable guide to what’s open on the day you plan to go.

World.title: Four in Ten Costa Ricans Hold Back Opinions on Social Media Out of Fear
World.content:
Four in ten Costa Ricans say they have held back from sharing their opinions on social media for fear of the consequences, according to a national survey released yesterday by the University of Costa Rica (UCR). The fourth National Survey on Freedom of Expression and Trust in the Media found that 40.1% of respondents have stopped expressing their views online out of fear, down from 46.5% in 2025 and the lowest level since the survey began in 2023.

For the first time, a majority, 56.2%, said they had not held back, after that figure hovered around 48% in the three previous editions. The survey does not specify what respondents fear, whether criticism, harassment, consequences at work or something else. Women were more likely to stay silent. After controlling for age, education and political attitudes, researchers found that women were 10 percentage points more likely than men to say they avoid expressing opinions on social media.

The findings matter because social media has become the main way Costa Ricans follow national news. According to the survey, 70.7% regularly or always use social networks to stay informed, compared with 46.2% who often watch television newscasts. The gap between the two has widened since 2025, when social media first overtook television, and radio news now ranks last.

Perceptions of free speech in general also improved. The share of people who believe freedom of expression is at risk in Costa Rica fell to 54.7%, from 73.4% in 2025. This year’s edition is the first carried out since President Laura Fernández took office in May 2026. According to the survey, 60.1% now believe the government respects freedom of expression, the highest share recorded by the study.

Trust in the press rose sharply. For the first time since the survey began, a majority of respondents, 56.2%, said they trust the news media, up from 43.4% in 2025, 35.6% in 2024 and 32.6% in 2023. Trust in journalists themselves reached 71.5%, the highest in the survey’s four editions.

At the same time, 58.1% said working as a journalist in Costa Rica is dangerous, the highest share since the question was first asked and up from 48% in 2023. The finding comes amid broader scrutiny of press freedom in Costa Rica. The survey also points to the reach of misinformation. One in three respondents, 33.5%, admitted recently believing information that later turned out to be false, up from 28.1% in 2025. Facebook was the platform most often cited as the source, followed by TikTok and WhatsApp.

Looking back at the 2026 election campaign, 49% said they had come across false content about presidential candidates and 43% about the Supreme Elections Tribunal. The study was carried out by UCR’s Freedom of Expression and Right to Information Program (PROLEDI), together with the university’s Communication Research Center (CICOM) and Center for Political Research and Studies (CIEP).

Researchers interviewed 993 adults with mobile phones, selected at random, between Sept. 2 and 14, 2026. The maximum margin of error is 3.1 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. Taken together, the results show fewer Costa Ricans censoring themselves online than a year ago, while a substantial share still hesitate to speak freely in the digital spaces where most of the country now gets its news.

World.title: San Ramón Forests Hold Nearly Half of Costa Rica’s Bat Species
World.content:
The forests around San Ramón shelter at least 56 bat species, nearly half of all those recorded in Costa Rica, according to researchers at the University of Costa Rica (UCR) who are studying how these often-misunderstood mammals cope as their habitat is broken up by farms, pastures and towns.

The work is led by UCR’s Western Campus in San Ramón, where scientists and students are tracking how bats respond to changes in their surroundings and what that means for forests and farming. One study sampled seven sites in and around the Alberto Manuel Brenes Biological Reserve to examine how forest fragmentation and degradation affect bat populations. Researchers captured and studied 407 bats from 39 species, including 10 species that had never before been documented in the area.

Those new records helped raise the known total for the wider San Ramón region to at least 56 species. UCR researcher Daniel Zamora said the findings show the importance of protecting not only large, continuous forests but also the smaller patches of vegetation that link one habitat to another. Landscapes that mix farms, pastures, forest and homes, he said, can still support remarkable biodiversity.

One encouraging result was the abundance of fruit-eating bats. By dispersing seeds, they help plants spread and drive the natural regeneration of tropical forests. Other species eat insects, which could make them valuable to farmers. UCR graduate student Katherine Álvarez is studying whether insect-eating bats help control pests that attack potato crops in Cartago, with the aim of producing evidence that supports conservation and encourages growers to see bats as allies.

The university is also looking at how bats adapt to cities, including the role of protected green spaces in San Ramón and Liberia. Researchers are combining field surveys with acoustic monitoring, which records bats’ echolocation calls, to map where different species live and how they respond to changing environments. A recent urban wildlife survey in Heredia found similar surprises in city green spaces.

Other studies are examining parasites carried by bats, and a project on their anatomy and evolutionary relationships is planned for 2027. Alongside the science, the program runs environmental education activities aimed at dispelling myths about bats. Researchers work with students, community groups, landowners and conservation organizations to share what they find and build support for protecting the animals.

World.title: Luisa Stefani Moves Closer to WTA Finals Semifinals After Dramatic Comeback
World.content:
Brazil’s Luisa Stefani and Canadian partner Gabriela Dabrowski moved closer to the WTA Finals doubles semifinals Wednesday after producing a dramatic comeback to defeat Wimbledon champions Guo Hanyu and Kristina Mladenovic in a match that lasted more than two hours.

The top-seeded Brazilian-Canadian partnership survived a tense encounter at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden, winning 7-6(5), 4-6, 10-5 to remain unbeaten in the round-robin stage of the season-ending championship. Their second consecutive victory put them in control of Group 1 and within reach of a semifinal berth, although their place in the final four was not yet mathematically guaranteed.

The result was particularly satisfying for Stefani and Dabrowski, who lost to the Chinese-French pairing in the Wimbledon doubles final earlier this year. Wednesday’s rematch gave them an opportunity to settle that score, but they needed a remarkable recovery in the deciding match tiebreak to secure the victory.

After splitting the opening two sets, Stefani and Dabrowski fell behind 5-2 in the 10-point match tiebreak. With the momentum favoring their opponents, the Brazilian and Canadian responded by winning eight consecutive points to complete the comeback. The victory took two hours and one minute and demonstrated the resilience that has helped make Stefani and Dabrowski one of the most successful doubles teams of the 2026 season.

The opening set was closely contested, with both teams struggling to hold serve consistently. Stefani and Dabrowski broke their opponents three times but also surrendered three service games of their own. They had an opportunity to serve out the set at 5-4, only for Guo and Mladenovic to respond and force a tiebreak.

The Brazilian-Canadian team eventually claimed the opening set 7-5 in the tiebreak after Mladenovic committed a double fault on set point. The Wimbledon champions responded strongly in the second set. Guo and Mladenovic increased the pressure on their opponents’ service games, breaking twice and establishing a 5-2 advantage. Although Stefani and Dabrowski fought back, the Chinese-French partnership closed out the set 6-4 to force a deciding match tiebreak.

For several minutes, it appeared the Wimbledon champions might repeat their Grand Slam victory. Instead, Stefani and Dabrowski raised their level when it mattered most, improving their serving and returns while putting their opponents under increasing pressure. Stefani acknowledged afterward that the match had been difficult and that the pair had needed to overcome several problems. She said their serving and returning improved during the closing stages, allowing them to regain control.

The victory was their second of the tournament following a 6-3, 7-6(5) win over Belgium’s Elise Mertens and China’s Zhang Shuai in Monday’s opening round. Stefani and Dabrowski now hold a 2-0 record in Group 1, putting them in a strong position to advance from the four-team group.

Their final round-robin match is scheduled for Friday, November 13, against Taiwan’s Hsieh Su-wei and Latvia’s Jelena Ostapenko, who defeated Mertens and Zhang 7-5, 6-3 on Wednesday. The top two teams in each group advance to Saturday’s semifinals, with the championship match scheduled for Sunday, November 15.

For Stefani, the tournament represents another opportunity to reach the season-ending final after finishing runner-up in 2025 alongside Hungary’s Timea Babos. Dabrowski already knows what it takes to win the championship. The Canadian captured the 2024 WTA Finals doubles title with New Zealand’s Erin Routliffe.

Their partnership has enjoyed an outstanding 2026 campaign. Before arriving at Indian Wells, Stefani and Dabrowski had collected six doubles titles together, including three WTA 1000 championships in Dubai, Beijing and Wuhan. They also won tournaments in Strasbourg, Eastbourne and São Paulo, establishing themselves as one of the most consistent teams on the women’s circuit.

Their success has extended beyond those victories. They reached the Wimbledon final and also finished runners-up at the Tokyo tournament earlier this month. The pair entered the WTA Finals as the top seeds, having built one of the strongest records in women’s doubles this season.

For Brazilian tennis, Stefani’s continued success is especially significant. The Olympic bronze medalist has become one of the country’s most accomplished doubles players and is seeking her first WTA Finals championship. Wednesday’s victory did not secure the title or eliminate the challenges ahead, but it moved Stefani and Dabrowski another step closer to their goal.

After surviving a difficult rematch against the Wimbledon champions, the Brazilian-Canadian team will enter Friday’s final group match with two victories, growing confidence and an opportunity to advance to the semifinals of women’s tennis’ season-ending championship.

World.title: Costa Ricans Could Vote on Reopening Crucitas to Gold Mining
World.content:
Costa Ricans could be asked to decide at the ballot box whether gold mining returns to Crucitas, after President Laura Fernández confirmed that her government is weighing a national referendum on the troubled northern mining zone. Speaking at her weekly press conference yesterday, Fernández said she has discussed the idea for months with Minister of the Presidency and Finance Rodrigo Chaves, the former president, and other members of her team.

She stressed that no decision has been made and said she would tell the country in due course whether she will call a referendum on Crucitas or on another issue. Chaves revived the idea earlier this month, saying he would recommend that Fernández put Crucitas to a public vote, while adding that he did not know whether she would. Fernández first said in July that she was studying a referendum as a way around stalled legislation and named Crucitas among the possible topics.

Crucitas, in Cutris de San Carlos near the border with Nicaragua, was the site of an open-pit gold project by Canadian company Infinito Gold that was halted in 2010, the same year Costa Rica banned new open-pit metallic mining. Since then the area has been overrun by illegal miners.

Authorities say the mercury and cyanide used to process illegally extracted gold are contaminating water sources and surrounding ecosystems, and they link much of the activity to organized criminal groups. The government has separately moved to treat illegal mining as organized crime.

Security Minister Mario Zamora has told lawmakers that about 200 police officers are deployed in the zone at a cost of roughly $1 million, and that the area affected by illegal extraction has grown by more than 200%. The government’s answer is Bill 24.717, which would authorize open-pit gold mining at Crucitas and award concessions through public auctions.

The administration argues that regulated mining would cut off illegal extraction and generate revenue it says would go to education, security and health. The bill has been stalled for months in the Legislative Assembly, where opposition lawmakers filed hundreds of motions to amend it.

Fernández blamed the National Liberation Party (PLN) and the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) for the delay. Opposition lawmakers favor alternatives centered on cleaning up and restoring the damaged land, and on issuing digital tokens linked to the gold that would stay in the ground. PLN legislator Diana Murillo has filed a proposal that combines remediation, the sale of gold recovered during cleanup and tokens tied to the remaining deposit.

Fernández argued that none of these approaches would stop illegal miners from entering the area. Costa Rica’s Constitution allows a referendum to be called in three ways: a citizen petition signed by at least 5% of registered voters, approval by two-thirds of the 57-member Legislative Assembly, or a joint call by the executive branch and an absolute majority of lawmakers.

The ruling Pueblo Soberano party holds 31 seats, enough to back a joint call without opposition votes. Opponents say the question cannot legally go to voters at all. Frente Amplio lawmaker Edgardo Araya, an environmental lawyer, has argued that reopening Crucitas to mining would be an environmental rollback, and that such a rollback cannot be decided by referendum.

Any consultation would have to meet constitutional and legal requirements, overseen by the Supreme Elections Tribunal, before voters could be called to the polls. Costa Rica has held only one national referendum, the 2007 vote that approved the Central American Free Trade Agreement with the United States. Earlier this year, the country’s geologists also called for a referendum on Crucitas.

World.title: El Niño Could Leave 306,000 People in Costa Rica Short of Water
World.content:
More than 306,000 people in Costa Rica could face problems getting drinking water as the strongest El Niño on record dries us out, according to estimates from the AyA. Nearly half of them, 48%, live in the Chorotega region, which covers Guanacaste, so if you live in that area, this matters now.

As we all know, the dry season is setting in across Guanacaste and the Central Valley, and the rains that refill wells and springs will not be back for months. AyA has tripled its fleet of water tanker trucks, from 21 to 64, to deliver water where local systems run short. It has also drawn up 149 water security plans for the community-run water associations known as ASADAS and handed out 25 storage tanks to 14 of them.

The utility says it is also bringing new wells online, adding storage, repairing leaks and arranging supply for schools and shelters. The figures were presented Wednesday at the government’s weekly press conference, where Alejandro Picado, president of the National Emergency Commission (CNE), outlined the response.

The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) has classified this El Niño as the most intense since the institute was founded in 1888. The CNE has declared four alerts since May and raised Costa Rica to a red alert on Oct. 22 and the government says more than 20 institutions are coordinating the response.

Every liter you save at home stretches what is left in the system. AyA has already asked households to cut back on water use as the dry season begins. Fire is the other risk and the fire department (Bomberos), bought five tanker trucks that hold about 34,000 liters (9,000 gallons) each and stationed them in Puntarenas and Guanacaste, after what the government describes as a historic rise in forest fires this year.

Farmers, ranchers and fishing families are already feeling the drought. The CNE and the fishing institute Incopesca have delivered food to more than 2,500 fishing families in 43 communities across 11 areas and Incopesca extended the fishing range for 40 boats to 12 nautical miles (22 kilometers, or about 14 miles).

The rural development institute Inder has put more than 645 million colones (about $1.4 million) into livestock feed, equipment, and water and pasture studies in Guanacaste, which it says benefit more than 6,000 families. The irrigation agency Senara says the reservoir serving the Arenal-Tempisque irrigation district can supply its farmers through the end of 2027.

Small businesses and community water systems can also get help. The Development Banking System will offer 5,000 million colones (about $11.2 million) in low-cost financing, with 4,000 million colones for small businesses and producers and 1,000 million colones for ASADAS, the first time those associations can borrow from the system.

With the dry season only beginning here, how far the water stretches will depend on how soon the rains return and how much households, farms and businesses conserve until then.

World.title: Major Microsoft Outlook outage disrupts email, including for businesses in Belize
World.content:
Major Microsoft Outlook outage disrupts email, including for businesses in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A widespread Microsoft outage disrupted email and other services for businesses on Thursday, and Belize was not spared.

Among those affected was one of Belize’s best known resorts on Ambergris Caye, which notified guests that it was having problems with its email because of the Outlook outage. The resort said responses may be delayed and asked anyone with an urgent matter to call directly.

Other businesses in Belize that rely on Microsoft’s services also reported issues.

According to WIRED, Microsoft’s 365 business and enterprise services suffered a major outage on Thursday that kept users from accessing their accounts. The company first reported problems with Microsoft Teams in North America in the morning, then confirmed that users across the Americas were having trouble reaching their Exchange Online mailboxes. Microsoft later said its network was under elevated load across multiple regions.

Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and going offline. The company paused all deployments, shifted traffic across its global network and began restarting the affected servers.

Services that may have been affected include Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR.

WIRED reported there was no indication the outage was caused by a cyberattack.

World.title: ‘Thank You For Your Patience’: Man who ‘punk’d’ runman out of $501 in fried chicken, dog chow, groceries and cash pleads guilty, sent to prison overnight pending sentence
World.content:
‘Thank You For Your Patience’: Man who ‘punk’d’ runman out of $501 in fried chicken, dog chow, groceries and cash pleads guilty, sent to prison overnight pending sentence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 24-year-old Belize City man who racked up a $501 bill with a deliveryman for fried chicken, barbecue, groceries, dog food and cash deliveries, but never paid a cent, has pleaded guilty to seven counts of obtaining property by deception and has been sent to the Belize Central Prison overnight pending sentencing.

Roy Earl Jones, also known as “Rayjaughn,” appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 on Thursday, November 12, where he admitted to deceiving a deliveryman who had repeatedly fulfilled his requests on the promise of being reimbursed.

As BBN previously reported, the deliveryman told police that between September 29 and October 12, Jones repeatedly contacted him through WhatsApp to request deliveries to his mother’s residence on Usher Street.

The requests included cash, a 55-pound bag of dog food, breakfast cereals, condensed milk, fried chicken from Benny’s Restaurant, rice and beans with pork, barbecue chicken and soft drinks.

Despite promising to make online payments, Jones never settled the outstanding bill. At one point, when the “runman” inquired about his money, Jones simply responded, “Thank you for your patience.”

The deliveryman eventually discovered Jones’ real identity and filed a formal police complaint on November 9, leading to his detention and subsequent charges.

In court, Jones apologized and pleaded for leniency, explaining that he supports his two children, his fiancée and his mother, who recently underwent surgery.

“I will never do any such thing again in my entire life,” Jones told the court, promising to repay the runman and asking for another chance to become a better person.

Jones, who described himself as self-employed and said he plans to open a car wash business, was nevertheless remanded to prison after the Magistrate deferred sentencing.

He is expected to return to court on Friday, November 13, when his sentence will be determined.

World.title: Orange Walk man charged after partner says he pushed her to the ground
World.content:
Orange Walk man charged after partner says he pushed her to the ground

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 34 year old Orange Walk Town man has been charged with common assault after his partner reported that he pushed her to the ground during an argument at their home.

Giovanni Reyes, a self employed resident of San Lorenzo Housing Site, was formally arrested and charged on Thursday, November 12.

According to the report, the woman, 36, said she was awakened around 7:00am by her 12 year old daughter, who told her that Reyes was talking about them on the phone.

The woman said she found him lying in a hammock with his phone to his ear and asked who he was speaking to. He denied speaking to anyone and ended the call. He later accused the child of lying.

The woman told him he needed to leave the house. As he gathered his things for work, she said, he insisted that she speak to her daughter and then began pushing her toward the girl’s bedroom.

She told police she asked him to stop and braced herself against the doorway, but he pushed her forcefully, causing her to fall.

She called the police and later made a formal report, requesting court action.

Reyes was detained and charged the same day. He remained silent when cautioned.

World.title: Woman, 64, robbed of phone while walking in Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Woman, 64, robbed of phone while walking in Orange Walk Town

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Orange Walk police are looking for a man who snatched a cellphone from a 64 year old woman as she walked along Otro Benque Road early Thursday morning.

The woman reported that around 2:31am on Thursday, November 12, she was walking from Central Park toward the Northern Regional Hospital while talking on her blue Samsung phone, valued at $500.

As she passed the Social Security building, she noticed a man following her.

After she walked past the police station, the man spoke to her in Spanish, saying, “Miss, I know you.”

When she turned around, he grabbed the phone out of her hand and ran up the hill onto San Francisco Street.

The woman was not injured. She described the thief as a dark skinned man with curly hair.

Police have recorded a statement. No one has been detained.

World.title: Ministry of National Security hands over 3 vehicles to Belize Police Department
World.content:
Ministry of National Security hands over 3 vehicles to Belize Police Department

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of National Security, Energy, and Ports handed over 3 vehicles for the Belize Police Department as part of ongoing efforts to strengthen the Department’s operational capacity, mobility, and response times.

Minister Michel Chebat handed over the three vehicles to the Commissioner of Police, Dr. A. Richard Rosado.

The Belize Police Department says that the vehicles will be deployed to three key locations: Corozal, Ladyville, and Independence, to enhance the department’s ability to respond to incidents and deliver policing services within these communities.

“This acquisition reflects the continued commitment of the Ministry and the Belize Police Department to ensuring that officers are equipped with the necessary resources to effectively carry out their duties and contribute to safer communities,” the Belize Police Department noted.

World.title: Julius Espat says no contractor selected for $74.4 million George Price Highway project, tendering to begin after parliamentary approval
World.content:
Julius Espat says no contractor selected for $74.4 million George Price Highway project, tendering to begin after parliamentary approval

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Minister of Infrastructure Development and Housing Julius Espat has confirmed that no construction contractor has been selected for the proposed BZ$74.4 million upgrading of the George Price Highway between Hattieville and La Democracia, explaining that the project has not yet reached the tendering stage.

Espat made the disclosure during today’s sitting of the House of Representatives while responding to questions raised by Opposition Leader Tracy Panton and Mesopotamia Area Representative Lee Mark Chang concerning the cost, financing and transparency of the project.

“Who gets the contract? Well, we don’t know,” Espat told the House, explaining that the government was first seeking parliamentary authorization for the US$30 million loan from the OPEC Fund for International Development.

He said the procurement process for the construction contract would commence after the loan motion receives the necessary parliamentary approval.

According to Espat, procurement will be conducted in accordance with the OPEC Fund’s requirements for the acquisition of goods, works and services, with oversight involving the Ministry of Finance and other relevant authorities.

The minister also revealed that an independent supervision company has already been contracted to oversee the highway works. He identified the company as NABCO, which he said is supervising the three sections of the George Price Highway upgrading programme.

Espat explained that the Hattieville–La Democracia project will involve two principal procurement arrangements: a civil works contract financed by the OPEC Fund and the Government of Belize, and a separate external audit contract financed by the government.

He said the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing’s Project Execution Unit will oversee implementation, reporting, withdrawals and project accounts.

The minister defended the government’s procurement procedures, saying the international lending institutions involved impose strict standards that must be followed.

Espat also responded to questions about the financing of the government’s contribution, saying payments required from the Treasury would have to be provided for in the upcoming fiscal year’s budget.

He maintained that the government is willing to share further technical and financial information with opposition parliamentarians, including arranging meetings with engineers and officials involved in the project.

The proposed upgrade covers approximately 23.6 kilometres of highway, including pavement reconstruction, improved drainage, flood mitigation works and replacement of the Colonel English Bridge.

The OPEC Fund’s published project information places the overall cost at US$37.2 million, equivalent to BZ$74.4 million.

The financing comprises two US$15 million loans, leaving approximately US$7.2 million of the total project cost to be financed from other sources.

Espat maintained that the project is necessary to improve one of Belize’s principal transportation corridors and strengthen connectivity between Belize City, Belmopan and the western border.
