World.title: Keep spending tight…
World.content:
The IMF has told Jamaica that revenue mobilisation and restraint in current spending growth are critical to preserve fiscal space for priority investment and return public debt to a sustained downward path.

THE International Monetary Fund (IMF) has applauded the Jamaican Government for its “strong policy frameworks and sustained reforms” which “have underpinned its resilience in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa”.

The category 5 system left severe damage in sections of the island after its rampage on October 28, 2025.

But the IMF has warned that addressing supply-side constraints is essential to raising Jamaica’s potential growth and enhancing the country’s resilience and has urged the Dr Andrew Holness-led Administration to ensure it contains non-priority recurrent spending.

Holness has already announced a pause on several government expenditure items, including non-essential travel, parties, and retreats at resorts, with the IMF agreeing that this should remain a priority.

“Revenue mobilisation and restraint in current spending growth are critical to preserve fiscal space for priority investment and return public debt to a sustained downward path. The authorities’ efforts to broaden the tax revenue base and strengthen administration are welcomed, along with the intention to develop a mechanism to anchor medium-term public wage growth in a manner consistent with the fiscal framework,” the IMF said on Wednesday as it released its ‘Jamaica: Staff Concluding Statement of its 2026 Article IV Mission’.

According to the IMF, its team, led by W Raphael Lam, held meetings in Kingston with Jamaican authorities, representatives of the private sector, civil society, and development partners during October 27-November 4 to conduct the 2026 Article IV consultation.

In his mission statement, Lam said the Jamaican authorities’ effective disaster risk financing framework, together with the strength of the country’s fiscal, monetary, and financial sector frameworks, have supported an appropriate policy response to cushion the severe impact of Melissa while preserving market access on favourable terms.

“The priority now is to advance reconstruction while preserving macroeconomic stability and deepening reforms, considering the more challenging external environment,” said Lam, who noted that economic activity is recovering gradually in Jamaica.

“Following a contraction of 1.2 per cent in fiscal year (FY)2025/26, growth is projected to recover moderately to 1.3 per cent in FY2026/27, with output returning to its pre-hurricane level by mid-2027, supported by reconstruction efforts and a recovery in tourism.

“Headline inflation, largely driven by higher energy and food prices, has risen above the Bank of Jamaica’s target band of 4-6 per cent, yet is projected to return within the target band by mid-2027 as supply pressures ease,” added Lam.

He pointed out that Jamaica’s risks to the growth outlook are tilted to the downside, while inflation risks remain on the upside.

“Higher energy and food prices from prolonged conflict in the Middle East and drought conditions from El Niño, and a further tightening in global financial conditions, could weigh on growth and intensify inflationary pressures. On the domestic front, delays in both reconstruction and restoration of tourism capacity would also weaken the recovery.”

Lam said the Jamaican Government correctly eased the fiscal stance in response to Hurricane Melissa, although accelerating reconstruction efforts remain essential.

“The multi-layered disaster risk financing provided rapid liquidity, including through IMF’s Rapid Financing Instrument. The Government appropriately activated the fiscal rule’s escape clause to support vulnerable households and hurricane-related reconstruction efforts. Revenue mobilisation efforts to broaden the tax base and strengthen administration are welcome,” said Lam.

“However, efforts are needed to accelerate reconstruction and build back better by closing long-standing infrastructure gaps and strengthening resilience to future natural disasters. The establishment of a new National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) provides an opportunity to do so, although work should continue in enhancing procurement, contract management, public investment management, and interagency coordination to address implementation bottlenecks.

“Meanwhile, containing non-priority recurrent spending remains essential, including by ensuring that the current fuel price smoothing mechanism continues to operate symmetrically to ensure cost recovery over time,” Lam added.

He pointed out that preserving debt sustainability should remain a priority for the Jamaican Government, with fiscal efforts shifted towards rebuilding buffers.

The IMF official applauded the Bank of Jamaica for its September policy rate hike which, it said, was appropriate, given above-target inflation and persistent commodity-price pressures.

“Monetary policy should remain focused on anchoring inflation expectations and limiting second-round effects, particularly as fiscal policy supports reconstruction efforts. Alongside an active monetary policy response to inflation risks, greater exchange rate flexibility would strengthen Jamaica’s capacity to absorb external shocks, including those coming from less favourable terms of trade.

“Over time, scaling back foreign exchange interventions would allow the exchange rate to play a greater buffering role and support foreign exchange market development,” Lam added.

He argued that Jamaica’s financial system remains resilient, but continued vigilance and reforms are needed.

“Continued close monitoring of credit and market risks, insurers’ financial positions, and vulnerabilities stemming from financial groups’ interconnectedness remains essential,” said Lam.

“In addition, cyber security risks require increased attention, building on the sector-wide cyber intelligence sharing hub.”

He called for the strengthening of the country’s energy security and electricity infrastructure, including by accelerating the transition towards renewable energy sources, which would reduce Jamaica’s exposure to imported fuel prices.

“Progress should continue in reducing crime, streamlining the regulatory burden for businesses, improving education outcomes and workforce skills, and addressing broader infrastructure bottlenecks. Continued implementation of reforms to strengthen climate resilience will help Jamaica better withstand future shocks,” declared the IMF official.

World.title: ‘Go make a song of it!’
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness speaking during the National Housing Trust’s (NHT) Construction Scholarship awards ceremony which was held at Jamaica House in St Andrew on Wednesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

WHILE acknowledging that thousands of Jamaicans remain without assistance in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has again firmly rejected claims that his Administration has failed to respond to the devastation, insisting that such assertions are false and must be challenged.

“I will continue to say it over and over again, and I don’t care who vex. Go make a song of it,” Holness declared in what appeared to be a pointed jab at dancehall entertainer Beenie Man amid their public disagreement over the Government’s handling of hurricane relief.

Speaking during the National Housing Trust’s (NHT) Construction Scholarship awards ceremony which was held at Jamaica House in St Andrew on Wednesday, the prime minister acknowledged that questions surrounding the pace of recovery and the adequacy of assistance were legitimate, but insisted that these concerns should not be conflated with allegations of Government inaction.

“That’s a perspective. We can debate that. You may feel $500,000 isn’t enough. Another one may feel, ‘I’m grateful’…We understand that, but don’t say the Government has not done anything,” he said.

“That’s false,” Holness insisted, warning that the repeated circulation of such claims threatened to undermine public confidence in the Government and, by extension, the stability of society.

His remarks come amid a public spat with Beenie Man, whose given name is Moses Davis, after the entertainer questioned — during an interview with British broadcaster ITV News — whether donated hurricane relief funds were reaching those who needed it most.

The dancehall artiste subsequently released a song titled Weh Di Money Deh, drawing attention to Jamaicans still struggling to rebuild their lives after the Category 5 storm which struck Jamaica a year ago.

Holness pointed to the NHT, which he said had spent approximately $13.3 billion on hurricane-related assistance, including $2.9 billion in grants distributed to 7,600 Jamaicans. Individual grants, he reminded, ranged from $75,000 to $500,000.

Holness also disclosed that the Government had spent close to $12 billion on direct assistance, with another $9.6 billion being sought to support outstanding needs.

He said the scale of destruction caused by Hurricane Melissa had presented an unprecedented challenge, with approximately 110,000 households identified as requiring assistance and just over 50,000 having received support so far.

“You would see that just the NHT alone has spent significant resources trying to assist Jamaicans. That is true, but it is also true that there are still many Jamaicans who have got no assistance,” he acknowledged.

Holness said the Government was working to secure the resources necessary to reach the remaining households, stressing that the magnitude of the disaster must be considered when assessing the pace of recovery.

“Did it happen quickly? That’s legitimate. Is $500,000 enough? We can debate that. That’s a legitimate debate. But it is patently untrue, false, to say the Government hasn’t done anything,” he said.

The prime minister further cautioned against the dissemination of misinformation, especially on social media, arguing that it could create widespread public distrust and undermine the country’s progress.

“And what that does is to undermine and destroy the legitimacy of Government. And in undermining the legitimacy of Government, your society ends up in chaos,” he said.

Addressing the 50 NHT scholarship recipients, Holness charged that they too must dismiss illegitimate claims against their country.

“I’m not asking you to defend the Government. But defend your society…Don’t believe that you can step out of the society and succeed in spite of the society. If you tear down your society, you are tearing down yourself. You must be vested in building your society,” he said.

“Ultimately, you will be in charge of the society. And what kind of society will you have if you tear it down?” asked Holness.

He maintained that while he is open to criticism over pace of recovery, he would continue to challenge what he described as inaccuracies presented as facts.

“As I’m talking to a group of young Jamaicans who are native to social media, you will see all kinds of untruths being spread. And the only way to deal with darkness is to shine the light. And at every opportunity, we must elucidate. We must shine light, challenge falsehoods and incorrectly held positions,” the prime minister said.

“Yes, we will always challenge falsehoods. Because in the current landscape of information, it is so easy to put things out which are not true. And it is so easy to have compelling perspectives which may have truth in them but are not contextually correct,” Holness added.

World.title: Macka Diamond pours her heart into new chapter
World.content:
Macka Diamond.

More than three decades in dancehall have given Macka Diamond plenty to celebrate, but behind the flamboyant persona and enduring stage presence is an artiste who says there is still much of her story left untold.

For the veteran entertainer, the next chapter will be a deeply personal one, with her forthcoming EP, The Rebirth, serving as an opportunity to share a more vulnerable side of herself with the world.

Scheduled for release in January 2027, the project is being shaped by experiences that have left a lasting impression on her, including the pain of being separated from her son for more than two years. It is an emotional experience she says has inspired her to pour her heart into the music.

“It was inspired by my son after not seeing him over two years, hurting me so bad, and I had to pour out my heart on this EP. And all the struggles as a female in dancehall I go through, I truly wanna show the world my true talent and another side of my talent they don’t see a lot of,” Macka Diamond shared.

The revelation offers a glimpse into the personal experiences informing The Rebirth, suggesting that the project will reach beyond the familiar sounds and personality that have defined much of her public career.

For an artiste who has spent more than 30 years navigating dancehall, the desire to reveal another dimension of her artistry is significant.

Macka Diamond has built a recognisable identity in a genre where women have often had to contend with their own set of challenges to establish and sustain their place.

Her comments suggest that those experiences, alongside the personal sacrifices and emotional struggles that have accompanied her journey, will form part of the story she hopes to tell through the EP.

While she is keeping much of the project under wraps, the self-styled “Diamond of Dancehall” has promised a musical experience that reflects both her years in the business and a willingness to explore a different creative direction.

“I am not at liberty to divulge much at this time, but all I can say is it’s going to be a very interesting project,” she said.

Details surrounding the track list, featured artistes, and exact release date have yet to be disclosed. However, Macka Diamond intends for the project to resonate with her established supporters while introducing her music to a younger generation of dancehall listeners.

The title The Rebirth is particularly fitting for a project rooted in reflection and personal expression. Rather than simply revisiting the career that has brought her this far, Macka Diamond appears intent on using the next phase of her musical journey to communicate something more intimate about the woman behind the artiste.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: Tighter controls coming for sex offenders
World.content:
Commissioner of Corrections Brigadier (Ret’d) Radgh Mason addressing Parliament’s Internal and External Affairs Committee during Wednesday’s meeting.

The Department of Correctional Services (DCS) is moving towards the use of electronic tags to track registered sex offenders as it seeks to strengthen its monitoring of more than 500 people on its watch list.

Commissioner of Corrections Brigadier (Ret’d) Radgh Mason said the department was working to acquire the equipment and put the necessary legal arrangements in place to introduce the system.

He disclosed that the DCS was monitoring 528 sex offenders, with just over 30 having breached their legal requirement to report to probation officers after leaving prison.

The offenders are required to report to the respective probation offices for up to 10 years after their release. Mason explained that monitoring currently centres largely on ensuring they meet that obligation.

The issue was raised by Member of Parliament for St Thomas Eastern Yvonne Rose-Marie Shaw during Wednesday’s meeting of Parliament’s Internal and External Affairs Committee. Shaw asked about the department’s success in monitoring offenders, particularly given that they may move between parishes and communities.

Mason said the department was looking to strengthen the system through electronic monitoring, which would allow authorities to track offenders’ movements and establish areas they should not enter.

“Our next step will be towards electronic monitoring, and so we are working with the acquisition and all the legislative underpinnings towards monitoring. That is effectively how the modern jurisdictions go about monitoring. They place these monitors on them, GPS trackers, and they geofence the areas that they are meant to remain within,” he told the committee.

Geofencing involves setting electronic boundaries around particular locations. A tracking device can then help authorities monitor whether an individual enters or leaves those areas.

Mason said the department was also developing a course specifically for sex offenders. He noted that preventing further harm, particularly to children, was a key consideration in managing this group.

He maintained that the department was meeting its responsibilities under the law, while acknowledging that offenders who fail to report must be dealt with through the police and courts.

“So the success rate has been good. When persons breach, it is then for the courts, the police, to find those persons, at which point they would be brought back into custody and possibly sentenced,” Mason said.

The commissioner did not provide a percentage success rate for the monitoring programme or explain how many of the 528 offenders had been successfully tracked over a particular period.

The disclosure comes as the DCS oversees approximately 2,678 non-custodial cases, including people serving sentences outside prison, while also monitoring the registered sex offenders.

Mason said probation offices across the country had designated officers responsible for monitoring those required to report. The department also provides confidential professional spaces for counselling sessions in each parish.

World.title: PROVE IT!
World.content:
West Indies’ players share a photo op with the trophy after winning the Test cricket series against Bangladesh at the Sylhet International Cricket Stadium in Sylhet on Monday. (Photo: AFP)

WHILE encouraged that West Indies completed a calendar year without losing a Test series for the first time since 1994, cricket commentator Joseph “Reds” Perreira says the ultimate proof of a turnaround would be success against the game’s top teams.

The Daren Sammy-coached West Indies team surprised some watchers by defeating hosts Bangladesh 1-0 in a two-Test series which ended days ago.

That success away from home followed a 1-1 Test series result against visiting Pakistan between July and August, and a 1-0 triumph over touring Sri Lanka earlier in the summer.

That success away from home pushed former kingpins West Indies up to sixth in the ICC Test rankings, closely followed by Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Pakistan, who hold the seventh, eighth, and ninth positions, respectively.

“Those teams are in the bottom half [of the Test rankings]. And we did well [against] them, but the opposition cannot be described as great,” Perreira told the Jamaica Observer on Wednesday.

“When we start beating the people above us, when we start beating the people in the top five, then you can really assess whether we’re getting back to being a competitive Test team.”

The top five ranked teams include world Test champions South Africa, followed by Australia, New Zealand, India and England.

Looking specifically at the Test tour of Bangladesh, the Guyanese-born Perreira said the signs were positive.

Left-arm finger spinner Jomel Warrican shone for the visitors with 16 wickets in the two matches to claim the player of the series award. Captain and all-rounder Roston Chase, who bowls off-break, was also influential with the ball in typical spin-friendly Asian subcontinent conditions.

The batting unit, spurred by Amir Jangoo, Kavem Hodge and Brandon King, more than held its own, particularly in the drawn second Test during which West Indies twice posted 350-plus scores. Batsman Kevin Wickham, who made his debut in the second encounter, was outstanding, scoring stylish half centuries in both innings. Wickham became only the eighth West Indian to score half-centuries in each innings of his first Test.

West Indies had a two-week camp in India prior to the tour of Bangladesh, which is widely believed to have significantly assisted preparations for the unique challenges of playing on pitches in that part of the world.

“I think you have to look at the series and accept that a one-nil win playing in Bangladesh on their home patch is a successful tour,” Perreira said.

While he noted West Indies could have pushed aggressively for a 2-0 series victory by declaring sooner when they built a big lead in their second innings of the final Test, the veteran commentator acknowledged that they took a safety-first approach.

“It’s easy to say [West Indies should have actively chased the win] when you’re watching from umpteen thousand miles away, [but] a win is a win. And they’re now number six in the Test match table,” Perreira said.

Wayne Lewis, a former Jamaica batsman and the West Indies Players’ Association secretary, credited the coaching staff for their efforts in crafting the positive results given the general struggles of regional Test teams since the mid-1990s.

Lewis pointed to the 3-0 series loss to visiting Australia last year, highlighted by West Indies being humiliatingly bowled out for 27 in the third and final Test.

“There was so much speculation around Daren Sammy taking charge of the red-ball team and all the scepticism around that, but he has delivered now. Yes, it was a rocky beginning when Australia bowled us out for 27 at Sabina Park. That was the lowest moment for West Indies cricket. But kudos to Cricket West Indies and him and his staff. We were not [playing] against Australia or England, but still, playing Test cricket and playing Bangladesh in Bangladesh is always very difficult,” the former player told the Observer.

He reasoned that the camp in India was a boost.

“Playing and getting acclimatised to the conditions will always help. So that’s a plus, and it’s good to see Cricket West Indies invested in the team to really allow the coaching staff to have that type of a camp going into a very important Test series,” Lewis said.

“It’s a happy moment for West Indies cricket, and I hope that come next year they can build on that. This is hopefully the beginning of something good for the future, but I’m quite pleased and happy that West Indies really went to Bangladesh and actually won the series.

“Don’t take Bangladesh lightly… they went to Australia and embarrassed Australia in that first Test match [in a drawn two-Test series in August]. They [Bangladesh] are a formidable team, particularly in their conditions,” Lewis said.

— Sanjay Myers

World.title: Palate Reimagined
World.content:
(Photo: Garfield Robinson)

At ROK Hotel Kingston, Palate is setting the table for its next chapter, with a refreshed menu, a new culinary vision and a renewed appetite for putting downtown Kingston on the dining map.

There is something to be said for a restaurant that knows how to reinvent itself without losing its sense of identity. At Palate, the signature restaurant at ROK Hotel Kingston, that philosophy is finding fresh expression through a reimagined menu, a considered refresh of the dining space and the arrival of new Executive Chef Oji Jaja.

With its fifth anniversary approaching next July, Palate is entering its next chapter with a renewed culinary perspective — one that looks to Jamaica’s rich larder, the restaurant’s waterfront setting and the possibilities of downtown Kingston as a dining destination.

To experience the evolution first-hand, the restaurant invited a particularly discerning table of guests, including Jamaica Observer Managing Director Dominic Beaubrun, Deputy Managing Director Natalie Chin-Samuda, Senior Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Social Content, and Table Talk Food Awards conceptualiser Novia McDonald-Whyte, alongside Food Awards judges. Familiar faces at Palate, the group was well-positioned to appreciate just how far the restaurant has come.

Since opening, Palate has collected some notable Jamaica Observer Food Awards accolades, including the Solomon Gardner Award for Outstanding Service, Best Sunday Spot and Chef of the Year — all within its first year of operation. The latest reinvention signals an ambition to build on that early success while giving diners new reasons to return.

“You’ve all been here before, several times. And I think if there’s anybody that can attest to how much we have reinvented ourselves… you are the guys that can tell those stories for us,” said Marlene Buckridge, director of sales & marketing, ROK Hotel Kingston.

“We really depend on you guys to put the word out there that this is one of the best, and safest places to dine in downtown Kingston… On behalf of our team Sherene Brown, director of Food And Beverage and Amit Mahbubani, our general manager, welcome back to Palate, our reimagined food and beverage outlet. And I hope you have a fantastic time tonight,” Buckridge continued.

Looking ahead to 2027, the team’s wider vision is to position its food and beverage offerings as a compelling reason to venture downtown. That means challenging perceptions, cultivating a stronger dining culture and creating an experience that extends beyond the plate.

The transformation is deliberately nuanced. Think: More inviting cushions, a newly introduced cocktail bar and a collection of rather enticing cocktails. The objective is not simply to refresh the restaurant’s appearance, but to elevate the entire experience.

In the kitchen, Jaja is bringing his own perspective to the table. Having joined the ROK team in July, the executive chef has spent his first months assessing the existing menu and identifying opportunities to give Palate a more distinctive culinary voice.

“Because we’re right here on the waterfront, seafood is really what I want to put forward on the menu — really fresh seafood dishes,” he explained.

That coastal sensibility informed several of the evening’s standout plates, including a crab cake and a turmeric-ginger snapper, the latter offering a fresh interpretation of curried fish, accompanied by bammy and coconut milk. There was also a distinctly Jamaican thread running through the bread service, with a Scotch bonnet and Scallion Milk Roll and roasted garlic pakasa making an appearance.

The seven-course tasting experience began with the warm, pepper-kissed milk roll before moving into a Scotch bonnet Pumpkin Bisque and Quinoa and Lentil Salad. A Scotch bonnet Thyme Crab Cake followed, bringing a familiar Jamaican ingredient into a more contemporary culinary expression.

The Turmeric-Ginger Snapper, served with turmeric-ginger coconut cream, steamed bammy, callaloo, okra and sweet corn, was another highlight. The Smoked Filet Mignon offered a change of pace before the evening concluded with Passion Fruit Pavlova — a bright, tropical finish to the menu.

Beyond the kitchen, the cocktail menu had its own moment in the spotlight. Bartenders Sean Hopkins and Odane Young kept the newly introduced bar in good company, mixing a selection of cocktails as guests took Buckridge up on her invitation to explore the “sexy” offerings.

For Jaja, the refreshed menu marks the beginning rather than the conclusion of the process. Although the new selections had only officially made their debut that day, the early response had been encouraging, with the chef looking forward to hearing what the wider dining public makes of the changes.

At Palate, then, reinvention is less about starting over than refining what is already there. With the waterfront as its backdrop, Jamaican ingredients informing its culinary direction and a renewed focus on hospitality, the restaurant is making a case for downtown Kingston as a destination worth dressing up, showing up and dining out for.

World.title: Gov’t cautions Jamaicans against employment offers linked to Russia-Ukraine war
World.content:
In this file photo Ukrainian soldiers drive in a military truck along a road in the Kharkiv region on July 30, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Roman PILIPEY / AFP)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Government of Jamaica has become the latest Caribbean nation to warn its citizens to avoid recruitment offers to participate in foreign wars or conflicts.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade issued the warning in a press release on Wednesday amid a wider caution regarding overseas employment opportunities advertised through social media, messaging platforms and other online channels.

The Government mentioned in particular those offering unusually high salaries, travel assistance or expedited immigration arrangements.

“It has come to the Government’s attention that there are international reports of foreign nationals being recruited to participate in Russia’s war against Ukraine including through s on social media,” it said.

Noting that the Government could not verify the legitimacy or authenticity of the reported overseas employment offers, it said it is however aware of international media reports of persons recruited from various countries to participate in that war, including accusations of ill-treatment of Africans and persons of African descent as well as misrepresentation of duties, difficulties in receiving payments and difficulties in returning to their home countries or onward travel.

“Jamaicans are therefore strongly encouraged to avoid such recruitment offers. The ministry further reminds that participation in foreign armed conflicts carries serious risks to personal safety including ultimately to life, and may also expose individuals to legal, immigration and consular complications,” it said.

“ The Government of Jamaica also wishes to advise that neither it, nor international humanitarian organisations can guarantee consular or humanitarian assistance or safe repatriation from active conflict zones,” the Government added.

The warning follows similar bulletins issued by the Dominican Republic.

READ: Lured to war: Caribbean men recruited by Russia with promises of work

The ministry is urging Jamaicans more widely to exercise due diligence in verifying the legitimacy of overseas employment offers, recruitment agencies and prospective employers before making travel arrangements or providing personal documents.

“Particular caution should be exercised where recruiters request passport information, advance payments or the signing of contracts that have not been independently verified or fully understood,” the ministry added.

Jamaicans at home who receive suspicious recruitment offers are encouraged to report the matter to the Ministry of Labour and Social Security. Those already overseas who believe they have been misled or coerced into military service should seek assistance from the nearest Jamaican diplomatic or consular mission, where it is safe to do so.

Persons may consult the Ministry of Labour and Social Security’s list of licensed employment agencies at www.mlss.gov.jm or contact its Employment Agencies Unit to seek verification of overseas employment opportunities.

World.title: 5 things to watch at the Dublin EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
Formal talks begin at 9:45 a.m. followed by lunch around 1 p.m. and a press conference provisionally scheduled for 4:15 p.m.

Here are the five issues that really matter — and what to watch for.

1. AI: Can Europe compete at the frontier?

Leaders will debate how Europe can build its own AI capacity, from computing power and cloud infrastructure to chips and models. European Council President António Costa framed the discussion around sovereignty, asking leaders to consider “how Europe can become a leading and sovereign player” across the AI value chain.

The central question is whether Europe should build frontier models to rival U.S. and Chinese developers, or focus on applications built on those models. Finland’s Petteri Orpo and Estonia’s Kristen Michal have argued that Europe “can compete at the frontier” and must aim beyond merely adopting AI.

The obstacle, however, is money. Leaders will discuss how to fund the computing capacity needed to turn European research into products. They will also hear from the CEO of French AI company Mistral, Arthur Mensch, who has railed against abandoning the frontier, and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton about global rules for the technology. The EU’s position is that its AI Act already provides a regulatory framework.

What to watch: Whether leaders back frontier AI development — and commit money to it.

World.title: Dissident leader wants Europe to consider Belarus in broader Ukraine peace deal
World.content:
Belarus has been a steadfast ally of the Kremlin, which also came to Lukashenko’s aid in August 2020 after a popular uprising threatened to unseat the longtime authoritarian ruler after he rigged an election against Tsikhanouskaya, who then fled the country. Now living in exile in Lithuania, she was handed a 15-year jail term after being convicted in absentia for treason.

The dissident leader criticized what she viewed as a lackadaisical approach to Belarus from Europe’s leaders, particularly before the 2020 election. “For us it looked like Europe just closed eyes, like ‘Lukashenko, you are son of the bitch, but you’re our son of the bitch. We know how to work with you, so okay. We are okay with this.’”

Asked if she blamed former German Chancellor Angela Merkel for the chain of events that led to the invasion of Ukraine, particularly the German leader’s role in the 2014 and 2015 Minsk agreements, which failed to deter Putin from further aggression, Tsikhanouskaya demurred.

“It’s not because of Angela Merkel that the war started against Ukraine,” she said. “It was because Russia was emboldened. I cannot judge politicians who have to make difficult decisions in difficult times. Maybe at that moment she was supported by German people … the policy of appeasement of Putin not only came from the side of Germany but from other [European] countries [and] brought us to the situation we are in.”

However, she accused Europe more broadly of turning a blind eye to the repression of the regime in Minsk. “For 30 years, Lukashenko was playing seesaw between Russia and Europe,” she said, seeking cheap oil and gas from Russia in winter and courting European investment for the rest of the year.

Tsikhanouskaya was attending the Freedom and Security Women Summit in Germany’s parliament during Berlin Freedom Week, which marks the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall and supports pro-democracy dissident movements.

You can hear the full interview here.

World.title: How to win friends and throw people: Judo’s big impact on politics
World.content:
The five-time Olympic gold medal-winning judoka — that’s someone who does judo, not a number puzzle — announced his candidacy by saying: “France doesn’t need a professional politician who recites talking points and spends all day bickering. It needs common sense, firmness, justice and a government that sets things right.”

As anyone who has ever tried to rewire a house or perform their own dentistry knows, many tasks very much do require a specialist. Politics is usually, though not always, one of them, and therefore Riner may be underestimating the challenge ahead. That said, he is a national hero and has already received an endorsement of sorts from President Emmanuel Macron — although that might not be great news for Riner, as Macron is about as popular in France as putting extra butter on a croissant or working 40 hours a week.

Most of the current crop of candidates have years of experience in political debates behind them, whether that’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon or any of the 430 centrist ex-prime ministers who want to replace Macron. To level the playing field for Riner, surely it’s only fair to hold a judo competition to see who makes it to the second round — my money would be on Le Pen to beat Riner in the runoff with a Hane-goshi, that’s a springing hip throw that uses the right side of the body.

But what if Riner wins? Could he be the answer to the question “who speaks for Europe when it comes to Russia”? Judo is, after all, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s favorite sport — well, second favorite after “bombing Kyiv.”

Judo is also fairly popular among politicians. Staying in France, David Douillet was a two-time Olympic champion who became a member of parliament and even sports minister. His predecessor as minister was karate champion Chantal Jouanno,, and the president while both were in government was Nicolas Sarkozy, who is reportedly a brown belt in judo — although for security reasons, they do make you remove your belt, no matter the color, when you go to prison.

Outside France, Pierre Trudeau, the former prime minister of Canada, and ex-Japanese Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda were serious judokas too.

World.title: What will a female president mean for Germany and Europe?
World.content:
A rare outbreak of cross-party unity has interrupted months of infighting surrounding Friedrich Merz’s embattled coalition in Berlin. His nomination of Ilse Aigner — a respected conservative from Bavaria — has united his own party and received support from the Social Democrats and the Greens. She is all but certain to become the country’s first female president in January.

A largely ceremonial role, the presidency of the Federal Republic represents the country abroad. The significance of a woman taking the highest office in the land has not gone unnoticed in other European capitals. In Berlin this week, Anne McElvoy talks to Gordon Repinski, chief political analyst for POLITICO, WELT and Business Insider. He’s been following the rise of Isle Aigner closely.

Berlin Freedom Week makes the connection between the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall and geopolitics today. As part of this week’s events, Anne attended the Freedom and Security Women Summit in the Bundestag, where she chaired panels of brave women who’ve been challenging autocratic regimes on Europe’s borders and beyond — and are calling on the EU to support their cause. Among them is Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, the Belarusian opposition leader, who has been forced to carry on her fight in Lithuania — despite defeating President Alexander Lukashenko in the country’s election six years ago. Anne also speaks with Hannah Neumann, a prominent Green MEP and campaigner for women’s rights, who supports Ilse Aigner’s nomination.

Questions? Comments? Message us on WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: EU leaders start Friday’s summit still at odds over who should lead on Ukraine
World.content:
Russia’s full-scale invasion started in February 2022 and as Trump’s enthusiasm for brokering peace has ebbed and flowed, the EU has found itself edged out of the picture ― despite increasingly picking up the tab.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who met with about 50 EU and non-EU leaders in Dublin on Thursday, warned that Russia was seeking to reshape Europe’s security architecture and insisted that European governments must have a voice in the negotiations, following two days of Russia-Ukraine-U.S. negotiations in Abu Dhabi that largely left out the EU.

Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, discussed the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier on Thursday before the American pair touched down in Dublin in the evening to offer Zelenskyy their thoughts.

The EU is united over the need to have a seat at the table as Ukraine’s main backer, but not on who it should send, with diplomats and officials telling POLITICO that the bloc has split into at least three camps.

In one, there is growing support for European Council President António Costa, whose role makes him the natural candidate to represent the bloc. In another, there’s France and Germany, both of which are reluctant to surrender their own places at the negotiating table to Brussels.

And then there’s the loneliest camp of all, the backers of Kaja Kallas. The bloc’s top diplomat would be the obvious pick, if not for her hawkishness on Russia, which some diplomats say could put off the Kremlin and make her a liability.

World.title: Jensen Huang’s fall further exposes EU leaders on AI
World.content:
Friday’s roundtable of European leaders in Dublin must reckon with the reality that the pursuit of AI superiority remains a two-horse race between the U.S. and China — and that Nvidia's leadership drama doesn’t change the fact that a single American company’s chips will continue to drive the artificial intelligence boom.

With the meeting meant to help forge a new direction for Europe on AI, leaders will mostly be in listening mode, with presentations by Arthur Mensch, CEO of French AI company Mistral, and computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, considered one of the “godfathers of AI” and an advocate for more stringent safety measures.

“We’re not going to pretend that we are experts,” an EU official said.

The session comes as Europe struggles to find its place in global AI. The rise of advanced U.S.-built proprietary models and open-weight artificial intelligence progress in China has created a new range of national security issues — and while the EU has proven to be a leader in regulating the technology, its own would-be frontier AI labs continue to play catch-up.

Although this week’s events are a reminder to European politicians that they are spectators in the AI race, an emerging split between top industry leaders in Europe is also dampening momentum on a bloc-wide effort to take on the competition.

“Switching dependency from California to France doesn’t solve Europe’s sovereignty problem, right?” Uljan Sharka, CEO of leading Italian company Domyn, said in an interview.

World.title: Not even old Andalusian heartlands can save Pedro Sánchez
World.content:
“We’re here to vote, we’re here to win, we’re here to govern,” Sánchez told the adoring crowd, which had been shown videos of the prime minister reciting poems by Federico García Lorca, the celebrated Andalusian poet and playwright murdered by Francoist forces in 1936.

Sánchez’s decision to launch his campaign in Seville is laden with historic symbolism. For 36 years, the Socialists dominated Andalusian politics, controlling the regional government and many of the region’s biggest cities.

That hold on power ended in 2018, after years of declining support and a string of corruption scandals paved the way for the center-right People’s Party to take control.

Since becoming regional president in 2019, Juanma Moreno has established himself as a steady, pragmatic leader, winning a landslide victory in 2022 and securing the most votes in snap elections earlier this year. His success in Andalusia has also elevated his profile nationally, making him one of the leading figures of the PP’s moderate wing.

Despite the PP’s consolidation of power in Andalusia, the Socialists are not ready to relinquish their claim on the region. Francisco Toscano, a Socialist candidate for congress in Seville, told POLITICO the party still considered Andalusia to be its bastion.

“This is an eminently progressive region, and one whose voters believe in progressive government,” he said.

World.title: AI and Ukraine to dominate EU leaders’ talks — live updates
World.content:
DUBLIN — It was supposed to all be about how Europe faces up to the challenges posed by artificial intelligence. Not for the first time at a summit of EU leaders, more pressing concerns are getting in the way.

And, as has so often been the case since Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it’s that conflict which is set to dominate proceedings in Dublin.

The EU is at odds over who should represent it in any peace talks. When officials from Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. met in Abu Dhabi earlier this week, Europe was only on the fringes. Most European leaders say that must change ― but working out how and with whom is easier said than done.

Friday is the second day of meetings in the Irish capital. Thursday’s gathering of 50 leaders under the banner of the European Political Community included several discussions involving smaller groups, chats with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and a debrief from Donald Trump’s envoys who had earlier met Putin in Moscow.



We’ll bring you the best of the action, from the latest on the Ukraine arguments to the AI discussions and other items which might crop up, like the race to succeed Christine Lagarde at the head of the European Central Bank and the never-ending back-and-forth over the EU’s next seven year budget.

World.title: US: New Congress members pose for traditional photo at Capitol
World.content:
Footage captures newly elected members of the US House of Representatives ascending the Capitol steps, mingling in clusters and exchanging warm greetings, some punctuated by enthusiastic high-fives. Drawn from Illinois, Iowa, Michigan, New York, Virginia and beyond, the freshman cohort gathered for a mandatory orientation programme designed to introduce first-time lawmakers to parliamentary protocol, their impending duties and life on Capitol Hill.

 

Their arrival in Washington follows November’s midterm elections, which yielded sweeping gains for the Democrats alongside a markedly smaller intake of Republicans. This transitional phase sees incoming politicians crossing paths with departing incumbents clearing their desks, signalling the formal handover to the next legislature.

Over the coming weeks, novices will immerse themselves in legislative mechanics and institutional operations before the 120th Congress convenes on 3 January 2027, when members will take the oath of office and formally assume their mandates.

World.title: Huang's exit, AI bubble and financial crisis fears in focus on Web Summit's last day
World.content:
Jensen Huang's sudden exit as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, the risk of an AI bubble and mounting US debt took the main stage on Thursday, a packed final day of the Web Summit in Lisbon, one of Europe's largest tech conferences.

 

Speakers on a panel moderated by Euronews warned that public debt markets could set off the next financial crisis.

The panel featured Adam Kobeissi, founder and editor-in-chief of The Kobeissi Letter, a capital markets publication with millions of followers, and economist James Galbraith, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

It was one of many sessions squeezed into Thursday after Wednesday's programme was called off on the advice of the Portuguese government, which had declared a state of emergency ahead of Storm Charles.

Ultimately, the storm did not hit Lisbon, which only saw heavy rain and minor flooding.

Huang's exit is "a net negative for investors"

Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of two extramarital affairs.

US intelligence reportedly suspects one of the women was spying for China, claims Beijing rejects. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.

Nvidia stock dropped roughly 15% at the open on Thursday but has since pared losses and is down a little over 5% on the day to around $164 per share, at the time of writing.

Since the all-time high price of $243 per share it hit on Monday 5 October, it is down over 30%.

FILE. Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, 22 May 2025 TVBS via AP

Kobeissi said Huang should not have resigned and that his departure "will be a net negative for investors" over the next couple of years, though he remained bullish on Nvidia overall.

He also did not expect Huang's exit to affect next week's stock market debut of Anthropic, the AI firm behind the Claude models, which is seeking a valuation of as much as $1.4 trillion (€1.25tn).

Nvidia is among seven tech companies that have agreed to buy Anthropic shares at the offer price.

AI, China, US debt and midterm elections

Professor Galbraith said there was a good possibility that Chinese technology would eventually undercut Nvidia's, which would raise questions about the hundreds of billions that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and other hyperscalers are currently pouring into AI infrastructure.

He framed the global economy as a contest between two systems.

The US makes it easy to raise private money quickly but is slower to set policy and take decisions, he explained, while China can centralise research, technological development and deployment, and intervene more directly in its economy.

For those reasons, Galbraith said he "would tentatively bet on China" to win the AI race, and perhaps to become the world's largest economy over the next few decades.

Beyond the AI boom, the panel pointed to public debt markets as a major concern.

Kobeissi warned that one in five dollars spent by the US government goes towards paying interest on the debt, "not even to pay down the debt". US Treasury data shows Washington spent $1.1 trillion (€988bn) on net interest in the fiscal year to September, or 19% of its revenue.

"US debt to GDP ratio is at World War II levels and there has not been a technical recession since the COVID-19 pandemic," Kobeissi said, adding that "the debt market has been screaming that it will be in a higher for longer environment in the foreseeable future," meaning interest rates are set to stay high.

"On the current path the US is on, there is a 100% chance of bankruptcy," he warned, adding that central banks cannot bring down interest rates in the current environment.

Adam Kobeissi on stage during day three of the Web Summit 2026 at the MEO Arena in Lisbon, 12 November Web Summit/Shauna Clinton

Still, "we are not in an imminent 2008 situation but the trends 10 or 20 years out are very concerning," Kobeissi said, although he remains "a huge bull" on the US, citing its resilient economy and accelerating innovation.

Professor Galbraith recalled how, during the COVID-19 pandemic, US President Donald Trump and a Democratic-controlled House agreed on relief to rescue the markets, but warned that the same cohesion might be lacking now.

In last week's US midterm elections, Democrats won 255 House seats to the Republicans' 169, according to AP's count as of the time of writing. Several US states are still tabulating ballots and Democrats can still flip the Alaska Senate seat and multiple of the 16 uncalled House seats.

When asked to make a prediction, Professor Galbraith stated that "the nature of financial crises is that we cannot foresee them," though he saw concerning signs.

World.title: Nvidia without Huang 'a significant loss' and puts the AI boom under a microscope, say economists
World.content:
Nvidia’s founder, Jensen Huang's resignation from the artificial intelligence giant has rattled a market already heavily dependent on a handful of AI companies but analysts do not expect the chip giant to have a long-term impact.

 

“It is a significant loss for the industry as a whole,” said investor and founder of financial publication The Kobeissi Letter, Adam Kobeissi.

Speaking at Web Summit in Lisbon on a panel moderated by Euronews, Kobeissi said Huang’s resignation was “a critical mistake,” adding that more time should have been taken for an investigation.

Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday as chief executive of Nvidia after the revelation of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee, marking a stunning fall from grace after being a global leader in the AI boom.

12 November 2026; Speakers, from left, James Galbraith, Adam Kobeissi, and Pascale Davies at Web Summit Lisbon 2026 Photo by Ramsey Cardy/Web Summit via Sportsfile

Kobeissi said that AI is the “biggest revolution in history” and that Nvidia will remain at the forefront.

As for the longer-term impact, James Galbraith, a professor at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs, University of Texas at Austin, who was also on the panel, said Nvidia is too important a company and that it will continue.

“The nature of large, successful corporations is that they are built to survive their founders or any mortal human who happens to be in charge,” Galbraith said. If the company is as strong as its reputation suggests, he said, the effects of the transition may not be long-lasting, he added

But Kobeissi warned that Nvidia’s troubles are unlikely to stay contained as much of the AI boom depends on just a few companies, making it “hard to say” whether anything involving Nvidia can be treated in isolation.

That could have implications for the industry’s next big moment. Kobeissi said he expects Anthropic to go ahead with its public offering, possibly as soon as next week.

Private debt markets are becoming “a little tapped out” as a source of capital, he said, and the next couple of quarters will be full of uncertainty, from the midterm election outcome to policy shifts and other headwinds.

“The notion that you can wait for uncertainty to dissipate in the AI world right now is kind of questionable,” he said.

World.title: Microsoft outage hits Outlook, Teams and Copilot, disrupting thousands
World.content:
A service interruption atMicrosoft caused disruption for thousands of users on Thursday 12 November, with access problems mainly affecting Outlook, the group’s email platform, but also Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 tools. The outage, particularly widespread in the Americas, affected users in several regions, according to reports collected by the Downdetector website.

 

In the United States, around 1.30 pm Eastern time (7.30 pm in Italy), more than 120,000 users had reported difficulties with Outlook. The number rose to over 130,000 according to data reported by Downdetector. The reports mainly concerned the inability to access their mailbox, send or receive messages and delays in email delivery.

Problems were also recorded for Microsoft 365, with more than 46,000 reports, and for Teams, the communications platform used mainly in workplaces, with around 3,000 users reporting access difficulties. Disruption was also reported for Copilot, Microsoft’s artificial intelligence based assistant.

Microsoft investigates: infrastructure overload

The company has confirmed that it is working to identify the source of the problem. In a series of updates posted on X, Microsoft initially said it had received reports from users who were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes through various connection methods in the Americas.

In a subsequent communication, the group identified a possible factor behindthe outage: part of its infrastructure was experiencing higher than normal load, probably responsible for the connection errors.

To limit the impact, Microsoft announced that it intended to redistribute traffic across its infrastructure, in order to rebalance the load and restore connectivity.

Issues for Teams too, first restoration in North America

The day had begun with reports of malfunctioning for Teams as well. Microsoft said it had resolved the issues affecting the service in North America, although some users were still complaining of connection difficulties.

The company did not immediately provide further details on the cause of the fault or an overall estimate of the users involved. The figures from Downdetector, which collects user reports, do not necessarily represent the actual number of people affected by the interruption.

World.title: Mercedes-Benz halts new investment in German plants, considers closures
World.content:
The future of Mercedes-Benz's production sites in Germany is coming under increasing pressure. Because of high labour costs and stalled talks with the works council and IG Metall, the Stuttgart carmaker is taking action. The management board has decided to suspend all further investment at German sites for the time being. Possible plant closures are now also being considered in more concrete terms.

 

Mercedes puts the brakes on spending

As bild.de reported on Thursday, HR director Britta Seeger justified the move by pointing to the strained cost situation. The group now has to examine which locations in Germany can still be operated profitably in the long term. Mercedes wants to avoid plant closures as far as possible, she said, but this option now has to be pursued more seriously than before.

The talks with employee representatives are considered deadlocked. A swift agreement is currently not in sight, Seeger explained in an internal interview that zeit.de reported on, citing the news agency Reuters. The aim remains a joint package that delivers noticeable savings while at the same time being socially acceptable.

At the heart of the dispute are production costs. According to Mercedes, an hour of labour in German plants can cost up to five times as much as at sites in Eastern Europe. The management board is therefore demanding concessions on working conditions. One proposal under discussion is to extend working hours without increasing pay.

Special payments such as profit sharing, holiday bonuses and Christmas bonuses could also be subject to cuts. The demands have already triggered protests among employees.

Sindelfingen, Rastatt or Bremen?

Head of production Michael Schiebe had already announced a few weeks ago that if cost reductions fail to materialise, two plants in Germany could be closed. Under current thinking, this would affect one vehicle assembly plant and one so called powertrain plant where vehicle components are manufactured.

According to zeit.de, Mercedes operates assembly plants among other places in Sindelfingen, Rastatt and Bremen. Powertrain sites include Stuttgart-Untertürkheim, Affalterbach, Berlin, Hamburg and Kamenz as well as locations in Thuringia. It is not yet known which specific plants could be affected by possible closures.

Volkswagen and subsidiary Audi are also cutting costs

The cost cutting is seen as driven not only by high site costs but also by the group's economic difficulties. In recent years Mercedes-Benz has struggled with falling sales and slumping profits.

The problems are not limited to the Stuttgart manufacturer. Volkswagen and Audi have also announced extensive savings programmes and job cuts.

Automotive expert Ferdinand Dudenhöffer sees these developments, according to bild.de, as a consequence of the long known competitiveness problems of Germany as a car manufacturing location. Without a fundamental change in cost structures, he warns, Germany's car industry risks losing even more of its competitiveness.

The dispute at Mercedes thus highlights the growing pressure on the German car industry. While the company is pushing for lower production costs, the works council and IG Metall are trying to safeguard jobs and collectively agreed benefits. An agreement is still not in sight.

World.title: Russia and Iran criticise US Caspian task force as study outlines joint sanction evasion
World.content:
As Iran issued fresh warnings about a widening military confrontation, Moscow and Tehran reacted to the creation of a new task force by the US military to monitor land and sea transit routes north of Iran and in the Caspian Sea, expanding its blockade.

 

Russia's Foreign Ministry described Washington's plan to form a task force to monitor and block Iran's trade and transport routes in the Caspian region as "a clear threat" to the rights and interests of the littoral states, adding that security in the Caspian Sea is an internal matter that concerns only the five states bordering it.

"We consider this latest escalatory and provocative step a blatant violation of the norms of international law and we declare our full support for the position of the Iranian authorities that continued economic pressure will not succeed in collapsing Iran's economy," the Russian foreign ministry said.

This reaction came after United States Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on 7 November the creation of the "Iron Gate" task force, a unit whose stated aim is to prevent the transfer of advanced weapons and dual-use items to Iran via land borders and the Caspian Sea.

CENTCOM also stressed in a statement posted on X on Wednesday that US forces are working around the clock to keep the Strait of Hormuz open to commercial shipping, to enforce rigorously an "Iron Maritime Blockade" against Iran, and to work with US partner institutions to prevent the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps from using land routes and the Caspian Sea to move advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned items and illicit revenue streams.

Meanwhile Kazem Gharibabadi, deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, said after meeting the Russian ambassador in Tehran that the two sides had discussed how to counter "unilateral US measures" and the "Iron Gate" programme and had emphasised the need for coordination in the face of common threats.

Gharibabadi stated that "Tehran and Moscow stress the need for coordination and cooperation in the face of common threats," adding that "the interests of the littoral states will also be served by maintaining stability and security in the Caspian."

ISW assessment and Tehran-Moscow economic relations

The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and the "Critical Threats Project" (CTP) said in their latest joint assessment that "Iran and Russia are cooperating to counter US efforts to stop weapons shipments to Iran via the Caspian Sea and land routes."

"Iran has used its Caspian Sea trade routes with Russia to import Russian arms before and during the 2026 US-Israel-Iran War, which prompted Ukraine to strike a shipment in July 2026," the ISW study said.

According to the think tank's analysis, the Caspian Sea is out of the Western monitoring bodies' reach allowing sanctioned Russian cargo ships to move consignments from the ports of Astrakhan and Olya to the ports of Anzali, Nowshahr and Amirabad.

An examination of recent maritime traffic data shows that, after loading in the ports of Astrakhan and Olya, sanctioned Russian cargo ships transfer their cargoes to the Iranian ports of Anzali, Nowshahr and Amirabad. As these ships approach the shores of the two countries, they switch off their Automatic Identification Systems (AIS) to conceal the nature of their cargoes.

Last summer Ukraine's Security Service also announced that the country's long-range drones had targeted two cargo ships in the Caspian Sea which, according to Kyiv, were involved in transferring military equipment between Iran and Russia.

In recent years Tehran and Moscow have sought not only to deepen their security and military ties but also to expand their economic and transit relations within the framework of the North-South corridor. Completing the Rasht-Astara railway, the missing link in this transit route which connects Russia to ports in the Persian Gulf, is one of the two countries' flagship projects.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said after his recent meeting with Russian president Vladimir Putin in Moscow that the council had approved the executive agreement for the construction of this railway.

He added that the meeting had also discussed building gas pipelines from Russia to Iran to address fuel shortages and allow exports to neighbouring countries.

Ongoing fragility of security in the Strait of Hormuz amid a continued "no war, no peace" situation in the region

Tensions over Iran's northern trade routes are rising at a time when the security situation in the southern waters and the Strait of Hormuz also remains fragile and volatile, despite an environment that observers describe as a "no war, no peace" situation.

The public relations office of the Revolutionary Guard Navy said in a statement on Thursday that two "supertankers" had been involved in an incident the previous night while passing through the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz and had been brought to a halt by a "massive explosion".

According to the Guard, the two vessels were carrying more than four million barrels of oil in total and had "ignored repeated warnings that the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz was unauthorised and unsafe".

Iran insists that vessels should pass only along the route it has designated in the Strait of Hormuz and says that the security consequences for "violating" ships are their own responsibility.

The Institute for the Study of War and the "Critical Threats Project" also said in their joint assessment that Iran has abandoned the claimed 2,000 kilometre limit on the range of its ballistic missiles, a move which, according to the think tanks, formalises Tehran's longstanding efforts to develop longer range systems.

This assessment comes as Tasnim news agency, which is close to the Revolutionary Guard, has reported the display of a new ballistic missile in the Guard's missile city which, by combining the warhead of the "Fattah" missile with the "Kheibarshekan 2" booster, has increased the range of the Fattah hypersonic missile from 1,400 to 2,000 kilometres.

At the same time Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, once again stressed the order attributed to Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei for "no geographical limitations in confronting the enemy".

In a post on the social network X he again warned Europe that "if the United States starts another war against Iran, every military base involved in this aggression, from West Asia to Europe, will be a legitimate target of Iran's lethal attacks. There will be no safe distance, no safe haven and no immunity."

Meanwhile Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of Iran's parliament, also criticised Washington's approach in the region, writing that despite the slogan "America First", in practice and in its strategies the Americans have prioritised "Israel First".

According to Ghalibaf, Washington's acceptance of Israeli intelligence and plans is the main cause of the United States' current military, political and economic problems in the region.

World.title: FIFA president says Qatar safe for U-17 World Cup despite US withdrawal
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino says Qatar is safe to host the upcoming Under-17 World Cup, despite the United States withdrawing its team over security concerns.

 

Speaking to Euronews and local media in Doha on Thursday, Infantino said the decision was up to US Soccer but insisted other teams had nothing to fear.

"Every country, every national team knows best by themselves what they want to do, they decide," he said.

"What I can say is that everyone is welcome in Doha, everyone is safe in Doha," the FIFA president added.

The tournament begins on 19 November, with teams already arriving in the Qatari capital.

US withdrawal leaves vacant spot

US Soccer informed players on Wednesday that it was withdrawing from the competition, citing security concerns in the Gulf region.

FIFA confirmed the withdrawal on Thursday but said its security assessment remained unchanged and that "no new developments affecting the security situation of the tournament have occured".

"FIFA understands that US Soccer’s decision was made in light of the existing US Level 3 travel advisory," the world football body said in a statement, adding that "as with all FIFA tournaments and events, we are in close contact with the relevant authorities and are looking forward to the tournament kick-off in Qatar."

The United States had been due to face Montenegro, Chile and Algeria in Group J.

A replacement has yet to be announced, although local organisers expect an update soon.

"This is a FIFA decision, a FIFA competition," said Jassim Al Jassim, CEO of Qatar's Local Organising Committee, adding that "I think they will announce something within the next few days."

Al Jassim said preparations were continuing as normal, with several teams already in Doha for training camps and friendly matches.

He pointed to other international events hosted in Qatar in recent weeks, including MotoGP and a United Nations technology conference.

"Everything is normal, business as usual for us," he said.

China's Under-17 football team arrives in Doha for its first FIFA U-17 World Cup appearance in 21 years. Local Organising Committee

Building on last year's tournament

This is the second of five consecutive Under-17 World Cups Qatar will host through 2029.

During a visit to Aspire Zone on Thursday, Infantino praised the preparations for the tournament, which will bring together young players from six continents.

"Qatar is ready, FIFA is ready," he said.

He highlighted the eight pitches that will host matches and encouraged fans to attend.

"Come to Qatar, come to Doha, enjoy the best young players in the world," he said.

The competition expanded from 24 to 48 teams last year, with matches played across eight pitches at Aspire Zone.

Cameroon's Under-17 football team arrives in Doha ahead of the FIFA U-17 World Cup Qatar 2026. Local Organising Committee

Infantino admitted FIFA had been unsure how the format would work when it was introduced in 2025.

"We did not really know what to expect," he said.

"The response from all the teams, from the managers, from everyone was absolutely fantastic."

He said the tournament drew an average of 10,000 spectators a day last year, and organisers have since made improvements to accommodate potentially larger crowds.

This year's competition is scheduled to feature 104 matches, with up to eight games a day during the group stage and Round of 32.

Seven countries are set to make their debut, including Greece, Montenegro and Vietnam. China is also returning after a 21-year absence.

Teams arrive ahead of kick-off

Saudi Arabia, Cameroon, China and South Korea are among the teams already in Doha, with more expected in the coming days.

Saudi Arabia's Under-17 football team trains in Qatar ahead of the FIFA U-17 World Cup, which kicks off on 19 November. Local Organising Committee

Most matches will take place at Aspire Zone, where fans can watch several games in a single day.

Hosts Qatar begin their campaign against Panama on 19 November, while the final is scheduled for 13 December at Ahmad bin Ali Stadium.

World.title: Russia plays down peace talks with Europe after Witkoff raises hopes of breakthrough
World.content:
Russia has played down comments made by US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner suggesting Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to accept a European presence in the peace negotiations to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

 

Instead, it has asked Europe to cease military aid to Ukraine as a condition.

Witkoff and Kushner landed in Moscow on Thursday to seek Putin's consent for Europeans to join a sought-after multilateral format. So far, the process has unfolded trilaterally between Ukraine and Russia with US moderation.

The trip came after two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi, during which Moscow's delegation refused to sit down with the European team.

"The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment because they are our partners and it's important to us that they take part," Witkoff told reporters at the end of the meeting, according to Reuters.

Kushner said the discussions had been "very fulsome and detailed" on all the topics and would "hopefully" feed into a multilateral format.

But Putin's aide, Yuri Ushakov, cautioned against the prospect of having Russians and Europeans at the same table, saying that, first, Europeans need to decide between "peace" or "war", referring to their military support to Ukraine.

Moscow has long equated Europe to a warring party due to the provision of weapons and ammunition that allies have sent to Kyiv.

"So far, all their practical actions point precisely to the latter," Ushakov said.

During the meeting, Putin made it clear that his real interest lies in revising the continent's security architecture, a complex topic that Europeans see as a ploy to divert attention from the war in Ukraine and realise Russia's great-power aspirations, including gaining veto power over NATO's future membership.

The Russian president cited US President Donald Trump's plan for a "big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe" to underline his point.

"President Trump offers to agree on instruments for European security as a whole," Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.

"What do we hear from the Europeans? No, only after there is peace in Ukraine," he said, seemingly in reply to comments by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and High Representative Kaja Kallas, both of whom have made the discussion on security architecture contingent on a ceasefire in Ukraine.

"But once there is peace in Ukraine, they intend to deploy troops into its territory, which would mean the continuation of the war."

Witkoff and Kushner argued that a European presence was necessary to advance the peace process, which has so far yielded limited progress beyond the prisoner swaps.

Kushner dangled the prospect of discussing security architecture as an incentive.

"The Europeans have a desire for this war to really be the end and for there to be a long peace after," Kushner told Putin.

"And understanding the long-term security between Russia, Ukraine, and Europe is a conversation that we started having with them."

Meanwhile, in Dublin, European leaders pushed back against Putin's revisionist attempt, arguing it was Moscow that breached the security agreements that had been in place for decades. Any discussion on architecture, they said, required a European presence.

"It is important that Russia comes to the table and that Russia is ready for talks," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.

EU leaders are set to discuss on Friday the possibility of appointing a special envoy for the diplomatic process. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has asked them to designate one common representative by the end of the month.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said such a designation was a pre-requisite for joining the negotiations.

"The Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar. If someone takes the initiative to establish contact with the Russian side, such people are facing ostracism," Peskov said.

Russia's opposition, though, is not a blanket ban: last month, Putin held a 90-minute phone callwith the leaders of Finland and Norway.

World.title: ‘Monstrous injustice’: King Charles condemns slavery as UK agrees to talks
World.content:
In this episode of Spotlight on Africa, we talked to scholars from the continent and the Caribbean about slavery reparations – a key topic discussed at this year’s Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

Advertising

The Commonwealth is a 56-nation group of mostly former British colonies, 21 of them in Africa. King Charles III remains head of state in 15 of them, including the UK.

Its biennial Heads of Government Meeting took place from 1 to 4 November 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda.

In a final communiqué issued on Wednesday, the group said the time had come for “meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation towards forging a common future based on equity”.

Timetable of talks

While no timetable for talks was announced, the group welcomed the United Kingdom’s willingness to engage “in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms”.

In his opening speech, King Charles III, who is politically neutral, called the slave trade “a monstrous injustice” that filled him with “profound personal sorrow”, but stopped short of a formal apology.

UN backs resolution calling slave trade ‘gravest crime against humanity’

For his part, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to saying sorry but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also said it was “not feasible” for the country to pay reparations for slavery, but that “there are things we can work on co-operatively”.

According to reports, Britain could issue a formal apology next year, during its G20 presidency.

Britain played a pivotal role in the slave trade, which saw between 10 and 15 million enslaved Africans taken to the Americas over four centuries.

The country abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833. It paid financial compensation, but to plantation owners rather than to the enslaved people themselves.

UN resolution

In March this year, the United Nations adopted a resolution recognising the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity”, in a motion spearheaded by Ghana.

Ghana backs Jamaica’s petition to push UK for slavery reparations

For many countries, the time has come for formal apologies and concrete plans for slavery reparations.

To find out how these issues are being tackled on the African continent and in the Caribbean, RFI spoke to a panel of four guests:

Edem Adotey: professor at the Institute of African Studies in Accra, Ghana,

Joel Kibazo: Commonwealth spokesperson,

Matiangai Sirleaf: professor at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law in the United States,

Verene A. Shepherd: Jamaican historian and one of three vice-chairs of the Caricom Reparations Commission.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.

World.title: Darth Vader strikes back at auction as his lightsaber from two original Star Wars films reclaims the record from Luke Skywalker's prop
World.content:
Darth Vader's lightsaber sold for nearly $5 million, breaking the record set by Luke Skywalker's in July. The hilt, made from a 1950s camera flash attachment, was used in two of the original trilogy's duels.

A lightsaber prop made for "Star Wars" villain Darth Vader sold for $4.875 million (€4.4 million) on Thursday, setting an auction record for a collectible from the franchise, according to Dallas-based Heritage Auctions.

The iconic prop was used in two defining duels between Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker in the original "Star Wars" trilogy.

Which scenes featured Vader's lightsaber?

Vader wielded the lightsaber in the climactic Cloud City duel in "The Empire Strikes Back" (1980), where he cuts off Luke's hand. When Luke accuses him of killing his father, Vader replies with one of the saga's most famous lines: "No. I am your father."

The same lightsaber returned for their final duel in "Return of the Jedi" (1983). This time, Luke cuts off Vader's hand but refuses to kill him.

Vader's lightsaber set an auction record for a screen-used "Star Wars" prop in 2025. Luke's lightsaber from the same Cloud City duel broke it in July. In the latest twist, Vader struck back to reclaim the record.

Luke and Vader's first lightsaber duel took place in Cloud City, a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away (FILE: 1980) Image: 20th Century Fox/Everett Collection/picture alliance

Actor David Prowse and stunt performer Bob Anderson both wielded the saber as Darth Vader. It may also have been used in the original 1977 "Star Wars" film, but the auctioneers could not confirm that.

What inspired the lightsaber?

"Star Wars" creator George Lucas drew on Errol Flynn swashbucklers and the legends of King Arthur. He imagined the Jedi as peacekeepers guided by chivalry and honor and wanted a weapon that suited that role.

In the original "Star Wars," Luke's Jedi mentor, Obi-Wan Kenobi, gives him his father's lightsaber, describing it as "not as clumsy or random as a blaster" and calling it "an elegant weapon for a more civilized age."
