She often handles about 28 bookings a month, with as many as four on a busy day, each lasting two to four hours. At Qingbeihu, a two-hour booking costs 188 yuan ($26), while four hours of surgery accompaniment costs 360 yuan.

Li previously worked in sales and became interested in medical companionship after accompanying a family member to hospital and struggling with some of the procedures herself.

“I had no medical background, so even understanding the doctors’ terminology was difficult at first,” she recalls. When she encountered unfamiliar terms, she consulted more experienced colleagues.

At Qingbeihu, training covers first aid, hospital procedures, and organizing patient records. Companions also attend training at a Red Cross first-aid center and must pass an assessment organized by the Shanghai Association of Elderly Care Services and Aging Industry to obtain a medical companion certificate.

Much of the initial training is theoretical. Even after certification, newcomers must shadow experienced colleagues before taking bookings on their own.

“Many elderly patients become anxious in crowded hospitals, especially when they don’t know their way around,” Li says. She learned to calm them through conversation or small gestures, such as offering a bottle of water or some snacks.

One elderly patient with mid- to late-stage cancer initially refused to engage with her. He believed his illness was incurable and saw little point in spending money on treatment.

Li began talking to him about his family, listening as he spoke about his grandchildren. As he grew more comfortable with her, she encouraged him to continue treatment, reminding him that his relatives wanted him to recover. Li says he eventually agreed to cooperate with treatment.

Ma Xunru, a 60-year-old Shanghai retiree, had reservations when she hired a medical companion while her daughter was away on a business trip. She needed to visit a hospital for dizziness and cervical spine problems but worried that the companion might not be professional.

The crowds at the top-tier hospital made her dizziness worse. But her companion arranged appointments with two departments so she could see the doctors and complete the necessary examinations. Ma says that if she had gone alone or with her daughter, they would have registered with only one department.

“It was such a relief to have the companion with me. Otherwise I wouldn’t have known where to go,” Ma says. She now plans to use the service again.

“I think in the future I’ll ask my daughter to book a companion as well, so that I don’t need to bother her, since she’s busy with her work and life.”

Doctor’s orders

When Wang, a rehabilitation doctor in Shanghai, needed someone to accompany her for a gastroscopy, she hired a medical companion. Most of her friends were doctors, too, and asking one of them to come along would have meant rearranging a hospital shift.

She expected help preparing for the procedure and someone to talk to while she waited. “When taking the order, they only asked what time and where. And they were on their phone the whole time,” she recalls.

The experience helped prompt Wang, 25, to establish Zhuoyu Health with Zhou, 30, a gynecology and reproductive medicine doctor. Both asked to be identified only by their surnames.

Both had seen elderly patients struggle with hospital equipment such as self-service machines. Zhuoyu now has more than a dozen part-time companions drawn from rehabilitation, gynecology, anesthesiology, and the medical device industry.

Wang and Zhou found that questions they considered straightforward could leave patients at a loss, from what to do if they lost their ID card at a hospital to how to prepare for a CT scan. During consultations, they also help patients ask questions they might otherwise overlook and, afterward, understand their doctors’ instructions.

Wang’s first booking, in early June, involved an elderly woman whose health had suffered, she says, from using folk remedies during a long illness.

Before the visit, Wang and the woman’s son-in-law reviewed her medical records and the remedies she had been taking. With heavy rain that day, Wang rented a wheelchair for her. During an echocardiogram, she helped the woman adjust her clothing and explained each step.

Wang admitted to the family that she was handling her first booking. “I was very nervous taking my first order, and the patient’s family comforted me instead,” she recalls.

Zhou encountered a different problem while accompanying an elderly woman with poor hearing and limited Mandarin for a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The patient struggled to follow instructions requiring specific movements, and her anxious daughter began scolding her.

Zhou took the woman out of the examination room and explained what she needed to do. The second attempt went smoothly. “She wasn’t being uncooperative. She genuinely didn’t understand what she was supposed to do,” Zhou recalls telling the daughter.

Yang Hanxue, 25, decided to become a medical companion after seeing elderly people living alone and out-of-town patients struggle through hospital visits while she was working as a nurse.

Now at Qingbeihu, she adjusts her approach to different patients, explaining delays to those who are anxious, listening to those who want to talk, and keeping small talk to a minimum with people wary of the service.

Yang recalls a family wanting an elderly relative to undergo a full set of examinations, although the patient might not have been able to tolerate them. In such situations, she says, companions should remain neutral, relay the doctor’s advice, help families raise questions during consultations, and work toward an arrangement that accounts for the patient’s condition and the family’s wishes.

“Many people don’t understand this profession and mistakenly think we are experts, consulting us on how to treat illnesses,” Yang says. She tells patients and families to follow their doctor’s advice rather than offering treatment recommendations herself.

Wang recalls a patient who fell into a deep coma. The family eventually decided to discontinue treatment. Wang and Zhou say companions should not influence such decisions, but can offer support to relatives struggling with the choices they face.

Despite being a practicing doctor, Wang believes the boundaries of medical companionship need to be more clearly defined, particularly when patients ask companions to weigh in on treatment decisions.

“Patients often ask me, ‘The doctor recommended this — should I do it? Should I keep taking this medicine?’” she says.

Contributions: Marianne Gunnarsson; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A trained medical companion explains prescribed medication to an elderly couple at a traditional Chinese medicine hospital in Beijing, May 22, 2025. Jade GAO/AFP/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.title: Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.content:
A pair of Chinese noodle shops serving free meals sparked debate this week after their popularity reportedly disrupted neighboring shops’ business.

“Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop,” which opened two outlets last month in the densely populated Jiangning and Yuhuatai districts of Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, offers only one dish: noodles with braised vegetarian chicken and shiitake mushrooms. Each restaurant has around 50 seats, and since opening have been frequented mainly by middle-aged and elderly customers, according to domestic media.

Jiangning is home to a large migrant worker population, while Yuhuatai has the city’s largest public housing project. Signs outside the restaurants read, “A bowl of pure intention, with no fixed price; three meals a day, offered with warmth to those in need.”

The owner, surnamed Zhang, told domestic media he opened the shops for two reasons: promoting vegetarianism and charity. He said he had previously donated to charities and operated low-cost vegetarian restaurants but found that offering free noodles was the most effective way to achieve his philanthropic goals.

The two shops have served more than 1,000 bowls of noodles each day, Zhang said. He added that he had initially planned to open 10 stores, each serving 500 bowls a day, but demand had exceeded his expectations.

“Our idea was simple: get more people to come eat,” he said.

The topic has garnered more than 10 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many questioning whether the measures can genuinely help those in need.

Asked what they thought about the initiative, a local resident told domestic media, “It’s both good and bad. The good thing is that people who are genuinely struggling can come here to get a meal and meet their basic needs. The bad thing is, how can you tell who has money and who doesn’t?”

Other users suggested requiring customers to show their ID cards to exclude locals and help migrant workers.

In an interview with domestic media, Zhang rejected the idea of screening customers. “We want to give people facing difficulties a sense of dignity and respect,” he said.

Domestic media reported that one nearby restaurant’s daily revenue had fallen from 3,000 yuan ($450) to just a few hundred yuan. Another shop owner said he was considering not renewing his lease over concerns about declining customer traffic.

However, some shop owners said customer traffic along the street had already fallen after the relocation of several nearby factories. Others said the free noodle shops had not significantly affected their business.

Zhang told domestic media that affected business owners could work at his stores if they were willing.

He added that the two shops could lose up to 10 million yuan a year. The stores do not have payment QR codes, and he has also turned down donation offers from friends.

The shops have reportedly recently installed barriers to keep lines orderly and stopped providing noodle refills and napkins to discourage those who don’t truly need help from taking advantage of the offer.

Authorities told domestic media they had found no evidence that the restaurants were providing free meals as a publicity stunt. Local authorities also said they had visited the shops to check food safety compliance and help maintain order among customers queuing outside.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Crowds gather at a “zero-yuan noodle shop” in Nanjing, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.title: What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.content:
Fufeng County, some 110 kilometers west of the northwestern Chinese city of Xi’an, is best known for its stunning Tang dynasty (618–907) relics, unearthed from an underground crypt beneath Famen Temple in the late 1980s.

But ask a Chinese archaeologist about Fufeng, and they’ll likely point you in another direction: toward a quiet cluster of more than 20 villages located along the border with neighboring Qishan County. There, hidden beneath unassuming farms and village houses, lies what a growing number of experts believe was the first capital of the Western Zhou (1046–771 BC) — one of China’s earliest and most important dynasties.

Known as Zhouyuan — literally “The Plains of Zhou” — its excavation sites have produced some of China’s most famous bronze ritual vessels. In the 1940s, those discoveries led archaeologist Shi Zhangru to survey the area and eventually propose that this was Qiyi, the center of Zhou culture before the Zhou toppled the Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC).

In the decades that followed, archaeologists worked on the site sporadically, uncovering large rammed-earth building foundations, cemeteries, craft workshops, bronze hoards, and oracle bones, all dating to the Zhou period.

Yet planned, continuous excavation at Zhouyuan began only at the turn of the 21st century, when the Institute of Archaeology at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, and Peking University’s School of Archaeology and Museology formed a joint team to systematically explore the site.

Why the delay? Part of the problem was historiographical. Chinese scholars have long relied on written texts to locate historic sites, and for more than 2,000 years historians placed the Western Zhou capital dozens of kilometers away, in a place called Fenghao, near Xi’an.

This drew attention and resources from other sites in the region, including Zhouyuan. But over the past decade or so, the joint archaeological team at Zhouyuan has made a string of breakthroughs that suggest Shi Zhangru’s near-century-old hunch might be right — and possibly even show that Zhouyuan, not Fenghao, was the Western Zhou’s first capital.

“Modern excavations are revealing more and more contradictions between the archaeological record and traditional accounts,” Cao Dazhi, a Peking University-based archaeologist and co-leader of the Zhouyuan team, wrote in a 2023 paper. Cao’s analysis attracted widespread attention in China for arguing that Zhouyuan was the Zhou capital, while the Fenghao region was merely an important hub and site of the royal hunting grounds.

But the dispute over ancient capitals may not be the biggest revelation to emerge from the Zhouyuan excavations.

While the exact significance of the discoveries remains a matter of debate even within the team, mounting evidence suggests the Zhou capital’s population was far more diverse than previously thought. In addition to the core Zhou population, it was home to large numbers of conquered Shang, as well as migrants from the northwest and south.

That matters because, over time, the Zhou would establish a very different political and moral order from the Shang, one combining military power with ritual, moral claims to legitimacy, and the incorporation of conquered peoples. This order would help shape Chinese political culture for the next 3,000 years, but where did it come from? And could the answer lie in the palaces, streets, and workshops of Zhou’s most prominent early settlement?

“Sweet as sugar”

Zhouyuan was founded by a people on the move.

According to legend, an ancestor of the Zhou people had served as an agriculture official under the Xia — a legendary state traditionally regarded as China’s first dynasty — and the clan made its living farming the land north of what is now Xi’an.

After the Xia declined, the clan lost its fief. For most of the Shang, the Zhou wandered from place to place.

Finally, around the 12th century BC, their leader Gugong Danfu set out with his people in search of a land where they could finally settle and prosper.

“Mian,” a poem from the “Book of Songs,” China’s oldest surviving poetry anthology, tells this story in just 400 characters: After a long journey, the Zhou arrive at a place called Mount Qi, where they find wild herbs “sweet as malt sugar.” They carve a turtle shell for divination, and the resulting oracle tells them to settle there.

Laborers toil under the direction of officials, stretching cords to mark straight lines and raising frames to tamp the earth. Soon, “a hundred walls rise together.” Ancestral temples, palaces, and homes are built, roads are laid down, and the local barbarian tribes, awed by the magnificent new city, can only flee in disarray.

The claim that Zhouyuan’s wild grass tasted as sweet as sugar may be poetic license, but modern archaeological discoveries support the outlines of the story. Archaeological and environmental evidence suggests that the region offered favorable conditions for early agriculture, with fertile loess soils and plentiful rainfall.

That supported the Zhou as they developed a mixed agricultural system dominated by millet and, later, wheat. The region’s abundance is reflected in the contents of a predynastic Zhou storage pit — a kind of primitive refrigerator with walls plastered in straw-tempered mud — containing some 500 apricot pits, more than 150 melon seeds, and a handful of plum pits, some still glossy after 3,000 years.

But the crucial evidence for Zhouyuan as the site of the Zhou’s foremost settlement only came in 2020, with the discovery of a building archaeologists call Wangjiazui No. 1. Covering more than 2,500 square meters, the compound is divided into front and rear sections, with a front courtyard framed by gatehouses, side chambers, and a front hall. In the rear lies another courtyard, surrounded by a hall, side chambers, and a back chamber.

It’s a structure of truly royal proportions, and Wangjiazui No. 1 quickly caught the attention of the archaeological team. “Ever since Shi Zhangru proposed in the 1940s that Zhouyuan was where Gugong Danfu migrated, the bronze hoards and large building foundations unearthed here have steadily reinforced that judgment — but hard proof of a high-ranking predynastic building was always missing,” Chong Jianrong, director of the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, tells Sixth Tone. “Large rammed-earth foundations are the most direct indicator of a settlement’s rank: Only a settlement with capital-level political functions could build such a structure. Wangjiazui No. 1 provides that key evidence.”

Based on stratigraphy and radiocarbon dating, the team confirmed that the building dated to the predynastic Zhou period, before the conquest of Shang, thereby verifying the existence of a “central settlement” within the Zhouyuan cluster. Wangjiazui No. 1’s size and clearly defined layout are unmatched among predynastic finds, and archaeologists were also able to trace a belt of predynastic structures stretching over 150 meters from north to south — evidence of a deliberately planned settlement that was developed continuously, rather than a temporary encampment.

Yet even the grandest predynastic building at Zhouyuan pales next to contemporary Shang architecture: the No. 1 palace at the Shang city of Huanbei, built at least a century earlier, covers some 16,000 square meters — six times the size of Wangjiazui No. 1.

The gulf in scale reflected a gulf in power. In the 12th century BC, the Shang were a powerful empire built on violence and tight state control, with formidable armies, complex cities, and impressive industry.

The Zhou, meanwhile, were still a small tribe on the distant fringes of the Shang cultural sphere. But after centuries of wandering, they had finally found land to farm and walls to call home. And within a few generations, their roles would flip as the Zhou destroyed the Shang and conquered the Chinese heartland.

A melting pot

In early 1046 BC, on a plain in what is now the central province of Henan, the Battle of Muye — a clash that would transform the course of Chinese history — was about to begin.

According to traditional accounts, Ji Fa, Gugong Danfu’s great-grandson, led a coalition of allied tribes numbering fewer than 50,000 men. Opposing them was a Shang army said to number hundreds of thousands. Yet despite its supposed numerical superiority, the Shang force offered little resistance, and its defenses collapsed almost immediately. The decisive battle was over in a single day — and with it, nearly six centuries of Shang rule.

Zhou’s conquest of Shang greatly expanded their territory. To administer their new lands, the Zhou established two capitals. One was Luoyi, near present-day Luoyang in Henan. Close to the conquered Shang heartland, it was intended to keep watch over Shang remnants and the eastern lords.

For centuries, the other was believed to be Fenghao, in what is now Xi’an’s Chang’an District, roughly 90 kilometers from Zhouyuan as the crow flies.

But recent finds at Zhouyuan have uncovered hard evidence against that view: in particular, the presence of a walled city of about 1.75 million square meters, with a palace complex at its core.

The palace lies at the exact center of the city’s northern half, says Cao, the Peking University archaeologist whose article kickstarted the Fenghao-Zhouyuan debate. Covering roughly 500,000 square meters, it is the largest and best-preserved pre-Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) palace complex ever discovered.

A comprehensive coring survey in 2023 revealed buildings across almost the entire site. Roads crisscross the area: the avenue leading into the city was paved with a foundation of large stones topped with soil and gravel, not unlike a modern gravel road. And in the moats outside the palace city’s walls, archaeologists found oracle bones used in royal divination.

“By comparison, no city walls have yet been found at Fenghao,” Cao says. “In fact, Zhouyuan’s remains of every kind are richer than Fenghao’s: more people, more nobles and officials, more wealth.” He adds that a building he is currently excavating is the largest structure ever found from the Western Zhou.

Inside the palace district, members of the royal house would have enjoyed the highest luxuries the age could offer. Beyond the palace walls, the settlement hummed with industry. Archaeologists have identified 61 craft production sites within the settlement, which produced bronzes, bone objects, pottery, jade ware, and lacquered wood.

Notably, many of the laborers staffing these workshops were not from the Zhou. Strontium isotope analysis of human bones and teeth from sites across the Yellow River basin found that populations at predynastic Zhou and Western Zhou sites were among the most heterogeneous on record in China, pointing to large-scale migration to Zhouyuan.

The influx began even before the conquest of Shang, says Chong of the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology. He identifies two early waves of migration: people associated with the Nianzipo culture to the north, whose graves featured distinctive vertical shafts, followed by people associated with the Liujia culture to the west, who used catacomb-style tombs.

Once the Western Zhou was established and Zhouyuan became a dynastic capital, people and cultural influences converged there from every direction — including the Chu from the south and the Qin from the west. Two shell carvings of human heads unearthed in 1980 feature high-bridged noses and deep-set eyes reminiscent of depictions of the Saka, a Scythian-related people of the Eurasian steppe — a hint that even more distant groups may have lived at Zhouyuan.

But the largest group of migrants came from the east: the conquered people of the Shang. In fact, the Shang may have been the city’s second-largest demographic after the Zhou themselves.

“The population structure of Zhouyuan was highly complex, and the available material doesn’t yet support precise ratios,” Chong tells Sixth Tone. “But what is certain is that, while the Zhou formed the ruling core, other groups from the northwest and south were integrated in different ways; and Shang remnants were a major group of considerable size.”

Learning from the conquered

So why were so many Shang people living in the Zhou capital?

Immediately after their victory at Muye, the Zhou were faced with a challenge: how to integrate this distant power center into their new state. They moved quickly to extend their rule east, building Luoyi to strengthen their position in the Shang heartland, while planting their agents and allies at strategic points throughout the new territory.

They also pursued a deliberate strategy of breaking up the close-knit Shang clans and resettling them across their empire.

It must have been a colossal undertaking. At its peak, the Shang capital alone is estimated to have had a permanent population in the hundreds of thousands. But in the eyes of the Zhou rulers, the effort of relocating large numbers of people hundreds of kilometers was worth the trouble. Not only did it allow them to keep a close eye on their new subjects, but it also made a powerful political statement: the remnants of the fallen dynasty had fully submitted to the Zhou order.

Then there were the practical reasons for the relocation: Archaeological finds suggest that Zhouyuan’s new Shang residents clustered around the city’s workshops, where they would have put their technological know-how and skills to work for their new rulers.

“In the predynastic period, bronze casting across the Guanzhong region (surrounding Zhouyuan) was scarce, and only very simple vessels could be made,” Cao tells Sixth Tone. “Then, at a certain point, large numbers of exquisite bronzes suddenly appear, essentially identical to late Shang products.”

Scholars such as Cao speculate that this sudden shift was connected to the Zhou bringing Shang artisans — along with bronzes seized in war — back to Zhouyuan.

Bronze was just one of many crafts and cultural practices the Zhou learned from the Shang. Li Xueqin, the late chief scientist of the state-sponsored Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project, compared the oracle-bone inscriptions of Yinxu and Zhouyuan and found them “more alike than different” — evidence of continuity in the writing system and divination practices across the two dynasties.

Song Jiangning, who heads the CASS Institute of Archaeology’s Zhouyuan project, argues that several early Western Zhou buildings imitate Shang architectural forms, and believes that their designers were most likely Shang people.

The evidence suggests the Zhou allowed these people to maintain many of their cultural practices. Excavations at multiple Zhouyuan workshops show that Shang people carried on key traditions, including burying their dead close to home and organizing production around clan lines.

Production and daily life were concentrated within the workshop quarters; the dead were buried there in their clan’s customary way; and children inherited the family trade. In other words, the Zhou rulers treated them with relative leniency — especially in contrast to the Shang’s own brutal treatment of outsiders, as attested by the large numbers of human sacrifice victims unearthed at the former Shang capital.

“The archaeological material tells us that the early Western Zhou inherited many Shang practices across the board — crafts, writing, architectural layouts, and even the ‘hereditary artisan clan’ mode of organizing production,” Chong tells Sixth Tone.

Running dry

As Zhouyuan attracted more and more people, its workshops continued to grow, eventually outpacing the city’s initially planned borders.

Toward the end of the Western Zhou period, the dynasty established a new, far larger settlement southeast of the original city, roughly tripling Zhouyuan in size and turning it into the largest known Chinese city of the Western Zhou. Excavations have uncovered walls and gates on a scale unprecedented for the pre-Qin period. It was a clear display of power and order.

Yet the city’s residents had little time to enjoy their magnificent new metropolis. In 771 BC, after 275 years of rule, the Western Zhou fell. Nomadic tribes from the west invaded the Guanzhong Basin, and King Ping fled east with his lords to the dynasty’s second capital of Luoyi. The Zhou would survive as the Eastern Zhou, but royal power quickly declined, and China descended into centuries of conflict and war.

Curiously, archaeologists have found almost no Eastern Zhou artifacts at Zhouyuan.

That might seem natural enough: after all, Zhouyuan was no longer the capital. But experts say it is highly unusual. “Think about it,” Song Jiangning of CASS tells Sixth Tone. “Chinese history is full of cities — Xi’an, Nanjing, Hangzhou — that were once capitals and later weren’t. When a city loses capital status, the royals and officials leave, sure. But do ordinary people leave? No. They go on with their lives. Zhouyuan is different. After the Western Zhou, the people of that city disappeared almost completely.”

The bronze hoards found densely packed across the site suggest the city’s abandonment was sudden.

“Picture the scene: the city suffers a sudden disaster, and the noble families must flee with the royal house,” Cao explains. “Their bronzes are incredibly precious — and far too heavy to carry — so they hastily dig pits and stash them away. The density of bronze hoards at Zhouyuan makes it easy to picture the rows of aristocratic mansions that once stood here, and the panic of their owners’ flight.”

But what exactly was the catastrophe? Many historians attribute the city’s fall to invasions by groups from the west. Song, however, wonders whether the city succumbed to something deadlier than war.

“Down through the ages, cities have generally met one of two fates,” he says. “The first is ‘rise and decline’: once a capital, then no longer; once prosperous, then decayed. That kind of story is common, and behind it are human factors.”

“The second fate, less common, is ‘life and death,’” he says. “Liangzhu died, Shimao died, Taosi died, the capitals of the 36 states of the Western Regions almost all died. Perhaps that is what happened to Zhouyuan. The death of a city means its people simply could no longer live there — and behind that usually lie forces of nature.”

For years, Song has studied the relationship between Zhouyuan’s water resources and its urban planning, hoping to crack the mystery of the city’s disappearance. Zhouyuan sits on a loess tableland, and its inhabitants drew water from two rivers descending from the mountains. To secure a sufficient, stable supply, they built a hydraulic system covering more than 30 square kilometers — enormous in scale and remarkably complex and refined in design.

For a time, the artificial canals worked well. But rivers rushing down from the mountains continually cut deeper into their channels; as the water levels fell, the canals had to be dug ever deeper, and at ever greater cost. Meanwhile, Zhouyuan kept expanding, and the demand for water kept growing.

To make matters worse, sediment analysis suggests that the city’s water-management authorities maintained the system diligently in the early Western Zhou, but grew lax in the middle period, and had ceased to function entirely by the dynasty’s collapse.

Although the evidence is inconclusive, water scarcity may be one reason Zhouyuan was abandoned. The same may have happened to several large Western Zhou dozens of kilometers to the west.

To Song, the quest to understand how Zhouyuan collapsed is almost as important as the answer itself. “To attend to one thing is inevitably to neglect another — and on that, we are no different from the ancients,” he says. “What the ancients did is done and cannot be redone. But we can study them, assess them, and learn from them. Zhouyuan is a modern-day revelation — how it rose, prospered, and died.”

A new order

The death of Zhouyuan was a catastrophe for the nobles and commoners who called it home. For archaeologists today, it has proven an unexpected gift.

One need only compare it with Luoyi — modern-day Luoyang — the Zhou’s eastern capital. Celebrated in China as the “ancient capital of thirteen dynasties,” Luoyang has served as a seat of power longer, and for more dynasties, than almost any other city in China. But that very longevity is the archaeologist’s headache: wave upon wave of construction has left cultural layers piled one atop another, making dating unearthed remains a thorny task.

Zhouyuan is different. No major city has stood there since the Western Zhou. The land has been farmed for nearly 3,000 years, and remains so today.

For China’s archaeologists and historians, that is rare good fortune, especially given that Zhouyuan may contain the answer to one of the longest-standing riddles in Chinese history: How China transitioned from the Shang to the Zhou, whose focus on ritual, order, and moral justifications for rule would shape future Chinese states for millennia.

Over a hundred years ago, the renowned scholar Wang Guowei called the Shang-Zhou transition “the most drastic transformation in Chinese politics and culture.” In essence, it shifted the basis of political order — from sacrificial ritual to political ethics. The Shang revered gods and ghosts, seeking to appease them with elaborate sacrifices, including human sacrifice; the Zhou, while not immediately breaking from Shang practices entirely, set out to build an alternative justification for their rule.

Historians have read this shift in many ways. According to one widely shared view, the Shang placed their faith in divination and sacrifice, trusting that so long as the rituals never lapsed, their ancestors and the spirits would protect them.

The Zhou advanced a different argument: Heaven favored virtue, and political legitimacy depended on the moral conduct of the ruler. Through the patriarchal clan system and the strategic allocation of titles and fiefs, they wove political and ethical order into a single fabric.

Dynasties rose and fell over the nearly 3,000 years that followed, and the machinery of government was rebuilt many times — but the Zhou ideal of “governing through virtue” endured. “By the Western Zhou, Chinese civilization had its ‘final draft,’” says Song.

Now, archaeologists can look for the physical evidence of that transition. The numerous tombs of Shang survivors found around Zhouyuan’s craft workshops, for instance, reveal a dynasty that inherited Shang culture and technology on a massive scale even as it labored to build a new ethical and moral order — one that could legitimize Zhou rule while incorporating conquered peoples and other groups.

“What did not change between Shang and Zhou dwarfs what did,” says Chong. “But that is precisely why we focus on the change — on how the Zhou built the ritual order that would define Chinese political culture for the next 3,000 years.”

(Header image: Visuals from Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, reedited by Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.title: ‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.content:
“Sisters, stand up!” reads a slogan written in pink on the mirror above three pink-and-white urinals. Alongside each sits a stack of disposable paper funnels, waiting for those willing to heed the call.

The scene, reportedly captured in the women’s restroom of a bar in China’s eastern city of Wuxi, began circulating online last week, sparking debate and prompting a related hashtag to garner over 54 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

“I stood there in disbelief for two minutes, thinking I’d walked into the wrong restroom,” one user wrote on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, attaching photos of the urinals. “I kept checking until a cleaner confirmed it was indeed the women’s restroom.”

The user, a Wuxi resident in her 30s surnamed Shi, told domestic media she was unsure how to use the urinals as there were no instructions nearby. She said she eventually opted for a traditional squat toilet in the same restroom instead because she worried about making a mess or soiling her clothes.

“I’d actually love to try this,” one commenter wrote. “In winter, it’s a hassle to squat with all those thick, long layers on, especially when you’re also carrying a bag.”

“Better yet, let the brothers sit down,” read another comment, which received nearly 1,400 likes.

On Tuesday, a woman surnamed Tang, who runs Gungun Folk Theater, the bar where the urinals were reportedly installed, told domestic media that they were intended for women who find it difficult to squat, including those wearing long dresses or with limited mobility. “We just wanted to make things easier and give women another option,” she said.

Studies suggest that standing to urinate may be easier for pregnant women and those with knee osteoarthritis, while standing, crouching, and sitting have been found to make no significant difference to bladder emptying in healthy women.

Standing urinals are increasingly common worldwide at music festivals to save space and reduce restroom queues, and at outdoor activities where toilets are scarce.

In China, efforts to introduce standing urinals for women reportedly date back to 2004. At that time, Ye Ganlin, a retired senior engineer, spent 10,000 yuan ($1,400) developing a portable standing urinal for all genders, and offered free disposable funnels to female users. She said the idea grew out of her own experience with a spinal condition that made squatting increasingly difficult as she aged.

Her toilet was tested in busy public areas of neighboring cities Xi’an and Xianyang, in the northwestern Shaanxi province, and reportedly drew around 200 users a day. However, women were in the minority, Ye said.

In 2010, Shaanxi Normal University, also in Xi’an, installed six standing urinals for women, an initiative championed by professor Qu Yajun to conserve water. Female students welcomed the idea but said it would take practice to get used to the fixtures.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Urinals installed in a women’s restroom at a bar in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019251/Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
World.title: Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019251/Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
World.content:
SHANGHAI — The ninth China International Import Expo ran from Nov. 5 to 10, with 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 162 countries, regions and international organizations.

More than 480 exhibits made global, Asian or Chinese debuts. Qualcomm brought a 6G terminal prototype out of the lab. Medtronic’s China-developed Kanghui orthopedic surgical robot had its world premiere. And a rare type of durian tree fruit, the Malaysian white durian, made its global debut.

Robots at the expo could be found working hotel front desks, taking photos for visitors, and running booth demos on their own — visibly more advanced than in past years. In place of the mechanical arm designed to play ping-pong featured last year, at this year’s expo, a company debuted an entire humanoid robot playing the sport. At the forum held alongside the expo, Xiong Jijun, Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology, said humanoid robots must be upgraded from performing simple actions to being “able to think and work.”

Sixth Tone photographers spent the week in the halls, capturing the new products, technologies and services on display.

(Header image: CIIE attendees play table tennis against a robotic opponent, Shanghai, Nov. 9, 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.title: From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.content:
The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday after showcasing cutting-edge technologies in artificial intelligence, commercial aerospace, and innovative drugs.

The six-day event drew exhibitors from a record 162 countries, regions, and international organizations. A total of 4,142 overseas companies took part — also a record high — with more than 480 representative products making their global, Asian, or China debut.

U.S. wireless chipmaker Qualcomm exhibited the world’s first 6G terminal prototype — the first time the device has been shown publicly outside the lab. The prototype has been used in joint tests with China Mobile, China’s largest telecom operator, and Chinese telecom equipment manufacturer ZTE. The prototype will provide the foundation for 6G chips and support the technology’s commercial rollout.

The event featured an expanded medical devices and health care exhibition area, acting as the stage for the China debut of pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca’s new hypertension medication baxdrostat. The oral medication works by inhibiting the enzyme aldosterone synthase, which helps synthesize the blood pressure-regulating hormone aldosterone, and was approved in the U.S. in May.

German optical giant Zeiss also made its global debut of its new non-spherical lens PT Lunana, designed for myopia correction. Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical company, showcased ianalumab, a drug used for treating the autoimmune illness Sjögren’s disease — also a China debut.

American electric vehicle company Tesla presented its Cybercab autonomous vehicle. Lacking a steering wheel or pedals, the vehicle relies on cameras and AI to drive. Hexagon — a global digital reality and metrology tech company — also displayed its industrial humanoid robot AEON.

Aerospace technology was also present, including the Zhuque-3 rocket developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace. The rocket’s reusable booster, which uses liquid oxygen and methane as fuel, can land vertically, first achieved by the company in August.

Beyond showcasing new tech, the expo held its first exhibition area for 100 long-established, reputable international brands — from Canadian shoe companies to Spanish wineries — as well as hosted a trade and investment “matchmaking” conference, where companies and buyers met to sign cooperation agreements. The latter conference attracted more than 600 exhibitors and over 2,000 buyers from 59 countries and regions.

The deals reached at this year’s expo are projected to be worth a total of $85.45 billion over the coming year, up 2.3% from last year and a record high.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, Nov. 6, 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.title: Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.content:
China has opened its first school dedicated to declining and obscure fields of study, with a focus on ancient and classical Chinese texts.

The School for Rare and Endangered Disciplines was inaugurated in Beijing on Nov. 6 under the University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (UCASS). At the opening, the university also announced the launch of a national alliance of more than 80 universities, museums, and cultural and research institutions to share resources, conduct collaborative research, and cultivate talent in related fields.

The school comes as the number of scholars studying ancient Chinese scripts dwindles. Nationwide, only about 500 people work in ancient Chinese writing studies, and of the roughly 4,500 known oracle bone characters — the oldest known fully developed form of Chinese writing and widely used for divination purposes during the Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) — nearly two-thirds remain undeciphered, underlining the need for further research.

The initiative also builds on previous attempts by UCASS to preserve such fields, such as establishing an institute for rare and endangered studies in 2024 to train future talent in fields such as bamboo and silk studies, which examines script on the two materials, as well as classical studies, Turkic studies, and Assyriology, or studies of the Ancient Near East.

Each student of the new school’s bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degree courses will be mentored by two members of the school’s more than 140 faculty members. UCASS has also built dedicated laboratories for the school’s use.

Students may pursue research in oracle bone studies, bamboo and silk studies, and classical studies. They may also train in over 10 ancient ethnic scripts, including Turkic, Tangut, Khitan, Jurchen, Manchu, Old Tibetan, Old Yi, Phags-pa, Naxi Dongba, and Zhuang.

“Ancient scripts like oracle bone script are on the verge of being lost, and some frontier history research relies on the survival of the country’s cultural roots and its long-term development,” Huang Dekuan, director of the Research and Conservation Center for Unearthed Texts at Tsinghua University, told state broadcaster CCTV.

Such disciplines are also hampered by scattered resources and research institutions working in isolation — key obstacles to research and transmission, according to CCTV.

China has called for increased focus on cultural heritage preservation in recent years. At an October press conference on cultural heritage protection, government officials called for advancing cultural heritage as a discipline, cultivating interdisciplinary talent in the field, and encouraging qualified universities to establish cultural heritage schools.

In a Nov. 7 commentary, domestic media outlet The Beijing News wrote that by emphasizing rare and endangered disciplines, the new school offers a lesson to other universities: schools should develop their own distinctive majors, resist the urge to offer only popular fields, and actively strengthen less mainstream majors.

“Only then can a university truly serve education,” it stated.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

World.title: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had a relationship with a second employee, sources say
World.content:
The revelation follows two other extramarital affairs that led to his resignation on Thursday, November 12

SAN FRANCISCO, USA – Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter, Reuters has learned.

The revelation follows two other extramarital affairs that led to his resignation on Thursday, November 12. The two women are Alice Huang, who US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care.

Reuters is not naming the second employee. Attempts to reach the woman were not successful.

Nvidia declined to comment. Powell, Jensen Huang, and a representative for Nvidia’s board did not reply to requests for comment. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment.

Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a November 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The former Nvidia CEO’s decision to resign from the company could disrupt the AI industry that he helped shape. Nvidia has used its financial strength to help create an industry around AI through complex financial arrangements that ease the purchase of the company’s chips. It has backed cloud computing companies and AI labs in order to do so.

Pressure on Jensen Huang, who is 63 and married, to resign mounted after reports of his affair with Alice Huang.

Nvidia’s board appointed finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search to replace Jensen Huang. The board is considering internal and external candidates for the job.

Earlier this month, Nvidia’s board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.

Shares fell 5.5% on Thursday in active trading. The stock has shed more than 30% of its value since its early October peak. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Market Rider] Quick fixes to relieve hurting households from high power costs
World.content:
Average residential electricity rate nationwide reached P12.43 per kilowatt hour (kWh) in June this year following intense summertime demand, compounded by the extensive power plant outages in the Visayas at the time.

Power cost rose once more in July owing to geopolitical tensions and rising global fuel prices. Typical residential rate within this time hit P14.82 per kWh. This slightly fell to P14.74 per kWh in September. But in October, standard residential rate peaked again to P15.0615 per kWh.

These rates dwarfed the cost structures of power prices in Thailand, Vietnam, and Malaysia from double to even triple depending on their reported respective prices of P7.41, P5.17, and P3.34 per kWh.

This situation has left the common Philippine household hurting sorely with the highest power rates in Southeast Asia in the last five months.

The math behind the price

The Philippine power sector was entirely privatized and deregulated under the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 or more commonly referred to as the EPIRA Law.

Like Singapore, the country does not artificially subsidize electricity. Instead, it passes the full economic cost of production, transmission, and delivery to consumers. In other words, Philippine consumers pay the “actual, unbundled market cost” of electricity.

In Malaysia, Indonesia, or Thailand, their governments heavily subsidize power costs. This structural policy for power in these countries enable their common households especially to enjoy lower electricity rates.

Based on the power rates implemented in the five-month period between June to October, the typical bill for a 200 kWh per month consumption would have been from P2,486.00 to P3,012.00, making the common household suffer as much as 21.15% increase in power billing.

Bundled into the common household’s electric bill are several cost items. These include the costs for generation, transmission, distribution, allocation for system loss, and charges for subsidies and taxes.

Generation charge is the cost of producing the electricity and buying it from the power companies. This often amounts to about 55% to 57% of total power cost. Between June and October, it swung from P6.84 per kWh up to P8.58 per kWh.

Transmission charge is the amount paid to the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) for its role as the “highway” for high-voltage power across the country. It usually amounts to about 10% of total electric bill. It scaled up from P248.60 to P349.20 for the period between June and October. Like generation cost, it can fluctuate depending on grid stability requirements and ancillary service costs.

Distribution cost is the actual share kept by the electric utility distribution company like Meralco and the electric cooperatives. It’s the money dedicated to operate, build, and maintain the poles, wires, transformers, and customer service lines in our neighborhood. This is about 15% of the electric bill. It added up to about P435.05 to P451.80 between June and October. This cost barely changes. It’s because distribution rates are strictly regulated by the government and do not fluctuate with global fuel prices.

Allocation for system loss is the cost of electricity lost during delivery due to old wires, transformers, or electricity theft. This is capped to 5% by law. This amounted to P124.30 up to P150.60 between June and October.

Subsidy is about 1% of the electricity bill. It’s called the “lifeline rate” share. This is a government-mandated socialized pricing mechanism and discount granted to low-income households and marginalized electricity end-users who struggle to pay power bills at full cost, as provided under Section 73 of the EPIRA Law and further strengthened by Republic Act No. 11552 or the Expanded Lifeline Rate Law. This added up to P24.86 up to P30.12 between June and October.

Taxes are roughly14% of the electricity bill. This includes the 12% value added tax (VAT) applied directly to the generation and transmission components, alongside the feed-in tariff allowance (FIT-All) used to fund renewable energy projects. This mandatory pass-through component charge amounted to approximately P430 to P450 between June and October.

On the average, generation, transmission, and distribution charges account for nearly 80% of the total electric bill of the common household.

Current government intervention measures

There are several legislative initiatives the government has triggered to lower household electricity bills, all of which are pointed to aggressively reform the country’s 25-year-old power policy framework.

One is House Bill No. 10430 otherwise called the “System Loss Charge Abolition Act.” This legislation seeks to completely amend the EPIRA law to prohibit distribution utilities from passing on these operational failures to household consumers. By removing the system loss charge from the monthly electric bill of the common household, this is projected to reduce total electricity costs by 5% to 10%.

Another is House Bill No. 10602. This legislative initiative is designed to legally exempt consumers from paying the 12% VAT on top of the system loss charge component.

Congress is furthermore fast-tracking the Sariling Kuryente Act or Self-Generated Power Act. This bill guarantees that households capable of generating and storing their own electricity are free to invest under uniform, highly simplified rules.

The bill also mandates standard net-metering nationwide. This forces our utility companies to buy back our excess daytime solar power at fair market rates, allowing middle-class families to wipe out their daytime consumption bills entirely and see a return on their solar investment in less than 5 years.

The Senate is also prioritizing the “ERC Strengthening Bill.” This bill aims to fundamentally alter how the ERC operates, shifting it from a reactive auditor into a proactive consumer-protection agency. It grants the ERC expanded teeth to dynamically freeze pass-through generation charges during severe economic downturns, heatwaves, or unexpected “bill shocks”.

To bypass legislative delays, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) already stepped in by issuing Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 97-2026, which actively removes the 12% VAT on allowable system loss charges within the cap approved by the ERC. This provides immediate, minor relief to household bills while Congress finishes codifying the permanent statutory ban.

Crucial to quick relief

Crucial to these efforts is to first cut red tape. Bureaucratic hurdles remain intense. The government should further simplify the bureaucratic process for residential as well as commercial solar installations.

Getting a solar system approved still involves navigating a mountain of paperwork aside from being subjected to long waiting periods for building permits, complex zoning laws, and slow utility company inspections. The government could skirt this issue with the “one-stop-shop” approval process. It cuts red tape, making permits faster and cheaper to get.

While waiting for formal legislative passage, the government could already speed up standard net-metering nationwide under existing laws. Under this method, when your energy system produces more than you can use, it enables you to send your excess energy into the grid and earn kilowatt-hour credits which you can use to offset future electricity bills.

Based on present costings, this will also enable you to realize massive savings that can completely cover your upfront cost of purchasing and installing your solar equipment in just 4 to 6 years. After this point, the electricity generated is practically free profit.

The Department of Energy (DOE) must aggressively penalize maintenance and grid-connection delays by NGCP. Dozens of completed power generation plants remain stranded simply because NGCP has failed to physically link them to the main transmission lines.

Next, during the dry summer months when supply squeezes hit the Wholesale Electricity Spot Market (WESM), the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) can deploy more rigid, temporary price mitigation caps to stop opportunistic price-gouging when plants experience un-scheduled outages.

Ruling out all the other options, the least the government can do to lower the equation in the electricity bill without disrupting the generation supply chain is to remove the 12% VAT specifically on the system losses, environmental fees, and cross-subsidies within the unbundled bill. That way, the common household may enjoy an immediate reduction in the electricity bill by at least 15%. – Rappler.com

A veteran stock market analyst, Den Somera has long years of professional experience in investment banking and stockbroking and founder-convenor of The Monday Circle. You may reach the writer at kapitaltek@gmail.com

World.title: ASEAN who’s who: Regional, global leaders converge in Manila for year-end summit
World.content:
FINISHING TOUCHES. Workers from various local government units and other agencies continue cleaning and organizing the area around the Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex in Pasay City on October 22, 2026, in preparation for the ASEAN Summit.

The Philippines wraps up chairmanship of ASEAN with a days-long summit that will see world leaders converge in Manila

MANILA, Philippines — Heads of state and governments, as well as heads of multilateral organizations, will be converging in Manila from November 15 to 17 for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits.

The week-long event is the biggest in Manila’s chairmanship of the regional bloc and the most consequential, at least in flexing the bloc’s “unique convening power and continued role as a platform for dialogue and cooperation with the wider international community,” according to a press statement from the Philippines’ Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA).

Leaders are expected to discuss “ASEAN’s collective capacity to address emerging regional and global challenges, including the situation in Myanmar.”

ASEAN has had to contend with instability in the supply and price of oil, no thanks to the war the US and Israel waged on Iran. ASEAN leaders are expected, as they had in previous years, to review progress or lack thereof in Myanmar’s adherence to the Five-Point Consensus or the ASEAN-adopted peace plan for its Southeast Asian sibling.

Manila had hoped to conclude the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea negotiations between ASEAN and China by 2026, as agreed upon by foreign ministers in 2023. Negotiations are far from over and no code is expected by mid-November 2026.

All meetings and summits, including bilateral or minilateral meetings on the sidelines between leaders, will take place at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City.

November 15 kicks off the event, with nine Southeast Asian leaders joining Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for the opening, plenary, and retreat sessions. Myanmar, which has not participated in ASEAN Summits since 2021 after a junta takeover, will be represented by the director-general of its Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ ASEAN Affairs Department.

For the plenary, ASEAN leaders will be joined by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Brazilian President Lula da Silva, and the International Monetary Fund as guests of the ASEAN chair.

“Their participation underscores the value of ASEAN’s engagement with key global partners in advancing regional economic resilience and addressing shared challenges in an increasingly interconnected global economy, in line with Philippines’ Chairship priorities particularly under its Prosperity Corridors,” said the DFA.

From November 16 to 17, Manila will host the related summits and plus-one summits under ASEAN. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Chinese Premiere Li Qiang, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Japan Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, New Zealand Primer Minister Christopher Luxon, Korean President Lee Jae-myung, and United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres will be flying in to co-chair those meetings with Marcos. Russia’s delegation will be led by Foreign Minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov.

This will be Guterres’ last engagement with ASEAN as the world’s chief diplomat. The 10th UN secretary-general is expected to be selected and appointed before the end of Guterres’ term on December 31, 2026.

US President Donald Trump is expected to arrive in Manila on November 17 yet and is unlikely to join the main summits under the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits. The Philippines is expected to host a Special ASEAN-US Summit on the same day.

Marcos will ceremonially hand over chairmanship to Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong at the end of the summit, although the Philippines will only officially cease its chairship by year’s end.

The Philippines had allocated over P17.5 billion for its chairmanship, although hosting duties were scaled down in the wake of the oil crisis earlier in 2026. Many meetings, including ones at the ministerial-level, shifted online.

Major meetings expected on the 17th include the ASEAN Plus Three (China, Japan, South Korea) Summit and the East Asia Summit, the premiere leaders-level forum in the region. – Rappler.com

World.title: Leah Santiago becomes first female PMA graduate to earn general’s star
World.content:
PROMOTED. The Superintendent, PMA, Lieutenant General Michael Logico PA (right) welcomes the newly promoted Commandant of Cadets, Brigadier General Leah Santiago PA at the Lim Hall Lobby.

The first female summa cum laude graduate of the PMA and its first woman Commandant of Cadets adds another first, 33 years after entering the Academy with its pioneering batch of women

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – Thirty-three years after entering the Philippine Military Academy with its first batch of female cadets, Leah Lorenzo Santiago has become the first woman PMA graduate to reach the rank of brigadier general.

Santiago formally donned her one-star rank on November 9 at Camp Aguinaldo, less than a month after becoming the PMA’s first female Commandant of Cadets and head of the Tactics Group on October 17.

The Academy rendered arrival honors for her at Fort Del Pilar the following day.

Her promotion puts another first beside a name already written several times into PMA history.

Santiago entered the Academy in 1993, the year PMA began admitting women under Republic Act 7192, or the Women in Development and Nation Building Act.

She graduated with the KalasagLahi Class of 1997, the first PMA class to include women. Santiago finished third overall and first academically, becoming the Academy’s first female summa cum laude graduate.

Commissioned into the Philippine Army, she went on to serve in infantry, field artillery, personnel management, and military education assignments.

Among her earlier posts were platoon leader, executive officer, and company commander of the 30th Infantry Battalion. She later returned to the PMA as a senior tactical officer, commanded the 9th Field Artillery Battery in Sulu, and held senior personnel positions in the Army.

The Cadet Corps Armed Forces of the Philippines welcomes the newly promoted Commandant of Cadets, Brigadier General Leah Santiago. Photo courtesy of the Philippine Military Academy

Santiago’s return to Fort Del Pilar this year brought another first.

As Commandant of Cadets, Santiago now oversees the military training, discipline, leadership development, and physical training of the Cadet Corps, the same institution she entered when women were only beginning to find a place in its ranks.

Santiago is not the first woman to become a general in the Philippine Army. Brigadier General Ramona Go achieved that milestone in 2011.

Rather, Santiago’s distinction is specific to the PMA — she is the first female graduate of the Academy’s four-year cadet program to reach general officer rank.

The achievement also carries particular weight for the women who followed the first female cadets through Fort Del Pilar.

What Santiago entered in 1993 as part of an experiment in opening a traditionally male institution to women is now part of PMA life. Women train alongside men, command cadet units, earn academic honors, and graduate into the different services of the Armed Forces.

Santiago now stands on the other side of that history.

She arrived at Fort Del Pilar as one of the first women allowed to become a PMA cadet. More than three decades later, she is back with a star on her shoulder, helping train those who will come after her. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] Follow VP Sara’s money, not her alibis
World.content:
(2nd UPDATE) While VP Sara Duterte was collecting annual checks from Gencorp, Gencorp was collecting tens of millions of pesos from City Hall run by her brother



Vice President Sara Duterte’s denial of franchise ownership leaves the central questions unanswered: why Gencorp paid her more than P2.14 million, what financial interest she retained, and how that interest fits with the company’s government contracts. Her explanations must withstand scrutiny against the records.

Leaving a politician’s name off a shareholder list does not make corporate checks cut in their favor any less suspect.

In Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, the defense panel’s own explanation for payments coming out of GenCorp Industries Inc. creates a contradiction no amount of legal hair-splitting can smooth over: if she owned no shares, held no office, and had no hand in the company, what financial right entitled her to pocket more than P2.14 million of its cash?

Duterte’s public response makes that question harder to dismiss. In October, she denied owning a Jollibee franchise and accused Rappler of disinformation. But her statement also acknowledged a previous investment in a company within a legitimate business organization. Her denial concerned direct franchise ownership; it did not establish that she had extinguished every financial interest connected to the business.

There is a valid corporate principle here. Shareholders do not personally own a corporation’s individual properties or contracts; the corporation has a separate legal personality.

Duterte could therefore distinguish an investment in a company from personal ownership of its franchises. But that distinction cannot answer the separate question of whether she retained a financial interest relevant to constitutional restrictions on the Vice President.

Play Video

At the Wednesday, November 11 hearing, Gencorp counsel Suzette Balucanag-Punay testified that Duterte was neither a shareholder nor a corporate officer from 2022 to 2025.

She nevertheless acknowledged disbursements totaling P2,142,369.14: P337,500 in 2022, P555,750 in 2023, P612,419.14 in 2024 and P636,700 in 2025. Duterte’s Statements of Assets Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) also identified Gencorp, or the related company names appearing in earlier declarations, as business interests. The payment explanation and sworn disclosures require reconciliation with the corporate records.

Attacking Rappler does not perform that reconciliation. Rappler defended its reporting by citing Duterte’s SALNs and the prosecution expert’s testimony. Every disputed assertion remains open to scrutiny, including the expert’s assumptions. But criticism of the messenger cannot explain the financial entitlement described by the defense’s own witness. Duterte’s response needs investment records, not merely objections to how a headline characterizes ownership.

The defense’s magic phrase for this arrangement is “loose investment,” which supplies no recognized accounting classification. Money placed in a business may represent equity, a loan, an advance, or another contractual entitlement. The arrangement can be informal, but the company must still explain how it recorded the obligation and calculated the payments. Calling the investment loose does not loosen the obligation to account for it.

The origin story makes the math even shakier. According to Balucanag-Punay, Duterte originally put P46,875 into Davao Bounty Foods Corporation in 2007 for a Jollibee franchise that never materialized, and that money was quietly rolled over across successor firms until it landed in Gencorp’s Times Square branch.

Yet when pressed by senator-judges and prosecutors, the company’s own lawyer admitted she had no records proving the original amount invested, no agreements documenting the rollover, and no formula showing how the payouts were computed.

As Senate Impeachment Court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero pointed out, receiving P2.14 million off a documented P46,875 contribution amounts to roughly 45 times the original stake. Under cross-examination by private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan, Balucanag-Punay eventually conceded that whether labeled a return of investment or a return on investment, the sum constituted income — and even admitted she had questioned the payouts herself. Without an opening ledger showing principal in and repayments out, “return of capital” is just a convenient label slapped onto unexplained cash.

Credibility problem

What turns a messy private ledger into a full-blown constitutional problem is public money. Testimony from PhilGEPS division chief Rendell Sopeña shows that between July 2022 and June 2026, Gencorp bagged 49 government contracts worth P35.88 million.

More than 95% of that money — roughly P34.22 million across 15 awards in PhilGEPS records, though Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte later testified the city’s total transactions with Gencorp reached P33.2 million across 19 contracts — came straight from Davao City Hall, with 11 of the PhilGEPS-listed deals awarded through negotiated small-value procurement rather than open competitive bidding.

Mayor Duterte insists he had no idea his sister had ties to the firm, while Gencorp’s counsel claims the city contracts went to a different branch and involved no intervention from the Vice President.

Those excuses miss the point of the 1987 Constitution. Article VII, Section 13 does not ask whether the Vice President personally called up a bids and awards committee or attended a board meeting. It flatly prohibits her from participating directly or indirectly in any business and from holding any financial interest in a government contract during her tenure.

A corporation is a single legal entity, not a collection of firewall-protected fast-food counters. While she was collecting annual checks from Gencorp, Gencorp was collecting tens of millions of pesos from City Hall run by her brother. (READ: Who is Tristan Domingo, the Davao official behind contracts awarded to Duterte’s company?)

Play Video

To be fair, the prosecution cannot afford to get sloppy either. Its forensic expert’s claim attributing more than P212 million in Gencorp deposits to Duterte rests on a disputed 20% ownership figure, and corporate gross receipts are not personal income.

Overreaching on unverified numbers only gives the defense an easy target to knock down while distracting from the facts already on the record — including the separate admission that Duterte remained on the books as a director and compensation committee member of Metro City Chow Foods during her vice presidency, even though the company’s bylaws do not provide for such a committee.

We do not need inflated projections to see where the paper trail leads. Until Vice President Duterte and Gencorp lay the original investment agreements, the accounting ledgers, the check vouchers, and the Davao City procurement files on the table, the claim that she walks away from this unblemished is not a defense.

It is an insult to basic arithmetic. – Rappler.com

(Note: This column has been updated to correct the calculations and clarify the figures discussed. The revisions distinguish corporate receipts from personal income and do not alter the central questions raised about the Vice President’s financial interests.)
