World.title: Azerbaijan’s proposed hourly wage system: Who stands to benefit – workers, employers or state?
World.content:
Introduction of hourly wages in Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan plans to introduce a minimum hourly wage from 2027. The announcement was made on 11 November by Deputy Minister of Labour and Social Protection Zaur Aliyev during a meeting of the Milli Majlis Committee on Labour and Social Policy. According to Aliyev, the new system will initially apply to agricultural production and the catering sector.

Back in 2024, we reported that the introduction of hourly wages was under discussion in Azerbaijan. The main provisions of the proposed amendments to the Labour Code have now emerged.

The government and MPs have presented the initiative as a way to make employment more flexible and bring informal employment into the formal economy. However, critics have raised a different question:

Who will benefit from hourly wages, and could the system be used to split full-time positions into part-time roles in the public sector?

What does the draft law propose?

According to media reports, the draft law provides for hourly wages in two cases: when an employment contract is concluded for less than one month or when the working week does not exceed 20 hours. The Cabinet of Ministers will determine which sectors the new system will apply to.

The draft law also includes several safeguards for employees:

If an employee works less than one hour in a day, they must be paid at least the minimum hourly rate. Any part of an hour must be paid as a full hour.

For part-time employees paid a monthly salary, wages cannot fall below the minimum wage calculated in proportion to their working hours.

In organisations funded by the state budget, hourly wages can only be introduced if the organisation’s existing pay system allows for them, according to APA.

The minimum hourly rate has not yet been announced. According to Musa Guliyev, chairman of the Milli Majlis Committee on Labour and Social Policy, the draft law stipulates that:

The minimum hourly rate cannot be lower than the hourly equivalent of the minimum monthly wage.

However, the deputy minister of labour and social protection said that the proposed minimum hourly rate would be set above this level.

Since January 2025, Azerbaijan’s minimum monthly wage has stood at 400 manats (approximately $235). According to calculations by economist Natig Jafarli, this translates into around 2 manats and 50 gapiks per hour (approximately $1.47) for a five-day working week, or around 2 manats (approximately $1.18) for a six-day working week.

What do authorities say?

Musa Guliyev believes that hourly wages could make it easier for women with young children, students and pensioners to enter the labour market. According to him, the current minimum monthly wage system creates “inequality and social injustice” for part-time, seasonal and short-term workers.

However, the minimum wage cannot serve as a universal benchmark for all working arrangements.

Guliyev described hourly wages as a “social instrument that helps formalise informal employment”. Deputy Minister Zaur Aliyev, meanwhile, said the changes would allow for greater flexibility in applying the minimum wage system and make wage calculations more transparent.

The introduction of hourly wages has not come as a surprise. In May 2026, the government, the Confederation of Trade Unions and the Confederation of Entrepreneurs of Azerbaijan signed a General Collective Agreement for 2026–2028, committing to securing legislative amendments introducing a minimum hourly wage.

What concerns have critics raised?

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the Republican Alternative Party, raised three questions in a social media post.

The first concerns the benefits for workers. What would they gain from the introduction of a minimum hourly wage? Jafarli gave an example: if someone were hired for two hours a day and paid 5 manats (approximately $3), “who would benefit from this?”

The second question concerns the public sector. According to Jafarli, nearly half of all salaried employees work in the public sector, and it would be difficult to introduce hourly working arrangements for teachers, doctors, police officers and judicial employees. According to figures from the State Statistical Committee, as of 1 September, 834,200 of Azerbaijan’s 1,776,800 salaried employees, or around 47%, worked in the public sector.

The third question concerns the private sector. Jafarli argues that hourly wages should not be “imposed on the private sector, but rather encouraged through incentives”. In his view, employers spend time and money recruiting and training staff and may therefore have little incentive to hire two or three hourly paid employees instead of one full-time worker.

Economist Akif Nasirli argued last year that Azerbaijan was not ready to introduce such a system. He identified the lack of effective mechanisms to monitor compliance with labour legislation as the main obstacle.

Human resources manager Royal Ahmadov told Bakupost on 6 November that introducing hourly wages would not automatically lead to higher salaries. According to him, much would depend on the minimum hourly rate and how working hours are recorded.

“The main goal is not to provide employers with cheaper labour,” he stressed.

Could full-time positions be split into part-time roles?

Jafarli’s most serious concerns relate to the public sector. He believes the new system will primarily be used in state-funded organisations.

The economist gives the following example: a ministry employing 100 people on an average salary of 1,500 manats (approximately $882) could hire another 100 employees without dismissing anyone. If each of the two employees sharing a position worked four hours a day and earned 600 manats (approximately $353), the cost of one full-time equivalent position would fall from 1,500 to 1,200 manats (approximately $706).

According to Jafarli, this would allow the authorities to report the creation of “new jobs”, while saving the state budget 300 manats (approximately $176) per full-time equivalent position.

The economist describes this as “an attempt to create the appearance of sweeping changes without changing anything in substance”.

Government representatives have not yet responded to the criticism. However, the draft law does not exclude state-funded organisations from the new system: hourly wages would be permitted where the organisation’s existing pay structure allows for them.

Jafarli’s example of a four-hour working day also falls within the conditions set out in the draft law, as it would amount to a 20-hour working week over five days.

These concerns come against a backdrop of declining public-sector employment. In 2025, the number of public-sector employees fell by 2%, equivalent to around 17,000 jobs. Employment also declined in education and public administration, while private-sector employment grew by 5.2%.

Who could benefit?

Supporters of the new system argue that workers currently employed without formal contracts stand to benefit the most. MP Razi Nurullayev explained the reasoning last year:

“Workers will be paid for the hours they actually work.”

Economist Khalid Kerimli said in May that the current monthly wage system is primarily designed for full-time employees. In his view, introducing a minimum hourly rate would help protect the rights of part-time workers and give the Labour Inspectorate greater scope to monitor compliance with labour legislation.

However, Kerimli stressed that “introducing a minimum hourly wage does not mean an increase in the minimum wage”.

The impact of the reform will therefore depend on two decisions that have yet to be made: setting the minimum hourly rate and approving the list of sectors in which it will apply.

The new system will first be introduced in agricultural production and the catering sector. If hourly wages help bring informal employment in these industries into the formal economy, supporters’ expectations will be met. However, if the system leads to full-time positions being split into part-time roles and lower labour costs, critics’ concerns may prove justified.

World.title: Court removes leaders of Coalition for Change from hearing on banning political parties in Georgia – day 10 recap
World.content:
Georgia opposition ban trial

On 11 November, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the tenth day of hearings on a lawsuit brought by ruling party Georgian Dream seeking to ban five opposition parties.

The hearing was at the question-and-answer stage, with judges questioning representatives of Georgian Dream, which brought the case.

Context. The case sets a precedent. The lawsuit was signed by 88 MPs from the ruling party. It seeks to ban five opposition groups: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties that seek to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. The ruling party cites their refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current government as one of its arguments. The application also accuses them of attempting to overthrow the government. The application also accuses Unity – National Movement of undermining the country’s independence and territorial integrity. The stated reason is the party’s alleged responsibility for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia, when the United National Movement was in power. All five parties deny the allegations. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the lawsuit, meaning at least four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

The main development on 11 November was the removal of Coalition for Change leaders Nika Gvaramia and Maia Kopaleishvili from the courtroom by Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraia for arguing with the court and the plaintiffs.

Unless their request to be allowed back into the proceedings is granted, Gvaramia and Kopaleishvili will be barred from attending further hearings until the case is concluded.

Both have been among the most active representatives of the defendants. Kopaleishvili is a former Constitutional Court judge.

What led to Gvaramia and Kopaleishvili being removed

Judge Eva Gotsiridze asked the plaintiffs whether they had evidence that the opposition parties had taken part in or incited violence. In response, Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze named Murtaz Zodelava and Paata Burchuladze. Both have been charged in connection with the events of 4 October 2025, when a group of activists attempted to storm the presidential palace.

Gorduladze said both men were linked to the United National Movement.

Nika Gvaramia objected: “Neither of them was a member of that party. If people were prosecuted simply because someone happened to be their former classmate, half of Georgia would be in prison – because all of you who have ruined this country were classmates!”

“As for those who have ruined it – well, here you all are!” Gorduladze retorted.

Gvaramia then asked whether being friends with someone meant belonging to the same political party: “If I acknowledge that someone is my friend, does that mean we are all conspirators plotting a coup?”

Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraia deemed the exchange disruptive and ordered Gvaramia, followed by Kopaleishvili, to leave the courtroom.

Maia Kopaleishvili: “This is a show of force”

Kopaleishvili described her removal from the courtroom as a restriction on access to justice. “This was a deliberate act. It was an instruction from Georgian Dream,” she said. She then asked Nadaraia: “Why are you laughing? Have you already made your decision?”

Nadaraia replied that a formal request could be filed, adding that it was regrettable that Kopaleishvili did not know the law despite having worked at the Constitutional Court for 10 years.

“This is an insult,” Tengiz Tevzadze, another representative of Coalition for Change, told the presiding judge.

“Keep your colleague in check,” Nadaraia retorted.

Before those ordered to leave the courtroom departed, Nadaraia asked them: “For the past two days, have you deliberately been trying to get yourselves removed? Are you perhaps just trying to avoid answering questions?”

As she left, Kopaleishvili told the judges that they should be guardians of the Constitution, not people who restrict the rights of participants in legal proceedings. “This is a show of force,” she said.

She added that Georgian Dream would probably be pleased that the defendants would no longer be able to ask questions.

A day earlier, on 10 November, Nadaraia had repeatedly threatened to remove Kopaleishvili from the courtroom and accused her of trying to discredit the court.

Gvaramia, meanwhile, threatened to file a motion to have the presiding judge recused.

170 injured police officers and photographs on a laptop

The first point of contention during the day’s hearing concerned the evidence.

Judge Vasil Roinishvili asked the plaintiffs whether they had calculated the material damage caused to the state by the defendants, both domestically and internationally.

He cited problems related to visa regimes, critical international resolutions and cases of law enforcement officers being injured during mass unrest.

Gorduladze replied that around 170 law enforcement officers had been injured in November and December 2024 alone.

Opposition representatives demanded to know where this figure appeared as evidence in the lawsuit.

“Did we not agree to skip the examination of evidence, Mr Chairman?” Gvaramia asked sarcastically, referring to a decision taken the previous day.

“The court did not skip anything. Please do not exaggerate,” Nadaraia retorted.

Gorduladze then opened photographs of injured police officers on his work laptop and showed them to the court.

This triggered another verbal clash with Gvaramia. The presiding judge issued him a warning and threatened to remove him from the courtroom.

Giga Lemondzhava, another representative of Coalition for Change, also tried to speak. Nadaraia refused to give him the floor, saying: “Take your seat, or I will order you to be removed. I am not giving you the floor.”

The presiding judge explained that at the questioning stage, the parties were required to accept their opponents’ answers, even if they found them unsatisfactory.

Ana Buchukuri, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, demanded that the court reprimand Gorduladze for making “offensive remarks” about the defendants.

Judge Gotsiridze: “Seeking to ban five parties at once is unprecedented”

Judge Eva Gotsiridze questioned the plaintiffs about the criteria for banning political parties.

She noted that seeking to ban five parties at once was truly unprecedented.

Gotsiridze also pointed out that the lawsuit describes several other parties as “anti-constitutional”, yet the plaintiffs are not seeking to ban them.

In her view, the term “anti-constitutional” was being applied to political parties too loosely. Following this logic, she said, more than 10 parties in Georgia – effectively a majority – could be classified as anti-constitutional.

The judge questioned whether the criteria proposed by the plaintiffs were sufficiently clear, suggesting they might be too vague, and asked how such an approach could be reconciled with democratic principles.

What happens next

The hearing will resume on 12 November at 12:00, with the question-and-answer stage continuing. This time, judges will question representatives of the opposition parties.

The presiding judge said the questioning is expected to continue until next Tuesday.

Hearings in the case have been held at the Constitutional Court in Batumi since 21 October. Since then, the defendants have filed around 14 motions, of which only one has been granted, and that only in part.

World.title: ‘Who could be closer friend to us than Armenia?’ – Key takeaways from Iran’s vice-president’s visit to Yerevan
World.content:
Вице-президент Ирана – об объемах поставок газа в Армению

Iranian Vice-President Seyed Hamid Pourmohammadi arrived in Yerevan to attend the 19th session of the Armenian-Iranian Intergovernmental Commission. Armenian journalists asked him about economic ties and Iran’s position on the Armenian-American TRIPP project project, known as the “Trump Route”, which would run through Armenian territory. Armenian media also wanted to understand why Iran’s religious and secular authorities hold different positions on the issue.

Seyed Hamid Pourmohammadi stressed that Tehran’s official position was reflected in statements by Iran’s Foreign Ministry.

“Armenia and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan are our reliable partners, and we remain in constant contact. Tehran considers it important that the countries of the region themselves ensure and maintain security and peace. Iran welcomes any steps aimed at preserving and strengthening peace and security among the countries of the region,” the Iranian vice-president said.

Just days earlier, Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, had sharply criticised Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan over the TRIPP project. Velayati accused Pashinyan of making Armenia increasingly dependent on the West, saying this “opens a new chapter of hostility and tension in the South Caucasus”. Velayati’s remarks prompted a response from Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. He stressed that the Armenian authorities had assured Tehran that the implementation of the TRIPP project, near Iran’s borders, would involve neither the deployment of US military forces in the region nor any changes to existing borders. Baghaei added that, although Iran enjoys excellent relations with Armenia, it would continue to monitor developments and make its position public if necessary.

On increasing Iranian gas supplies to Armenia

Against the backdrop of discussions about a possible increase in the price of Russian gas supplied to Armenia, journalists asked whether Iran could increase its gas exports to the country.

“Iran is one of the countries with the largest gas reserves in the world. And if we have the capacity to export gas, who could be a closer friend to us than Armenia, to whom we would export it?” the Iranian vice-president replied.

Pourmohammadi said that one of the commissions established under Armenian-Iranian cooperation deals specifically with energy issues. According to him, the two sides discussed all possible areas of cooperation in this sector, including supplies of gas and diesel fuel, as well as issues related to Armenia’s long-term energy security.

However, the specific details of the agreements reached with Iran have not been disclosed.

Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan, who co-chairs the intergovernmental commission on the Armenian side, offered only the following details:

“There is not a single area in which we have not reached agreements. These include trade, energy (particularly gas and electricity), opportunities to expand existing project agreements, as well as infrastructure development and its mutual integration.”

The Iran–Armenia gas pipeline has a designed capacity of more than 2 billion cubic metres of gas a year. However, only a small fraction of this capacity is currently being used. Since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline has been under the control of Russian company Gazprom. Some experts believe that Iran cannot increase its gas exports without Russia’s consent. However, in July this year, Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan said there were no restrictions on receiving gas under the Armenian-Iranian “gas-for-electricity” programme. The programme began in 2009 and has already been extended until 2030. The minister assured that Armenia could at least double its gas imports from Iran.

Outcomes of the intergovernmental meeting

The Armenian government said that the intergovernmental meeting covered the implementation of joint projects in the following areas:

energy;

transport;

trade;

infrastructure;

business ties.

Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan particularly emphasised Armenia’s readiness to develop regional connectivity. He expressed confidence that unblocking regional transport links “would create new opportunities for the countries of the region”. In this context, he stressed the importance of Iran’s support for the Crossroads of Peace initiative. The Armenian government’s project aims to fully unblock transport links to and from Armenia in all directions.

The two sides also signed a memorandum of understanding following the intergovernmental commission meeting.

Connectivity also on the agenda of bilateral meetings

According to the Armenian prime minister’s office, Nikol Pashinyan discussed joint Armenian-Iranian programmes during his meeting with the Iranian vice-president. He said their successful implementation would “help develop and expand bilateral relations”.

“The interlocutors discussed issues related to the development of Armenia-Iran border infrastructure, joint road construction projects, as well as cooperation in energy, agriculture and other sectors,” the statement said.

Pashinyan and Pourmohammadi also discussed the unblocking of regional transport links and the opportunities this process could create for both countries.

Armenian Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan also discussed regional connectivity and the unblocking of transport links with the Iranian vice-president. Following their meeting, officials said that both countries saw “great potential” for further developing trade and economic ties and elevating bilateral relations to a strategic level.

World.title: Kazakhstan increases electricity generation by 2.3% in January-October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Kazakhstan generated 102 billion kWh of electricity in January-October 2026, an increase of 2.3% compared with the same period last year, the press service of the country’s government reported.

According to Trend’s calculations based on official data, electricity generation in October alone grew by 5.1% compared with the same month in 2025, totaling approximately 10.3 billion kWh.

In January-September 2026, Kazakhstan generated 91.7 billion kWh of electricity, representing a 2% increase year-on-year. Thus, the overall growth rate accelerated by 0.3 percentage points in the first ten months of the year.

Meanwhile, electricity generation in Kazakhstan in the first 10 months of 2026 exceeded the figure for the first nine months by 11.2%. In turn, electricity generation in January-September was 46% higher than in January-August, Trend’s calculations show.

For reference, Kazakhstan’s electricity generation remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, particularly coal. According to the Ministry of Energy, coal-fired power plants account for 62.1% of total electricity generation, while gas-fired facilities contribute 23.4%. Hydropower accounts for 7.5%, and renewable energy sources make up a further 7%.

To address growing electricity demand and modernize its generation capacity, Kazakhstan approved a National Project for the Development of Coal-Fired Generation in March 2026. The program considers the construction of eight new energy facilities and the modernization of 11 existing plants, adding or upgrading a combined 7.8 GW of capacity by 2030. The government expects the projects to strengthen baseload generation and improve the reliability of the power system.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s outstanding bank loans rise 13% to $54.68B
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Outstanding loans of Uzbekistan’s commercial banks increased 13% year over year to 659 trillion soums (about $54.68 billion) as of October 1, 2026, with lending growth varying across economic sectors, according to the Central Bank of Uzbekistan.

According to Trend’s calculations based on the reported figures, loans to individuals accounted for approximately 37.6% of the total portfolio, while trade and general services represented about 8.2% and industry approximately 20.2%. The shares of individuals and trade and general services increased by 2 and 1 percentage points, respectively, while industry’s share declined by 5 percentage points.

Outstanding loans to the construction sector recorded the fastest growth, increasing 33% year over year to 23 trillion soums (around $1.9 billion). Lending to trade and general services rose 32% to 54 trillion soums (approximately $4.48 billion), with the sector’s share of the total loan portfolio increasing from 7% to 8%.

Outstanding loans to individuals grew 19% to 248 trillion soums (about $20.58 billion), raising their share of total loans from 36% to 38%. Meanwhile, lending to agriculture increased 15%, while loans to transport and communications rose 16%.

Outstanding loans to the industrial sector amounted to 133 trillion soums (around $11 billion). However, the sector’s share of the total loan portfolio declined from 25% to 20% over the reporting period.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s oil exports to Switzerland down 2.18% in January-August
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Kazakhstan's crude oil and petroleum product exports to Switzerland declined by 2.18% year on year to 1.15 million tonnes in January-August 2026, according to Trend's calculations based on official statistics.

The data was provided by Kazakhstan's Bureau of National Statistics.

In value terms, crude oil exports to Switzerland increased by 23.46% year-on-year to $684.99 million from $554.85 million.

In August 2026 alone, Kazakhstan exported 136,740 tonnes of crude oil to Switzerland valued at $97.57 million.

Overall, Kazakhstan exported 46.96 million tonnes of crude oil and crude oil products obtained from bituminous minerals in January-August 2026, down 3.65% from 48.74 million tonnes in the same period of 2025. In value terms, total crude oil exports grew by 16.31% to $30.09 billion compared to $25.87 billion a year earlier.

Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover reached $102.96 billion in January-August 2026, up 12.8% in nominal terms compared with the same period of 2025.

Exports totaled $60.39 billion, increasing by 19.5% in nominal terms, while imports reached $42.57 billion, up 4.5%.

Crude oil and crude oil products obtained from bituminous minerals accounted for 49.8% of Kazakhstan’s exports in January-August 2026. Other major export commodities included refined copper and unwrought copper alloys (6.4%), radioactive chemical elements and radioactive isotopes (5.1%), copper ores and concentrates (4.4%), and ferroalloys (2.2%).

Passenger cars and other motor vehicles accounted for the largest share of imports, at 3.3%. Other major imported commodities included telephone equipment (2.7%), pharmaceutical products (2.5%), petroleum gases and other gaseous hydrocarbons (2.4%), and electric generating sets and rotary converters (2.2%).

Italy was Kazakhstan’s largest export destination, accounting for 18% of exports, followed by China (17.6%), Russia (8.5%), Türkiye (7.9%), France (6.1%) and the Netherlands (5.9%).

Russia was Kazakhstan’s largest import partner, accounting for 31% of imports, followed by China (29.8%), Germany (4.6%), the United States (3.9%), South Korea (2.5%) and Türkiye (2.1%).

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva holds series of meetings at COP31 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. On November 12, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and founder and head of the IDEA Public Union Leyla Aliyeva met with Director of the UN-Habitat Regional Office for Eastern Europe and Central Asia Erfan Ali on the sidelines of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).

During the meeting, Leyla Aliyeva provided insight into Azerbaijan’s measures in sustainable urban development, environmental protection and climate change adaptation. In this context, the projects and initiatives of the IDEA Public Union aimed at improving the urban environment, expanding green spaces and promoting environmental awareness were highlighted.

The discussions emphasized the importance of strengthening the climate resilience of coastal cities, assessing related risks and taking environmental factors into account in urban planning.

The sides also discussed opportunities for cooperation between the IDEA Public Union and UN-Habitat in urban greening, creating a sustainable living environment and adapting to climate change. They also explored the possibility of implementing joint initiatives in these areas.

xxx

On November 12, Leyla Aliyeva also met with Secretary-General of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Celeste Saulo on the sidelines of COP31.

During the meeting, the sides exchanged views on assessing the impacts of climate change, improving meteorological observations and making effective use of scientific data. They highlighted the importance of strengthening climate monitoring in Azerbaijan, applying modern technologies and developing early warning systems for climate-related events.

The discussions also covered opportunities for the scientific study of observed changes in the Caspian Sea level and for expanding international cooperation in this area. In particular, the sides discussed prospects for jointly analyzing long-term climate observations, meteorological data and wind patterns to gain a deeper understanding of changes in the sea level.

Furthermore, they exchanged views on opportunities for cooperation between the IDEA Public Union and the WMO to enhance the climate research knowledge and skills of young researchers in Azerbaijan, facilitate international scientific exchanges and organize relevant training programs.

World.title: Footage of President Ilham Aliyev's meeting with UK Prime Minister posted on his social media (VIDEO)
World.content:
Photo: Press service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Footage about President Ilham Aliyev's meeting with Prime Minister of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland Andy Burnham has been published on his social media pages.

The post reads: "President Ilham Aliyev held a meeting with the Prime Minister of United Kingdom in Dublin."

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva participates in discussions on improving air quality in cities at COP31 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. An event titled “Clean Air, Healthy Cities: From Urban Planning to Climate Action” was held at the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), in partnership with the IDEA Public Union and the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat).

Participants were first shown a short documentary film prepared by IDEA on the importance of clean air in urban environments.

Speaking at the opening of the event, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and founder and head of the IDEA Public Union Leyla Aliyeva discussed the impact of air pollution on human health and emphasized the importance of taking environmental factors into account in developing healthier and more sustainable cities.

Leyla Aliyeva also highlighted Azerbaijan’s experience in sustainable urban development, including measures to expand green spaces and promote environmentally friendly transport. She noted the role of the IDEA Public Union’s “Our Courtyard” project, tree-planting campaigns and other initiatives aimed at greening urban areas.

Speaking at the event, COP29 President and Representative of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan on Climate Issues Mukhtar Babayev underscored the link between improving air quality and combating climate change. He stressed the importance of strengthening international cooperation to reduce harmful emissions in cities, develop sustainable transport systems and promote environmentally friendly technologies.

Addressing the official part of the event, Director of the UN-Habitat Regional Office for Eastern Europe and Central Asia Erfan Ali highlighted issues related to air quality monitoring, reducing harmful emissions, improving environmental governance in cities and applying international best practices in this field.

The event continued with a panel discussion moderated by Patricia Scotland, a member of the UK House of Lords and the Nizami Ganjavi International Center. The panel featured Robb Butler, a University of Copenhagen representative and expert on climate and health issues; Timur Sabitov, Deputy Director of the National Center for Climate Change under the Ministry of Ecology, Environmental Protection and Climate Change of the Republic of Uzbekistan; and Renee Gift, a legal specialist in air quality regulation and management at the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).

The panelists exchanged views on reducing air pollution, developing environmentally friendly transport systems, integrating green infrastructure into urban development and the positive effects of climate change mitigation measures on human health.

The event highlighted the importance of strengthening international cooperation, applying sustainable urban planning principles and aligning climate policies with public health measures to improve air quality and create healthier urban environments.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev meets with UK Prime Minister in Dublin (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

DUBLIN, Ireland, November 13. On November 12, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev met with Prime Minister of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland Andy Burnham in Dublin, Trend's special correspondent reports.

They first exchanged the “Joint Declaration on Strategic Partnership between the Republic of Azerbaijan and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.”

During the conversation, it was emphasized that the adoption of the Declaration would formally elevate relations between the two countries to a qualitatively new level. They noted that even before the adoption of the document, relations between Azerbaijan and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland had already been characterized by a strategic partnership.

Touching upon more than 30 years of successful energy cooperation between the two countries, the head of state said that the United Kingdom is the largest European investor in Azerbaijan.

The sides noted that broad opportunities also exist for cooperation in renewable energy, high technologies and artificial intelligence. In this regard, the two leaders highlighted the importance of high-level official visits from the United Kingdom to Azerbaijan and discussions held in recent months.

The meeting also included an exchange of views on issues on the international agenda.

World.title: Head of Baku Media Center Arzu Aliyeva attends presentation of film “Steps in Silence” (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. On November 12, the Nizami Cinema Center hosted the presentation of the documentary film “Steps in Silence,” produced by the Baku Media Center.

The event was attended by Arzu Aliyeva, head of the Baku Media Center, government officials, cultural figures, and members of the film’s creative team.

Guests first viewed an exhibition highlighting the film’s subject matter, demining efforts, and the daily lives of women working in this field.

Addressing the audience before the screening, military journalist Heydar Mirza emphasized that the threat of landmines is one of the most serious humanitarian challenges facing Azerbaijan. He highlighted the importance of demining operations in the liberated territories and the mission carried out by those involved in this work.

He noted that in 2021, AZERTAC correspondent Maharram Ibrahimov and Azerbaijan Television (AzTV) cameraman Siraj Abishov were killed in a landmine explosion while performing their professional duties in Kalbajar. The tragedy once again demonstrated the serious threat posed by landmines to military personnel, civilians, and journalists.

Speaking at the event, Vugar Suleymanov, chairman of the board of the Mine Action Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan (ANAMA), noted that since November 2020, a total of 444 people in Azerbaijan have become victims of landmines, 73 of whom have lost their lives.

He added that, according to the agency’s analysis, approximately 60 percent of mine incidents have occurred beyond the front line, indicating that the liberated territories were mined in a haphazard manner.

According to Vugar Suleymanov, 11,667 square kilometers of the liberated territories are currently classified as suspected areas contaminated by landmines and other unexploded ordnance (UXO).

Umud Mirzayev, president of the International Eurasia Press Fund and a member of the board of the Azerbaijan Press Council, highlighted the importance of the film in drawing international attention to the landmine issue.

He stressed that the ongoing landmine threat in the liberated territories is a serious humanitarian issue requiring the attention not only of Azerbaijan but also of the international community.

Such films demonstrate the scale of the danger and bring the dedication and daily struggles of demining personnel, particularly women, to a wider audience.

The guests then watched the full-length documentary “Steps in Silence.”

The documentary tells the story of an all-female demining team. It follows the women’s lives, showing how, despite their extremely dangerous work, they set aside their professional responsibilities at home to spend time with their loved ones as mothers and wives.

The film has already received international recognition. It had its world premiere in the competition programme of the 66th Krakow Film Festival, one of Europe’s oldest film festivals, where it won the Best Cinematography award.

The documentary has also been featured in Modern Times Review, a Europe-based digital and print magazine specializing in documentaries and books. International audiences can find detailed information about the film on the platform.

The film also received a Special Jury Mention at the NNW International Film Festival in Gdynia, Poland, and was screened for international audiences at the Astra Film Festival in Romania.

These achievements have created further opportunities for “Steps in Silence” to reach international audiences and bring its important story to viewers in more countries.

The film attracted considerable interest at its presentation at the Nizami Cinema Center. The creative team was invited onto the stage after the screening.

In their remarks, screenwriter Fariz Ahmadov and director of photography Mateusz Czuchnowski thanked everyone involved in bringing the project to life, particularly executive producer Arzu Aliyeva, President of the Baku Media Center, for her support.

The film is co-produced by the Baku Media Center, Drygas Film Production, and Polish Television (TVP), with financial support from the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Azerbaijan, ARKA, and the Polish Film Institute.

Arzu Aliyeva is the film’s executive producer. The production team also includes co-producer Vita Żelakevičiūtė (Poland), producer Orman Aliyev, screenwriters Fariz Ahmadov and Ismayil Iman, director of photography Mateusz Czuchnowski, editor Rasim Ismayilov, and creative producers Maciej Drygas (Poland) and Tahir Aliyev.

Since its establishment, the Baku Media Center has attached great importance to preserving Azerbaijan’s historical heritage and conveying the truth.

The Center has produced numerous films covering various chapters of the country’s history, many of which have attracted considerable public interest. These include “Target Baku,” “Heritage,” “The Last Session,” “Eternal Assignment,” “We,” “Shusha, You Are Free!” and “Taghiyev.”

The trailer for “Steps in Silence” is available here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EE9l5z_QahQ

World.title: Mt Isa's $145 million critical minerals pitch one step closer
World.content:
Mount Isa's push to reinvent its regional economy with a new mineral research hub has secured state and federal backing for a feasibility study.

Mount Isa City Council and the University of Queensland released a business case earlier this month for a $145 million critical minerals research centre.

The facility would allow mining companies to analyse rock samples from local mineral deposits to see what minerals were present and if they would be viable to mine.

The $145 million centre is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs. (Supplied: Mount Isa City Council)

In July 2025, Mount Isa's underground copper mine closure saw nearly 500 workers sacked in the 19,000-strong community, forcing the council to search for economic alternatives.

While Mount Isa's economy has been affected, exploration and investment across the wider North West Minerals Province has boomed, with about 85 critical minerals projects underway.

Sustainable Minerals Institute director at the University of Queensland Rick Valenta said the proposed hub would allow industry to scale operations quickly.

Rick Valenta (right) says the facility will help mines understand what minerals are in deposits and how they could be mined. (ABC Rural: Eric Barker)

"The reason you can't just find a deposit and put it into production in a year is because you've got to answer … 'What's the content of the metal that you're after? And … how do we get the metals out of that rock?'" Professor Valenta said.

"[At the moment], those rocks would be going elsewhere in Queensland … Australia or the world … [and] that involves a cost and a delay.

"This centre is aimed at providing a local solution to that sort of thing."

The proposed research centre would be situated between the George Fisher Mine and Mount Isa Airport. (Supplied: Mount Isa City Councill)

Search for new ideas

Mount Isa Mayor Peta MacRae said she hoped the research hub would help future-proof the city by giving mining companies a dedicated site to research problems locally.

"[Currently] minerals are just going to be ripped up and shipped," she said.

"What we want to do is add the value and do as much processing as we can … to help us secure the future for our communities."

Peta MacRae hopes the project will centralise some of the regions' mining investment into the town's economy. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

The proposed hub is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs and would be located near the Mount Isa Airport.

On Friday morning, Federal Assistant Minister for Resources Anthony Chisholm confirmed funding would be released to consider the proposal.

"We want to make the most of these opportunities … and ensure that Mount Isa remains a great place to live and work and attract people at the same time," he said.

"We know that there is enormous potential, but it's about proving that and then also ensuring that we can attract the industry investment."

Anthony Chisholm says the cenrre is about proving Mt Isa's potential and attracting industry investment. (ABC News: Tim Little)

The federal and state governments have agreed to tip in $241,250 each to fund a feasibility study, with an additional $482,500 to come from Mount Isa City Council.

If successful, the hub would operate in conjunction with similar facilities in Mackay and Townsville.

Initial testing and analysis would start at Mount Isa's centre, before small-scale piloting took place in Mackay followed by large-scale trials in Townsville.

World.title: Police arrest two men behind nine-day copper theft heist
World.content:
Police have arrested two men who stole 239 kilograms of copper wire in an Ipswich shopping Centre heist, after one of the men tried to hide in a closet.

Detective Inspector Mick Manago said Town Square Redbank Plains security equipment was sabotaged over nine days in a "coordinated" attack.

Inspector Manago said police alleged around 11pm on November 1 a masked man was captured on CCTV deliberately damaging a security camera at the site before leaving.

Detective Inspector Mick Manago said police were searching for more possible colluders. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

He said on November 5, offenders allegedly cut through perimeter fencing before forcing a door open using a crowbar.

He said inspection of the site on November 9 identified extensive damage to electrical infrastructure, including a severed main earthing cable and additional wiring.

Inspector Manago said two Redbank Plains men had been arrested, a 42-year-old and a 46-year-old.

More potential colluders

Inspector Manago said police were investigating the possibility that there may have been other people involved.

"There was some planning, which is quite concerning for us," Inspector Manago said.

"I would expect that amount of copper cabling would need a vehicle to remove it, so we're appealing to anyone in the area at the time who saw any suspicious vehicles to come forward.

"There is every chance that further persons will need to be held to account for what's occurred."

The 46-year-old was arrested by police after hiding in a closet. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

The 42-year-old has been charged with two counts of possessing tainted property and fraud, one count each of entering premises to commit an indictable offence, possessing dangerous drugs, possessing property suspected of having been used in the commission of a drug offence, and possessing utensils.

He was remanded in custody and is due to appear in Ipswich Magistrates Court on December 2.

The 46-year-old was arrested by police after trying to hide in a clothes closet.

He was charged with three counts of possessing tainted property, two counts of fraud, and one count each of entering premises to commit an indictable offence, and possessing utensils.

He was remanded in custody and is due to appear in Ipswich Magistrates Court on January 8.

Inspector Manago said copper theft was a serious offence.

"The theft of copper is not a victim less crime," Inspector Manago said.

"The financial impact of this type of offending extends well beyond the value of the copper stolen.

"There are businesses that face costly repairs, but also they face a financial impact due to the loss of trading."

The copper theft caused most of Town Square Redbank Plain's shops to lose power on Tuesday, causing businesses to close and food to spoil.

World.title: NT teenage girl charged with terror offence makes bid for bail
World.content:
The diary entries of a 15-year-old Northern Territory girl charged with a terrorism related offence allegedly reveal she "had plans to shoot her school", a court has heard.

The 15-year-old girl has been in custody since being charged with collecting or making documents likely to facilitate a terrorist act 10 days ago.

Commonwealth prosecutor Hadi Mazloum opposed the bail application, telling the court the main concern was a risk to community safety.

"That's because of the risk of the infliction of ideologically motivated violence and an online presence which could be seen to encourage extreme violence," he said.

The girl was charged with collecting or making documents likely to facilitate a terrorist act. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Mr Mazloum referenced diary entries allegedly made by the teenager which he said included plans to carry out a school shooting and while the proposed bail conditions were strict, parental supervision would be "inadequate".

Mr Mazloum acknowledged detaining a young girl was a "grave step" and said her writing showed "a child in real distress with a history of being bullied".

However, he opposed the characterisation of the diary entries as that of a "young girl who was bullied and venting, not planning".

"She names a particular student and says she wants her dead; she names a particular place and school," Mr Mazloum said.

"She writes that she and the other young person had plans to shoot her school.

"All of this happened within the family home."

Mr Mazloum also raised concerns about the teenager's access to online devices which he said would be difficult to control through parental supervision in a home environment.

Defence says 'psychological circumstances' warrant bail consideration

The girl's lawyer, Brooke Houen, put forward a plan she described as "extremely stringent" and would impose conditions akin to "house arrest" including "24/7 parental supervision" and electronic monitoring.

Ms Houen said her client's young age and her "psychological circumstances" were important considerations for the court.

Australian Federal Police are involved in the joint counter-terrorism investigation. (Supplied)

The court heard the teenager had been diagnosed with ADHD and was likely to be diagnosed with autism.

Ms Houen said her client's "educational difficulties" and "psychological needs" were unlikely to be met due to "rolling lockdowns" at the Holtze Youth Detention Centre.

"This is a matter where part of the issue is [the youth] has tendencies to be isolated, disaffected and struggling personally and putting her on remand in a youth detention facility is not the way to address those issues," Ms Houen said.

"The way to address those issues is through structured psychological supports which are now in place, returning her to her family, allowing them to support her."

The court heard the case was likely to proceed to a jury trial in the NT Supreme Court which Ms Houen said could take more than a year.

"That is a significant amount of time to remand a young child with her particular vulnerabilities," Ms Houen said.

She also told the court guns owned by family members had all been removed from the property and the girl would have "no access" to any firearms.

Ms Houen emphasised that her client was "well aware" of the seriousness of the charges and the strictness of the bail conditions.

The AFP has warned of a 'tsunami' of youth crime is hitting the country, due to rapid online radicalisation (Unsplash: Gilles Lambert)

"Her primary goal is returning home to her family and she is willing to do whatever is necessary to achieve that," she said.

The girl was supported in court by a group of family members, including her mother, and at one point during the hearing Judge Greg Macdonald asked the girl how she was.

"Good," the girl said.

Judge Macdonald explained the bail conditions would include "lots of rules".

"Are you willing to stick with them, to comply with them, to follow the rules and not break them?" Judge Macdonald asked.

"Yes," the girl said.

Judge Macdonald said he required additional time to consider all the submissions from the prosecution and defence before deciding whether to release the girl from custody.

The girl was remanded in custody and is expected to return to court later this afternoon.

World.title: ATSB releases preliminary report into young pilot's NT crash
World.content:
Fishermen witnessed young Tasmanian pilot Bob Bramley's plane crash in waters off the Northern Territory in August "at very high speed", a report has revealed.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) today released its preliminary report into the crash in the Gulf of Carpentaria on August 25 this year, which is believed to have killed 23-year-old Bramley.

Northern Territory Police conducted extensive marine and air searches at the time, which recovered parts of the plane, but Bramley has never been found.

At the time, 23-year-old Bob Bramley was working as a charter company pilot. (Supplied.)

As a teenager, he became a passionate advocate for suicide prevention, and sought to raise awareness by becoming the youngest person to circumnavigate Australia solo by plane.

Friends and family expressed their shock and sadness in the wake of the crash, remembering Bramley as a "beacon of hope", and for his love of flying.

The ATSB report detailed the circumstances of the August crash, but noted the investigation is continuing and that a final report will be published at its conclusion.

Fishers found plane parts in sea after crash

The report, which refers to "the pilot" but does not identify Bramley, details his movements on the morning of August 25, as he prepared to fly between the small communities of Gove and Nambulwar in the Northern Territory.

At the time, Bramley had been working as a pilot for aviation operator Air Frontier for more than a year, and had been the company's senior base pilot for the Arnhem region since April.

The report noted that after fuelling the plane and lodging a flight plan, the Beechcraft 58 Baron plane departed from the Gove Airport at about 11am, with only the pilot on board.

"The flight plan for the return to Gove indicated four passengers were to be on board," the report noted.

The ATSB's map of Bob Bramley's final flight on August 25, 2026. (ATSB/Google Earth)

About half an hour later, at 11:27am, fishermen in a boat south-west of Isle Woodah in the west of the Gulf of Carpentaria watched the plane pass overhead.

"The witnesses observed the aircraft descending toward the water at an estimated 35–45° nose-down attitude, with its wings-level," the report said.

"They expected the aircraft to pull up; however, it did not change trajectory, and it impacted the water at very high speed.

"The witnesses motored to the impact point and found a fuel/oil slick on the water surface along with many small floating fragments of shattered airframe."

NT Police image of wreckage underwater at the crash site. (NT Police)

No audio recording of cockpit before crash

The report noted that the Baron was not fitted with, and was not required to have, a flight data recorder or a cockpit voice recorder.

The ATSB said the flight wasn't detected by radar, and data tracking the flight was recorded by Bramley's iPad, which it was transmitting to the online platform OzRunways.

The final data point was transmitted at 11:24am, about 23 kilometres north of the crash site.

Bramley made two radio broadcasts during taxi and take-off, and phone records indicated "maintained a messaging stream with their partner" throughout the flight.

"The records identified that the final message was sent from the pilot at 11:21 while the aircraft was in the cruise," the report said.

The report noted Bramley's qualifications to operate the Baron aircraft, that he held a valid medical certificate and that he had completed a multi-engine instrument proficiency check the previous month.

Bramley had more than 1,138 hours total flight time, more than 300 of which were in the Baron.

The Baron itself was initially built in 1978 and had been serviced most recently in June in Darwin.

The report noted no significant weather activity was observed on the day, consistent with the witnesses and other pilots flying in the area.

The report noted Bramley made two radio broadcasts during taxi and takeoff, and "maintained a messaging stream with their partner" throughout the flight. (Supplied: Lachlan Bennett)

Large parts of plane, including engine, found in sea floor

In August, NT Police Acting Assistant Commissioner Peter Malley said the search for Bramley and the crash site had been particularly difficult, adding that "tiger sharks and crocs" had complicated efforts.

NT Police confirmed today human remains had not been found.

Police divers had to contend with sharks and crocodiles during search efforts. (Supplied: NT Police)

The ATSB report said diving operations recovered parts of the aircraft at a depth of 17 metres, and some of Bramley's personal items including his logbook, flight crew licence and "a significantly damaged iPad".

"The diving confirmed the aircraft had separated into many large and small fragments, with that damage consistent with witness reports of a high-velocity impact into the water," the report said.

Included in the report was a photo of the plane's engine, which was found "embedded into the sea floor".

Other parts of the plane, including the cockpit area, parts of the wing, the fuselage and the vertical stabiliser were also found.

The ATSB said the investigation was ongoing, and that it will examine aircraft maintenance records, aircraft and pilot documentation, items recovered from the crash and similar occurrences.

A further report will be released at the end of the investigation.

World.title: Vandals increasingly targeting Melbourne's bus shelters, data suggests
World.content:
Reports of vandalism across Victoria's public transport network have increased by 50 per cent over the past year according to a popular app.

The creator of Snap Send Solve claims it received more than 5,700 reports of vandalism and graffiti on public transport across Victoria between October 2025 and last month.

That was up from 3,760 the year prior.

Bus shelters were the most common target for vandals, with nearly 3,700 reports received in the past 12 months — double those of bus shelter vandalism reports from the previous year.

Bus shelters are commonly damaged in Victoria. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

"This isn't a general rise in vandalism, and it isn't app growth," said Snap Send Solve chief executive Danny Gorog, whose app launched in 2013.

Vandals were targeting "shelters specifically", he said.

Where in Melbourne is worst affected by bus shelter vandalism?

Snap Send Solve's bus shelter figures include all reports of vandalism or graffiti to the app in Victoria which describe bus shelters or stops.

Mr Gorog said they received about two million reports annually for issues ranging from potholes to graffiti, from some 1.25 million registered users across Australia and New Zealand.

In Melbourne, suburbs in the north-east and south-east recorded the highest number of bus shelter vandalism reports.

Graffiti and broken glass were the issues most frequently flagged by users.

The Victorian government confirmed bus shelter vandalism was the most common type of vandalism across the state's public transport network, but did not provide a figure for the repair cost.

It said about $10 million was spent each year removing and repairing graffiti on the train network.

Public Transport Users Association spokesperson Daniel Bowen said bus shelter vandalism was a particular nuisance, especially during hot and wet weather extremes.

"Anecdotally, there are too many cases of vandalism," Mr Bowen said.

" We all want a reliable public transport system, one that is pleasant to use and [where] every seat is available for passengers. "

Bus shelters are often spray-painted or scratched by vandals. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

While bus shelter vandalism accounted for fewer than half of all public transport vandalism reports Snap Send Solve received in 2024-25, it was nearly two-thirds of reports in 2025-26.

"There's clearly a problem there," Mr Gorog said.

Responsibility for repairing or removing bus shelter vandalism across Melbourne varies between location.

Shelters with electronic billboards are often the responsibility of the advertising company leasing them.

Vandalism destroys Melbourne cricket pitch A local cricket club in the south-western suburbs has expressed dismay after its turf pitch was destroyed by suspected vandals on e-bikes.

The ABC contacted several local governments within the areas with the highest number of bus shelter vandalism reports made to Snap Send Solve.

Most declined to comment and deferred to the Department of Transport and Planning, or to oOh!media, which leases shelters for advertising.

Mr Gorog said one theory was that lingering damage, such as graffiti not immediately removed, could encourage further vandalism.

"There is a thesis that there's this repair lag ... and when something has deteriorated and has been vandalised, it creates a bit more vandalism," Mr Gorog said.

Drones, CCTV used in monitoring

The Shire of Nillumbik, which contains suburbs including Eltham and Diamond Creek, is in the north-east of Melbourne where the highest number of shelter vandalism reports originated.

The Shire said it had received 130 vandalism reports since January — roughly one every two days.

It said shelters were inspected and cleaned twice weekly, "with graffiti removed as quickly as possible".

Officials at Frankston City, in Melbourne's south-east, said they had removed more than 37,000 square metres of graffiti across all property types last financial year.

The council has been running a trial offering locals $500 if their graffiti reports result in a guilty finding in court.

Another scheme offered offered free graffiti removal supplies to locals.

Public Transport Users Association spokesperson Daniel Bowen said "there are too many cases of vandalism" on Victoria's bus network. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

The Department of Transport and Planning said it used more than 14,000 CCTV cameras across the public transport network.

A spokesperson said the department was "cracking down" on vandalism using drones and "new tracking technology" along train routes.

“We encourage anyone who sees vandalism or damaged property on our network to report it to Victoria Police," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Government back to the drawing board on backpacker crackdown
World.content:
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has all but confirmed the government is going back to the drawing board on its proposed backpacker crackdown, as it grapples with the twin issues of a surge in UK working holiday-makers and pressure to rein in overall migration.

On Friday, Mr Burke said Australia must "find a way" to reduce the number of UK backpackers arriving and staying in the country under a free trade deal introduced in 2023, which allows British citizens to live in Australia for up to three years without specific work requirements.

"We can find a way to bring that back to something more sensible and in the national interest, without jeopardising the other parts of the free trade agreement," he said.

In August, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ruled out imposing regional work requirements on backpackers from the UK, which apply to other working holiday-makers seeking to extend their visas beyond 12 months.

The favourable treatment has led to a steep increase in the number of British backpackers coming to Australia, up from 47,238 in 2023/24 to 79,412 in 2024/25 according to Home Affairs data.

"The conversations with the United Kingdom continue," Mr Burke said.

Backpacker ballot could be delayed

The government had also proposed introducing a ballot system for non-British backpackers seeking to extend their stay into a second or third year, to dramatically reduce visa numbers.

The Australian newspaper reported the government was now considering delaying the rollout of the ballot system until early next year, after farming, tourism and hospitality groups warned the changes could cripple their industries.

The report suggests the government is considering lifting the cap on third-year visas from the proposed 5,000 to 20,000 (down from the current 31,000) and imposing longer regional work requirements on visa-holders.

Mr Burke said the government was continuing to engage with industry stakeholders, but the "parameters" around reducing the overall number of working holiday-makers were unchanged.

"The total number of working holiday or backpacker numbers that I've announced at the National Press Club, I cannot shift from," he said.

He described potential changes to the implementation as "tweaks" that would allow businesses to "get the best possible use out of people, while they are here".

"I am completely open to that," he said.

Industry urges government to make quick decision

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said there had been "extensive discussions" between the government and affected industries about the backpacker issue.

He warned the original proposal risked disrupting businesses outside major cities, particularly in regional areas that relied on working holiday-makers to fill jobs.

"And those regional areas really need those people to be coming out there and to be undertaking that work, supporting work in those areas," he said.

Andrew McKellar says the government must move quickly to grant businesses certainty. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr McKellar said business groups wanted the government to "make a decision", warning the "clock is ticking" for businesses seeking certainty ahead of summer.

"Let's ensure that those people who are already here can continue with their plans … and that there's a fresh set of rules for anyone else who's coming in," he said.

Community Strong MP Allegra Spender said growing uncertainty was becoming increasingly painful for businesses.

"What I'm seeing in the migration system more broadly is very slow processing times and not real honesty about where this is all going," she said.

"When you're employing someone where you've in the past been able to get some money in pretty quickly, and now it's taking months, there's that uncertainty that is really damaging for businesses".

The government paused working holiday-maker visa applications from 24 countries in August.

Mr Burke said the government was "very close" to a resolution.

World.title: Victorian Labor MP 'sick to death' of council approach to new Maryborough pool
World.content:
Labor's Ripon MP Martha Haylett has called on Central Goldfields Shire Council Mayor Ben Green and CEO Peter Harriott to "reconsider their positions" amid controversy surrounding the redevelopment of Maryborough outdoor swimming pool.

The pool has been closed since 2022 after an independent assessor deemed it was at "end of life".

The Labor MP announced yesterday if re-elected, the government would match a Liberal Party promise of a further $5 million to fund the Central Victorian pool under "very strict conditions".

"We will not release a single cent of taxpayer funding until the council is able to explain how they have so dramatically mismanaged this project, and provide the community with a fully transparent and detailed plan as to how they intend to actually deliver it," Ms Haylett said.

"We are sick to death of this council repeatedly coming and asking for further money.

Martha Haylett has accused the council of mismanaging the Maryborough outdoor pool project. (Supplied)

"Due to ongoing issues, we think it is appropriate that Liberal Mayor Ben Green and CEO Peter Harriott reconsider their positions."

Yesterday, Liberal Party candidate Megan Read pledged $5 million to demolish the existing pool and build a new 50-metre outdoor pool.

$9 million in funding has already been secured for the project, comprising $4.5 million federal commitment, $3 million from the state government and $1.5 million from the Central Goldfields Shire Council.

Nationals candidate Jo Armstrong has also promised to "deliver the pool to the community".

Ben Green is the Central Goldfields Shire mayor. (Supplied)

An assessor previously recommended the Maryborough pool be demolished and rebuilt, estimated to cost $9 million.

Last year, the estimated cost of reopening the pool jumped to about $14 million, which the council attributed to soaring construction prices and site complexities.

The 50-metre pool is the only outdoor facility of its kind for the town of 8,000 residents.

Maryborough is facing its fourth summer without an outdoor pool. (ABC News: Sarah Lawrence)

Central Goldfields Shire Council did not respond to the ABC's questions about the call for the mayor or CEO to resign or to allegations the council had "dramatically mismanaged" the pool project.

In a statement to the ABC, a Central Goldfields Shire Council spokesperson welcomed the Coalition and Labor's commitment to provide $5 million for the pool.

"Additional community engagement will occur around all aspects of the project when funding is secured," the spokesperson said.

"After the election outcome is known, we'll seek the local member's support to work collaboratively and get on with delivering."

Speaking to the ABC this morning, CEO Peter Harriott said the $5 million commitment was "fantastic", but he denied wrongdoing.

"There has been no mismanagement of this project. If you are talking about the costs … look at some of the tunnels in Melbourne that go [over the budget]. We are nowhere in the league of those increases," Mr Harriott said.

World.title: Not-so-happy campers: Queanbeyan council's crackdown on caravan parking
World.content:
The Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council has begun enforcing strict residential parking rules banning large caravans, boats, and trailers from long-term parking in residential streets.

The push is part of the council's effort to crackdown on large vehicles being left for long periods of time in prime parking spots.

Under the new rules, which came into effect last month, vehicles longer than 7.5 metres cannot park in residential streets for more than an hour.

Vehicles smaller than 7.5 metres will be allowed to park in residential streets for up to 28 days before being required to move.

The council's push is aimed at reclaiming street space, and is being met with mixed reactions. (ABC News: Ruby Thomas)

Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council Mayor Kenrick Winchester said the issue was prominent in the NSW town of Googong, where he said people were using on-street parking to store large vehicles.

The mayor said people had "bought houses where they can't fit their boat or their trailer in their own backyards, or sheds, or driveways, and so they're parking them randomly throughout the suburb".

"You bought a house out at Googong and you didn't plan to fit your big boat or caravan on the property that you bought, then that's all on you I guess," he said.

The new council rules also ban any vehicles from parking on the verge — the area between the road and the boundary of a property.

The council's pursuit to reclaim street space has been met with mixed reactions.

The council is concerned that vehicles are being left for long periods of time in prime parking spots. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

'A good thing': home owners

Local couple, Sarah and Parveen, have lived in Googong for nine years and said they had recently seen more caravans parked on their street, for months at a time.

The couple said they now referred to their street as a "caravan park".

Googong residents Sarah and Parveen welcome the enforcement of strict residential parking rules, targeting caravans, boats, and trailers. (ABC News)

"In the beginning it was not bad, but now this whole street sometimes is full of caravans," Sarah said.

"Most of the year they just stay there, except the few times people will take them for holidays."

Parveen said the vehicles, which he speculated were not always owned by people who lived on the street, created a safety hazard.

"This street … has a bend in it and caravans are a bit wider, they take [up the] whole lane. It's hard to see over the bend ... so I think [the decision] is a good thing," Parveen said.

'Drive around the corner, don't be afraid to exercise'

But the move has also resulted in some not-so-happy campers.

The Campervan and Motorhome Club of Australia (CMCA) has criticised the crackdown as heavy-handed and unnecessary.

Chief executive Richard Barwick said people would now have to pay for storage sites for the vehicles, on top of rising fuel costs.

Vehicles longer than 7.5 metres can no longer park in residential streets for more than an hour. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"Don't pick a certain market because they think it's an easy target and that they are wealthy because not all people that own an RV or that own a boat are wealthy people," he said.

" We have a lot of pensioners in our organisation that are struggling with the cost of living and this extra burden will affect [them]. "

Mr Barwick said he also did not believe that the area had the population or density to warrant the new rules, saying there was likely plenty of parking available for local residents.

"I know Queanbeyan reasonably well; to me there'd be parking. Drive around the corner, don't be afraid to exercise."

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer, alleged double murderer’s cross-examination continues; grilled by Crown over texts to Jesse Baird
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Thank you for reading our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial. The former NSW police officer’s cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, is continuing.

A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon this week. Rocco Fazzari

The former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant.

Here is his evidence so far today:

Lamarre-Condon has denied his messages to a friend about the movie Saltburn in the days before the alleged murders resonated with him because he had a plan to murder Baird. “Watch the movie salt burn,” he messaged his friend after 9pm on February 15, 2024. “I see myself playing the lead role of the nerd.” He told the court it was a reference to his acting classes.

He denied that hiring a car the evening before the alleged murders was also part of a plan to murder Baird. “Mr Crown, if I wanted to plan a murder, I would have two stolen vehicles ready to go, I would have a gun that’s not linked to me, I know exactly how to do it,” he said. “I work with youth gangs. It was never a plan to murder anybody.”

He said he bought a new SIM card in the name of “Bob Ballard” in January 2024 to talk to current and former police officers about a complaint they were preparing to lodge against NSW Police. He said it was “a second phone” rather than a burner phone.

The court heard Lamarre-Condon tried to contact a man he met on Hinge on the burner phone on January 26, 2024. The accused has admitted he attempted to dispose of the bodies of Baird and Davies at a family property linked to the man on February 21, 2024. His former Hinge date was unaware of this, the court has heard. The accused said he was trying to “catch up” with the man and did not want to discuss the farm.

Lamarre-Condon denied that he pretended to return his gun to a safe at Balmain police station on February 18, 2024, the night before the alleged murders. He does not dispute that he kept his gun with him that night and took it to Baird’s house but has told the court he was considering taking his own life due to work-related trauma.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Father and daughter team adds fuel to familial fire in play of ideas
World.content:
Old Fitz Theatre, November 11, until November 15

If you’ve ever wondered why Australia’s last remaining pub theatre – tucked in the basement of Woolloomooloo’s Old Fitzroy Hotel – would run a ‘late-night’ series of shows alongside its main season of plays, look no further than this 9pm offering.

A Number, by acclaimed British playwright Caryl Churchill, has a run time of just 60 minutes and doesn’t follow conventional narrative arcs, making it difficult to slot into main theatre seasons. It’s something we may never see in Sydney if not for its home in a later time slot, when it layers a few props and a new seating configuration over the set of the main season show Scenes from a Friendship, which plays before it every night at 7pm.

There’s clearly a hunger in Sydney for something a little riskier that can only come out late at night: this production sold out before it even opened.

World.title: Big Build royal commission LIVE updates: Rail Projects official says Allan’s office told them to handle CFMEU dispute or they ‘can’t have more work’
World.content:
The Big Build royal commission has just resumed after a lunch break and the inquiry is discussing text messages between senior public servants after the CFMEU stopped work at the Gap Road level crossing removal.

Peter Wilkinson, then a senior Rail Projects Victoria (RPV) official, sent a group text to RPV chief executive Evan Tattersall and RPV communications director Amanda Correy on the afternoon of June 6, 2022.

The royal commission’s first block of hearings is focusing on the Gap Road level crossing removal project.

The inquiry heard Wilkinson’s message said: “FYI police are on their way to the Gap Road site to remove union organisers.”

Correy responds: “Thanks for the heads-up – I’ll let MO know. Are works still continuing?”

Wilkinson said: “Works are being greatly disrupted.”

The inquiry heard that “MO” referred to the minister’s office.

World.title: From fairy invasions to political intrigue, 10 new books worth your time
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There’s no shortage of strange goings-on in this week’s books. Fairies are laying siege to Durham, a time traveller is playing havoc with Napoleon’s plans and two elderly Irishmen are expecting answers from the afterlife. And that’s just the fiction. In non-fiction, we encounter some very spooky ladies, a parade of political performers and a world order that’s looking decidedly disorderly. Fiction Photo: O Now! by Niall Williams (Bloomsbury, $23)

The power of this book belies its short-story length – just 57 pages. Set in the fictional Irish village of Faha, which Williams has explored in previous novels, the novella centres on two lifelong friends, elderly Ganga Crowe and Bat Considine. Four times a week, Bat visits Ganga’s home; though their conversation is sparse, they take comfort in each other’s company through a well-worn ritual of tea, newspapers and staring into the fire. The two have made a pact: whoever dies first must let the survivor know why the world exists and what lies in the mind of God. When death finally claims one of them, the survivor initially refuses to leave his side, faithfully waiting for word from the afterlife. The remainder of the story traces the customs and traditions of Irish mourning as neighbours gather to celebrate a life, proving true the local adage that “in Faha, a funeral beat two weddings”. Williams also appends an essay detailing the genesis of the story, which, though interesting, feels somewhat unnecessary. Ultimately, the work is infused with lyricism, beauty and quiet spirituality, its sadness gently balanced by the warmth and solidarity of a tight-knit community. Photo:



Daughters of the Tide by Arianne James (HarperCollins, $33)

This work of historical fiction is set in and around the coast of Tasmania and follows the lives of three generations of women from the late 1800s to the early 1920s. The setting, a ramshackle mansion, is suitably Gothic as the back-and-forth narrative tracks 21-year-old Isla fighting for independence from her mother, Clara, whilst preparing for the return of her estranged aunt, Adelaide. The two share similar sensibilities – in particular, an obsession with the ocean and its mysterious depths. The folklore and mythology of selkies – shapeshifting creatures that can transform between seal and human – carry the narrative and imbue it with a magical-realist tint.
