Why does Isla keep dreaming about swimming in a different shape and eating the glittering, metallic flesh of fish? Arianne James’ debut novel melds fact and superstition as it explores a range of themes, including mother-daughter relationships, sibling bonds and rivalry, love, loss and mental illness. You need to settle into its rhythm, as it is a slow-moving, atmospheric book that gradually teases out long-held family secrets, leaving no easy answers and plenty of ambiguity. Photo: You’ll Love It Here by Natalie Sue (HarperCollins, $35)

Mona doesn’t exactly love her neighbours – in fact, she does her best to avoid them, giving them uncharitable nicknames like “Old White Perve” and “Weird Girl”. She lives in a less-than-salubrious, 16-unit complex called Valleyview in Calgary, Canada (contrary to expectations, it offers no such vista). Though she is one of the old-timers, having lived there for five years, she makes no attempt to beautify her flat, seeing it as a temporary stopgap rather than a permanent home. After a series of unfortunate events, including a meltdown at her marketing job and a fire at the building in which her live-in landlady is injured, Mona reluctantly agrees to take on superintendent duties for a spell – cue all manner of unavoidable interactions and hijinks with her fellow tenants. Though the narrative arc is predictable, You’ll Love It Here is a light, funny, and warm-hearted tale about an insecure, lonely character finding a sense of belonging in the community she once shunned. Mona’s slow-burn romance with Sami, the cute cook at the local diner, also offers a welcome distraction from managing the motley crew of residents whose life stories she finally deigns to understand. Photo:



The Bishop of Durham Attempts to Surrender the City by Susanna Clarke, illustrated by Victoria Sawdon (Bloomsbury, $33)

This is a strange little novella – or extended short story – by Susanna Clarke, known for her bestseller Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell. It combines history with folklore as it imagines the Northern English city of Durham being overtaken by fairies, enchanted trees that move and withstand the axes of woodchoppers and rivers that block the passage of boats. In the middle of the siege is the Bishop of Durham, one Ranulf Flambard, who does his best to capitulate to the invaders, only to find the fairy folk have vanished. Ranulf then sets out on a quest to find their king. Victoria Sawdon’s black-and-white illustrations border the pages like medieval manuscripts and add interest to a story that feels somewhat insubstantial and unfinished. The final chapter explores the intersection of children’s literature, fantasy, landscape and nature, and is actually more engaging than the tale itself. “I still keep company with magicians and giants, fairies and fauns,” Clarke points out, explaining her predilection for writing magic realism, and how she is drawn to what she calls “liminal creatures” between the non-human and human worlds. Photo: As We Fall Through Time by Claire North (Hachette, $35)

Time-traveller and gender-bender Cal meets Olivier in 1789 during Revolutionary France and falls in love with the young soldier. Olivier dies when Napoleon invades Russia, but Cal is determined to change this fate and enlists the help of another time traveller, Fadimatu, an archivist trying to catalogue and preserve human knowledge. As We Fall Through Time is an entertaining read – after all, who doesn’t want to escape a world governed by the strict laws of chronology? It does, however, demand close attention: without it, the constant jumping across non-linear timelines quickly becomes disorienting. There are paradoxes and multiple incarnations of the same characters that the reader must keep track of. Olivier may live to spend more time with Cal, but tampering with history brings its own set of consequences, as we soon discover. Fadimatu has her own complications to unravel when she stumbles across her own mummified body, prompting the narrative to swerve into a murder investigation. Ultimately, the book feels slightly overambitious, with Claire North attempting to juggle too many threads across the space-time continuum. Non-fiction Photo:



Betrayal by Luke Harding (Faber, $37)

A preparatory part of Vladimir Putin’s imperialist grab to colonise Ukraine in 2022 involved Russian special forces storming the presidential building in Kyiv, and either capturing or executing Volodymyr Zelensky and other heads of government. Like the rest of the war, it didn’t go to plan. Putin’s invasion is one part of Luke Harding’s examination of the betrayal of the rules-based international system – encoded in the 1945 UN Charter that instructed all members to “refrain” from “threat or force” for territorial gains – that has brought the world relative peace since the end of World War II. The Ukraine war is a pivotal case study in charting this alarming trend (and the book includes a face-to-face with Zelensky). It also incorporates Donald Trump’s war in Iran, his Greenland threats, China and Taiwan and North Korea. Karl Marx wrote that history does repeat itself, the second time around as farce. Today’s unstable world bears eerie similarities to the 1930s, with a right collection of thugs, war criminals, dictators and would-be dictators rearing their ugly heads once again. History will reveal if it results in farce, or a category that Marx didn’t mention – tragic farce. A compelling piece of superior analytic journalism, timely, urgent and just a bit scary. Photo: Australian Girls by Catherine Gay (Monash University Publishing, $40)

As often as not, the term “girl” can be a put-down, but this study of 19th-century girls reclaims the word to empower them. It tells the stories of settler and Aboriginal girls (mostly between the ages of five and 15) from the 1840s to Federation – united, where possible, by surviving artefacts the girls made themselves, such as a handmade Commonwealth dress, school exercise books and diaries. Academic Catherine Gay maintains that most histories write girls out of the narrative, asserting that she “takes girls seriously” and that her subjects “participated in and contributed to their families and society … and were key actors who contributed to historical change”. Whether she is documenting the activism of, say, Ellen, an Indigenous girl in the 1860s, or the impact of free education in the 1870s, the stories are told firmly from the girls’ point of view. While it may have started life as an academic study, Gay brings a welcome lightness of touch to a previously neglected history. Photo: Jacques Miller by Caitlin McInnis (The Miegunyah Press, $50)

This is not just a portrait of a great scientific mind, but of the relentless drive behind a game-changing discovery. The scientist is Australian Jacques Miller and, to a large extent, this is the story of his groundbreaking work on the thymus – an organ vital to the immune system – which transformed the study of immunology worldwide. Many argue that he ought to have received the Nobel Prize, and the fact that he was overlooked remains a sore point.



Yet, Caitlin McInnis’ biography is equally a portrait of the era that moulded him, particularly the tumultuous years leading up to the Second World War. Born in France, Miller had lived in Switzerland, Shanghai, and Australia by the age of 20; his family not only navigated wartime upheaval but also endured profound personal tragedy in the premature death of his beloved sister. Tumultuous though those years were, they proved instrumental in sharpening an intensely inquiring mind, while instilling in Miller a lifelong appreciation for art and beauty. Drawn from meticulous research and extended conversations with Miller himself, McInnis’ book is an evocative, thoughtful and engaging account that captures the rich complexities of its subject. Photo: Spooky Ladies by Kaz Cooke (Scribner, $38)

Author and cartoonist Kaz Cooke describes this survey of women and magic as a “riotous galumph” through the lives of a long list of “spooky” ladies. That phrase captures the spirit of the book rather well. Spanning the mid-19th to the mid-20th century, it showcases a gallery of larger-than-life, frequently overlooked figures – from the “wildly entertaining” to “shameless frauds and shimmering visions who held their audiences spellbound”. Two notable examples, often cast into the shadow of their famous husbands, are Bess Houdini (who continued performing long after Harry’s death) and Lady Conan Doyle, who took on the role of medium during Arthur’s world tours to promote spiritualism. It is a rollicking chronicle that takes in Madame Blavatsky, witches, seances, mind-reading, mesmerism and more, while examining how the supernatural and superstitious continue to haunt the modern imagination. Photo: Performance Politics by Joshua Black (NewSouth, $40)

When Paul Keating likened himself to Placido Domingo he was, playfully and self-consciously, invoking performance politics and the concept of the politician as performer. Joshua Black, a historian and former political adviser, draws on a wide range of sources – including political memoirs, autobiographies, television documentaries, and interviews – to examine the rise of this phenomenon.

World.title: ‘This is the benchmark’: A rediscovered concert film shows George Michael at his peak
World.content:
‘He’s at the top of his game’: George Michael, pictured on his Faith tour in Perth in 1988.

For almost 40 years, 30 canisters of film footage of George Michael in concert on his iconic Faith tour sat untouched – until now.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As far as pop images go, it’s indelible. The Ray-Ban aviators. The stubble. The leather jacket. The cocked hip. Onstage in Paris in May 1988, just months after Faith became a global chart-topping smash, George Michael playfully teases an audience of 20,000 fans, striking a silhouette to impassioned screams. “He knew the strength of that image he created, and he just played to it,” says Andy Morahan, who directed Michael’s iconic Faith music video. “He’d already plotted his solo image as he was exorcising himself away from Wham! and the big blonde hair and all that stuff. It was like, ‘Right, this is who I am now.’” The new concert film, George Michael: The Faith Tour, captures the late singer at his pop peak. He’s 24 and firmly in the midst of his Faith tour, which took in 109 shows across 16 countries, including Australia, between February 1988 to July 1989. “He’d served his apprenticeship with Wham!, and he knew how to write these songs that jumped out of the radio,” says David Austin, Michael’s longtime friend and manager, who co-directed the film with Morahan. “He was sparring with the greats – Michael Jackson, Prince, Madonna, his three great contemporaries – and he was outselling them all. By the time he got to Faith, he was pretty polished and he knew what he was doing.” The concert was shot in Paris in May 1988. Ahead of the 10th anniversary of Michael’s death this December – the singer died on December 25, 2016, aged 53 – the film is a wild feat of resurrection. It was assembled from restored and remastered 35mm footage shot during two performances at Paris’ Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy on May 30 and 31 in 1988 which sat untouched in 30 film canisters in Michael’s archives for almost 40 years.



Morahan had originally captured the concert for Michael’s video for Monkey, the funked-out fifth single from Faith. “It was never designed to be a concert film. George had just wanted me to shoot the best bits from the show that he could pick out,” he explains. “It wasn’t until 40 years later that David came to me and said, ‘Have a look at this, we might have something here’.” The footage proved a treasure trove. Since it wasn’t a scripted shoot, Morahan had approached the original job with a looser brief. He had Michael’s permission to light the audience during certain sections of songs. He also had a director of photography and a 16-camera crew situated throughout the arena. “I was talking to them on headphones, and they were asked to really go for it, to get the flares and silhouettes and really capture the energy of George’s performance.” No phones, just 20,000 lighters and a handful of worried OHS workers. The audio for both nights had also been recorded on a 24-track mobile studio for a French radio broadcast. “When we revisited it all, it was like, wow,” says Morahan. “George was really comfortable with where he was at that time, which is why this film is so joyous. He’s at the top of his game. He literally runs around like an Olympic athlete. He’s got the audience in the palm of his hand.” As a pristine time capsule, the footage is remarkable. Michael paces nonstop across three stages as he peels through classics such as Father Figure, Careless Whisper and I Want Your Sex (three times). He bounces like a glistening jackhammer, doing MTV dance moves choreographed by Paula Abdul. The singer was 24 years old and riding the wave of chart-topping success that was Faith. As a cinematic event, it’s immersive. In the arena, we’re surrounded by 20,000 fans swaying cigarette lighters in a way that might horrify young phone addicts and OHS officers alike. Cameras shoot the action from all over, including inside the audience pit with Michael hovering above.



The footage was cut together by editor Ben Wainwright-Pearce, who edited concert films including Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour and Billie Eilish’s Hit Me Hard and Soft. Between the sound and vision, it feels like you’re right there. “The technology helped us in that we can clean everything out, we can do amazing things,” says Morahan. “In a funny kind of way, this is probably a better film for having waited all these years.” Opening the concert film is a short documentary, Finding Faith, from photographer and filmmaker Mary McCartney, the eldest daughter of Paul and Linda. Her film sets the context around the concert, using previously unseen archive photos and unreleased clips from interviews Michael did with Tony Parsons between 1989 and 1990 for the book Bare. McCartney says she was drawn to how casual and unguarded Michael was in the interviews. The concert film opens with a short documentary, Finding Faith. “He’s really young, 24 and just out of Wham!, and we see a very reflective George Michael. He’s thinking, ‘What’s my next move? I want to do this, but what am I willing to sacrifice for this?’ He’s a sensitive person at an interesting time in his life and career, and I think that comes across.” McCartney had known Michael for years, but the two became close around 2005 when Michael and his then partner, art dealer Kenny Goss, invited her to exhibit her photography at their gallery in Dallas. “I got to understand his humour. You’d ask him a question and he was very honest, very funny and slightly self-deprecating,” McCartney recalls. “I wanted this piece to show the emotion of George and the vulnerability, and also his talent and craft, and then just release him live into the auditorium.” In the years since his death, there’s an added wrinkle to seeing Michael in his pure element. Recent documentaries, such as Netflix’s 2023 film Wham!, have reflexively reframed Michael as a tortured artist, the pop star whose teen idol success forced him to conceal his sexuality until his infamous arrest in a public bathroom in 1998. In the Faith concert, Michael’s staging plays like a metaphor: he emerges from a barred cage, lives his best life onstage, only to return to his cage at the show’s end. Was he trying to tell us something?



“No, he wasn’t tortured at all!” says Austin with a laugh. “He absolutely owned who he was throughout his career. Everything was very calculated.” Related Article Australian music ‘Total surrender, that’s what healed me’: Daine came back from the brink and made a pop classic Morahan agrees. “There’s a thing in Mary’s opening film where he says, ‘I consider myself one of my generation’s high achievers, but I want to be known as a musician and an artist,’ and I think that was his motivation. When he won his first Ivor Novello award in 1985, he burst into tears because to be recognised by his peers was absolutely everything to him.” Michael’s estate has proven generous in promoting his legacy to a new generation. Last year, Taylor Swift interpolated Father Figure on her song of the same name on The Life of a Showgirl, while Haim gained permission to sample Freedom! ’90 on their album I Quit. At September’s MTV Video Music Awards, young artists including Sombr and Raye joined in a medley of Michael’s biggest hits. The film offers another chance to refocus Michael’s legacy, away from cheap narratives and sordid storylines, and back to his craft. “For me, it’s like, ‘Didn’t see the Faith concert the first time? Well, here’s your chance to see it’,” says Austin. “I hope young people can feel what George was doing and understand the excellence on show. Because this is the benchmark.” George Michael: The Faith Tour is in cinemas now.

World.title: Microsoft outage cuts Queensland Health from emails, Teams
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health Microsoft outage cuts Queensland Health from emails, Teams Dominique Tassell November 13, 2026 — 1:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Queensland public servants’ communication channels have been crippled by the global Microsoft outage but the state government insists emergency health services and patient care have not been compromised. Government departments do not have access to platforms including Outlook, Teams and Copilot as a result of the outage. Minister for Health and Ambulance Services Tim Nicholls said the Microsoft outage had no significant impact to Queensland Health. Dominique Tassell Health and Ambulance Services Minister Tim Nicholls confirmed the health system was run on Microsoft Outlook, but maintained the outage had no significant impact. Queensland Health has 135,000 staff members across 16 hospital and health services, who cannot email each other because of the outage.



“As we all know, we got up early this morning to find the Outlook system was not performing as anticipated and as we all expected to do every day when we log in, sign in, and start looking at what the day ahead holds,” Nicholls said about 9.30am on Friday. Related Article Updated

Network outage Almost 20,000 reports a minute as Microsoft hit by widespread outage “We have stood up the State Health Emergency Command Centre, and we are monitoring the situation continuously, and have been since early this morning, when the outage was first alerted to Queensland Health.” Nicholls said no disruption had been detected to patient care or the delivery of services in hospitals, and the Triple Zero service was not affected. “People can have confidence that Triple Zero and the dispatch service continue to operate as intended,” he said.



“There are back-up systems in place, but we have not had need to call on those back-up systems. So we continue to monitor the system.” The Queensland Police Service was dealing with the outage by adopting an “old school” approach using phones and radios, a spokesman said. The Queensland Education Department was unable to access emails, and families across Brisbane were sent texts from their schools advising them that emails were not working. A department spokesperson advised parents to keep an eye on their school’s social media pages, and only call for urgent inquiries. Brisbane City Council uses Outlook, and was also affected by the outage.

World.title: Almost 20,000 reports a minute as Microsoft hit by widespread outage
World.content:
Updated TechnologyNetwork outage Almost 20,000 reports a minute as Microsoft hit by widespread outage Elias Visontay, Jack Gramenz and Emily Kaine Updated November 13, 2026 — 1:18pm ,first published November 13, 2026 — 7:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Microsoft has prioritised restoring services to government systems as it struggles to issue a broad fix to return full functionality to its apps and platforms after a global outage, as Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke insists the issue is not the result of a cyberattack. The widespread outage hit Microsoft Outlook, Teams and Copilot, causing users to have issues accessing or sending emails, while other errors affected the tech giant’s apps. Microsoft users were hit with a widespread outage overnight. AP Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook and other Microsoft services, beginning just before 5am (AEDT). At one point, reports to the platform reached almost 20,000 per minute, stemming from outages across five Microsoft services in 74 countries. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they still couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes.



Issues among Australians were still common on Friday. Affected users told this masthead that their Outlook email access had stopped working early on Friday, then resumed working for several hours, before subsequently failing again. Related Article Exclusive

Telecommunications ‘Didn’t foot the bill’: Telstra outage cost the economy half a billion dollars, modelling finds By afternoon, email access was still patchy, while other Microsoft platforms such as Teams appeared functional - prompting memes on social media from frustrated workers lamenting the split-level of functionality. A swathe of corporate Australia as well as government departments and agencies were among those affected. They included the Australian Federal Police and the ABC. While they were still able to function, email issues also plagued national supermarket chain Coles as well as government agencies in New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Tasmania and Western Australia. The US tech company was reported to be focussing on restoring services to government first given its large user base. “Microsoft are prioritising life, safety and government services,” a Western Australian state government spokesperson said.



Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services. To fix the issue, Microsoft said it had so far attempted to restart its servers, and validate a change. But initial efforts to fully restore services proved unsuccessful. “We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the company said. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.” Loading A subsequent update issued shortly after 10am AEDT said the company had “begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far”.



“We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions,” it said. Microsoft said it was implementing “protective traffic management measures” region by region to test if it helped with restoring its services. “[We are] fully isolating a portion of our service infrastructure, restarting the affected components, and gradually reintroducing traffic to confirm our services remain stable before applying this approach more broadly. “We’re also analysing traffic patterns across our entire service infrastructure and evaluating whether isolating traffic within each region may allow affected regions to recover independently.” At a press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, Burke said he had been briefed by Australia’s cybersecurity coordinator and the head of Microsoft Australia and that they did not believe they were dealing with a cyber threat.



“The perspective of Microsoft at this stage … they believe in some ways [similar] to what we saw with CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke said. View post on X Microsoft said it was “also investigating why affected servers are experiencing elevated processor usage while handling requests”. In updates posted earlier, it said it was aware of users “experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes”. Microsoft later explained that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load”, which it said was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors”. The company determined several servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” due to a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.



“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X. The company earlier said it had “successfully restored” problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues. World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer, alleged double murderer’s cross-examination continues; grilled by Crown over texts to Jesse Baird
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Thank you for reading our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial. The former NSW police officer’s cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, is continuing.

A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon this week. Rocco Fazzari

The former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant.

Here is his evidence so far today:

Lamarre-Condon has denied his messages to a friend about the movie Saltburn in the days before the alleged murders resonated with him because he had a plan to murder Baird. “Watch the movie salt burn,” he messaged his friend after 9pm on February 15, 2024. “I see myself playing the lead role of the nerd.” He told the court it was a reference to his acting classes.

He denied that hiring a car the evening before the alleged murders was also part of a plan to murder Baird. “Mr Crown, if I wanted to plan a murder, I would have two stolen vehicles ready to go, I would have a gun that’s not linked to me, I know exactly how to do it,” he said. “I work with youth gangs. It was never a plan to murder anybody.”

He said he bought a new SIM card in the name of “Bob Ballard” in January 2024 to talk to current and former police officers about a complaint they were preparing to lodge against NSW Police. He said it was “a second phone” rather than a burner phone.

The court heard Lamarre-Condon tried to contact a man he met on Hinge on the burner phone on January 26, 2024. The accused has admitted he attempted to dispose of the bodies of Baird and Davies at a family property linked to the man on February 21, 2024. His former Hinge date was unaware of this, the court has heard. The accused said he was trying to “catch up” with the man and did not want to discuss the farm.

Lamarre-Condon denied that he pretended to return his gun to a safe at Balmain police station on February 18, 2024, the night before the alleged murders. He does not dispute that he kept his gun with him that night and took it to Baird’s house but has told the court he was considering taking his own life due to work-related trauma.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Father and daughter team adds fuel to familial fire in play of ideas
World.content:
Old Fitz Theatre, November 11, until November 15

If you’ve ever wondered why Australia’s last remaining pub theatre – tucked in the basement of Woolloomooloo’s Old Fitzroy Hotel – would run a ‘late-night’ series of shows alongside its main season of plays, look no further than this 9pm offering.

A Number, by acclaimed British playwright Caryl Churchill, has a run time of just 60 minutes and doesn’t follow conventional narrative arcs, making it difficult to slot into main theatre seasons. It’s something we may never see in Sydney if not for its home in a later time slot, when it layers a few props and a new seating configuration over the set of the main season show Scenes from a Friendship, which plays before it every night at 7pm.

There’s clearly a hunger in Sydney for something a little riskier that can only come out late at night: this production sold out before it even opened.

World.title: Big Build royal commission LIVE updates: Rail Projects official says Allan’s office told them to handle CFMEU dispute or they ‘can’t have more work’
World.content:
The Big Build royal commission has just resumed after a lunch break and the inquiry is discussing text messages between senior public servants after the CFMEU stopped work at the Gap Road level crossing removal.

Peter Wilkinson, then a senior Rail Projects Victoria (RPV) official, sent a group text to RPV chief executive Evan Tattersall and RPV communications director Amanda Correy on the afternoon of June 6, 2022.

The royal commission’s first block of hearings is focusing on the Gap Road level crossing removal project.

The inquiry heard Wilkinson’s message said: “FYI police are on their way to the Gap Road site to remove union organisers.”

Correy responds: “Thanks for the heads-up – I’ll let MO know. Are works still continuing?”

Wilkinson said: “Works are being greatly disrupted.”

The inquiry heard that “MO” referred to the minister’s office.

World.title: From fairy invasions to political intrigue, 10 new books worth your time
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There’s no shortage of strange goings-on in this week’s books. Fairies are laying siege to Durham, a time traveller is playing havoc with Napoleon’s plans and two elderly Irishmen are expecting answers from the afterlife. And that’s just the fiction. In non-fiction, we encounter some very spooky ladies, a parade of political performers and a world order that’s looking decidedly disorderly. Fiction Photo: O Now! by Niall Williams (Bloomsbury, $23)

The power of this book belies its short-story length – just 57 pages. Set in the fictional Irish village of Faha, which Williams has explored in previous novels, the novella centres on two lifelong friends, elderly Ganga Crowe and Bat Considine. Four times a week, Bat visits Ganga’s home; though their conversation is sparse, they take comfort in each other’s company through a well-worn ritual of tea, newspapers and staring into the fire. The two have made a pact: whoever dies first must let the survivor know why the world exists and what lies in the mind of God. When death finally claims one of them, the survivor initially refuses to leave his side, faithfully waiting for word from the afterlife. The remainder of the story traces the customs and traditions of Irish mourning as neighbours gather to celebrate a life, proving true the local adage that “in Faha, a funeral beat two weddings”. Williams also appends an essay detailing the genesis of the story, which, though interesting, feels somewhat unnecessary. Ultimately, the work is infused with lyricism, beauty and quiet spirituality, its sadness gently balanced by the warmth and solidarity of a tight-knit community. Photo:



Daughters of the Tide by Arianne James (HarperCollins, $33)

This work of historical fiction is set in and around the coast of Tasmania and follows the lives of three generations of women from the late 1800s to the early 1920s. The setting, a ramshackle mansion, is suitably Gothic as the back-and-forth narrative tracks 21-year-old Isla fighting for independence from her mother, Clara, whilst preparing for the return of her estranged aunt, Adelaide. The two share similar sensibilities – in particular, an obsession with the ocean and its mysterious depths. The folklore and mythology of selkies – shapeshifting creatures that can transform between seal and human – carry the narrative and imbue it with a magical-realist tint. Why does Isla keep dreaming about swimming in a different shape and eating the glittering, metallic flesh of fish? Arianne James’ debut novel melds fact and superstition as it explores a range of themes, including mother-daughter relationships, sibling bonds and rivalry, love, loss and mental illness. You need to settle into its rhythm, as it is a slow-moving, atmospheric book that gradually teases out long-held family secrets, leaving no easy answers and plenty of ambiguity. Photo: You’ll Love It Here by Natalie Sue (HarperCollins, $35)

Mona doesn’t exactly love her neighbours – in fact, she does her best to avoid them, giving them uncharitable nicknames like “Old White Perve” and “Weird Girl”. She lives in a less-than-salubrious, 16-unit complex called Valleyview in Calgary, Canada (contrary to expectations, it offers no such vista). Though she is one of the old-timers, having lived there for five years, she makes no attempt to beautify her flat, seeing it as a temporary stopgap rather than a permanent home. After a series of unfortunate events, including a meltdown at her marketing job and a fire at the building in which her live-in landlady is injured, Mona reluctantly agrees to take on superintendent duties for a spell – cue all manner of unavoidable interactions and hijinks with her fellow tenants. Though the narrative arc is predictable, You’ll Love It Here is a light, funny, and warm-hearted tale about an insecure, lonely character finding a sense of belonging in the community she once shunned. Mona’s slow-burn romance with Sami, the cute cook at the local diner, also offers a welcome distraction from managing the motley crew of residents whose life stories she finally deigns to understand. Photo:



The Bishop of Durham Attempts to Surrender the City by Susanna Clarke, illustrated by Victoria Sawdon (Bloomsbury, $33)

This is a strange little novella – or extended short story – by Susanna Clarke, known for her bestseller Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell. It combines history with folklore as it imagines the Northern English city of Durham being overtaken by fairies, enchanted trees that move and withstand the axes of woodchoppers and rivers that block the passage of boats. In the middle of the siege is the Bishop of Durham, one Ranulf Flambard, who does his best to capitulate to the invaders, only to find the fairy folk have vanished. Ranulf then sets out on a quest to find their king. Victoria Sawdon’s black-and-white illustrations border the pages like medieval manuscripts and add interest to a story that feels somewhat insubstantial and unfinished. The final chapter explores the intersection of children’s literature, fantasy, landscape and nature, and is actually more engaging than the tale itself. “I still keep company with magicians and giants, fairies and fauns,” Clarke points out, explaining her predilection for writing magic realism, and how she is drawn to what she calls “liminal creatures” between the non-human and human worlds. Photo: As We Fall Through Time by Claire North (Hachette, $35)

Time-traveller and gender-bender Cal meets Olivier in 1789 during Revolutionary France and falls in love with the young soldier. Olivier dies when Napoleon invades Russia, but Cal is determined to change this fate and enlists the help of another time traveller, Fadimatu, an archivist trying to catalogue and preserve human knowledge. As We Fall Through Time is an entertaining read – after all, who doesn’t want to escape a world governed by the strict laws of chronology? It does, however, demand close attention: without it, the constant jumping across non-linear timelines quickly becomes disorienting. There are paradoxes and multiple incarnations of the same characters that the reader must keep track of. Olivier may live to spend more time with Cal, but tampering with history brings its own set of consequences, as we soon discover. Fadimatu has her own complications to unravel when she stumbles across her own mummified body, prompting the narrative to swerve into a murder investigation. Ultimately, the book feels slightly overambitious, with Claire North attempting to juggle too many threads across the space-time continuum. Non-fiction Photo:



Betrayal by Luke Harding (Faber, $37)

A preparatory part of Vladimir Putin’s imperialist grab to colonise Ukraine in 2022 involved Russian special forces storming the presidential building in Kyiv, and either capturing or executing Volodymyr Zelensky and other heads of government. Like the rest of the war, it didn’t go to plan. Putin’s invasion is one part of Luke Harding’s examination of the betrayal of the rules-based international system – encoded in the 1945 UN Charter that instructed all members to “refrain” from “threat or force” for territorial gains – that has brought the world relative peace since the end of World War II. The Ukraine war is a pivotal case study in charting this alarming trend (and the book includes a face-to-face with Zelensky). It also incorporates Donald Trump’s war in Iran, his Greenland threats, China and Taiwan and North Korea. Karl Marx wrote that history does repeat itself, the second time around as farce. Today’s unstable world bears eerie similarities to the 1930s, with a right collection of thugs, war criminals, dictators and would-be dictators rearing their ugly heads once again. History will reveal if it results in farce, or a category that Marx didn’t mention – tragic farce. A compelling piece of superior analytic journalism, timely, urgent and just a bit scary. Photo: Australian Girls by Catherine Gay (Monash University Publishing, $40)

As often as not, the term “girl” can be a put-down, but this study of 19th-century girls reclaims the word to empower them. It tells the stories of settler and Aboriginal girls (mostly between the ages of five and 15) from the 1840s to Federation – united, where possible, by surviving artefacts the girls made themselves, such as a handmade Commonwealth dress, school exercise books and diaries. Academic Catherine Gay maintains that most histories write girls out of the narrative, asserting that she “takes girls seriously” and that her subjects “participated in and contributed to their families and society … and were key actors who contributed to historical change”. Whether she is documenting the activism of, say, Ellen, an Indigenous girl in the 1860s, or the impact of free education in the 1870s, the stories are told firmly from the girls’ point of view. While it may have started life as an academic study, Gay brings a welcome lightness of touch to a previously neglected history. Photo: Jacques Miller by Caitlin McInnis (The Miegunyah Press, $50)

This is not just a portrait of a great scientific mind, but of the relentless drive behind a game-changing discovery. The scientist is Australian Jacques Miller and, to a large extent, this is the story of his groundbreaking work on the thymus – an organ vital to the immune system – which transformed the study of immunology worldwide. Many argue that he ought to have received the Nobel Prize, and the fact that he was overlooked remains a sore point.



Yet, Caitlin McInnis’ biography is equally a portrait of the era that moulded him, particularly the tumultuous years leading up to the Second World War. Born in France, Miller had lived in Switzerland, Shanghai, and Australia by the age of 20; his family not only navigated wartime upheaval but also endured profound personal tragedy in the premature death of his beloved sister. Tumultuous though those years were, they proved instrumental in sharpening an intensely inquiring mind, while instilling in Miller a lifelong appreciation for art and beauty. Drawn from meticulous research and extended conversations with Miller himself, McInnis’ book is an evocative, thoughtful and engaging account that captures the rich complexities of its subject. Photo: Spooky Ladies by Kaz Cooke (Scribner, $38)

Author and cartoonist Kaz Cooke describes this survey of women and magic as a “riotous galumph” through the lives of a long list of “spooky” ladies. That phrase captures the spirit of the book rather well. Spanning the mid-19th to the mid-20th century, it showcases a gallery of larger-than-life, frequently overlooked figures – from the “wildly entertaining” to “shameless frauds and shimmering visions who held their audiences spellbound”. Two notable examples, often cast into the shadow of their famous husbands, are Bess Houdini (who continued performing long after Harry’s death) and Lady Conan Doyle, who took on the role of medium during Arthur’s world tours to promote spiritualism. It is a rollicking chronicle that takes in Madame Blavatsky, witches, seances, mind-reading, mesmerism and more, while examining how the supernatural and superstitious continue to haunt the modern imagination. Photo: Performance Politics by Joshua Black (NewSouth, $40)

When Paul Keating likened himself to Placido Domingo he was, playfully and self-consciously, invoking performance politics and the concept of the politician as performer. Joshua Black, a historian and former political adviser, draws on a wide range of sources – including political memoirs, autobiographies, television documentaries, and interviews – to examine the rise of this phenomenon.

World.title: ‘This is the benchmark’: A rediscovered concert film shows George Michael at his peak
World.content:
‘He’s at the top of his game’: George Michael, pictured on his Faith tour in Perth in 1988.

For almost 40 years, 30 canisters of film footage of George Michael in concert on his iconic Faith tour sat untouched – until now.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As far as pop images go, it’s indelible. The Ray-Ban aviators. The stubble. The leather jacket. The cocked hip. Onstage in Paris in May 1988, just months after Faith became a global chart-topping smash, George Michael playfully teases an audience of 20,000 fans, striking a silhouette to impassioned screams. “He knew the strength of that image he created, and he just played to it,” says Andy Morahan, who directed Michael’s iconic Faith music video. “He’d already plotted his solo image as he was exorcising himself away from Wham! and the big blonde hair and all that stuff. It was like, ‘Right, this is who I am now.’” The new concert film, George Michael: The Faith Tour, captures the late singer at his pop peak. He’s 24 and firmly in the midst of his Faith tour, which took in 109 shows across 16 countries, including Australia, between February 1988 to July 1989. “He’d served his apprenticeship with Wham!, and he knew how to write these songs that jumped out of the radio,” says David Austin, Michael’s longtime friend and manager, who co-directed the film with Morahan. “He was sparring with the greats – Michael Jackson, Prince, Madonna, his three great contemporaries – and he was outselling them all. By the time he got to Faith, he was pretty polished and he knew what he was doing.” The concert was shot in Paris in May 1988. Ahead of the 10th anniversary of Michael’s death this December – the singer died on December 25, 2016, aged 53 – the film is a wild feat of resurrection. It was assembled from restored and remastered 35mm footage shot during two performances at Paris’ Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy on May 30 and 31 in 1988 which sat untouched in 30 film canisters in Michael’s archives for almost 40 years.



Morahan had originally captured the concert for Michael’s video for Monkey, the funked-out fifth single from Faith. “It was never designed to be a concert film. George had just wanted me to shoot the best bits from the show that he could pick out,” he explains. “It wasn’t until 40 years later that David came to me and said, ‘Have a look at this, we might have something here’.” The footage proved a treasure trove. Since it wasn’t a scripted shoot, Morahan had approached the original job with a looser brief. He had Michael’s permission to light the audience during certain sections of songs. He also had a director of photography and a 16-camera crew situated throughout the arena. “I was talking to them on headphones, and they were asked to really go for it, to get the flares and silhouettes and really capture the energy of George’s performance.” No phones, just 20,000 lighters and a handful of worried OHS workers. The audio for both nights had also been recorded on a 24-track mobile studio for a French radio broadcast. “When we revisited it all, it was like, wow,” says Morahan. “George was really comfortable with where he was at that time, which is why this film is so joyous. He’s at the top of his game. He literally runs around like an Olympic athlete. He’s got the audience in the palm of his hand.” As a pristine time capsule, the footage is remarkable. Michael paces nonstop across three stages as he peels through classics such as Father Figure, Careless Whisper and I Want Your Sex (three times). He bounces like a glistening jackhammer, doing MTV dance moves choreographed by Paula Abdul. The singer was 24 years old and riding the wave of chart-topping success that was Faith. As a cinematic event, it’s immersive. In the arena, we’re surrounded by 20,000 fans swaying cigarette lighters in a way that might horrify young phone addicts and OHS officers alike. Cameras shoot the action from all over, including inside the audience pit with Michael hovering above.



The footage was cut together by editor Ben Wainwright-Pearce, who edited concert films including Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour and Billie Eilish’s Hit Me Hard and Soft. Between the sound and vision, it feels like you’re right there. “The technology helped us in that we can clean everything out, we can do amazing things,” says Morahan. “In a funny kind of way, this is probably a better film for having waited all these years.” Opening the concert film is a short documentary, Finding Faith, from photographer and filmmaker Mary McCartney, the eldest daughter of Paul and Linda. Her film sets the context around the concert, using previously unseen archive photos and unreleased clips from interviews Michael did with Tony Parsons between 1989 and 1990 for the book Bare. McCartney says she was drawn to how casual and unguarded Michael was in the interviews. The concert film opens with a short documentary, Finding Faith. “He’s really young, 24 and just out of Wham!, and we see a very reflective George Michael. He’s thinking, ‘What’s my next move? I want to do this, but what am I willing to sacrifice for this?’ He’s a sensitive person at an interesting time in his life and career, and I think that comes across.” McCartney had known Michael for years, but the two became close around 2005 when Michael and his then partner, art dealer Kenny Goss, invited her to exhibit her photography at their gallery in Dallas. “I got to understand his humour. You’d ask him a question and he was very honest, very funny and slightly self-deprecating,” McCartney recalls. “I wanted this piece to show the emotion of George and the vulnerability, and also his talent and craft, and then just release him live into the auditorium.” In the years since his death, there’s an added wrinkle to seeing Michael in his pure element. Recent documentaries, such as Netflix’s 2023 film Wham!, have reflexively reframed Michael as a tortured artist, the pop star whose teen idol success forced him to conceal his sexuality until his infamous arrest in a public bathroom in 1998. In the Faith concert, Michael’s staging plays like a metaphor: he emerges from a barred cage, lives his best life onstage, only to return to his cage at the show’s end. Was he trying to tell us something?



“No, he wasn’t tortured at all!” says Austin with a laugh. “He absolutely owned who he was throughout his career. Everything was very calculated.” Related Article Australian music ‘Total surrender, that’s what healed me’: Daine came back from the brink and made a pop classic Morahan agrees. “There’s a thing in Mary’s opening film where he says, ‘I consider myself one of my generation’s high achievers, but I want to be known as a musician and an artist,’ and I think that was his motivation. When he won his first Ivor Novello award in 1985, he burst into tears because to be recognised by his peers was absolutely everything to him.” Michael’s estate has proven generous in promoting his legacy to a new generation. Last year, Taylor Swift interpolated Father Figure on her song of the same name on The Life of a Showgirl, while Haim gained permission to sample Freedom! ’90 on their album I Quit. At September’s MTV Video Music Awards, young artists including Sombr and Raye joined in a medley of Michael’s biggest hits. The film offers another chance to refocus Michael’s legacy, away from cheap narratives and sordid storylines, and back to his craft. “For me, it’s like, ‘Didn’t see the Faith concert the first time? Well, here’s your chance to see it’,” says Austin. “I hope young people can feel what George was doing and understand the excellence on show. Because this is the benchmark.” George Michael: The Faith Tour is in cinemas now.

Well, we’re ready for the first ball and it feels like it’s the calm after the storm. Who’d have thought? The cricket has taken the back seat during this remarkable and explosive past week, where the scars and baggage of that tour in 2018 have roared back into the headlines.

Spencer Johnson is taking the ball from the other end.

England are 0-5 - 1 over

World.title: Microsoft outage cuts Queensland Health from emails, Teams
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health Microsoft outage cuts Queensland Health from emails, Teams Dominique Tassell November 13, 2026 — 1:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Queensland public servants’ communication channels have been crippled by the global Microsoft outage but the state government insists emergency health services and patient care have not been compromised. Government departments do not have access to platforms including Outlook, Teams and Copilot as a result of the outage. Minister for Health and Ambulance Services Tim Nicholls said the Microsoft outage had no significant impact to Queensland Health. Dominique Tassell Health and Ambulance Services Minister Tim Nicholls confirmed the health system was run on Microsoft Outlook, but maintained the outage had no significant impact. Queensland Health has 135,000 staff members across 16 hospital and health services, who cannot email each other because of the outage.



“As we all know, we got up early this morning to find the Outlook system was not performing as anticipated and as we all expected to do every day when we log in, sign in, and start looking at what the day ahead holds,” Nicholls said about 9.30am on Friday. Related Article Updated

Network outage Almost 20,000 reports a minute as Microsoft hit by widespread outage “We have stood up the State Health Emergency Command Centre, and we are monitoring the situation continuously, and have been since early this morning, when the outage was first alerted to Queensland Health.” Nicholls said no disruption had been detected to patient care or the delivery of services in hospitals, and the Triple Zero service was not affected. “People can have confidence that Triple Zero and the dispatch service continue to operate as intended,” he said.



“There are back-up systems in place, but we have not had need to call on those back-up systems. So we continue to monitor the system.” The Queensland Police Service was dealing with the outage by adopting an “old school” approach using phones and radios, a spokesman said. The Queensland Education Department was unable to access emails, and families across Brisbane were sent texts from their schools advising them that emails were not working. A department spokesperson advised parents to keep an eye on their school’s social media pages, and only call for urgent inquiries. Brisbane City Council uses Outlook, and was also affected by the outage.

World.title: Almost 20,000 reports a minute as Microsoft hit by widespread outage
World.content:
Updated TechnologyNetwork outage Almost 20,000 reports a minute as Microsoft hit by widespread outage Elias Visontay, Jack Gramenz and Emily Kaine Updated November 13, 2026 — 1:18pm ,first published November 13, 2026 — 7:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Microsoft has prioritised restoring services to government systems as it struggles to issue a broad fix to return full functionality to its apps and platforms after a global outage, as Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke insists the issue is not the result of a cyberattack. The widespread outage hit Microsoft Outlook, Teams and Copilot, causing users to have issues accessing or sending emails, while other errors affected the tech giant’s apps. Microsoft users were hit with a widespread outage overnight. AP Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook and other Microsoft services, beginning just before 5am (AEDT). At one point, reports to the platform reached almost 20,000 per minute, stemming from outages across five Microsoft services in 74 countries. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they still couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes.



Issues among Australians were still common on Friday. Affected users told this masthead that their Outlook email access had stopped working early on Friday, then resumed working for several hours, before subsequently failing again. Related Article Exclusive

Telecommunications ‘Didn’t foot the bill’: Telstra outage cost the economy half a billion dollars, modelling finds By afternoon, email access was still patchy, while other Microsoft platforms such as Teams appeared functional - prompting memes on social media from frustrated workers lamenting the split-level of functionality. A swathe of corporate Australia as well as government departments and agencies were among those affected. They included the Australian Federal Police and the ABC. While they were still able to function, email issues also plagued national supermarket chain Coles as well as government agencies in New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Tasmania and Western Australia. The US tech company was reported to be focussing on restoring services to government first given its large user base. “Microsoft are prioritising life, safety and government services,” a Western Australian state government spokesperson said.



Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services. To fix the issue, Microsoft said it had so far attempted to restart its servers, and validate a change. But initial efforts to fully restore services proved unsuccessful. “We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the company said. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.” Loading A subsequent update issued shortly after 10am AEDT said the company had “begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far”.



“We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions,” it said. Microsoft said it was implementing “protective traffic management measures” region by region to test if it helped with restoring its services. “[We are] fully isolating a portion of our service infrastructure, restarting the affected components, and gradually reintroducing traffic to confirm our services remain stable before applying this approach more broadly. “We’re also analysing traffic patterns across our entire service infrastructure and evaluating whether isolating traffic within each region may allow affected regions to recover independently.” At a press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, Burke said he had been briefed by Australia’s cybersecurity coordinator and the head of Microsoft Australia and that they did not believe they were dealing with a cyber threat.



“The perspective of Microsoft at this stage … they believe in some ways [similar] to what we saw with CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke said. View post on X Microsoft said it was “also investigating why affected servers are experiencing elevated processor usage while handling requests”. In updates posted earlier, it said it was aware of users “experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes”. Microsoft later explained that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load”, which it said was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors”. The company determined several servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” due to a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.



“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X. The company earlier said it had “successfully restored” problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues. World.title: Country's largest vape retailer under investigation over advertising concerns
World.content:
Audio player for " NZ's biggest vape retailer allegedly operating in advertising grey area " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/health/2579219%2Fcountry-s-largest-vape-retailer-under-investigation-over-advertising-concerns

NZ's biggest vape retailer allegedly operating in advertising grey area Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

The country's largest vape retailer is under investigation by the Ministry of Health over concerns it's operating in advertising grey area.

Regulations that came into place in June 2025 banned retailers from advertising vaping products, which included showing pictures of product on their websites, or social media.

However, one week earlier, Shosha sent out an email to its mailing list informing customers that it's local .co.nz domain would no longer feature product images due to incoming regulations.

Instead, subscribers were directed to a newly created .com "global" website, listed at a US address, where product displays remained fully visible and available for direct order.

At the time, Associate Health Minister Casey Costello referred Shosha's "global" website to the Ministry of Health to investigate.

MoH said the investigation indicated that the shosha.com website was hosted and registered in the USA and did not deliver regulated products to New Zealand.

But with the website still active, a group of researchers said it is clear that the website is being used to bypass the regulation, and is marketed at a local audience, according to their research.

The email sent out to Shosha customers a week before advertising regulations came into effect in June 2025. Screenshot

Researcher at Auckland University's school of population, Lucy Hardie, said when they took a deeper dive into the website, there were many things that indicated it was simply a workaround rather than a completely new marketing venture for a global market.

"One of the first things was, there was a product availability tool, so you can check in store whether your favourite product is available in your nearest store, but none of the stores listed are outside of New Zealand."

Hardie said a number of test purchases were made on the .com website, which arrived at local addresses within three days. Despite being ordered on the global site, postage documentation showed the orders were dispatched directly from Auckland.

"Effectively this website can be used in exactly the same way [as the .co.nz website] but has full view of all the products."

Hardie also assessed the Instagram account associated with the global website. Under the new legislation it is an offence for retailers to display vaping products on social media.

The Instagram page, shosha.global, is linked to and accessible via the .com website.

The shosha.global Instagram bio shows it's based in New Zealand, and products in posts feature NZ warning labels Screenshot

Location information accessible via the 'about this account' section of the account's bio showed it was based in New Zealand.

Hardie and the other researchers analysed 67 posts on the account, posted between 17 June 2025, when the regulation came into effect, and May 2026.

She said the posts displayed pictures of vaping products in breach with the regulation, and many of them seemed to be targeted at a New Zealand audience.

Forty-six-point-three percent of the posts featured bilingual Te Reo Māori warning labels, 5.9 percent posts included references to Matariki, and 40.3 percent of posts regularly displayed New Zealand-specific nicotine concentration restrictions.

"All of those things sort of put together indicate that these tools are being used as a workaround for this company to continue promoting their products in full view, but sit outside of the law." Hardie said.

When Checkpoint last attempted to access the Instagram account on 6 November, two days after Hardie's research was released, the account had been taken down.

A product in full view on shosha.com (top), and the same product advertised in line with regulations on shosha.co.nz Screenshot

A Ministry of Health spokesperson said they reviewing whether their position on the shosha.com website has changed.

Despite the previous investigation, they said the Ministry had no knowledge of the shosha.global Instagram account.

In terms of issuing infringement notices the Ministry said its focus for websites has been on advertising, by companies registered in New Zealand.

Seventy-one infringement notices for advertising breaches on websites were issued between June 2025 and July 2026.

"New Zealand law applies to a website that is accessible in New Zealand. However, where a company is registered overseas, there are practical and jurisdictional challenges when investigating and taking enforcement action."

Hardie said Shosha's website showed that the regulation was too loose.

The find in store option on shosha.com only lists New Zealand locations. Screenshot

"One of the first things that we should be looking at is strengthening our laws and making sure we're not always playing catch up to whatever the companies are doing at the time. We've seen them adapt to every regulation and law that we put up and then we have to keep changing it.

"We knew that [the Ministry of Health] were already aware of this situation well over a year ago and nothing has happened. So it just seems to me that if one of our most prominent vape companies can operate then what's stopping every other company from operating in this way. It makes our legislation completely meaningless if there's no enforcement, if our health authorities know about it but nothing is ever done."

Hardie said having product images available meant retailers could continue to target their advertising at young people.

"We've got really high rates of youth vaping in NZ and part of the product appeal is that they are marketed really slickly in a range of flavours and colours and designs that we know appeal to young people. So the intent of the law was to prevent those kinds of appeals from being used in NZ."

World.title: 'Great news': Auckland Airport strike notice withdrawn
World.content:
Strikes that would have disrupted travel at Auckland Airport have been called off, with talks between staff and the airport making progress.

E tū union issued a strike notice last week for two 24-hour strikes by the Airport Emergency Services (AES) team - firefighters and emergency responders.

They were to take place on Tuesday 24 November and Friday 27 November, potentially disrupting travel plans for thousands.

E tū on Friday withdrew the strike notice, citing an improved offer from the airport, and would go back to its membership.

"As always, reaching a resolution without the need to take industrial action is the preferred path for everyone involved," E tū assistant national secretary Mat Danaher said.

There are 69 AES members whose work is vital for flights to come and go safely. Danaher earlier this week said the workers wanted pay that recognised their specialist work, and fair compensation for the two five-day training trips firefighters must make to Singapore each year to meet Civil Aviation Authority requirements.

Auckland Airport chief operations officer Chloe Surridge said it was "great news" the strike notice had been withdrawn.

"Our priority throughout has been to avoid disruption for travellers and the New Zealand aviation sector, and to keep the airport operating safely.

"People can now travel as planned, whether they're heading away on holiday, travelling for work, or coming home to see family.

World.title: Voters in areas with large Pacific populations clear on who should lead country
World.content:
While the general election result might be too close to call, voters in areas with large Pacific populations have once again shown a clear preference on who should lead the country.

National and Labour finished in a near dead heat for the party vote - with Labour on 29.4 percent percent and National on 29.2 percent, but with almost 400,000 special votes still to be tallied, who can form a coalition is not yet certain.

Based on preliminary results it's fairly clear there will be eight Pacific members of Parliament (MPs), increasing representation in the previous term from the previous seven.

And for those Pacific Labour MPs who won their electorates, support for many of them has also significantly increased since 2023 - assuming special votes don't swing back to the right.

Labour's Barbara Edmonds, who is of Samoan descent, won Kenepuru with 17,294 votes, almost ten-thousand more than the next best placed candidate (which she won by 7324 votes in 2023 when the electorate was called Mana) and fellow Samoan Lemauga Lydia Sosene regained Māngere with 14,815 votes and an increased 11,970 margin (having previous won by 11,712).

Three-term Tongan MP Jenny Salesa is also back, winning Ōtāhuhu for Labour with 13,826 votes with a margin of over ten-thousand (having previously won by 7,970) and Labour's Samoan-Tongan deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni won Glendene with 14,478 votes with a 6,940 margin (having won by 4,396 when her electorate was previously called Kelston).

Labour's Tangi Utikere, who is Cook Islands descent, also retained his seat of Palmerston North with a similar margin as 2023, while fellow Cook Islander and former National Party minister Alfred Ngaro re-enters Parliament after a six year absence, but this time under the NZ First banner thanks to his fifth place ranking on its list.

The Greens won 13.3% of the party vote according to preliminary results, meaning Teanau Tuiono, who is of Cook Islands descent, returns to Parliament thanks to his third place ranking, while first-time MP Tania Waikato, who's of Māori, Samoan and Hawaiian heritage, also enters due to her list placing of 13.

None of National's three Pacific list candiates of Rosemary Bourke, Angee Nicholas and Agnes Loheni will make it into Parliament, given their party's lower party vote percentage and the unusual situation where the party won 42 electorates - creating an overhang

Fania Kapao, Labour Party volunteer who is Cook Islands and Samoan descent at one of Labour's post-election events on November 7, 2026. RNZ Pacific/ Justin Latif

Pacific Labour voters react

While election night didn't fall strongly in Labour's favour, it was clear for Pacific voters at Labour's post-election event in Tamaki why their support swung left.

For Rua Rio and Koro Tuarae, Cook Islanders from Glen Innes, Labour was who they felt would do the most to address the cost of living.

"There's a lot of things we've seen that this government has been doing that makes it hard," Tuarae said.

"Things like the length of stay with hospital, there's [a shortage of] nurses, doctors and so when you go to hospital you can sit there for so many hours before they see you."

For Rio, the lack of jobs and the price of petrol were two factors in his support for a left-wing government.

"It's so hard to get a job now because three years ago I had a factory job, but it was closed but I know if Labour comes on board, people always work aye."

While failure to turn around cost of living pressures during this term has hurt the National Party electorally, its finance spokseperson told the public that the signs of a turnaround in the economy are starting to appear.

Nicola Willis, who has not made it back into parliament, said that the National-led coalition has been laying the foundations for a economic rebound during trying times, but that improvement can take time.

Labour's Tamaki candidate Max Harris, left, with a campaign volunteer at his post-election event on November 7, 2026. RNZ Pacific/ Justin Latif

Fania Kapao, who is of Cook Islands and Samoan descent, volunteered for Labour in Glendene. She felt excited to see more young people involved in this campaign than in previous years even though overall voter turn out was down almost 4 percent from last election.

"I hope that Pacific people feel a lot more represented and seen [by this result]," Kapao said.

"And I'm feeling very hopeful with the new and fresh blood that's coming through."

For Gloria Tu'itupou, a 24-year-old Tongan-New Zealander youth leader, she was inspired by how Labour's Tamaki candidate Max Harris engaged the Pacific community in her neighbourhood.

"I loved what Max Harris has been doing, centring Pacific communities in Glen Innes and Point England," she said.

"I like that he's been out and about in the community and talking to heaps of people in the community about what problems we have been facing, especially because our problems might get overshadowed by the wealthier areas."

She was also concerned how the turnout was impacted by the decision to scrap same-day voter enrollment.

"I feel like the way that they've set it up not being able to enrol and vote on the same day really impacts a lot of our communities.

"Our Pacific communities are more disenfranchised by this government and that's what motivated me to get out and be a bit more vocal.

World.title: Why MAPAS still matters after 50 years: 'Bringing everyone to the same starting point'
World.content:
For more than 50 years, the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme, commonly known as MAPAS, has aided Māori and Pacific students into the healthchare system.

As those behind the scheme take stock of what has been achieved to date, they remember the contribution of Emeritus Professor Colin Mantell (Ngāi Tahu), whose work helped shape MAPAS and different aspects of Māori and Pacific healthcare, generations of health leaders gathered at Waipapa Taumata Rau on Wednesday.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408259785112

For current and former MAPAS students and graduates, Prof Mantell's lifelong commitment to Māori and Pacific health was a stark reminder of why the programme continues to matter.

"The biggest thing is that MAPAS provides the foundation to be able to unify one another," Joshua Jay Matenga, 22, said.

"The idea of MAPAS is to make a collective empowerment to bring us together, but also to be able to celebrate both the diversity and the academia as well, of our achievements.

"It's more of a platform that raises the ability to emphasise the Māori success and the Pacific success that we have ... so if anything, it's more about trying to embrace what we already have and bringing it to a higher light."

Te Paea Ma'u, 20, agreed with Matenga's sentiments, describing MAPAS as a programme focused on equity.

"It's so important that we have a health system that is representative of the populations that we have, and just due to the systemic effects of colonisation and the inequities that have persisted from that, we don't currently have that healthcare system," Ma'u said.

"The whole role of MAPAS is to just ensure that we do have that for the future... it is just giving the opportunity for tauira who do want to get into healthcare that opportunity, that they can if that's what they want."

ACT leader David Seymour has called ethnicity-based admission pathways discriminatory, while the National-ACT coalition agreement led to a government review of targeted medical school admission programmes.

Seymour's criticism has not extended to the Rural Admissions Scheme, which selects students based on their attendance at rural primary and secondary schools.

"I oppose racial discrimination. I don't oppose living in the country. I don't oppose, for example, trying to train rural GPs. I don't oppose bonding people to work in the countryside where it's hard to get people … those are separate issues," he previously told RNZ.

The review has reportedly been completed and is awaiting release.

2025 MAPAS graduate, Joseph Johnston. Coco Lance

Samoan doctor Joseph Johnston graduated through MAPAS in 2025, and is now in his first year as a house officer at Waitākere Hospital.

He will move to Middlemore Hospital next year as he works towards his long-term goal of becoming a surgeon.

Since leaving university, Johnston said the importance of having Māori and Pacific health professionals had become even more apparent.

While in medical school, tauira are taught about health inequities and the wider social and economic factors influencing Māori and Pacific health.

But Johnston said that real-life experience in hospitals had clearly shown him what representation could mean in those everyday interactions with patients.

"I think just being a voice and actually representing our people and advocating for our people in spaces that there's not a lot of advocacy for ... is something that's really important," Johnston said.

Disproportionate statistical representation

Māori experience a life expectancy gap of around seven years and greater barriers to accessing healthcare.

The current gap in representation shows that Māori make up less than 6 percent of the medical workforce, despite making up around 18 percent of the population.

Pacific representation among doctors is even lower.

Across a variety of measures, Māori and Pacific peoples continue to experience substantially worse health outcomes. Māori women have more than three times the lung cancer registration of non-Māori women. Māori adults have twice the rate of ischaemic heart disease.

Pacific life expectancy remains about six years behind that of non-Māori, non-Pacific people. They also have the highest rates of diabetes and gout examined in the ethnic groups observed in Tupu Ola Moui.

Professor David Tipene-Leach (Pōrangahau, Ngāti Kere and Ngāti Manuhiri). RNZ / Coco Lance

Professor David Tipene-Leach, who was involved in the programme's early development, said the ultimate goal was a Māori and Pacific health workforce capable of serving its own communities.

"What we need is allies who are there with us in the battle for good health for Māori [and] Pacific people. In fact, for everybody in Aotearoa New Zealand who, at the moment, don't get a fair deal," he said.

"MAPAS graduates pass at the same rates. They stay in New Zealand. They don't go overseas. They are more likely to become general practitioners, and we know there's a shortage of that," Tipene-Leach added.

"They're more likely to go into the regions and to rural medicine, and we know there's a shortage there. So the argument is that, and I've heard [Prof Paparangi Reid] say this time and time again, is that these are exactly the doctors that we should be training in New Zealand."

Johnston shared a similar sentiment - that much of the criticism of MAPAS comes from a misunderstanding of the programme, including a misconception that Māori and Pacific students face lower standards.

"There's the misunderstanding that we get in easier and that we don't have to meet the same requirements," he said.

"Our graduates meet those requirements and go above and beyond those requirements. And actually as we enter the workforce, some of the best doctors that I've been lucky enough to work with this year have been MAPAS graduates."

Current students made a similar distinction, clarifying that MAPAS is not about giving somebody an advantage, but rather addresses an existing disadvantage.

"Removing one aspect will eventually lead to the removal of a bigger kaupapa there, so I'd say it would be very hard for us to be involved in this field or in this profession if this wasn't here in the first place," added Matenga.

"I think that when you stand in a place of privilege, to provide equity feels like you're providing inequality to that person.
