World.title: Live cricket: Black Caps v India fourth ODI
World.content:
The Black Caps take on India at Bay Oval in Mt Maunganui for their fourth of five One Day Internationals.

On Tuesday the Black Caps were looking to make a comeback after consecutive losse in the first two matches, but play was abandoned without a ball being bowled at Hamilton's Seddon Park due to rain.

First ball is at 3pm.

Follow all the action in our live blog below:

Embedded content removed for printing

New Zealand has been forced to make numerous changes during the T20 and ODI series mainly due to injuries and Central Districts pace bowler Brett Randell is the latest to be called up.

Randell has been called into the squad to bolster their bowling stocks for the fourth and fifth ODIs at Mt Maunganui this weekend.

The 31-year-old right-arm bowler has 145 professional caps to his name including five appearances for New Zealand A, and recently returned from a County Championship stint with Derbyshire.

Fellow Central Districts allrounder Josh Clarkson will also come into the squad for the fifth and final ODI against India on Sunday.

"We're very pleased for Brett, he's been a consistent performer in domestic cricket for some time now and has earned this opportunity," said head coach Rob Walter.

"There's been a few movements throughout the series so we're fortunate to be able to bring in Brett and Josh."

World.title: Police still seeking key witness in Myers Park attack
World.content:
Police say they're yet to hear from a crucial witness in the attack on a five-year-old girl at an Auckland park.

A 20-year-old man has been charged with the attempted murder of the girl at Myers Park playground.

Police on Thursday put out a public appeal for a man seen on CCTV talking to the alleged attacker. They say he was present when the attack began but left a little later.

A police spokesperson told RNZ they were still appealing for the man and any other witnesses to come forward.

Meanwhile, the girl has been discharged from Starship Hospital after being critically injured in the attack. Her father posted online and said the whole family was struggling with the psychological aftermath.

The girl's father has set up a Givealittle page seeking financial support for his daughter and family. He said his daughter had numerous lacerations to her head, along with injuries to two fingers.

The money would be used for long-term family recovery - which could include day-to-day support, therapy, and potential cosmetic surgery. The Givealittle page has passed $14,500 in three days.

World.title: KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals hit record levels, but some could be avoided
World.content:
A researcher says if governments want to look at making Kiwisaver changes, they should also look at the high increase of hardship withdrawals.

A Victoria University report led by senior lecturer of law Victoria Stace, and commissioned by FinCap shows hardship withdrawals rose sharply in the 12 months to June 2026.

More than 52,000 KiwiSaver members withdrew, which is up from just over 20,000 in 2023.

Total hardship withdrawals have increased from $65 million in 2016 to $443.6m in 2025 and Inland Revenue said the withdrawals now outpace withdrawals for first home deposits.

Stace told Nine to Noon concern over the increase in hardship withdrawals had been expressed by various groups including Retirement Commission, Consumer New Zealand and Financial Markets Authority.

Audio player for " KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals not always necessary: report " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2574701%2Fkiwisaver-hardship-withdrawals-hit-record-levels-but-some-could-be-avoided

KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals not always necessary: report Nine To Noon Download MP3 20m

This helped launch the research report which interviewed stakeholders, financial mentors and Kiwisaver providers and looked into superanuation arrangements around the world.

Stace said the research found that those who make KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals often would not have done so had they been made aware of other support options.

Kiwisaver contributions have been a part of the recent elections with both major parties proposing policies.

National proposed increasing contributions up to 12 percent total and making it compulsory for both the employer and employee. Labour's policy would not make it compulsory for the employee.

Stace said if any party was making changes it was an opportunity to look at other issues regarding hardship withdrawals.

"I think the main issue is if the government's serious about helping people get through times of hardship without accessing their KiwiSaver, then they seriously need to consider how that's going to be funded and how financial mentors are going to be incorporated into the process in a way that is sustainable and recognise the value that they can provide in this space."

Lilley said their research showed that financial mentors were concerned if these policies go into place and more money is going into Kiwisaver it would lead to more people looking to take Kiwisaver out.

He said there were around 750 financial mentors with at least 318 full-time equivalents worth of work.

Of those 318 around 181.5 were funded by the Ministry of Social Development. Lilley said this showed a "chronic underfunding " of the sector.

What are the options?

"There are a number of options, whether it's an intermediate step or, I mean, for example, you could have that it was a requirement that you'd spoken to a financial mentor as part of your application process," Stace said.

She said another option was to have all financial hardship withdrawal applications processed by a central clearinghouse or hub, which has financial mentoring expertise built into it.

This was a model already used by six of Kiwisaver providers, Stace said.

She explained applications were made to the Kiwisaver provider who then put a formal application to the supervisor. There were three supervisors, the main one being public trust, who make the final decision.

FinCap's senior policy advisor Jake Lilley says there needs a to be a system where budget advisors can be involved and check all options before a hardship withdrawal.

"You might have entitlement at, say, working income or another government agency or local charity you weren't aware of, or it had been hard to navigate in the first place, that actually means you can get on top of things.

"Sometimes people have had their consumer rights breached and actually there's an underlying issue or they have options."

The average hardship withdrawal amount had been $10,000

Stace said the report also found that the idea of "sidecar savings" should be explored which means setting aside money in a Kiwisaver account ring-fenced for an emergency.

World.title: Cummins hits out at Khawaja in passionate hour-long press conference
World.content:
Pat Cummins has labelled Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering allegations "utter nonsense", revealing he has received legal advice that the claims are "probably defamatory".

In an extraordinary 70-minute press conference on Friday, Australia's Test captain ruled out legal action against his former teammate, but was scathing in response to the bombshell revelations in Khawaja's book.

Cummins repeated he and the bowlers' stance that he had no prior knowledge of plans for illegal ball tampering, until Cameron Bancroft was caught with sandpaper during a Cape Town Test match in 2018.

Sandpapergate live updates: Cummins says Khawaja's ball-tampering claims '100 per cent wrong'

He agreed the bans handed down to Bancroft, David Warner and Steve Smith were too harsh after an investigation found they were the only players behind the plot, but rejected Khawaja's assertion that the entire team knew.

"When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins told a packed press conference in Sydney.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

Pat Cummins has rejected Usman Khawaja's claims that everyone knew about ball tampering in 2018. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"But Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper.

"That's complete and utter nonsense."

Cummins said he did not remember any conversations around the team taking collective responsibility, as Khawaja said in his book he had pushed for.

The 33-year-old said he had exchanged some messages with Khawaja over recent days and planned to speak to him at some point.

Pat Cummins says Usman Khawaja has been "casual" with people's lives. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

But the pair's relationship is now considerably rocky.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," Cummins said.

"In his book, Uzzy's been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket.

"I support his right to tell a story. I'm really glad that he feels like he can. But we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Cummins said it was up to Cricket Australia whether they would reopen the investigation into the matter, something the organisation has already ruled out.

Usman Khawaja's secret illness Cricket great Usman Khawaja could barely walk and thought he had a terminal illness when he was just starting out his Test career. He was soon diagnosed with a crippling disease, which he has kept secret for 17 years.

But he made it clear he wanted to move on from the scandal, declaring his willingness to take every question on Friday should make it the last time he has to speak about it.

"I did get advised this week that some of the things that were said are probably defamatory," Cummins said.

"But I won't be doing that. Like, you've got to move on. It's been eight years.

"We're moving on. You've got to draw a line at some point."

Now the Australia Test captain, Cummins pointed out that at the time of the scandal in South Africa, he was a 24-year-old just 13 Tests into his career.

Cummins said he had also not yet spoken to Warner since his backing of Khawaja's claims, and could not explain why their position was so different to his.

"That sounds like a pretty good question for those two," he said.

"Again, there's quite a few different accounts here, so they've got two accounts.

"There's 11 players in that room, so that means there's nine other guys who I think it's appropriate you give an equal amount of weight into their story as well."

World.title: Sydney Swans players will not face charges over sex assault investigation
World.content:
Sydney Swans players embroiled in a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault in a Melbourne hotel will not face criminal charges.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Nick Blakey had been under a police investigation over the alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel in late August.

Several adult entertainers are understood to have joined players at the East Melbourne hotel after being hired in the hours after the Swans' win against Essendon on August 17.

The ABC understands the investigation centred on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

The police investigation centred on events at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne in August. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

Multiple police sources previously told the ABC they understood an arrangement was reached in the hotel room for players to pay extra to take drugs, believed to be cocaine, from the women's breasts and buttocks.

It is unclear how many players, or which players, had allegedly participated.

It is understood a woman was seen leaving the hotel room in a distressed state in the early hours of the morning, with a Triple Zero (000) call made to police soon after.

This morning, Victoria Police confirmed no charges would be laid over the incident.

"Following a thorough investigation and based on legal advice, Victoria Police will not proceed with criminal charges due to insufficient evidence," a police spokesperson said.

Victoria Police said due to an "ongoing civil matter", no further comment would be made.

Sydney 'stands by' decision to suspend players

Sydney Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich told a press conference today it had been a difficult period for everyone involved and affected by the hotel incident.

"We appreciate and understand that everyone has been dealing with it in their own way, and we thank them for their support during that time," he said.

Matthew Pavlich says the outcome of the police investigation marks a moment to move forward. (ABC News)

"We've been in constant contact with the players through the whole process.

"Today's a moment for them to move forward. It's a time for everyone to move forward, and at some point, they'll be back here at training, back with their teammates, and that's going to be an important step."

The players were sidelined by the Sydney Swans in the days after the incident, for staying out late drinking and inviting women back to the team hotel in breach of club standards.

Fellow Swans player Riley Bice, who was also stood down for breaching club standards, was earlier cleared in the police investigation.

In an earlier statement today, Sydney Swans management said they stood by the decision to stand down the players "because their conduct fell short of the standards of behaviour expected at the club".

"The club was clear from the outset that this decision was separate from the police investigation, and it stands by that decision.

"The club has commenced a comprehensive examination of its AFL program and is committed to acting on the findings and implementing meaningful change to build an environment that players, staff, members, supporters and corporate partners can be proud of," the statement said.

Pavlich said that work was the club's express focus.

"This is not a day for anyone to really celebrate — we're still looking very hard at the program and understanding where we need to get better for the future and examining that in real thorough detail," he said.

"I can guarantee everyone out there that we'll be doing everything we can to restore the standards and behaviours that this club has held for a long period of time."

Blakey last month moved from the Swans to North Melbourne football club, apologising for "the events that led up to my exit from Sydney".

"I know I have to win back the trust of the broader community, football and otherwise," he said at the time.

Women to proceed with civil claims, lawyers say

The police update came as lawyers confirmed three women were still pursuing civil lawsuits related to the allegations.

Lawyers representing one of the women who alleges she was sexually assaulted said she was "devastated" by the decision.

Slater and Gordon lawyer Jackson Pannam said what had occurred had a "profound impact" on her.

"She reported the incident immediately, provides a formal statement and cooperated fully with the investigation," he said.

"She has shown enormous courage in coming forward."

Mr Pannam confirmed the woman would proceed with a civil case, which must be proved on a "balance of probabilities" rather than the higher criminal standard of "beyond reasonable doubt".

"The absence of criminal charges does not prevent a civil claim from proceeding," Mr Pannam said.

"Slater and Gordon Lawyers is continuing to prepare a civil claim against the relevant parties and will continue to support our client through this extremely difficult time."

Victoria Police said a thorough investigation into the incident concluded there was insufficient evidence to lay charges. (ABC News)

John Karantzis from Carbone Lawyers, who is acting for two of the women in a civil claim against the club, said his clients were "very disappointed and distressed" over the outcome of the police investigation.

He said the women would still forge ahead with their civil claim.

"My clients' civil claim is based on a different burden of proof, it is based on the balance of probabilities," he said.

"We will vigorously pursue this claim."

Asked about how the club might handle related civil claims, Mr Pavlich contained his comments to the outcome of the police investigation.

"Any future aspects, we'll deal with that as it comes," he said.

Isaac Heeney welcomes police update

In a statement, Heeney welcomed the police announcement.

"The past three months have been incredibly difficult for my family, Steffie and those close to me," Heeney said.

"Watching my family carry the weight of this has been heartbreaking.

"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice.

Swans player Isaac Heeney was among those spoken to by police during the investigation. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"To those that have never doubted me and stood by my side in solidarity — thank you. I know it has not been easy in the face of such intense public scrutiny. I will never forget your support.

"To the entire Sydney Swans Club — my teammates, coaches, the board, our sponsors, and our loyal members and fans — thank you for keeping faith in me.

"The Swans have given me an opportunity to live out a childhood dream and I am fully focused on repaying that faith by being the best person and player I can be."

World.title: Cummins says Khawaja's ball-tampering claim '100 per cent wrong'
World.content:
(Getty)

Before the questioning, Cummins read what seemed like a prepared statement and signalled his intentions for what he wanted to achieve with his address.

Here is that statement in full:

Loading...

"I've taken a bit of time this week to respond to Usman's allegations. I've been trying to understand exactly what those allegations have been, that's why it's taken me a few days.

"When he says 'we all knew', if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong. I've said that consistently for the last eight years; I did not know that was happening.

"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper; that's complete and utter nonsense.

(Getty)

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not the Usman that I know, it's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book Ussie's been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell a story, 100 per cent. I'm really glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do.

"So I'm here, I'm happy to answer all your questions. I'll stay here until you have no more questions. I don't want to talk about this again after today. So even if it takes all day — I've got to bowl at some stage — but I'll answer all of them because at some point we got to move on.

(Getty)

"Today I'll talk as Australian captain right now but I'll also talk about the 24-year-old young guy and his recollections playing my 13th Test back in 2018 in a team that at that stage I think had a win-at-all costs mentality, had an ugly underbelly, and there was too many silos within the team, traits that I hope that everyone has seen and I try very hard to eradicate for the last six years as captain.

"So I'm happy to take all your questions about sandpaper, ball tampering, changerooms, international cricket, whether my wife and I did have a spat out the front, whatever you want, hit me, I'm here."

World.title: Sixers win WBBL clash despite Ellyse Perry's strange run-out
World.content:
New Zealand captain Melie Kerr has starred with the bat and ball to keep the Sydney Sixers unbeaten in the WBBL with a victory over the Melbourne Renegades.

In the second match of a double-header at Melbourne's Junction Oval, Kerr set up the Sixers' 11-run win by top-scoring with 53 off 34 balls and finishing with tidy figures of 1-29.

It lifted the Sixers to 5-0 at the season's halfway mark and into second spot alongside the also unbeaten Perth Scorchers.

Kerr was the only batter to pass 50 in the game, sharing a crucial 56-run partnership with opener Ellyse Perry before the Australian star was undone in unusual circumstances.

In the 18th over, Kerr chipped a ball into the deep on the leg side and pushed for two with Perry, as Georgia Wareham swooped on the ball in the deep and fired it into the bowler's end.

Sophie Molineux fielded cleanly and whipped the bails off as Perry dove to make her ground, and there was only half an appeal from the Renegades to umpire Louise Broadfoot, who shook her head.

Former Australia captain Lisa Sthalekar in commentary credited Broadfoot and fellow caller Aaron Finch prophetically said: "There must be something in the back of the umpire's mind that goes 'what if I just haven't quite got it right though?'."

As the slow-motion replay on the big screen at Junction Oval showed Perry's dive bouncing over the line, rather than being grounded, the crowd and everyone on the field raised their eyebrows, with Broadfoot consulting fellow umpire Malcolm Wood before sending it to the third umpire.

Perry had already started making her way off the field before the decision was made, with her team adding 16 in the final two overs to set up the chase.

As the pitch slowed, the Renegades got off to a horror start chasing 141 to win after collapsing to 3-22 by the fifth over.

Molineux inched her way to 18 off 21 and was livid when caught trying to cut away Caoimhe Bray (1-17), but Tess Flintoff (44 off 33) breathed life back into the Renegades.

Needing 17 off the last over to win, spinner Ashleigh Gardner (3-13 off three overs) shut the door as the Renegades were bowled out for 129.

In the earlier game, a captain's knock from Georgia Redmayne propelled Brisbane past the Melbourne Stars and into the top four.

Set 166 for victory, skipper Redmayne (74 not out off 50 deliveries) and Irish young gun Orla Prendergast (52 not out off 36) put the Stars to the sword.

It was the Stars' fourth straight loss, while the Heat are sitting pretty in third with three victories on the bounce after going 706 days without a triumph.

World.title: AFLW has come a long way but this player 'doesn’t want to settle'
World.content:
When Jenna Richardson scrolls through TikTok, she's now starting to come across AFLW content — and lots of it.

To the inaugural Hawthorn defender, it's a sign of the game's evolution and how it's connecting to fans.

"There are videos of people analysing the games … It's nice because they analyse the men's game, so then to see them do it for the W, [it's good]," Richardson tells ABC Sport.

AFLW club culture AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

After securing Hawthorn's first finals win last week (against Gold Coast), the side are now gearing up for a semi-final against Carlton on Saturday at Princes Park, a ground that drew 5,000 fans for the weekend's prior qualifying finals.

This season, the overall AFLW home-and-away attendance record was broken in round 10, helped by the introduction of double-headers, with the two crowds at Docklands drawing 20,455 and 14,573, respectively.

Excluding the matches with men's games, standalone games were at an average of 2,500 per game, similar to the 2025 figures.

"I'm pretty level-headed in being able to see the games come a long way," Richardson said.

"So whilst I am so grateful for everything we get, and I feel quite spoiled at times, I also know there's a lot of room for growth — and not to settle."

The biggest change Richardson wants to see is the number of regular season rounds increase from 12 — which she really feels during finals.

Hawthorn are the only team to have beaten North Melbourne in three years. (Getty: Emily Barker)

"At least playing every team once to make a more realistic ladder at the end of the season," she said.

Every team's fixture is dependent on where they finished the year before, meaning sides that finished lower theoretically play more fellow-lower sides, and vice versa with the top sides.

It can result in some teams making finals that get caught out straight away, and some that could make a finals run with more rounds, missing out.

"Playing the top teams, we always get the most out of… the more you play the best teams, the better you becomel. We did," Richardson said, noting Hawthorn were the only team to beat North Melbourne in three years.

"We played Adelaide (not in finals) and got beat. I thought they were really good to play against.

"They have shown in the past, for however many years, that they're up for finals contention. I feel like if there were more games, I wouldn't be surprised if they were in there too."

Hawthorn are playing in its first semi-finals in AFLW history. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

Richardson said, she'd then like to see increased salaries for support staff and assistant coaches in women's programs.

Richardson notes how stretched programs can be, which adds pressure on coaches, assistant coaches and support staff.

"They [line coaches] sacrifice a lot from their other jobs, like they're usually losing money to come and help our program," she said.

"They have to do so much for us... (and) those two days a week where they're at our club, they're taking a massive pay cut from their other job."

Jenna Richardson joined Hawthorn as an expansion signing in 2022. (Getty: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

With the W awards coming up, Richardson is also not opposed to the introduction of a defender award, given the best and fairest generally goes to a midfielder and there is a medal for leading goalkicker.

"Why not?" Richardson asked.

"That'd actually be cool because we're never in those, you know, fun photos or celebrating goals that are down there — so that'd be fun."

World.title: Are we really going to shoot the messenger over Sandpapergate?
World.content:
Consider a famous scene from the heat of a Test cricket battle. The South African team manager calls the opposition chairman of selectors into a room and says: "You'd better have a look at this." The pair sit down to view some sinister television footage.

The chairman of selectors is aghast at the replays: something comes out of one of his players' trousers and is rubbed against the ball. The ball-tampering player and his own team manager are promptly dispatched to the match referee. What the player has to say for himself, the chairman of selectors later admits, isn't "completely honest".

Sandpapergate live updates: Cummins says Khawaja's ball-tampering claims '100 per cent wrong'

The player is duly excoriated and his punishment doubled on account of his lying. The press goes into overdrive. Career-ending sackings are called for but don't quite eventuate. And then, eventually, everyone moves on.

The player is not Cameron Bancroft, in case you haven't already guessed. It is Michael Atherton, about whom most of us probably hold far more positive views: a brave opening batter, a thoughtful and perceptive TV and newspaper analyst and something close to a conscience figure in the game, beyond reproach despite that regrettable interlude at Lord's in 1994.

Then-England captain Michael Atherton (right) was caught in his own ball-tampering firestorm during a South Africa tour in 1994. (Getty Images: PA Images/Adam Butler)

This raises questions about recent events that were not adequately answered in 2018, when Australia's tampering crisis exploded. Firstly, in these tumultuous, adversarial times, can we no longer hold multiple ideas in our heads at once?

Are we really not mature and reasonable enough to say that in the unending and sometimes bitter pursuit of the success Australians demand of them, our cricketers occasionally take things too far, just as Atherton did?

Are we really to put aside the plainly obvious truth that Sandpapergate was, in and of itself, a trifling matter for which a select few got stung with the compound interest on decades of accumulated grievances against entitled, poorly behaved Australian cricketers?

What is in Usman Khawaja's book Sabr and what did he actually say about Sandpapergate? Much has been written and said about Usman Khawaja's new book — but what's actually in the pages of Sabr?

And are we really going to keep shooting the messenger? We might think Usman Khawaja naive, but in our heart of hearts, have we ever really believed that three batters were the only ones who knew about a minor cheating scheme that was of no direct personal benefit to them?

It is possible this entire affair now says far more about the Australian cricket public than it does our cricketers. It certainly says more about their bosses.

As was the case in 2018, the public expressions of dismay, both informed and not, speak of one positive: Australians care deeply about Test cricket and take it personally when they feel its honour is being sullied.

Equally, the defensiveness, the reflexive and faintly sinister demolition of Khawaja's character, and the "leave it in the past" mentality show that an unfortunately large cohort are in favour of administrators burying any form of dishonesty or wrongdoing by their own team, no matter the strength of the evidence in front of their eyes.

Usman Khawaja has faced a character assassination from parts of Australia after the release of his book earlier this week. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

It is precisely this dogma that got Australia in this mess in the first place: there is a line, but we decide where it is and whether or not we've crossed it. And when we do, we will bully into submission anyone who talks about it more honestly.

So many people have made this issue about themselves; perhaps you can permit me two personal anecdotes that illustrate broader points that have not been taken seriously enough.

In the first, I am, from memory, nine years old, down at the local cricket club, standing with other boys in a semicircle around our coach. He has in his hand a two-piece Red King cricket ball that has been battered so often against our cyclone fencing practice nets that it looks like roadkill. The coach is showing us what to do when a ball has degenerated beyond spit and polish treatment: pick the seam, gouge one side, hope for the best.

In the second, I'm in my mid-30s, working as a publisher but engaged in the unliterary task of searching the abrasives aisle of the local hardware store for the perfect piece of yellow sandpaper. It will be torn into small pieces and photographed to feature on the cover of Gideon Haigh's Sandpapergate book, Crossing the Line: How Australian Cricket Lost Its Way.

The roughing-up of a cricket ball via unconventional and illegal methods is commonplace in park cricket around Australia. (Supplied: Cricket NSW)

The first scenario was a point made with possibly unnecessary force this week by Stuart MacGill: everybody does it and always has (although perhaps not on the wall of the SCG dugout). Any club cricketer who says they are unfamiliar with at least some form of ball alteration is either an extremely disengaged teammate or a member of Pinocchio's Invitational XI.

As for the second, and putting aside the claim that Australian batsmen were using sandpaper on their bats — not beyond the realms of possibility, but behaviour that would be "rare" in both senses that cricketers use that word — it prompted a feeling that has never left me: "Someone in the Australian cricket team made this exact trip to Bunnings warehouse."

There were, in other words, both subconscious cultural factors and very obvious acts of premeditation at play in 2018 that always made the denials appear ludicrous.

Frankly, it is time that a lot of people grew up and acknowledged that a messy pile of accumulated facts are occasionally going to contradict each other, and that the truth is not as neat as a cricket scorecard. Some key points we should always bear in mind:

It is unlikely that Warner (left), Smith (centre left) and Bancroft (centre right) were the only players who knew the ball was being tampered with in South Africa. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

One: it is implausible that only Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were aware the ball was being altered.

Two: many lies were, and since have been, told in service of Cricket Australia's process of "investigation", which put public relations priorities well ahead of the truth.

Three: having committed to a PR version of punishment, acting not in response to a case of ball tampering but to a public relations disaster, Cricket Australia was bound to hand out disproportionate penalties that have warped our rational sense of wrongdoing.

Four: the actual truth — or at least a version of it that did not insult our intelligence — was always bound to come out eventually. That it has occurred when some of the extremely well-remunerated players are still main characters should not mean it is buried again.

Mitchell Starc (centre) this week offered a strong rebuke to Khawaja's (right) allegations that the whole team knew of the sandpaper being brought into the field. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Five: Test cricketers are human beings, as prone to white lies and interpersonal dramas as the rest of us, with the added burden of intense scrutiny of their every move. The idea that any one of them would experience, process and recall certain events the same way as another is preposterous.

Six: It is equally preposterous to think every Australian player gets on with his teammates all the time, or that inevitable frictions are as dramatic as they have been made out to be. Australian Test stars of previous generations have, in books and post-career media work, detailed threatened (and actual) lawsuits against each other, exposure of infidelities, even death threats. Most of them have hugged it out in the end.

What many fans are left with, probably, is the similarly vague sense of anger and resentment — "This again? Really?" — that followed the original events. Cricket is a game for soul-searchers and its history is pockmarked with these moral eruptions.

Anger, in this case as in others before it, needs a target. The easiest one is Khawaja, because it is less practical and cathartic to direct it at faceless administrators. But make no mistake: back then, they absolutely bottled a situation that demanded level heads, and now they claim there is nothing else to see here.

Loading...

What would a level-headed reaction have looked like in 2018? That was the question faced by English chairman of selectors Ray Illingworth when he dealt with the Atherton affair.

To go with the media's lashings, Atherton was fined £2,000 — a proactive measure to ward off the suspension that was the preference of the Australian match referee, Peter Burge.

Years later, Illingworth pondered what a suspension would have meant for Atherton. "It could have finished him off as captain," he wrote in 2006. "[But] I don't think he would have been happy no matter the outcome."

"We were the first country to step in on the matter. Richie Benaud came up to me afterwards and said: 'Well done, you've handled it brilliantly.'"

It is something nobody would say of Cricket Australia.

World.title: Marsh dodges Sandpapergate questions in testy press conference exchange
World.content:
Australia's one-day captain, Mitch Marsh, has refused to address key aspects of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal as journalists peppered him with questions at a press conference.

Marsh, who was bowling when Cameron Bancroft was spotted hiding a piece of sandpaper in his pants during the 2018 series, spent most of the 12-minute press conference straight-batting questions about the infamous South Africa tour and Usman Khawaja's explosive allegations.

The very first question put to Marsh was: "Did you know that sandpaper was being used to tamper with cricket balls in South Africa?"

"Jeez, you hit a six off the first ball there, mate. Well done," Marsh replied.

Loading Instagram content

"I respect that certain people have told their stories, but I'm not here to share mine.

"I know that might sound weird, but it's a big week for us, and it's an important time for this one-day group.

"I really respect that Uzzy has told his story. He's written his book, and my focus is really on tomorrow."

Marsh was continually peppered with questions about why he was not willing to speak on the topic.

"I've personally moved on," he said.

Mitch Marsh says he has no ill feelings towards Usman Khawaja for the allegations made in his book. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

"I respect that others probably haven't, but I have, and I hope that's respected.

"This is my choice to not go back there. Who knows? Maybe I'll write a book one day."

Marsh insisted he held no grudges against Khawaja.

"I respect Uzzy for telling his story and for writing his book, and I don't sit here coming from a place of judgement," Marsh said.

"Everyone's got their story. Some will be willing to share it, and others might not, purely on the basis of the fact that they've moved on.

"It's really important that at some stage we do."

Australia's Test captain, Pat Cummins, is set to front a press conference in Sydney tomorrow morning and has promised to answer "any and all media".

AAP

World.title: FA scrambles for Jordan alternative with Socceroos reluctant to travel
World.content:
Socceroos players remain unwilling to travel to Jordan as Football Australia (FA) scrambles for alternatives to playing an upcoming friendly in Amman.

But US Soccer's decision to withdraw its team from the under-17 World Cup in ‌Qatar over safety concerns is not expected to affect either the Socceroos or their Joeys counterparts.

The Socceroos and Joeys are both in camp in Doha ahead of their respective friendlies and World Cup campaigns.

Popovic refuses to blacklist Socceroos who pull out of Jordan friendly Australia coach Tony Popovic insists Socceroos players who are reluctant to play Jordan due to security concerns will not be blacklisted from the national team set-up if they elect to withdraw from his squad.

The senior team is due to face Qatar on Saturday (AEDT) before travelling to Amman to face Jordan on November 18.

The latter is the issue, with PFA boss Beau Busch saying last week that Socceroos players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan "due to the unpredictable security situation" and the "threat of terrorism".

FA had been keen for the game in Jordan to proceed, but has said it was monitoring the security situation in the area.

The friendlies against Qatar and Jordan were arranged as preparations for January's Asian Cup, but the postponement of the tournament to December 2027 due to conflict in Saudi Arabia has decreased their significance.

Martin Kugeler has flown to Doha to find a solution. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar)

FA heavy hitters including chief executive Martin Kugeler and football director Heather Garriock flew to Doha this week, as did Busch and men's head of player relations Jon McKain.

Players are not expected to back down and agree to play in Jordan, likely leaving cancellation or relocation as the options.

One option is Australia remaining in Qatar and playing Jordan in Doha.

But that proposal is understood to have been met with some reluctance from both the Qatari and Jordanian football associations.

Jordan has already had to deal with Indonesia pulling out of a friendly this window.

Playing the Jordan game somewhere in southern Europe is another option, along with cancelling or postponing the game altogether.

Coach Tony Popovic, due to speak to media in his pre-match press conference on Thursday night, has indicated no players would be blacklisted from future selection if they withdrew from his squad for security reasons.

Elsewhere, in ‌a letter sent to players, US Soccer said it was cancelling its team's pre-tournament camp and its participation in the under-17 World Cup "in light of current circumstances".

US Soccer cited US State Department's Level 3 travel advisory for Qatar and related ‌directives for ‌embassy ⁠staff and families.

But the Joeys are not expected to follow the US in withdrawing from the under-17 tournament in Qatar, while the Socceroos are understood not to have issues with being in Qatar.

AAP

Tech.title: Xbox announces Wolfenstein 3
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s been nearly a decade since Bethesda’s MachineGames released Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus in 2017, and now Xbox is ready to announce a sequel from the studio. Wolfenstein 3 was officially announced today, just days after Bethesda also confirmed that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel.

In a post, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the name and a photo of a script. “Looking forward to sharing more,” she said. MachineGames also announced the game in a post, saying the game is “in production” and sharing a photo from a motion-capture session. IGN reports that Brian Bloom (who plays protagonist William Joseph “BJ” Blazkowicz) and Debra Wilson (who plays Grace Walker) are reprising their roles, and they appear to be the featured actors in the photo.

The last mainline entry, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus, launched in 2017 and continued the story of Blazkowicz in an alternate 1960s where Nazi Germany had won the Second World War. Wolfenstein: Youngblood also debuted in 2019 as a co-op spinoff, starring Blazkowicz’s twin daughters.

Tech.title: Whoop launched a social network where every user has a ‘verified heartbeat’
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Starting Thursday, Whoop members can share their data from its wearables on the app’s new Whoop Humans social network. Users can make their metrics, activities, and achievements visible to other Whoop wearers, post Story-like “Moments” with photos and captions, and add comments and reactions on other members’ posts.

Whoop claims its platform is “entirely human,” unlike other social media platforms that are “saturated with artificial intelligence, automated accounts and bots, and manufactured content.”

Whoop CEO Will Ahmed says Humans is “the most verifiably human network ever launched. Every account represents a real person with a verified heartbeat.” Whoop says its existing Teams social feature “will remain available,” allowing people to share strain, recovery, and sleep data along with group leaderboards.

In the Community tab in Whoop’s app, users can scroll through Moments from people they’re following, like tapping through your Stories feed on Instagram but with your friends’ fitness tracker data. In one of Whoop’s examples, swiping up on a user’s Moments post with a photo from their run shows a map with their route and details like their pace and distance. The Community tab also shows cards for people in your “community” with their sleep, recovery, and strain scores.

Whoop says users choose which activities, achievements, and metrics they want to share on Humans, including Recovery, Strain, Sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate. Any activities marked as sensitive aren’t shared by default. There’s also an option to keep Moments posts private and a “Stealth Mode” for temporarily hiding health and performance data without changing your sharing settings.

Tech.title: Humble Bundle redesign removes two-factor verification from settings
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Humble Bundle storefront for buying games and other software recently got a new look, but on the settings page, it no longer offers a way to add or update two-factor verification methods, as reported by Kotaku. PC Gamer also points out that there are Humble Bundle support pages discussing two-factor verification, and the writer for the publication said that they had set up two-factor verification on the old version of the site.

However, it does appear that, at least as of now, there is some form of two-factor verification. When I tried logging into my Humble Bundle account while writing this article, I was prompted to check my email for an access code before I could access my account. While logged in, I was able to update my password, but I didn’t have to enter my old password to be able to do so.

For what it’s worth, my passwords app also shows that I set up a rotating two-factor code for Humble Bundle at some point. I was not asked to input that at any part of my login process today.

Humble Bundle owner IGN Entertainment and IGN parent company Ziff Davis didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

Tech.content:
We’ve begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far. We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions.

We’ve streamlined our recovery process to expedite returning the remaining affected servers to service. To further support recovery, we’re implementing protective traffic management measures in a specific location to reduce load on the affected infrastructure, and we’ll expand these measures to additional locations if we observe positive results.
